documents.text: 教材・研究資料 読みたい内容や、確かめたい計算から始める。 理論天文学の道具箱 高校数学から標準問題へ。入門16章、発展35章、解ライブラリーを日英で読む。 日本語・英語 入門編を読み始める 数値計算アトラス 手法・数式・計算例から探す。前提、一次文献、コードと検証をたどる。 日本語・英語。一部の日本語訳はドラフト 手法の見取り図へ 熱的不安定性 星間ガスの物理を、論文・研究図・動画・公開計算から読み解く。 本文は英語 図と論文を見る 資料・記録を調べる 原本や一次資料に戻れるアーカイブ。 大学ノート 学生時代の手書きノート41冊・1,170ページ。科目と原本画像から探す。 本文は日本語 Gordon Bell Research Archive 歴代の候補・応募記録、論文と性能の条件を調べる。 本文は英語 計算科学政策の記録 HPCI・ポスト「京」・AI for Scienceの委員会と関連業務を公開資料でたどる。 日本語・英語 目的に合わせて使う 研究課題から資料を選ぶ 数値計算と熱的不安定性の資料を選び、抜粋と出典を自分のAIへ渡す。 Academic Roots 出典付きの完成例から学術系譜をたどり、いつものAIで自分のルーツも調べる。本文は日本語。 研究者について 博士論文 星間物質の物理過程と分子雲の形成理論 所属学協会 日本天文学会、理論天文学宇宙物理学懇談会（理論懇） 研究プロフィール 資料の使い方・引用 利用条件・AI方針 Learning & research Start with a topic to understand or a calculation to check. documents.title: Academic Roots — 4代先に、湯川秀樹。
documents.text: KOYAMA'S ACADEMIC ROOTS 小山 洋の学術系譜を、たどってみた。 4代先に、 湯川秀樹。 自分の先生から、そのまた先生へ。 研究のつながりをたどると、思いがけない人に出会える。 あなたも、いつものAIと自分のルーツを探してみよう。 自分のルーツを調べる ↗小山の完成例を見る ↓ ここでの「4代」は4つの学術上の関係。すべてが博士論文指導ではありません。 小山 洋 → 湯川 秀樹 4つの関係を たどった先に。 小山 洋↓犬塚 修一郎↓観山 正見↓林 忠四郎↓湯川 秀樹 01 / FOLLOW THE ROOTS 小山 洋から、湯川 秀樹へ。 完成例 · 公開資料＋本人申告 矢印は 研究者 → 指導を受けた相手。人物や線を選ぶと、根拠が開きます。 公開資料で確認 本人申告5人 · 4つの関係 あなたの先生の、その先は？ いつものAIで調べてみる ↓ 02 / BRING YOUR OWN AI 調べるのは、いつものAI。 ここで、あなたの系譜に。 登録・APIキー入力不要 Web検索ができるAIに調査を頼み、回答をこのページに貼り戻します。 指導教員が小山の例に登場しなくても、どの研究室からでも始められます。 01依頼文を作る 02自分のAIで調べる 03回答を取り込む 入力は運営者へ送信しません。依頼文をAIへ貼り付けたり、作成結果を共有したりすると、その相手に内容が渡ります。 保存・外部AI・共有の詳しい扱い 氏名・所属・貼り付けたAIの回答を、当サイトの運営者が収集・保存することはありません。作成した系譜は、このブラウザ内に保存されます。保存データは、下の「このブラウザの作成データを消す」から削除できます。 調査依頼文を自分のAIに貼り付けると、その内容は利用するAIサービスに送信されます。また、文章・画像・リンク・データを誰かに共有すると、そこに含まれる情報が相手に伝わります。 01 / MAKE A RESEARCH REQUEST まず、知っている先生まで。 あなたの名前 必須 指導を受けた先生 必須 大学・研究室 人物を見分けるヒント 学位取得年・在籍年 先生との関係 コピーした依頼文を、普段使っているAIのチャットに貼ってください。 調査依頼文を見る・手動でコピーAIに渡す調査依頼文 02–03 / RETURN WITH YOUR ROOTS AIの回答を、ここに。 依頼文には、調査のルールと回答形式も入っています。AIが返したJSON全体を、そのまま貼り付けてください。 AIの回答（JSON） 実例データでも、取り込み後は確認前として表示します。AIが出典を付けても、自動的に確認済みにはなりません。 あなたの調査は、あなたのAIで。 このページからAIを呼び出すことはありません。AIの利用条件・料金や、貼り付けた情報の扱いは、ご自身が利用するサービスに準じます。 系譜を知っているので、手入力する起点となるあなたの名前指導教員から順に、1行に1人 YOUR ACADEMIC ROOTS 選択してコピー リンクと保存データには、名前・所属・根拠・出典が含まれます。共有先では「確認前」に戻り、元の作成者のチェックは引き継ぎません。 この非公開プレビューのリンクは、同じ端末での再現用です。ほかの人に渡す場合は文章・画像・データ保存を使ってください。 自分のルーツを、文章・画像・データで持ち出せます。 つながりの根拠を、1本ずつ確かめる。 出典の該当箇所が、この2人の関係を本当に示しているか確認してください。チェックは作成者による確認であり、このサイトによる独立検証ではありません。申告や推測には、出典確認のチェックは付けられません。 03 / EVIDENCE, NOT ASSUMPTION 実例のつながりと、その根拠。 確認日 2026.11.10 学位の指導、研究室での師弟、共同研究は、それぞれ異なる関係です。 このデモでは、資料が示している範囲と未確認の点を一緒に表示しています。 3つの関係を 公開資料で確認 1つの関係は 本人申告 「博士の系譜」とは限りません。すべての線が博士論文指導を意味するわけではありません。 「4ステップ」は、種類の異なる学術上の関係を数えたものです。 ABOUT THIS DEMO 小山洋の実例は、公開資料と本人申告を人が照合してまとめた完成例です。このページのAI依頼文で自動生成・検証された結果ではありません。訪問者は自分のAIに調査を依頼し、回答を取り込んで系譜を作成できます。共通データベースへの投稿・合流には対応していません。日本の天文学者の系図を経路発見の参考にし、各関係を別の公開資料または本人申告で記録しています。元の図・文章・データ全体は転載していません。 出典付きデータを保存（JSON） ↓ 誤りに気づいた場合は、GitHubで訂正を知らせることができます（GitHubアカウントが必要です）。

Copyright © 2026 Hiroshi Koyama. Text, figures and photographs are excluded from that code license. No exclusive rights are asserted over names, public facts or source URLs. Quoted and linked material retains the providers’ terms. Your work stays under your control The operator does not relicense visitor-entered, imported or exported lineage data under MIT. Inputs and AI responses are not sent to the operator; your lineage is saved in your browser. Use the tool’s delete control to remove locally saved work. Using your own AI & sharing When you paste a research request into your AI service, that service receives the request. Recipients of shared text, images, JSON and links receive the information they contain. Check the external service’s terms and choose what you share. Distinguish self-reports, public-source evidence and unverified inferences, and check the evidence for each relationship.

documents.title: Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: AN OPEN NOTEBOOK OF ASTROPHYSICS Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step. From school algebra to classical problems with differential equations. A Japanese–English series connecting atoms, stars, cosmic expansion, and the physics of equilibrium and change. Start the foundations ↗Explore the advanced volume Starts with school algebraFoundations to advanced topics日本語 / English FIG. 01 — THE BALANCE THAT HOLDS A STAR VOLUME I16 lessons available Foundations Exploring the universe through school algebra Light and distance, quantum physics and radiation, stars and their limits, and cosmic expansion—one algebraic step at a time. Open the foundations ↗ VOLUME II35 worked chapters available Advanced Equilibrium, instability, transport, and similarity solutions Lane–Emden, collapse, cluster relaxation, rotating ellipsoids, alpha disks, and Toomre Q—a path toward learning through equations. View chapters and learning guide ↗ SOLUTION LIBRARY Solution library Compare astrophysical solutions by assumptions, boundary data, mathematical form, and validity. ↗ READING GUIDE Textbooks & review volumes Explore your next question with standard references and PP III. ↗ SUPPLEMENT · NUMBERS & UNITS Numbers and units for astrophysics From parsecs to the fine-structure constant: values, scales, and SI versus Gaussian CGS. ↗ 01 Build intuition Start with a concrete question. 02 Follow every algebraic step See the steps between formulas. 03 Understand the assumptions Know what a model can explain. TWO LIMITS, TWO STORIES Two limits. Two physical stories. Two destinations for your journey through the physics. QUANTUM PHYSICS × RELATIVITY How massive can a white dwarf be? Balance electron pressure against gravity. When radius cancels, a limiting mass emerges. MCh ≈ 1.4 M☉ The Chandrasekhar mass↗ ELECTROMAGNETISM × GRAVITY Can light push a star apart? Count the momentum light transfers to electrons, then find where it balances gravity. LEdd = 4πGMc / κ The Eddington limit↗ FOUNDATIONS / I Small equations. A vast universe. Foundations: exploring the universe through school algebra. All 16 chapters are available. 16 Search chapters0 / 16 chapters complete OBSERVATIONS & TOOLS — Measuring the universe 00 A small mathematical toolkit for the universe Powers, proportions, and units—one algebraic step at a time. About 8 min↗01 Measuring light, measuring distance From the inverse-square law to the cosmic distance ladder. About 12 min↗02 Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature Why does gravity govern stars when electromagnetism is so strong? About 9 min↗ ATOMS & RADIATION — Understanding light 03 Atomic light and starlight: why 10.2 eV? From the Rydberg formula to the wavelength of Lyman alpha. About 12 min↗04 Why spectral lines have width Read finite lifetimes and thermal motion as two distinct effects. About 13 min↗05 The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering How a tiny effective area helps set a star’s luminosity limit. About 15 min↗06 Mean free paths, thermal equilibrium, and Boltzmann factors From the chance of a collision to the distribution of energy. About 16 min↗07 From Einstein A and B coefficients to Planck’s law Solve the balance of absorption, spontaneous emission, and stimulated emission. About 18 min↗ STARS & THEIR LIMITS — From micro to macro 08 The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up Connect gravitational energy to thermal motion and explore negative heat capacity. About 18 min↗09 Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation Connect gravity, pressure, and the random walk of radiation. About 17 min↗10 Why is the Sun’s surface about 6,000 degrees? Calculate 5,772 K from luminosity and radius. About 11 min↗11 The Eddington limit: when light balances gravity Use Thomson scattering to derive a characteristic luminosity limit. About 15 min↗12 The Chandrasekhar mass: a white dwarf’s limit Quantum pressure meets relativity—and radius disappears from the balance. About 20 min↗13 An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity From escape-speed estimates to black-hole radii and gravitational time dilation. About 16 min↗14 Nucleosynthesis and why helium is about 25% Count protons and neutrons to estimate a primordial abundance. About 11 min↗ COSMOLOGY — Reading the expanding universe 15 Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law From fractional distance growth to v = HD, redshift, and the Hubble time. About 20 min↗ ✳ An equation is another kind of telescope. When a law needs more advanced mathematics, we name it as an input. Connect what you can follow, then take the next step.

documents.title: About this series | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ABOUT THE SERIES Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step is a Japanese–English series for learning the shared tools of astrophysics. It pairs foundations through school algebra with an advanced volume using differential equations. VOLUME I16 lessons available Foundations Exploring the universe through school algebra Light and distance, quantum physics and radiation, stars and their limits, and cosmic expansion—one algebraic step at a time. Open the foundations ↗ VOLUME II35 worked chapters available Advanced Equilibrium, instability, transport, and similarity solutions Lane–Emden, collapse, cluster relaxation, rotating ellipsoids, alpha disks, and Toomre Q—a path toward learning through equations. View chapters and learning guide ↗ Foundations: exploring the universe through school algebra All 16 lessons, questions, references, and four interactive panels are available. No differential equations are solved. The optional entropy-maximization extension uses derivatives. Supplied laws from quantum mechanics and relativity are distinguished from the algebra developed here. Advanced: equilibrium, instability, transport, and similarity solutions 35 worked chapters are available in a 35-topic learning guide, covering cloud equilibrium, gravitational instability, cosmic structure, spherical accretion and winds, disk transport, MRI, Toomre Q, fluid interfaces, shocks, radiation, and ionization. Each topic shows its publication status. Supplement: numbers and units The supplement covers pc, h and ℏ, electron rest mass, solar mass, H₀, the fine-structure constant, G, and c. Compare values and equations in SI and Gaussian CGS. Open numbers and units ↗ Further reading Find standard references on galactic dynamics, radiation, stellar structure and evolution, cosmology, compact objects and fluid stability, plus PP III reviews on star and planet formation. Each entry includes preparation and connections to this site. Open the reading guide ↗ Teaching principles Astrophysical phenomena are the focus. Equations of state, opacities, and recombination coefficients are used with their meaning and validity stated; microscopic material-property derivations are not a separate theme. Connect intuition, assumptions, algebra, and questions. Distinguish estimates, exact results, and supplied coefficients, stating their conditions. Build advanced chapters in three stages: understand the phenomenon, formulate the equations, and solve and check. Plot provenance and validation The figures are conceptual illustrations or teaching plots recomputed from theoretical models. Checks against known solutions and conservation laws are distinct from reproducing a specific paper figure. A figure comparison requires its number, physical conditions, axes, normalization, and data scope. The same place in two languages Language switching keeps the current chapter and expanded syllabus entries. Language and completion records stay in your browser. Advanced chapters have separate progress from the foundations. Open the foundations ↗

documents.title: Advanced — Chapters and learning guide | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: BROWSE BY AREA Choose a chapter by field Advanced progress: 0 / 35 Open a chapter by its title. Expand “Question, prerequisites and sources” to see what it covers, which tools it uses, and its references in the same place. 01Understand the phenomenon Use diagrams, conservation, and dimensions. 02Formulate the equations Track assumptions, scaling, and boundaries. 03Solve and check Explore solutions and their limits. Mathematical preparation Calculus, introductory ordinary differential equations, vectors, and matrices. The treatment introduces partial differential equations through conservation laws, followed by linearization, nondimensionalization, and similarity transformations. The foundational chapters on the virial theorem, stellar structure, and cosmic expansion provide useful physical context. AREA 01 Equilibrium and limits of stars and clouds From the foundational virial theorem and white dwarfs to the internal structure of spheres and filaments. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ 01 Lane–Emden equation and polytropes Solve a stellar interior and recover the coefficient of the Chandrasekhar mass. 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Lane–Emden equation and polytropes TOOLS Calculus, the chain rule, and introductory ordinary differential equations READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How does a pressure–density relation determine stellar mass and radius? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Reduce hydrostatic balance and mass conservation to a dimensionless equation. Connect central regularity, the surface zero, and the n = 3 model to the Chandrasekhar mass. Read the chapter → Reference: Princeton · Polytropes ↗ 02 Bonnor–Ebert spheres and a cloud’s limiting mass How much self-gravity can a pressure-confined isothermal cloud support? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Bonnor–Ebert spheres and external pressure TOOLS The Lane–Emden chapter, ODEs, exponentials, and nondimensionalization READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION When does an externally compressed isothermal gas cloud become unstable? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Truncate an isothermal sphere at a specified external pressure and follow equilibrium sequences. State the quantities held fixed when assessing stability. Read the chapter → Reference: Bonnor (1956) ↗ 03 Ostriker’s isothermal cylinder and critical line mass Remembering J. P. Ostriker through an analytic model of filament gravity and its limiting mass per length. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Ostriker’s isothermal cylinder and critical line mass TOOLS Hydrostatic balance, Gauss’s law, differentiation and integration READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How much mass per unit length can a long gaseous filament support? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive an analytic equilibrium from cylindrical Gauss’s law and hydrostatic balance. Connect the flat centre, r⁻⁴ envelope and line mass 2cₛ²/G, distinguishing pressure truncation and projected column density. A chapter remembering J. P. Ostriker. Read the chapter → Reference: Ostriker (1964), §III, equations (56)–(61) ↗ 04 Hayashi limit and Hayashi tracks Why can a contracting pre-main-sequence star fade at nearly constant effective temperature? 35 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Hayashi limit and Hayashi tracks TOOLS Lane–Emden, ideal gas, calculus and powers READING TIME 35 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why can a contracting pre-main-sequence star fade at nearly constant effective temperature? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Connect an n = 3/2 polytrope to approximate full convection, photospheric boundary conditions, and H⁻ opacity. Use L = 4πR²σT_eff⁴ to read the contracting track, separating the atmospheric physics setting the Hayashi limit from the energy budget setting its timescale. Distinguish Henyey tracks when a radiative core develops. Read the chapter → Reference: Princeton · Hayashi limit ↗ AREA 02 Rotation and nonspherical gravitational equilibrium Move beyond spheres and connect shape to motion along different axes. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ 05 Gravitational potentials of ellipsoids At fixed mass, how does flattening or elongation change the internal gravity? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Gravitational potentials of ellipsoids TOOLS Newtonian gravity, integration and Poisson’s equation READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION At fixed mass, how does flattening or elongation change the internal gravity? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Begin with homogeneous ellipsoids, relating their potentials to axis ratios and comparing axisymmetric and triaxial shapes. Read the chapter → Reference: Binney · Dynamics of elliptical galaxies ↗ 06 Tensor virial theorem and Maclaurin/Jacobi sequences Which rotating fluid shapes can be in equilibrium, and are they stable? 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Tensor virial theorem and Maclaurin/Jacobi sequences TOOLS The ellipsoid chapter, matrices and equations of motion READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Which rotating fluid shapes can be in equilibrium, and are they stable? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use directional balances to study spheroidal and triaxial fluid figures. Separate equilibrium, bifurcation, and stability, and distinguish fluid figures from stellar systems. Read the chapter → Reference: Lebovitz (1961) ↗ AREA 03 Gravitational instability and cosmic structure Separate background from perturbations and ask which disturbances grow. Connect to foundations: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law ↗ 07 Jeans instability and the Jeans swindle Derive the wavelengths dominated by gravity and inspect the treatment of the uniform background. 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Jeans instability and the Jeans swindle TOOLS Fluid conservation, partial derivatives, linearization, and plane waves READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Which wavelengths can pressure stabilize, and how should the gravity of a uniform background be treated? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Linearize continuity, momentum, and Poisson equations to obtain a dispersion relation. Compare a static background assumption with an expanding cosmological background. Read the chapter → Reference: Falco et al. · Why does the Jeans swindle work? ↗ 08 Zel’dovich approximation and pancakes Why does gravitational clustering not necessarily begin by forming spheres? 30 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Zel’dovich approximation and pancakes TOOLS Cosmic expansion, mass conservation, derivatives and determinants READING TIME 30 min PHYSICAL QUESTION Why does gravitational clustering not necessarily begin by forming spheres? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Use a Lagrangian map and mass conservation to obtain density and study one-axis compression. Explain the breakdown at shell crossing. Read the chapter → Reference: Zel’dovich (1970) ↗ 09 Press–Schechter theory and the halo mass function Count cosmic density fluctuations to predict the abundance of dark-matter halos by mass. 40 min↗Question, prerequisites and sources Available Press–Schechter theory and the halo mass function TOOLS Cosmic expansion and Jeans chapters, calculus, normal distributions, and logarithms READING TIME 40 min PHYSICAL QUESTION How can initial density fluctuations predict halo abundances by mass? MATHEMATICAL APPROACH Derive the linear spherical-collapse threshold, relate Gaussian tails to mass fractions, and explain cloud-in-cloud accounting and the factor of two. Obtain the mass function and power-law self-similarity, with limits for galaxy formation. documents.title: Alpha disks and viscous-type accretion | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive scale height from vertical balance, define the ν = αcsH convention, and connect steady mass, angular-momentum, and energy budgets. Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Specify transport strength without choosing its cause The transport chapter related inward accretion to outward angular-momentum flux. A viscous-type disk prescribes an effective kinematic viscosity ν instead of deriving its stresses microscopically; ν need not represent molecular collisions. ν ≡ αcsH, [ν] = m² s−1 This equation defines our alpha convention. It is a dimensional closure using a velocity cs and length H, not a derivation of alpha’s value. MRI, self-gravity, winds, or other mechanisms must be assessed separately. 02Derive thickness from vertical balance For a thin disk dominated by a central mass M, vertical gravity is −ΩK²z at |z| ≪ r, with ΩK² = GM/r³. A vertically isothermal closure P = ρcs² gives a Gaussian density profile. cs²d lnρdz = −ΩK²z ρ(z) = ρ(0)exp(−z²2H²), H = csΩK H is a Gaussian scale height, not a sharp edge. Substitution gives ν = αH²ΩK. A small aspect ratio H/r makes radial viscous evolution slow compared with orbital motion. tν ∼ r²ν = 1α(rH)²ΩK−1 03Keep the stress sign and alpha convention explicit Define W as vertically integrated stress transporting angular momentum outward, with positive sign for outward transport. Keplerian shear has dΩ/dr < 0, so W = −νΣr dΩ/dr is positive for positive ν. Surface density Σ has different units from volume density ρ. W = −νΣrdΩdr = 32νΣΩ, 𝒢 = 2πr²W = 3πνΣj Our viscosity convention gives W = (3/2)αΣcs². A convention defining stress directly as αΣcs² has a different alpha by a factor of 3/2. The same symbol does not guarantee the same numerical normalization. 04Connect the torque to a steady accretion rate Assume steady flow with no wind or mass sources and zero torque at an inner radius rin. Combine 𝒢 = Ṁ(j−jin) with j = √(GMr) to obtain the relation between viscosity, surface density, and accretion. νΣ = Ṁ3π[1−√(rinr)] r ≫ rin : Ṁ ≈ 3πνΣ, vr ≈ −3ν2r The panel assumes a one-solar-mass central object and Σ = 100 g cm−2, with aspect ratio, alpha, and radius as inputs. It does not solve a radiative equilibrium for temperature or surface density. Changing alpha alone is different from recomputing an entire disk structure. 05Where is the released energy radiated? Dissipation combines stress with shear. If a thin disk radiates the dissipated energy locally from its two faces, the flux from one face is given below. Advected heat and energy carried off by a wind are neglected. 2F = νΣ(rdΩdr)² = 94νΣΩ² F(r) = 3GMṀ8πr³[1−√(rinr)] L = ∫rin∞4πrF(r)dr = GMṀ2rin The area 4πr dr includes both faces. The effective temperature defined by F = σSBTeff⁴ need not equal the internal temperature setting H. Additional emission from a stellar surface or boundary layer is not included in this disk luminosity. 06What alpha does not determine Alpha provides a useful closure, but does not replace a theory of the transport mechanism. Ideal-MHD MRI cannot simply be imposed when gas is poorly coupled to fields; a disk dominated by vertical wind torques is not fully described by radial viscosity alone. MRI examines linear extraction of differential-rotation energy; Toomre Q examines linear gravitational instability. Neither by itself uniquely specifies a saturated alpha. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed radius, central mass, H/r, and surface density, triple alpha. Far from the inner edge of a steady disk, what happens to viscosity, accretion rate, and viscous time? Show the answer and reasoning Viscosity and Ṁ ≈ 3πνΣ triple; tν ∼ r²/ν falls to one-third. Temperature and surface density have not been allowed to change simultaneously. The comparison requires an explicit convention and fixed inputs. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. Shakura & Sunyaev (1973) · Black holes in binary systems ↗ Princeton · Accretion disks ↗ Lesur (2021) · Wind-driven protoplanetary discs ↗ Advanced progress: 0 / 35 ← PreviousAngular-momentum transport and accretionNext →MRI: magnetic fields and differential rotation

documents.title: Ambipolar diffusion: magnetic fields and neutral gas | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive a diffusion clock from charge–neutral drift and check strong-coupling and small-drift assumptions. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Neutrals do not directly feel the magnetic force Most particles in a molecular cloud are neutral. A small charged component couples to the magnetic field and transfers momentum to neutrals through collisions. Different velocities allow magnetic flux to move relative to neutral material. Here ambipolar diffusion specifically means this ion–neutral drift in a weakly ionized astrophysical gas. Assume charges are sufficiently tied to the field and neglect ion inertia. This model does not solve charge separation. Omit Ohmic resistance, Hall effects, and a distribution of charged dust grains. 02Balance magnetic force against drag Let vD = vᵢ−vₙ. Drag on the ions is −γρᵢρₙvD. Balancing it against the Lorentz force determines the drift. Use Gaussian CGS units below: densities in g cm⁻³ and field strength in gauss. The drag coefficient is a supplied material input with dimensions, not a dimensionless efficiency. γρᵢρₙvD ≈ (∇×B)×B4π ηAD=B²4πγρᵢρₙ, tAD∼L²ηAD ηAD has units cm²/s and is a magnetic diffusivity, rather than an electrical resistance. At fixed number ionization fraction, increasing gas density strengthens drag and slows the relaxation of a fixed field pattern. A stronger field increases the magnetic force as well as the diffusivity. 03A single Fourier mode makes diffusion solvable Prescribe a static, uniform neutral background and a z-directed field varying weakly along x. Linearize about B₀ and hold ηAD at its background value. Define L = 1/k and wavelength λ = 2πL; using the wavelength in place of L would introduce a factor of 4π² in the decay clock. ∂δB∂t=ηAD∂²δB∂x² BzB₀=1+ε cos(x/L)e−t/tAD, tAD=L²ηAD Charges and field drift away from magnetic maxima toward minima, flattening the pattern. Set ε = 0.1. The neutral background is externally prescribed, so this is a diffusion benchmark, not a self-consistent collapsing cloud. Terms beyond linear order in ε are omitted. vD,x≈εηADLsin(x/L)e−t/tAD 04Compare field smoothing with a gravitational clock Inputs are neutral-particle number density nₙ and number ratio χᵢ = nᵢ/nₙ, not an ion mass fraction. Set ρₙ = 2.33mₚnₙ and ρᵢ = 29mₚχᵢnₙ for a representative molecular ion. Supply γ = 3.5 × 10¹³ cm³ g⁻¹ s⁻¹, B₀ = 30 μG, and T = 10 K. These composition-dependent choices are illustrative inputs, not universal constants. tff=√3π32Gρₙ, tin=1γρₙ, tni=1γρᵢ Borrow the free-fall time of a uniform sphere at the same density solely as a gravitational clock. tᵢₙ measures ion momentum adjustment to neutrals; tₙᵢ measures neutral adjustment to ions. Neglecting ion inertia requires tᵢₙ to be short relative to field evolution. Strong coupling does not require exactly zero drift. 05Dissipation and limits of the approximation The wavelength-averaged perturbation energy is ε²B₀² exp(−2t/tAD)/(16π). Its loss rate equals the averaged drag heating γρᵢρₙ⟨vD²⟩ to the retained order. This provides an energy check. Dissipated energy would heat matter, although the panel does not evolve temperature or neutral motion. The constant low-drift coefficient also assumes drift well below particle thermal speeds. Inspect vD,max/cₛ and tᵢₙ/tAD. Large values signal that interpreting the fixed-coefficient result physically requires more care. Sound speed is a thermal-speed proxy here, and the displayed flag is a heuristic validity check, not a sharp stability threshold. Compare with ideal MHD in MRI and the unmagnetized isothermal filament. This identifies where flux freezing enters an argument. A short diffusion time alone does not prove that a cloud must form a star; forces, geometry, and boundary conditions still matter. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed density, ionization, and field, double the perturbation scale L. How do diffusion time and initial drift speed change? Show the answer and reasoning With fixed η, tAD = L²/η grows fourfold and vD,max = εη/L halves at fixed fractional amplitude ε. L is 1/k, not the wavelength. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Angular-momentum transport and accretion | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the relation between specific angular momentum and circular radius, distinguish radial exchange from wind removal, and explain torque, accretion rate, and the role of alpha. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Fast rotation and large angular momentum are different Consider gas in a thin disk on nearly circular orbits around a fixed central mass M. Neglect disk self-gravity and radial pressure corrections and use Newtonian gravity. The model describes radii away from the immediate relativistic vicinity of a black hole. Balance centripetal acceleration against gravity. The orbital speed vφ, angular velocity Ω, and angular momentum per unit mass j then follow: vφ²r = GMr² vφ = √(GMr), Ω = vφr = √(GMr³) j ≡ rvφ = √(GMr) At one-quarter the radius, orbital speed doubles but j halves. Gas accreting through nearly circular orbits must therefore transfer angular momentum elsewhere. Gas that loses energy while retaining j circularizes at rc = j²/(GM). This argument concerns a sequence of circular orbits. An eccentric orbit can change radius during a revolution at fixed angular momentum. Do not generalize the result to every inward motion. 02Outward exchange can release orbital energy Specific orbital energy e is kinetic plus gravitational potential energy. Replacing r by j connects energy directly to angular momentum. e = vφ²2−GMr = −GM2r = −(GM)²2j² dedj = (GM)²j³ = Ω For a ring of fixed mass, the same relation gives dE/dJ = Ω. If an inner ring transfers a small positive δJ to an outer ring, their orbital energy changes are −ΩinδJ and +ΩoutδJ. Since Ωin > Ωout in a Keplerian disk, the total orbital energy decreases. δEorb = (Ωout−Ωin)δJ < 0 δEreleased = (Ωin−Ωout)δJ > 0 The lost orbital energy goes into fluctuations, magnetic fields, heat, radiation, or other channels. The transport mechanism determines where and how much becomes heat. Tracking both angular momentum and energy is the starting point for understanding luminous accretion disks. 03Check conservation with two rings Take equal ring masses m with initial radii r₀ and 4r₀. Use J₀ = m√(GMr₀) and E₀ = GMm/r₀ as angular-momentum and energy units. Transfer δJ = δJ₀ outward and compare circular end states. JinJ₀ = 1−δ, JoutJ₀ = 2+δ rinr₀ = (1−δ)², routr₀ = (2+δ)² The slider controls exchanged angular momentum, not time. Ring masses and central mass remain fixed; the panel compares circular end states. It does not simulate the forces, intermediate trajectories, or disk density evolution. 04Torques and stresses carry angular momentum Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. Forces between disk regions increase the angular momentum of one and decrease that of the other. Internal exchange does not destroy total angular momentum. 𝒢 = dJdt, [𝒢] = kg m² s−2 Correlated radial and azimuthal velocity fluctuations transport angular momentum through Reynolds stress. Magnetic tension links regions and exchanges angular momentum through Maxwell stress. In sufficiently self-gravitating disks, spiral structure can exert gravitational torques. Transport includes correlations and forces on astrophysical scales, beyond molecular collisional viscosity. The presence of fluctuations alone does not determine the magnitude or direction of transport; the relevant stresses and torques must be identified. 05Build the steady-disk angular-momentum budget Let Σ be surface density and vr radial velocity, positive outward. In a steady disk with no wind or mass sources, the accretion rate dot M, defined positive for inward mass flow, is independent of radius. Ṁ = −2πrΣvr > 0 The outward-positive angular-momentum flux FJ across radius r combines stress transport 𝒢 and inward advection −dot M j. With no accumulation in a steady annulus, FJ is constant with radius. FJ = 𝒢−Ṁj = constant With the boundary condition 𝒢 = 0 at an inner edge rin, the constant is −dot M jin. Rearranging relates inward accretion to the outward stress torque. 𝒢 = Ṁ(j−jin) Zero inner torque is a boundary assumption. Stellar magnetic fields, boundary layers, and stresses near a black hole can change it. A wind removes both mass and angular momentum, so constant dot M and FJ cannot simply be imposed on a wind-driven disk. 06A disk wind provides another route Transferring angular momentum to a wind leaving the disk surfaces can allow the remaining gas to accrete. A magnetically coupled wind can carry rotational angular momentum vertically out of the disk. Distinguish radial exchange within the disk from flux through its surfaces. Ĵwind = Ṁwindjwind Here jwind is angular momentum removed per unit wind mass flux, including the magnetic contribution. A small wind mass flux alone does not imply small angular-momentum removal. Conservation applies to the combined disk and wind, while the disk’s own angular momentum can decrease. Which route dominates a protoplanetary disk depends on its conditions. A magnetized disk wind is distinct from a spherical, thermally driven Parker wind; their driving and angular-momentum budgets need not be the same. 07Connect to alpha, MRI, and disk spreading The alpha model parametrizes transport through an effective kinematic viscosity ν = αcsH, where cs is sound speed and H a vertical scale height. This definition alone does not select the mechanism or determine alpha. ν = αcsH, tν ∼ r²ν H ≈ csΩ ⇒ tν ∼ 1α(rH)²Ω−1 A timescale assuming vertical balance in a thin Keplerian disk and viscous-type radial transport. MRI is a mechanism involving magnetic fields and differential rotation; its requirements differ from self-gravity or winds. Lynden–Bell–Pringle similarity solutions follow accretion and outward spreading with conservation laws and a prescribed ν. Toomre Q introduces gravitational instability. The advanced learning guide connects to alpha disks, MRI, viscous-disk similarity, and Toomre Q. Alpha disks, MRI, and Toomre Q have worked chapters. Viscous-disk similarity develops time evolution from these conservation laws. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Gas around a fixed central mass moves between nearly circular orbits at r and r/4. How do orbital speed and specific angular momentum change? Does radiating energy alone ensure the required angular-momentum change? Show the answer and reasoning vφ ∝ r−1/2 doubles, while j ∝ r1/2 halves. A torque must transfer angular momentum to other gas or a wind; energy loss alone does not ensure this. The transferred angular momentum remains part of the total budget. Radiation can carry angular momentum in other settings, but that effect is omitted here. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Bondi accretion and the sonic point | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive spherical isothermal flow, find the regular transonic accretion solution and its rate, and distinguish it from pressure-free free fall. Connect to foundations: The Eddington limit: when light balances gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Isolate a flow without angular momentum Let a mass M be surrounded by gas nearly at rest far away, with specified density ρ∞ and sound speed cs. Assume steady spherical flow, neglect the gas’s self-gravity, angular momentum, and magnetic fields, and first use the isothermal closure P = cs²ρ. Write the inward speed as u > 0. The mass passing through each sphere per unit time is constant. The changing area 4πr² links the increase of speed to the increase of density. Ṁ = 4πr²ρu, d lnρdr = −2r−1ududr 02Eliminate the density gradient Pressure opposes infall. Insert the isothermal relation into momentum balance and use mass conservation to eliminate d lnρ/dr. Although u is positive, its radial derivative is negative for an inflow accelerating toward smaller radius. ududr = −cs²d lnρdr−GMr² (u−cs²u)dudr = 2cs²r−GMr² At u = cs, the coefficient on the left vanishes. A smooth solution with finite slope requires the right-hand side to vanish there too. This regularity selects the sonic point rather than merely identifying a division-by-zero failure. rs = GM2cs², rB ≡ GMcs² = 2rs Some authors include a factor of two in the Bondi radius. Here rB = GM/cs². Do not mix a radius convention from one source with a dimensionless rate coefficient from another. 03Integrate and select the critical branch Use x = r/rs and Mach number 𝓜 = u/cs. Integrate the flow equation and choose the constant so that x = 1 and 𝓜 = 1 coincide. (𝓜−1𝓜)d𝓜dx = 2x−2x² 𝓜²−ln(𝓜²) = 4ln x+4x−3 Bondi inflow from a quiet reservoir joins the subsonic branch at x > 1 to the supersonic branch at x < 1. Expansion at the sonic point gives d𝓜/dx = −1. The opposite slope, +1, belongs to the Parker wind branch. Instead of dividing the ODE across its critical point, the panel bisects the integrated relation. Solving for ln(𝓜²) preserves positive Mach numbers even at small speeds. Substituting each plotted point back into the relation provides a direct residual check. 04Obtain the accretion rate from sonic density Integrating momentum in another form gives an isothermal Bernoulli relation. Set its constant using u → 0 and ρ → ρ∞ at infinity, then evaluate at the sonic point. u²2+cs²ln(ρρ∞)−GMr = 0 ρsρ∞ = e3/2 ṀB = 4πrs²ρscs = 4πλ(GM)²ρ∞cs³, λ = e3/24 ≈ 1.1204 The dimensional estimate rB²ρ∞cs does not determine λ. Its value comes from connecting the outer reservoir through pressure support and sonic regularity. Doubling the density normalization leaves the velocity profile unchanged and doubles the mass flux. 05What changes for a polytropic flow? For P = Kργ with constant K, the local sound speed a² = γP/ρ varies with radius. Combining mass conservation, sonic regularity, and Bernoulli balance yields the following standard relations in terms of the outer sound speed a∞. rs = (5−3γ)GM4a∞², as² = 2a∞²5−3γ λ(γ) = 14[25−3γ](5−3γ)/[2(γ−1)] (1<γ<5/3) The limit γ → 1 recovers the isothermal coefficient; γ → 5/3 gives λ → 1/4. In the latter limit the Newtonian sonic point moves to r = 0, so a formula for a finite regular critical point cannot simply be evaluated there. The panel displays only the isothermal solution. Angular momentum, fields, cooling, radiative feedback, and motion through the gas can alter real accretion. A Bondi rate is not automatically the mass reaching a black hole or the luminosity seen by an observer. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed outer density, double both the central mass and the outer sound speed. How do Bondi radius and isothermal accretion rate change? Show the answer and reasoning rB ∝ M/cs² halves. The rate scales as M²ρ∞/cs³, giving 4/8 = 1/2. Increased sound speed strengthens pressure support; the isothermal dimensionless coefficient λ stays fixed. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Bonnor–Ebert spheres and a cloud’s limiting mass | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFormulate an isothermal sphere, locate the maximum mass at fixed external pressure, and distinguish a finite cloud from an infinite isothermal sphere. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A cloud has pressure at its boundary Consider a dense core inside a molecular cloud. Its surface need not have zero pressure: surrounding gas confines it. Truncate the cloud where its pressure equals an external pressure Pext. Assume a static, spherical, isothermal, nonrotating gas without magnetic or turbulent support. P = cs²ρ, dPdr = −GM(r)ρr², dMdr = 4πr²ρ Treat the sound speed as a spatially constant input. Heat exchange maintaining that temperature is a closure condition, not solved here. Raising external pressure can produce a denser core, but does not imply that any mass can remain in equilibrium. 02Construct the dimensionless isothermal sphere Write the density decrease as ρ = ρcexp(−ψ). Hydrostatic balance becomes cs²dψ/dr = GM/r². Choose a length a and dimensionless radius ξ, then express the problem as two first-order equations that can be integrated from the centre. a = cs√(4πGρc), r = aξ, M = 4πa³ρcm dψdξ = mξ², dmdξ = ξ²e−ψ 1ξ²ddξ(ξ²dψdξ) = e−ψ This differs from finite-index polytropes in both length scaling and boundary definition. Isothermal density does not vanish at a finite radius. Here the surface is where pressure matches the confining pressure. 03Start regularly at the centre Symmetry requires ψ(0) = ψ′(0) = m(0) = 0, but directly evaluating m/ξ² gives 0/0. Insert a series ψ = Aξ² + Bξ⁴ + … into the equation and compare coefficients to obtain regular starting values. ψ = ξ²6−ξ⁴120+ξ⁶1890+… m = ξ³3−ξ⁵30+ξ⁷315+… The panel starts with this series and integrates using fourth-order Runge–Kutta. Determine the dimensionless structure before matching physical density or mass. Halving the integration step also lets you check that the critical point is numerically resolved. 04Compare masses at fixed external pressure At an edge ξb, Pext = cs²ρcexp(−ψb). Eliminate central density to separate physical mass into a dimensional scale and a function μ. This μ denotes dimensionless mass, not mean molecular weight. M = cs⁴G3/2Pext1/2 μ(ξb), μ = m e−ψ/2√(4π) R = cs²√(GPext)ξb e−ψb/2√(4π) Varying ξb compares equilibria at fixed sound speed and external pressure, while central density and mass change. It is not a time animation of a single cloud moving along the curve. 05The mass maximum marks a stability boundary Differentiate μ and insert the two first-order equations. A turning point satisfies m² = 2ξ⁴exp(−ψ). The first maximum encountered along the regular central solution gives the following values. ξcrit ≈ 6.451, ρcρb ≈ 14.04 MBE ≈ 1.182 cs⁴G3/2Pext1/2 For this pressure-confined isothermal model, configurations before the first maximum are stable to small radial compression, whereas those beyond it are unstable. Identifying the turning point with radial stability uses a result of dynamical perturbation analysis; hydrostatic integration alone is not a proof about every possible disturbance. Magnetic fields, temperature gradients, rotation, and turbulence change the threshold. An observed contrast above 14 alone does not establish ongoing collapse. The Jeans chapter compares this finite cloud with an unbounded local model. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed sound speed, quadruple the external pressure. How do critical mass, critical radius, and the central-to-edge density contrast change? Show the answer and reasoning Critical mass and radius both scale as Pext−1/2, so both halve. The critical dimensionless radius is unchanged and the contrast stays near 14.0. Both absolute central and edge densities quadruple. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Gravitational potentials of ellipsoids | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNExpress a homogeneous ellipsoid’s interior gravity through three coefficients and check axis ratios, positions and the spherical limit. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Let the shape depart from a sphere Consider a homogeneous Newtonian ellipsoid with semiaxes a, b and c. It isolates the effect of shape rather than modelling a realistic star or galaxy. Interior points satisfy x²/a²+y²/b²+z²/c² ≤ 1. M = 4π3ρabc, Φ = Φ₀+πGρ(A₁x²+A₂y²+A₃z²) A quadratic interior potential gives forces linear in coordinates. This expression does not describe the exterior. The constant Φ₀ uses the convention that potential vanishes at infinity. 02Define three coefficients by quadrature Δ(u) ≡ √[(a²+u)(b²+u)(c²+u)] Aᵢ = abc∫0∞du(aᵢ²+u)Δ(u), Φ₀ = −πGρabc∫0∞duΔ(u) Use the integral representation as the supplied solution obtained from Newtonian potential theory. u has units of length squared; the Aᵢ are dimensionless and depend only on axis ratios. A common rescaling of all axes leaves them unchanged. gᵢ = −∂Φ∂xᵢ = −2πGρAᵢxᵢ The panel maps the infinite integration interval to a finite one. It computes each coefficient independently and checks the sum below rather than enforcing it by renormalization. 03Check Poisson’s equation Differentiate 1/Δ to obtain −(1/2Δ)Σ1/(aᵢ²+u). Its integral fixes the coefficient sum from endpoint values. Inserting it into the interior Laplacian checks Poisson’s equation. A₁+A₂+A₃ = −2abc[1Δ(u)]0∞ = 2 ∇²Φ = 2πGρΣAᵢ = 4πGρ The panel fixes abc = 1, comparing shapes at fixed mass and density. Flattening can increase A₃ while shortening c, so surface acceleration depends on both the coefficient and position. 04Binding energy and the spherical limit W = −3GM²10∫0∞duΔ(u) a=b=c=R : Aᵢ=23, W=−3GM²5R W includes the factor of one half preventing double counting of pair energy. −W/(GM²) has inverse-length units. The panel fixes the equal-volume radius to one; its displayed energy factor is not in joules. The spherical limit and permutations of the axes give independent checks. Verify the sum of two and each spherical value of two thirds before examining elongated shapes. 05Add rotation and pressure A prescribed homogeneous shape need not be an equilibrium. Pressure and rotation must support an equipotential boundary. The tensor-virial chapter constructs this additional condition. The plot recomputes the homogeneous-ellipsoid integrals, not observations or N-body figures. A collisionless stellar system also needs a velocity-dispersion tensor and an orbital distribution. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For a = b = c = R, what are the three A coefficients and the interior gravitational field? Show the answer and reasoning Symmetry and the sum rule give Aᵢ = 2/3. Thus gᵢ = −(4π/3)Gρxᵢ: interior gravity grows linearly with distance. This differs from the exterior inverse-square field. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Fokker–Planck equation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConstruct drift–diffusion from small stochastic increments and check conservation and limits for star clusters. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From trajectories to a probability density Suppose x receives stochastic increments Δx in short intervals Δt. Define drift A and diffusion B from the first two increment moments per unit time. This small-increment approximation fails when large jumps dominate. A(x,t)=lim⟨Δx⟩Δt, B(x,t)=lim⟨(Δx)²⟩Δt Let f integrate to one over the full real line. The one-step squared increment defining B is distinct from the total squared displacement since the initial time. 02Expand the evolution through second order Expand the transition-probability evolution in Δx. When higher increment moments can be neglected, the first two terms give the Fokker–Planck equation. Its apparent factor of two depends on the convention used for B. ∂f∂t=−∂(Af)∂x+12∂²(Bf)∂x²=−∂J∂x J=Af−12∂(Bf)∂x Zero boundary flux conserves total probability; an absorbing boundary removes it. Conservation depends on boundary conditions as well as the differential equation. 03A solvable model: restoring drift plus diffusion Choose A = −γx, B = 2D, γ ≥ 0 and D > 0. This Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model combines restoring drift with random excitation. A Gaussian initial distribution remains Gaussian while its mean and variance evolve. d⟨x⟩dt=−γ⟨x⟩, dVdt=−2γV+2D μ(t)=μ₀e−γt V(t)=V₀e−2γt+Dγ(1−e−2γt) (γ>0) Multiply the PDE by x or x² and integrate by parts to derive the moment equations. At γ = 0 the variance is V₀ + 2Dt and keeps growing. 04Animate the distribution and its stationary state f(x,t)=1√(2πV(t))exp[−(x−μ(t))²2V(t)] γ>0 : feq∝exp[−γx²2D] The panel uses dimensionless x,t, D = 0.5, μ₀ = 2 and V₀ = 0.0625. It plots an analytic solution, not self-consistent cluster collision coefficients. Tails outside the window are retained mathematically; the visible area is not renormalized to one. 05Additional ingredients for star clusters Clusters require position–velocity distributions or orbit-averaged energy distributions. Even at fixed potential, phase-space f(E) differs from number per energy N(E) = g(E)f(E); the density of states g(E) matters. Encounter coefficients depend on the stellar distribution and the potential must be updated with Poisson’s equation. An evolving potential also changes energy coordinates. Escape boundaries, binaries and multiple stellar masses can be important. The OU model exchanges energy with a bath and generally does not conserve kinetic energy. It is not a calculation of cooling or gravothermal collapse in an isolated cluster. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For A = −γx and B = 2D, let γ = 2 and D = 0.5. Find the limiting mean and variance. What changes at γ = 0? Show the answer and reasoning Mean tends to zero and variance to D/γ = 0.25, giving standard deviation 0.5. With γ = 0, variance grows as its initial value plus 2Dt; no normalizable stationary Gaussian is reached on the full real line. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Goldreich–Julian density and corotation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive corotation charge density, compare SI and Gaussian units, and distinguish light-cylinder limits, net charge and pair plasma. Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Rotation creates a corotation electric field A highly conducting corotating plasma satisfies E+v×B = 0 locally. Insert v = Ω×r and first examine a flat-spacetime, quasistatic approximation to the required charge density. E=−(Ω×r)×B, ∇·E=ρeε₀ (SI) ρe denotes charge density, not mass density. Corotation can require a net charge; this alone does not determine the total electron–positron population. 02Apply a vector identity to obtain GJ density ∇·(v×B)=B·(∇×v)−v·(∇×B), ∇×(Ω×r)=2Ω ρe=ε₀[−2Ω·B+v·(∇×B)] Neglecting the current-related curl-B term in the near zone gives the Goldreich–Julian density scale. Keeping the omitted term visible clarifies where the approximation fails. ρGJ≈−2ε₀Ω·B (SI) ρGJ≈−Ω·B2πc (Gauss) nGJ≡|ρGJ|e Gaussian corotation includes 1/c and Gauss’s law reads ∇·E = 4πρe. Inserting a magnetic field measured in gauss directly into the SI formula is incorrect. 03Estimate the scale from period and field Ω=2πP, nGJ≈6.94×1010B∥ / 1012 GP / s cm−3 (magnitude) B∥ is the magnitude of the local component parallel to Ω. An aligned dipole with polar field Bp has surface Bz = Bp(3cos²θ−1)/2. The approximate charge changes sign near θ = 54.7°. The panel estimates the near field at the surface of a 12 km star using an aligned dipole. It does not solve field back-reaction, relativistic frame dragging or the global magnetospheric current. 04The light cylinder and a polar-cap estimate Rigid corotation has speed Ωr⊥ at cylindrical radius r⊥ and cannot extend beyond the light cylinder. The dipole line r = req sin²θ gives a geometric estimate of the open polar cap. RLC=cΩ≈4.77×10⁴(Ps) km sin²θpc≈R*RLC, rpc≈R*√(R*RLC) This cap estimate assumes an aligned dipole whose last closed line reaches the light cylinder. Real fields open and carry currents; a vacuum dipole is not an exact exterior solution. 05Connect net charge to acceleration and radiation A dense pair plasma can supply the required net charge through n₊−n₋ while n₊+n₋ greatly exceeds nGJ. The GJ number scale is not automatically the total density to use in scattering rates. Insufficient charge can leave an unscreened field along B and permit particle acceleration, radiation and pair creation. A density scale alone does not determine gap locations or the emitted spectrum. These diagrams recompute the corotation approximation, not global paper magnetospheres or observed pulses. Use them to inspect local validity and charge sign. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed field and location, double the spin period. How do GJ charge magnitude, light-cylinder radius and aligned-dipole polar-cap radius change? Show the answer and reasoning Charge magnitude halves, light-cylinder radius doubles, and the aligned-dipole cap radius decreases by √2. The last result is a geometric estimate, not a solution for the global magnetosphere. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Gravothermal catastrophe | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConnect negative heat capacity to heat flow and distinguish isothermal-sphere stability under different constraints. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Losing energy can increase temperature With negligible surface pressure, virial equilibrium gives E = K+W = −K. Losing energy makes E more negative and can increase kinetic energy and temperature: self-gravity permits negative heat capacity. K=32NkBT, C≡dEdT=−32NkB (negligible surface pressure) Outward heat flow can further heat and contract the core, increasing the temperature difference and reinforcing transport. Negative heat capacity alone does not imply immediate collapse of every gravitating system. 02Specify the constraints before asking about stability The classical model confines mass M inside a spherical box of radius R. It differs from a fixed-pressure Bonnor–Ebert sphere. A fixed-temperature bath and an insulating fixed-energy wall also lead to different stability criteria. Point-particle gravity admits arbitrarily concentrated configurations, so there is no global entropy maximum without short-distance regularization. Stability here concerns local or metastable smooth mean-field equilibria. 03Add an energy scale to the isothermal sphere Integrate the same ψ,m,ξ equations used for Bonnor–Ebert spheres to a box boundary ξb, with ρ = ρc exp(−ψ). This sequence instead compares equilibria at fixed M and R. u=ξ³e−ψm, v=mξ, η≡GMRcs²=v Wall pressure Pb means E = −K no longer applies. Use 2K+W = 3PbV and K = 3Mcₛ²/2 to obtain the energy. E=4πR³Pb−32Mcs²=Mcs²(u−32) Λ≡−ERGM²=3/2−uv 04Locate two different turning points The first maximum of η occurs near ξb = 8.99 and contrast 32.1. The first maximum of Λ is near ξb = 34.4, contrast 709 and Λ = 0.335. Their identification with the first fixed-temperature and fixed-energy stability limits uses supplied thermodynamic/perturbation results. Moving along this sequence is not time evolution. Equilibria have different energies and temperatures at fixed M,R; the selected ensemble specifies perturbation constraints. Contrasts 14, 32.1 and 709 refer to distinct boundary/thermodynamic conditions. 05Connect to core collapse in real clusters In a cluster, two-body relaxation transports energy. A core losing heat can contract, raise its density and accelerate relaxation, driving core collapse. This is not the same timescale as collisionless orbital instability. Hard binaries can release binding energy during encounters, halting collapse and contributing to post-collapse expansion or oscillation. Tides and mass loss matter in open systems; 709 is not a direct observational classifier for real clusters. The panel recomputes boxed isothermal equilibria and stability landmarks. It does not simulate binary formation, a time-dependent core collapse, or paper particle data. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For a boxed isothermal sphere with density contrast 100, distinguish fixed-temperature from fixed-total-energy stability. Show the answer and reasoning 100 exceeds 32.1 but is below 709: it lies beyond the first fixed-M,R,T stability limit but before the fixed-M,R,E limit for a local entropy maximum. These boxed-model values do not directly classify an open star cluster. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Hayashi limit and Hayashi tracks | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConnect photospheric and convective assumptions to a nearly constant effective temperature and a contraction timescale. Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A cool photosphere and convective interior A pre-main-sequence star can shine through contraction before nuclear reactions dominate. Approximate a fully convective monatomic ideal-gas interior by an n = 3/2 polytrope. Its surface temperature also requires a boundary condition where light escapes. P = Kρ5/3, P = ℛρT, ℛ ≡ kBμmp K ∝ GM1/3R The last scaling follows by eliminating central density from the n = 3/2 Lane–Emden structure. Hold composition fixed. Partial ionization and a superadiabatic surface layer limit this idealized adiabat. 02Supply a photospheric pressure In a thin plane atmosphere dP/dτ = g/κ. Taking representative g and κ at optical depth about 2/3 gives Pph ≈ 2g/(3κph). Supply an approximate low-temperature H⁻ opacity per unit mass; microscopic opacity theory is outside this chapter. Pph ≈ 2g3κph, g = GMR² κ = κ₀ρaTb, a = 12, b = 7.7 The opacity power law has a limited temperature/composition range, and κ₀ carries units. Approximate the photospheric temperature by effective temperature to connect the atmosphere and interior; do not extrapolate the law to all stars. 03A strong opacity power gives a weak temperature scaling Eliminate density with ρ = P/(ℛT). The adiabat then gives P = (ℛT)⁵ᐟ²K⁻³ᐟ². Substitute into the photospheric condition and collect the powers of K, M and R. Pa+1 ∝ gκ₀−1ℛaTa−b Teff3a+2b+5 ∝ κ₀−2Ma+3R3a−1 Teff ∝ M3.5/21.9R0.5/21.9, ε ≡ 143.8 ≈ 0.02283 L = 4πR²σSBTeff⁴ ∝ R2+4ε (fixed M) A large radius change produces little temperature change, giving a nearly vertical H–R path. The cool boundary is the Hayashi limit. This scaling estimates its slope; it does not replace a detailed atmosphere calculation or establish every forbidden configuration. 04Use luminosity to time contraction Omit nuclear burning, accretion and mass loss, and take total energy E = −3GM²/(7R). Integrating L = −dE/dt gives a contraction law. Write ℓ = 2+4ε and use initial radius R₀ and luminosity L₀. L = −3GM²7R²dRdt, RR₀ = (1+tt₀)−1/(ℓ+1) t₀ = 3GM²7(ℓ+1)R₀L₀ The teaching model chooses R₀ = 3 solar radii and T₀ = 4000 K × (M/M☉)3.5/21.9. The temperature normalization is supplied, not calibrated from κ₀. Main-sequence arrival, radiative-core formation and realistic stellar tracks are not computed. 05Leaving a Hayashi track A radiative interior invalidates a single n = 3/2 convective model. Following a hotter Henyey track requires radiative transport and internal structure. Different nearly vertical curves need not describe the same mass or evolutionary phase. Playback advances the specified energy model. It is more than moving an observational point, but it does not reproduce published numerical tracks. Separate the weak temperature dependence from the energy budget that sets elapsed time. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. With this chapter’s opacity powers, halve radius at fixed mass. How do effective temperature and luminosity change? Show the answer and reasoning With ε = 1/43.8, temperature changes by 2−ε ≈ 0.984 and luminosity by 2−(2+4ε) ≈ 0.235. The small temperature change leaves area as the main luminosity factor. These powers belong to the stated atmosphere approximation, not a detailed evolution calculation. documents.title: Larson–Penston and Shu isothermal collapse | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFormulate similarity collapse and distinguish Shu/LPH boundary conditions, sonic points and asymptotic profiles. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01The same equations can select different flows Begin with continuity, momentum and mass for a spherical self-gravitating isothermal gas. Cooling maintaining isothermality is supplied; rotation and fields are omitted. Enclosed M includes any central point mass. ∂ρ∂t+1r²∂∂r(r²ρu)=0 ∂u∂t+u∂u∂r=−cs²∂lnρ∂r−GMr², ∂M∂r=4πr²ρ Shu and Larson–Penston are not automatically successive stages of one cloud. The sign of time relative to central formation and the outer density/velocity select the solution. 02Introduce post-formation similarity variables Set central formation at t = 0 and use t > 0 here. Match time powers in each term to reduce partial differential equations to ordinary equations in x. x=rcst, u=csv(x), ρ=α(x)4πGt², M=cs³tGm(x) m=x²α(x−v), m′=x²α [(x−v)²−1]v′=[α(x−v)−2x](x−v) [(x−v)²−1]α′α=[α−2(x−v)x](x−v) A regular sonic point x−v = 1 also requires α = 2/x. Directly dividing by the vanishing denominator fails; select a regular critical branch together with global boundary conditions. 03Shu: inside-out collapse from a singular isothermal sphere x≥1 : v=0, α=2x², ρ=cs²2πGr² x→0 : m→m₀, v≈−√(2m₀x), α≈√(m₀2x³) The exterior is a static singular isothermal sphere, with an expansion wave at x = 1 marking the onset of infall. Inner r⁻³ᐟ² density and free-fall velocity apply where central mass dominates. Use the supplied global-solution result m₀ ≈ 0.975. Ṁ=m₀cs³G, Mcentral=m₀cs³tG 04LPH: an envelope already flowing inward The Larson–Penston flow continued through central formation by Hunter has α ≈ 8.86/x² and v ≈ −3.28 far away. The envelope is about 4.43 times denser than Shu’s static sphere and is already infalling. Its central coefficient is m₀ ≈ 46.9. The panel numerically computes the post-formation Shu and LPH similarity ODEs. Compare log–log density and inward-speed profiles, switch to similarity coordinates, and animate labelled mass shells. The approximate LPH central accretion coefficient 46.9 differs from the pre-formation LP flux and is not a universal finite-cloud rate. 05Separate the derived equations from supplied eigenvalues The similarity equations and free-fall powers can be followed here. Coefficients 0.975 and 46.9 depend on boundary conditions and critical branches, not dimensions alone. The plots integrate the intermediate region from Shu’s A → 2⁺ limit and the LPH outer data, measuring the inner m₀. Checks use Shu (1977), Table 2, free-fall limits, mass conservation and half-step convergence. Rounded LPH outer coefficients give m₀ ≈ 46.97. Finite reservoirs, disks, fields and heating change real accretion. Compare with collapse from a finite initial equilibrium such as a Bonnor–Ebert sphere, and inspect what was imposed at infinity. Compare high-density molecular conversion with a gravitational clock in three-body chemistry. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Within one solution family, double sound speed and compare at the same time after central formation. How do rate, central mass and similarity radius scale? Show the answer and reasoning The rate and central mass increase by eight; cₛt doubles. The coefficient m₀ depends on the solution family. Changing sound speed alone does not switch between Shu and LPH. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. documents.title: Ostriker’s isothermal cylinder and critical line mass | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the cylindrical density profile, verify its r⁻⁴ envelope and finite limiting line mass, and distinguish spherical geometry, projection and external pressure. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01In memory of Jeremiah P. Ostriker Jeremiah P. Ostriker (1937–2025) died on 6 April 2025, aged 87. We remember his work on dark matter, galaxy formation and the interstellar medium, and his contributions to teaching and collaboration, by working through his 1964 isothermal-cylinder solution. In memory of Jeremiah P. Ostriker — Princeton University tribute ↗ (14 April 2025). The article describes his scientific contributions and shares recollections from colleagues and former students. Approximate a long molecular filament by a cylinder uniform along its axis. Gravity still balances pressure, as in a star, but changing geometry alters the density envelope and mass limit. Here the tribute takes the form of deriving and using a result, rather than only remembering its name. We follow §III of the original paper. Ostriker’s footnote acknowledges the same solution obtained by Stodółkiewicz (1963); it is also called the Stodółkiewicz–Ostriker solution. Notation and length scales below are chosen for this guide. 02From spherical mass to cylindrical line mass Let r measure distance from the axis, and λ(r) be the enclosed mass per unit length. Line mass is mass divided by length, distinct from volume density or projected column density. Assume a long, static, isothermal, nonrotating cylinder, neglecting ends, magnetic fields and turbulent support. Divide the mass in a segment by its length L. Gravity points toward the axis, perpendicular to it. λ(r)=∫0r2πr′ρ(r′)dr′, dλdr=2πrρ gr=−2Gλ(r)r A cylindrical Gaussian surface has side area 2πrL, so gravity times 2πrL equals 4πGλL. This differs from spherical GM/r². Near a regular centre λ ∝ r², so gravity tends to zero linearly rather than diverging. 03Reduce isothermal balance to one equation P=cs²ρ, cs²dlnρdr=−2Gλr 1rddr(rdlnρdr)=−4πGρcs² Write ρ = ρce−ψ, H = cₛ/√(4πGρc), and ξ = r/H. Regular central conditions are ψ(0) = ψ′(0) = 0. The spherical isothermal Lane–Emden term 2ψ′/ξ becomes ψ′/ξ for a cylinder. ψ″+1ξψ′=e−ψ This is not the spherical solution with a relabelled radius. Geometry changes the growth of Gaussian surface area, leaving a different coefficient in the differential equation. 04Verify the analytic solution and its r⁻⁴ envelope ψ=2ln(1+ξ²8), ρ(r)=ρc(1+r²8H²)−2 a≡√8H, ρ(r)=ρc(1+r²/a²)² ψ′=4ξ8+ξ², ψ″+ψ′ξ=64(8+ξ²)²=(1+ξ²8)−2 Density is nearly constant for r ≪ a and falls as r⁻⁴ for r ≫ a, unlike the r⁻² singular isothermal sphere. The scale a marks a smooth transition rather than an abrupt density boundary. Unlike a profile known only by numerical integration, this closed form can be substituted to verify the equation identically. This also makes it a useful numerical benchmark. 05Infinite radial extent but finite line mass λ(r)=2πρc∫0rr′dr′(1+r′²/a²)²=πρca²r²r²+a² λ(r)=2cs²Gr²r²+a², λcrit≡λ(∞)=2cs²G Increasing central density narrows the cylinder, cancelling ρc from its full line mass. Radius a encloses half that line mass. The total mass of an infinitely long cylinder is still infinite: the finite quantity is mass per unit length. cs²=kBTμmp, λcrit≈16.5(T10 K)(2.33μ) M☉ pc−1 This static cylinder supported only by thermal pressure cannot support a larger line mass. Axial fragmentation, end-driven contraction and magnetic, rotational or turbulent support are separate questions; this one formula does not determine every real filament’s fate. 06Pressure truncation and observational projection Truncating at radius R with external pressure gives a line mass below the limit. Set f = λ(R)/λcrit to obtain the surface-to-central density relation algebraically. R=a√(f1−f), ρ(R)ρc=(1−f)², Pext=cs²ρ(R) The side-on projected column density Σ integrates volume density along the line of sight. For the radially unbounded analytic model, it follows the formula below at projected distance b and falls as b⁻³, not r⁻⁴. A pressure-truncated cylinder has a different, finite line-of-sight integration range. Σ(b)=∫−∞∞ρ(√(b²+z²))dz=πρca2(1+b²a²)−3/2 The panel compares static equilibria. Sliders are not time and do not animate physical contraction. Compare geometry with Bonnor–Ebert spheres and time evolution with LPH/Shu collapse. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed temperature, quadruple central density. How do the critical line mass and the radius enclosing half the full line mass change? Show the answer and reasoning The critical line mass 2cₛ²/G is independent of central density and stays unchanged. The half-line-mass radius a = √8H scales as ρc−1/2 and halves. A narrower, denser cylinder has the same line mass integrated to infinite radius. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Jeans instability and the Jeans swindle | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNLinearize continuity, momentum, and Poisson equations, derive the Jeans length and growth time, and explain the limits of subtracting background gravity. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Two responses compete in a compression A small overdensity attracts additional gas, while its pressure increase tends to erase the contrast. Examine individual wavelengths to determine where gravity wins. Exclude rotation, magnetic fields, viscosity, and expansion of the background in this model. ρ = ρ₀(1+δ), P = P₀+cs²ρ₀δ cs² = (∂P∂ρ)background The density contrast δ is dimensionless and satisfies |δ| ≪ 1. Isothermal and adiabatic responses have different sound speeds. Use the constant cs appropriate to the chosen closure rather than silently switching between them. 02What happened to background gravity? An infinite uniform density at rest creates a background problem: its pressure gradient vanishes, but ordinary Poisson gravity requires ∇²Φ₀ = 4πGρ₀, not zero. A static homogeneous background with zero gravitational field is not self-consistent without an additional prescription. Define a background-subtracted local model with ∇²φ = 4πG(ρ−ρ₀). The treatment of background gravity is the issue behind the Jeans swindle. Cosmological perturbations include Hubble damping and are not governed by the same static-background equation. To solve a finite cloud with its boundary conditions, use a different model such as a Bonnor–Ebert sphere. The purpose here is the local competition between pressure and gravity at each wavelength. 03Eliminate velocity from three equations Let u denote perturbation velocity. Linearize continuity and momentum, discarding quadratic terms such as δu. Differentiate continuity in time and substitute the divergence of momentum to obtain an equation for density contrast alone. ∂δ∂t+∇·u = 0 ∂u∂t = −cs²∇δ−∇φ, ∇²φ = 4πGρ₀δ ∂²δ∂t² = cs²∇²δ+4πGρ₀δ The gravitational term reinforces a density peak. The spatial second derivative of a wave is negative at that peak, so the sound-speed term restores it. Checking these derivative signs explains the competition without memorizing the final criterion. 04Replace derivatives with wavenumber and frequency Insert a plane wave δ = δ₁exp[i(k·r−ωt)]. The second time derivative supplies −ω² and the Laplacian supplies −k². Positive ω² gives oscillations; negative ω² allows growing and decaying solutions with ω = iσ. ω² = cs²k²−4πGρ₀ kJ = √(4πGρ₀)cs, λJ = 2πkJ = cs√(πGρ₀) Wavelengths longer than λJ are unstable. At short wavelengths the pressure term increases as k². The exact k = 0 mode changes the mean density and is excluded from the background-subtracted perturbations; the plotted long-wave endpoint is a formal limit. 05Define length, mass, and time separately MJ ≡ 4π3ρ₀(λJ2)³ = π5/26cs³G3/2ρ₀1/2 tJ ≡ 1√(4πGρ₀), σtJ = √[1−(k/kJ)²] The numerical coefficient in a Jeans mass depends on the geometry and length used to convert a wavelength into mass. Here the sphere’s radius is half a wavelength. The wavelength criterion itself follows directly from the dispersion relation. When δ approaches order unity, the omitted nonlinear terms matter. A linear growth rate does not predict the number or masses of the eventual stars. For a rotating thin disk, include the rotational response as in Toomre Q. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed sound speed, quadruple density. How do Jeans wavelength, the mass convention used here, and the gravitational timescale change? Show the answer and reasoning All three scale as ρ₀−1/2, so all halve. The mass here is that of a sphere of radius λJ/2. Defining it as ρλJ³ changes a numerical coefficient, not its density and sound-speed scaling. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. Falco et al. documents.title: Kelvin–Helmholtz instability | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNInclude advection in interface conditions, derive KH growth and pattern speed, and compare gravitational stabilization with shear driving. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Shear can drive waves even at equal density Two fluids moving at different speeds along an interface can transfer bulk kinetic energy into interface waves. This is Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. RT uses density ordering relative to effective acceleration; KH is driven by shear. Use the RT chapter’s incompressible, inviscid, infinitely deep half-spaces, upper density ρ₁ and lower density ρ₂. Background velocities U₁ and U₂ are uniform and parallel to x, discontinuous at the interface. Initially set g = 0, with no surface tension or magnetic field and k > 0 parallel to the flow. Rewrite the RT chapter’s potential flow and pressure conditions to include advection. 02Use the frequency seen by each stream Following each stream changes the time derivative to ∂/∂t + Uj∂/∂x. Acting on ei(kx−ωt) gives −i(ω−kUj). Define this stream-relative frequency as Ωj. Ω₁ = ω−kU₁, Ω₂ = ω−kU₂ a₁ = iΩ₁ζ₀k, a₂ = −iΩ₂ζ₀k Pressure perturbations also use δpj = −ρj(∂/∂t + Uj∂/∂x)φj. Matching interface pressures gives, for g = 0: ρ₁(ω−kU₁)² + ρ₂(ω−kU₂)² = 0 03Complete the square to separate drift and growth Subtract the density-weighted mean velocity Ū and complete the square. With ΔU = U₁ − U₂: Ū ≡ ρ₁U₁+ρ₂U₂ρ₁+ρ₂ (ω−kŪ)² = −ρ₁ρ₂(ρ₁+ρ₂)²k²(ΔU)² ω = kŪ ± iσ, σ = √(ρ₁ρ₂)ρ₁+ρ₂k|ΔU| The pattern drifts at Ū while one branch grows as eσt. Equal densities still give σ = k|ΔU|/2. Adding the same velocity to both streams changes drift but not growth. Larger density contrast reduces growth at the same shear. 04Combine gravity and shear in one relation Restore the RT chapter’s downward g. Pressure matching becomes ρ₁Ω₁² + ρ₂Ω₂² = (ρ₂−ρ₁)gk. Completing the square again puts gravity and shear in a single relation. (ω−kŪ)² = −Agk − ρ₁ρ₂(ρ₁+ρ₂)²k²(ΔU)² A ≡ ρ₁−ρ₂ρ₁+ρ₂ A positive right-hand side gives advected oscillations; a negative value gives growing and decaying branches. For A > 0, RT and KH both destabilize. For A < 0, gravity supports long waves, but the shear term proportional to k² wins at sufficiently short wavelengths. A zero-thickness inviscid velocity jump has σ ∝ k and no finite fastest-growing wavelength. Finite shear thickness, compressibility, magnetic fields, and viscosity change this. The statement that all wavelengths are unstable applies here to the ideal g = 0 model. 05A linear wave is not a vortex simulation Wave roll-up, vortices, and mixing are nonlinear stages. Jets and surrounding gas or gas clouds moving at different speeds are applications, but their stability depends on actual density, sound speed, magnetic field, and velocity profiles. The panel draws a single linear mode of the derived dispersion relation, not a nonlinear fluid simulation. Comparing RT, KH, Jeans, and Toomre instabilities asks the same useful questions: what supplies energy, and what opposes the disturbance? CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For equal densities, no gravity, ΔU = 2 m/s, and λ = 2π m, what is the growth rate? What happens if the wavelength halves? Does linear theory determine the eventual vortices? Show the answer and reasoning σ = k|ΔU|/2 = 1 s⁻¹. Halving the wavelength doubles k and σ. Linear theory describes initial small-amplitude growth; rolled-up vortices and mixing are nonlinear. An ideal zero-thickness interface without viscosity or another small-scale regulator has no finite fastest-growing wavelength. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
