documents.title: Kerr: rotation, the ergoregion, and the ISCO | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish the horizon from the static limit and compute the spin dependence of circular orbits. Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A ruler for rotating spacetime Take the stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat Kerr vacuum metric as a supplied exact solution. Set electric charge to zero and neglect disc and test-particle self-gravity. Use G = c = M = 1: restore physical lengths with GM/c² and times with GM/c³. Let χ = cJ/(GM²) be nonnegative and label the orbital direction separately. Σ = R² + χ² cos²θ, Δ = R² − 2R + χ² ds² = −(1−2R/Σ)dt² − (4χR sin²θ/Σ)dt dφ + (Σ/Δ)dR² + Σdθ² + [R²+χ²+2χ²R sin²θ/Σ]sin²θ dφ² The mixed coefficient is 2gₜφ. Setting χ = 0 recovers Schwarzschild. R is a Boyer–Lindquist coordinate, not an areal radius when the spin is nonzero. We derive consequences of the metric; its construction from the Einstein equations is left to the references. 02Separate the horizon and static limit The outer horizon is the larger root of Δ = 0. An observer at fixed R, θ, and φ has ds² = gₜₜdt² and can be timelike only where gₜₜ < 0. The outer root of gₜₜ = 0 defines the static limit. R₊ = 1 + √(1−χ²) Rₑ(θ) = 1 + √(1−χ²cos²θ) The surfaces meet at the poles; the equatorial static limit remains at R = 2. Between them static observers are impossible, but rotating timelike observers can exist. The static limit is not a no-escape boundary. The panel stays in the exterior and does not evolve horizon-crossing or exactly extremal orbits. 03Allowed angular velocities and frame dragging Hold R and θ fixed and rotate at Ω = dφ/dt. Substitution into the metric gives a quadratic that must be negative. Its null endpoints bound the allowed angular velocities of stationary timelike observers. gₜₜ + 2gₜφΩ + gφφΩ² < 0 Ω₋ < Ω < Ω₊, Ω± = [−gₜφ ± √(gₜφ²−gₜₜgφφ)]/gφφ ΩZ = −gₜφ/gφφ = 2χR / [(R²+χ²)²−χ²Δsin²θ] Even zero angular momentum pφ = gₜφuᵗ + gφφuφ generally requires a nonzero ΩZ. This describes frame dragging of a locally nonrotating observer. Such a fixed-radius observer generally needs acceleration; ΩZ is not the angular velocity of a freely orbiting particle. 04From circular orbits to the ISCO For a massive equatorial test particle, conserved specific energy E and angular momentum L separate the radial motion. The Carter constant vanishes in the equatorial plane. Combine the two circular-orbit conditions with marginal radial stability. Σ²(dR/dτ)² = ℛ(R) ℛ = [E(R²+χ²)−χL]² − Δ[R²+(L−χE)²] ℛ = ∂Rℛ = ∂²Rℛ = 0 ⇒ R² − 6R + 8sχ√R − 3χ² = 0 Differentiate at fixed E and L, then eliminate them. Set s = +1 for prograde and s = −1 for retrograde motion. Selecting the physical exterior branch yields the closed expression below. Z₁ = 1 + (1−χ²)1/3[(1+χ)1/3+(1−χ)1/3] Z₂ = √(3χ²+Z₁²) RISCO,s = 3+Z₂−s√[(3−Z₁)(3+Z₁+2Z₂)] At χ = 0 both branches give six. As χ approaches one, the prograde limit is one and the retrograde limit is nine. This does not place an ordinary timelike orbit on the exactly extremal horizon. Infall can occur inside the ISCO; pressure and magnetic stresses make a disc inner edge a different question. 05Compare different spins Curves show coordinate radii computed from the equations, not an observed shadow or integrated trajectories. Changing inputs compares stationary spacetimes; it is not a time evolution of a spinning-up black hole. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If the equatorial static limit stays at R = 2 while the horizon moves inward, what changes? Show the answer and reasoning An exterior ergoregion opens up. It forbids static timelike observers, rather than escape itself; permitted stationary timelike motion must co-rotate. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Lane–Emden equation and polytropes | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNNondimensionalize hydrostatic balance, integrate from centre to surface, and explain why mass is independent of central density for n = 3. Connect to foundations: The Chandrasekhar mass: a white dwarf’s limit ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From global balance to a thin shell A global estimate P ∼ GM²/R⁴ treats a star as a whole. Now distinguish the enclosed mass m(r), local pressure P(r), and density ρ(r). Assume a static, spherical, nonrotating object with Newtonian gravity. A shell of thickness Δr has mass about 4πr²ρΔr. Its net outward pressure force is −4πr²ΔP; the inward gravitational force is (Gm/r²)4πr²ρΔr. Balance them and take the thin-shell limit. dPdr = −Gmρr² dmdr = 4πr²ρ dP/dr is the local change in pressure with radius. Its negative sign means pressure decreases outward. The second equation expresses mass conservation as successive shells are added. 02Eliminate mass and close the model Multiply the first equation by r²/ρ to get r²P′/ρ = −Gm. Differentiate with respect to r and use the second equation; here a prime means an r derivative. 1r²ddr (r²ρdPdr) = −4πGρ We still need a pressure–density relation. Adopt a polytropic relation with K and n constant throughout the object. The index n is not a particle count: it specifies the density dependence of pressure. P = Kρ1+1/n (n > 0) This is a structural model, not a universal law with constant K and n for all stars. An isothermal sphere P = cs²ρ requires a different scaling; it is distinct from the finite-n models considered here. 03Remove the units, step by step Let ρc be the central density and use θ(ξ) to describe the profile. The scale a is a length; ξ and θ are dimensionless. Use d/dr = (1/a)d/dξ. ρ = ρcθn, r = aξ P = Kρc1+1/nθn+1 1ρdPdr = (n+1)Kρc1/nadθdξ Substitute into the previous equation. Transforming the outer 1/r² and derivative leaves a factor (n+1)Kρc1/n/a² on the left and 4πGρc on the right. Choose a so that these factors match. a² = (n+1)K4πGρc(1−n)/n 1ξ²ddξ(ξ²dθdξ) = −θn θ″ + 2ξθ′ + θn = 0 The Lane–Emden equation; primes now denote ξ derivatives. 04Start at a regular centre By definition θ(0) = 1. A smooth spherical centre has no preferred direction, so θ′(0) = 0. Direct numerical evaluation at ξ = 0 would nevertheless give 0/0 in 2θ′/ξ. Insert θ = 1 + Aξ² + Bξ⁴ + … . Constant terms give 6A + 1 = 0; ξ² terms give 20B + nA = 0. This supplies starting values just outside the centre. θ = 1 − ξ²6 + nξ⁴120 + … θ′ = −ξ3 + nξ³30 + … Start at a small ε > 0 and integrate outward using two first-order equations, θ′ = q and q′ = −2q/ξ − θⁿ. The first zero ξ₁ defines the surface. Here we consider 0 < n < 5. 05Integrate and compare with a known solution For n = 1, θ = sinξ/ξ is a solution. Differentiating ξ²θ′ = ξcosξ − sinξ gives −ξsinξ = −ξ²θ, as required. The central limit is one and the surface is ξ₁ = π. This provides an independent check on the numerical method. The numerical recipe: fourth-order Runge–Kutta For y′ = F(x,y), y can be a scalar or a vector such as (θ,q). With step h, calculate these four slopes in order. k₁ = F(x,y) k₂ = F(x+h/2, y+hk₁/2) k₃ = F(x+h/2, y+hk₂/2) k₄ = F(x+h, y+hk₃) y(x+h) ≈ y(x) + h6(k₁+2k₂+2k₃+k₄) The panel uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta: evaluate four slopes over a short interval and combine them with weights 1:2:2:1. It starts at ε = 10⁻⁴ and interpolates the surface between neighbouring points. Halve the step to check convergence. 06Turn the dimensionless shape into radius and mass Integrating the equation from centre to surface expresses the density integral through the surface slope. Call this dimensionless mass μₙ. μn ≡ ∫0ξ₁ ξ²θndξ = −ξ₁²θ′(ξ₁) R = aξ₁, M = 4πa³ρcμn R ∝ K1/2ρc(1−n)/(2n) M ∝ K3/2ρc(3−n)/(2n) Scaling along a sequence at fixed n; G is also constant. For n = 3/2, M ∝ ρc1/2 and R ∝ ρc−1/6, giving R ∝ M−1/3 at fixed K. For n = 3, the density exponent in M vanishes: changing radius does not change the equilibrium mass at the same K. 07Recover the Chandrasekhar coefficient In the cold, completely degenerate, ultrarelativistic electron limit, P = KURρ4/3, so n = 3. Quantum statistics supplies KUR below. Here μe is mass per electron in units of the atomic mass constant mu, and ℏ = h/(2π). KUR = ℏc4(3π²)1/3(μemu)−4/3 Numerical integration gives ξ₁ ≈ 6.89685 and μ₃ ≈ 2.01824. Cancel the central density in a³ρc to recover the structural coefficient supplied in the foundation lesson. M = 4πμ₃(KURπG)3/2 MCh ≈ 5.83μe² M☉ ≈ 1.46 M☉ (μe = 2) This is an idealized limiting mass. General relativity, electron capture, Coulomb effects, finite temperature, and rotation are omitted. The n = 3 equilibrium equation alone does not establish dynamical stability. The n = 5 solution has no finite zero; the uniform-density n = 0 model also needs separate treatment. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed K and composition, increase the central density eightfold. How do a, R, and M change for n = 3? What about n = 3/2? Show the answer and reasoning a and R scale as ρc(1−n)/(2n); M scales as ρc(3−n)/(2n). For n = 3, a and R halve while M stays fixed. For n = 3/2, a and R decrease by 1/√2 and M increases by √8. The dimensionless surface ξ₁ and mass μₙ stay fixed because each sequence keeps n and K fixed. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Lin–Mestel–Shu: collapse of a uniform spheroid | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCompute axis evolution and compare spherical, oblate, and prolate collapse. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Let a slightly nonspherical cloud fall Shape changes the directional gravitational field even at fixed initial density. Consider an isolated, homogeneous, nonrotating pressure-free spheroid: no expansion, magnetic field, turbulence, or shocks. Follow it only before an axis collapses. A spheroid is a shape; it does not imply that the cloud rotates. a₁ = a₂ = a(t), a₃ = c(t), q = c/a M = (4π/3)ρa²c = constant ρ(t)/ρ₀ = a₀²c₀/[a(t)²c(t)] Use the homologous velocity field vᵢ = (ȧᵢ/aᵢ)xᵢ. The interior gravitational acceleration of a homogeneous ellipsoid is also linear in xᵢ, so this gives a self-consistent homogeneous evolution before caustics. It is not an exact description of arbitrary nonuniform clouds. 02From gravitational coefficients to axis motion Use the coefficients Aᵢ from the ellipsoidal-potential chapter. Inside the cloud gᵢ = −2πGρAᵢxᵢ and their sum is two. Applying the pressure-free equation of motion to surface elements produces two ordinary differential equations. Aᵢ = a₁a₂a₃∫₀∞du/[(aᵢ²+u)√((a₁²+u)(a₂²+u)(a₃²+u))] 2Aₐ+Ac = 2 ä = −2πGρAₐa, c̈ = −2πGρAcc For oblate q < 1 use e = √(1−q²); for prolate q > 1 use e = √(1−q⁻²). Use series near the sphere to avoid cancellation. The acceleration includes the axis length as well as its gravitational coefficient. q < 1: Ac = 2[1−q arccos(q)/e]/e² q > 1: Ac = (1−e²)[ln((1+e)/(1−e))−2e]/e³ q = 1: Aₐ = Ac = 2/3, Aₐ = (2−Ac)/2 03Specify initial conditions and a time unit Use a₀ as the length unit and t₀ = (2πGρ₀)⁻¹/² as the time unit. The dimensionless initial conditions are a = 1, c = q₀, with both velocities zero. Primes denote derivatives with respect to dimensionless time τ. D = ρ/ρ₀ = q₀/(a²c) a″ = −DAₐa, c″ = −DAcc Changing the initial density rescales physical time by ρ₀⁻¹/². Varying q₀ at fixed a₀ and initial density also changes the mass. The panel integrates this stated family; it does not allow arbitrary initial contraction velocities or external pressures. 04Check against spherical collapse and energy conservation For a sphere, a = c = b and b″ = −2/(3b²). The initially stationary solution has the parametric form below, providing an independent numerical benchmark. b = (1+cosη)/2, τ = (√3/4)(η+sinη) τff = π√3/4, tff = √[3π/(32Gρ₀)] Total energy supplies a second check. The mean squared coordinate along an axis is aᵢ²/5, which determines the kinetic energy per unit mass. Combine it with the potential-energy integral to obtain a dimensionless invariant. ℋ = (2a′²+c′²)/10 − (q₀/5)I(a,c) I = ∫₀∞du/[(a²+u)√(c²+u)] q < 1: I = 2 arccos(q)/(a√(1−q²)) q > 1: I = 2 arcosh(q)/(a√(q²−1)) Oblate clouds flatten further; prolate clouds become more elongated. A vanishing axis makes the density diverge and ends the smooth homogeneous flow. Stop when either the smallest initial-normalized axis or the current short/long axis ratio reaches 0.03. This is a numerical cutoff, not a measured singularity time. 05Follow shape and density Teaching plots integrate the axis equations; they do not reproduce a particular original figure or particle simulation. Assumptions differ from pressure-supported Shu collapse and from the pre-crossing Zel’dovich approximation. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed initial shape, quadruple the initial density. What happens to the physical time needed to reach the same shape? Show the answer and reasoning The time unit (2πGρ₀)⁻¹/² halves. With the same dimensionless initial velocities, the dimensionless track is unchanged and physical times halve. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: MRI: magnetic fields and differential rotation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the dispersion relation from local tension and Coriolis forces, find the unstable band and maximum growth, and distinguish linear growth from transport saturation. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Connect a faster inner orbit to a slower outer orbit A Keplerian disk has angular velocity decreasing outward, but specific angular momentum j = r²Ω increasing outward. Even when hydrodynamic axisymmetric radial exchanges are stable, magnetic coupling changes the problem. This is the starting point of magnetorotational instability, MRI. q ≡ −d lnΩd ln r, κ² = 4Ω²+dΩ²d ln r = 2(2−q)Ω² Keplerian rotation has q = 3/2. The epicyclic frequency κ describes the oscillation of a slightly radially displaced orbit. Restrict the model to 0 ≤ q < 2, separating MRI from hydrodynamic Rayleigh instability. 02Magnetic tension acts like a weak spring Imagine two fluid elements connected by a field line. The faster inner element stretches the connection, so tension slows the inner element and accelerates the outer one. Losing angular momentum lets the inner element move inward, while the outer element moves outward. The separation can reinforce itself. Quantify this using a local rotating frame, ideal MHD, incompressibility, a uniform vertical field B, and axisymmetric disturbances with vertical wavenumber k. Define the Alfvén speed and a tension frequency squared K. vA = B√(μ₀ρ), K = k²vA² These are SI expressions. K is not a spring constant in force per length; it is a restoring coefficient per unit mass with units s−2. Even a weak field can provide appreciable tension at a sufficiently large wavenumber. 03Coupled displacement equations Let ξx be radial displacement and ξy azimuthal displacement. The linear local equations contain Coriolis forces, the differential-rotation tidal term, and tension. Take these equations as the ideal-MHD input, then derive their eigenvalues explicitly. ξ̈x−2Ωξ̇y = (2qΩ²−K)ξx ξ̈y+2Ωξ̇x = −Kξy Substitute ξ ∝ exp(st), replacing first and second derivatives by s and s². A nonzero displacement requires the determinant of the coefficient matrix to vanish. (s²+K−2qΩ²)ξx−2Ωsξy = 0 2Ωsξx+(s²+K)ξy = 0 s⁴+(κ²+2K)s²+K(K−2qΩ²) = 0 04Solve a quadratic in s squared Set b = kvA/Ω, z = s²/Ω², and κ̂² = 2(2−q). The quartic in s is a quadratic in z. A positive larger root permits an exponentially growing solution with s > 0. z²+(κ̂²+2b²)z+b²(b²−2q) = 0 z+ = −(κ̂²+2b²)+√(κ̂⁴+16b²)2 For 0 < q < 2, the interval 0 < b² < 2q makes the constant term negative, producing one positive and one negative root. There is no growth at exactly b = 0; sufficiently strong tension, b² ≥ 2q, also suppresses this mode. 05Find the fastest-growing wavelength Differentiate z+ with respect to b² and set the derivative to zero: −1 + 4/√(κ̂⁴+16b²) = 0. Rearrangement gives the optimum tension and maximum growth rate. bmax² = q(4−q)4, smax = qΩ2 q = 32 : bmax² = 1516, smax = 3Ω4 For Keplerian rotation the e-folding time is 4/(3Ω), about 0.21 of an orbit 2π/Ω. This is the linear growth time of a small perturbation, not a prediction of unlimited exponential amplification. 06MRI growth does not fix a saturated alpha A real mode must fit within the disk thickness. Resistivity, ambipolar diffusion, and other nonideal effects alter the result when field–gas coupling is weak. The ideal unstable band alone cannot establish activity throughout a protoplanetary disk. Linear eigenvalues do not determine nonlinear saturation or the mean transport stress. Obtaining the alpha used in an alpha disk requires additional calculations including field geometry, nonlinear interactions, and boundary conditions. Compare the clock for magnetic flux to slip relative to weakly ionized gas in ambipolar diffusion. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Fix the fastest-growing Keplerian mode. At fixed density and wavenumber, double the magnetic field. Does that mode still grow? Have all disk modes become stable? Show the answer and reasoning Its b² rises from 15/16 to 15/4, outside b² < 3, so that mode stops growing. Other, longer wavelengths can have smaller b; this is not stability of every mode. The wavelength must also fit within the real disk. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Parker wind and transonic outflow | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNSelect the outflow branch of the equation shared with Bondi flow and separate sonic regularity, heating, and outer boundary conditions. Connect to foundations: Why is the Sun’s surface about 6,000 degrees? ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Can a hot atmosphere remain static? In a hot atmosphere such as the solar corona, a pressure gradient pushes gas outward. Begin with Newtonian gravity from a mass M and an isothermal, spherical, steady gas. Magnetic fields, rotation, and electron–ion temperature differences are not yet included. cs² = kBTμmp Here μ is the mean mass per particle in proton-mass units; the example specifies μ = 0.6. This is the isothermal sound speed, so do not insert the heat-capacity ratio used in an adiabatic sound speed. 02Apply mass and momentum conservation to a wind Now define u > 0 as the outward velocity. A steady wind has constant mass-loss rate 4πr²ρu. Eliminating the density gradient yields the same speed equation as in the Bondi chapter; the branch and boundary conditions distinguish the physical flows. Ṁwind = 4πr²ρu (u−cs²u)dudr = 2cs²r−GMr² The right-hand side is negative inside rs and positive outside. On the subsonic branch the left-hand coefficient is also negative, so du/dr can be positive even inside the critical radius. Inward gravity does not forbid outward acceleration: include the pressure gradient in the force budget. 03The smooth accelerating sonic branch rs = GM2cs², x = rrs, 𝓜 = ucs 𝓜²−ln(𝓜²) = 4ln x+4x−3 Connect a subsonic branch at x < 1 to a supersonic branch at x > 1. Expanding numerator and denominator together at the sonic point gives d𝓜/dx = +1, compared with −1 for Bondi’s inward speed. Choosing the wrong branch reverses the physical interpretation. The plot compares the two critical curves. Each point is obtained by bisection of the integrated relation, avoiding a numerical division by zero at the sonic point. 04Why hydrostatic balance can be insufficient The static isothermal equation can also be integrated. Given a base radius r₀ and density ρ₀, its density profile is: ρ(r)ρ₀ = exp[GMcs²(1r−1r₀)] Density tends to a finite nonzero value at infinity. Such a static atmosphere cannot match a sufficiently low-pressure exterior. A confined outer boundary can permit a subsonic breeze, so writing the differential equation alone does not uniquely demand the transonic wind. Critical regularity is important, but heating, base conditions, and the outer connection also matter. Dynamical selection of a stable flow is a larger problem than the steady equations solved here. 05Solar scales and the cost of isothermality For one solar mass, T = 106 K, and μ = 0.6, the isothermal sound speed is about 117 km/s and the sonic point about 6.9 solar radii. Raising temperature moves the sonic point inward as pressure becomes stronger relative to gravity. A velocity profile still leaves density normalization unspecified, so a base density or equivalent boundary condition is needed for mass loss. Expansion requires heating to remain isothermal; this model does not solve an energy equation. At large radius 𝓜² ≈ 4 ln x, so it does not even predict a finite terminal speed. Real solar wind is magnetized, with heating, conduction, and weak collisionality also important. Use Parker flow as a basic transonic outflow model, distinct from a magnetized disk wind extracting rotational angular momentum. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed central mass and mean molecular weight, quadruple the isothermal temperature. How do sound speed and sonic radius change? Does the sonic point alone fix mass loss? Show the answer and reasoning Sound speed doubles because cs ∝ √T; sonic radius decreases by four. The mass-loss rate 4πr²ρu still needs a density normalization, such as a base density. The critical velocity curve alone does not fix it. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Press–Schechter theory and the halo mass function | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConnect spherical collapse, Gaussian tails, and mass-to-number conversion, explaining the factor of two and model limits. Connect to foundations: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From small fluctuations to halo abundances Regions slightly denser than the cosmic mean can attract more matter. Press–Schechter theory combines fluctuation statistics with a collapse criterion to estimate halo abundances by mass. A halo here means a gravitationally bound dark-matter structure. Define density contrast δ, initially with |δ| ≪ 1. Include cosmic expansion and pressureless matter growth, extending beyond the static gas in the Jeans chapter. The statistical variable is the linearly extrapolated contrast; the actual late nonlinear density field is not assumed to remain Gaussian. δ ≡ ρ−ρ̄ρ̄, δL(t) = D(t)δL(t₀), D(t₀) = 1 Playback uses a flat, matter-only Einstein–de Sitter universe: D = a, a(t₀) = 1, and a ∝ t2/3. This is not an assertion that D = a remains exact at low redshift in ΛCDM. 02Choose a mass scale by smoothing Averages over small and large regions need not agree. Smooth the field with a normalized window W and call its rms fluctuation σ(M,t). A real-space top-hat averages uniformly within a comoving radius R, which differs from the final halo radius. M = 4π3ρ̄m,0R³, σ²(M,t) ≡ ⟨δL,R²⟩ σ(M,t) = D(t)σ(M,t₀) Here ρ̄m,0 is the mean matter density at the reference epoch, matching the comoving volume used for number densities. Linear smoothing of an initially Gaussian field gives a zero-mean Gaussian with variance σ². p(δL|M,t) = 1√(2π)σexp(−δL²2σ²) σ measures fluctuation strength at a mass scale, not the density of an individual halo. A larger σ places more of the distribution above a fixed threshold. 03Spherical collapse gives a threshold of 1.686 Model a uniform overdense region as a pressureless sphere. Before shell crossing, each shell encloses constant mass M and obeys R̈ = −GM/R². The growing-mode solution can be written parametrically: R = A(1−cos θ), t = B(θ−sin θ), A³ = GMB² The sphere turns around at θ = π and formally reaches R = 0 at θ = 2π. Divide its density 3M/(4πR³) by the background density 1/(6πGt²) to obtain the nonlinear contrast. 1+δNL = 92(θ−sin θ)²(1−cos θ)³ At small θ, θ−sinθ ≈ θ³/6 and δNL ≈ 3θ²/20. Match this to linear growth proportional to t2/3, then extrapolate: δL(θ) = 35[34(θ−sin θ)]2/3 δc = δL(2π) = 35(3π2)2/3 ≈ 1.68647 1.686 is a linearly extrapolated contrast at the formal collapse time, not the actual halo overdensity. Real halos undergo shell crossing and virialization; the singular R = 0 solution does not describe their internal evolution. 04Relate a Gaussian tail to a mass fraction Define peak height ν = δc/σ. A smaller σ makes the same threshold rarer. First compute the probability P of exceeding it at one smoothing scale by substituting u = δL/σ. P = ∫ν∞e−u²/2√(2π)du = 12erfc(ν√2) The Press–Schechter prescription assigns mass fraction F(>M) = 2P to halos above M. The complementary error function erfc is a name for this Gaussian-tail integral, not an additional physical law. F(>M,t) = erfc(ν√2), ν = δcσ(M,t) For ν = 1, P ≈ 0.1587 and F ≈ 0.3173; at ν = 2, F ≈ 0.04550, and at ν = 3, F ≈ 0.002700. The Gaussian tail makes high-ν objects rare. The factor of two has not yet been derived; it requires the next section. 05The factor of two and cloud-in-cloud accounting A region below threshold on one scale can lie inside a larger collapsing region. Smaller regions inside a larger halo can also be counted as separate objects. A single-scale tail probability alone does not consistently assign matter to halos. Even as σ → ∞, P approaches only 1/2. Doubling restores total-mass normalization, but symmetry between positive and negative contrasts alone does not solve the nested-region problem. Excursion-set theory follows one position from large smoothing scales to small ones and assigns mass at the first threshold crossing. A Gaussian field with a sharp-k window and constant barrier has independent random-walk increments; a reflection argument yields the factor of two. Extension: the first-crossing distribution S ≡ σ², ffirst(S) = δc√(2π)S3/2exp(−δc²2S) F(>M) = ∫0S(M)ffirst(S)dS We supply the reflection-principle result without solving a diffusion equation here. Real-space top-hat and Gaussian windows correlate the steps, so this simple derivation cannot be transferred unchanged. Distinguish the PS prescription, including its mass–window mapping, from the conditions of an exact first-crossing solution. 06Convert mass fractions into number densities Let n(M,t)dM be the number of halos per comoving volume in the interval [M,M+dM]. Minus the differential of F gives the mass fraction in this interval. Multiply by mean comoving matter density and divide by the mass per halo. M n(M,t)dM = −ρ̄m,0∂F∂MdM When ν increases with M, ∂F/∂ν = −√(2/π)exp(−ν²/2) and ∂ν/∂M = (ν/M)|∂lnσ/∂lnM|. Apply the chain rule: n(M,t) = √(2π)ρ̄m,0M²ν|∂lnσ∂lnM|e−ν²/2 n has units of inverse comoving volume per unit mass. Number per natural-log mass is Mn(M), whereas mass fraction per natural-log mass is ψ = M²n(M)/ρ̄m,0. These are distinct vertical axes and give different curve shapes. ψ(M,t) ≡ M²n(M,t)ρ̄m,0, ∫0∞ψ(M,t)dlnM = 1 This is the distribution of halos present at each epoch, not a formation rate per unit time. Merger histories require further ingredients such as conditional mass distributions. Total-mass normalization assumes monotonically increasing σ reaching infinity as M → 0. Do not impose it unchanged on a model with a small-scale cutoff. 07Use a power-law spectrum to expose time scaling The power spectrum describes fluctuation strength by wavenumber. For P(k) ∝ kn and a window W(kR), substitute q = kR to factor out the radius dependence. Spectral index n is distinct from the mass-function notation n(M). σ²(R) = 12π²∫0∞k²P(k)|W(kR)|²dk ∝ R−(n+3) σ(M,t) ∝ D(t)M−p, p = n+36 For a real-space top-hat, a pure power law extending over all wavenumbers converges for −3 < n < 1. The panel stays within this idealized range; it does not compute a transfer function or calibrate σ₈ for precision cosmology. σ(M,t) = δcD(t)(MM₀)−p, ν = (M/M₀)pD(t) σ(M*,t) = δc ⇒ M*M₀ = D1/p M₀ is an arbitrary reference mass where ν = 1 at D = 1. M* also maximizes the mass-weighted logarithmic distribution ψ. For n = −2, p = 1/6 and M* ∝ D⁶. Scaling the horizontal axis by M* makes curves at fixed n overlap. 08What the plots do and do not reproduce These teaching plots recompute the equations above. To compare with Bond et al. (1991), equation (3.9), identify their A with S = σ², their fᵥ with δc, and |dlnA/dlnM| with 2p. This gives the same ψ = √(2/π)pνexp(−ν²/2). Equivalently, keep A = σ²(t₀) fixed and use barrier fᵥ = δc/D(t) to obtain the same ν. Checks cover the analytic expression, standard Gaussian-tail values, mass normalization, and time scaling. These are not copies of paper figures, N-body data, or curves using a CDM transfer function. For example, Bond et al. Figure 5a uses a CDM spectrum, unlike this power-law model. Distinguish recomputing an equation, reproducing a named figure, and comparing measured data. A citation alone does not make curves computed under different conditions identical. 09From dark halos to luminous galaxies PS theory bridges initial fluctuations and halo statistics. It does not specify gas cooling, star-formation efficiency, supernova or active-galactic-nucleus heating, or post-merger morphology. One halo cannot automatically be equated with one observed luminous galaxy. Predictions depend on spherical-collapse assumptions, filtering, and nonspherical dynamics. Use this chapter to understand exponential rarity and hierarchical formation, with simulation-calibrated mass functions needed for more precise observational predictions. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For P(k) ∝ k⁻², halve D from 1. How does M* change? At fixed M = M₀, what happens to ν and F(>M)? Show the answer and reasoning p = 1/6, so M* ∝ D⁶ and decreases by 64. At fixed M₀, ν rises from 1 to 2 and F falls from about 0.3173 to 0.04550. This is a fraction of mass in halos heavier than M₀, not a fraction of halo counts. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Rayleigh–Taylor instability | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the interface dispersion relation from kinematic and pressure conditions, estimate growth from Atwood number and wavelength, and identify the linear regime. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Denser fluid above can lower its potential energy Denser fluid below lighter fluid is a stable arrangement under gravity. If the denser fluid is above, a small downward deformation lets dense fluid sink while lighter fluid rises. Releasing potential energy amplifies the deformation: Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Take z upward and acceleration −g with g > 0. The upper and lower half-spaces have constant densities ρ₁ and ρ₂. Both are infinitely deep, incompressible, and inviscid, with no surface tension, magnetic field, or background flow. Unlike Jeans instability, we prescribe g rather than calculate perturbed self-gravity. ζ(x,t) = Re[ζ₀ei(kx−ωt)], k = 2πλ > 0 ζ is interface height. Complex exponentials are a calculational tool; the physical displacement is the real part. For ω = ωr + iσ, e−iωt = e−iωrteσt, so σ > 0 means growth. Linearization requires k|ζ| ≪ 1. 02Build a flow that decays away from the interface In each fluid take potential perturbations δu = ∇φ. Incompressibility, ∇·δu = 0, gives ∇²φ = 0. With x dependence eikx, the vertical equation is φ″ − k²φ = 0. Choose solutions that decay far from the interface. φ₁ = a₁e−kzei(kx−ωt) (z > 0) φ₂ = a₂ekzei(kx−ωt) (z < 0) The interface moves with the fluid, so its vertical speed ∂ζ/∂t equals ∂φ/∂z on either side. At first order evaluate at z = 0. Removing the common exponential gives: −iωζ₀ = −ka₁ = ka₂ a₁ = iωζ₀k, a₂ = −iωζ₀k 03Keep the background pressure gradient Spatial integration of linearized momentum gives δpj = −ρj∂φj/∂t = iρjωφj. Pressures match at the displaced interface z = ζ. The equilibrium gradient dp₀/dz = −ρg adds a term −ρgζ when evaluating there. δp₁−ρ₁gζ = δp₂−ρ₂gζ δp₁−δp₂ = (ρ₁−ρ₂)gζ The amplitudes above give δp₁ = −ρ₁ω²ζ₀/k and δp₂ = +ρ₂ω²ζ₀/k. Subtract them and cancel nonzero ζ₀. −(ρ₁+ρ₂)ω²k = (ρ₁−ρ₂)g ω² = −Agk, A ≡ ρ₁−ρ₂ρ₁+ρ₂ A is the Atwood number. Denser fluid on top gives A > 0 and ω = ±i√(Agk); the growing branch has σ = √(Agk). If A < 0, ω is real and the interface supports gravity waves in this model. τgrow = 1σ = √(λ2πAg) (A > 0) 04Explore density contrast and wavelength Multiplying both densities by the same factor leaves A unchanged. Reducing wavelength by four increases k by four and growth rate by two. The doubling time is ln2/σ; 1/σ is the e-folding time. With A = 0 and no shear, this ideal interface has neither restoring force nor growth. 05Separate linear growth from nonlinear mixing This calculation describes only the small-amplitude stage. Large bubbles, dense spikes, and entrainment require nonlinear dynamics. At contacts in supernova remnants, examine density ordering relative to the effective acceleration in a frame following the decelerating flow. Without surface tension, viscosity, magnetic effects, or finite interface thickness, σ ∝ √k has no finite fastest-growing wavelength. If a numerical result changes with resolution, check the physical small-scale regulator and the prescribed initial perturbations. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Let the top fluid have three times the bottom density, downward g = 1 m/s², and wavelength λ = 2π m. What are the growth rate and e-folding time? What if the fluids are exchanged? Show the answer and reasoning A = (3−1)/(3+1) = 1/2 and k = 1 m⁻¹. Thus σ = 1/√2 s⁻¹ and the e-folding time is √2 s. Swapping the fluids makes A = −1/2, giving positive ω² = gk/2: oscillation instead of exponential growth in this idealization. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Two-body relaxation and gravitational encounters | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNIntegrate weak encounters over impact parameter to derive the Coulomb logarithm and relaxation scaling, distinct from crossing time. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Smooth gravity and discrete encounters A star orbits in a cluster’s mean field and is weakly deflected by individual neighbours. Relaxation measures accumulated velocity changes becoming comparable to the original velocity. It is distinct from direct physical collisions. Two-body refers to an encounter approximation, not a two-star model of the cluster. Assume equal masses, roughly isotropic velocities and many weak deflections. 02One deflection and its encounter rate For a nearly straight passage with relative speed v and sufficiently large impact parameter b, integrate the transverse gravitational acceleration over the encounter. Δv⊥≈2Gmbv, dΓ=2πb n v db n is stellar number density. Add squared, randomly directed kicks. The larger number of distant encounters compensates their smaller individual deflections, giving comparable contributions per logarithmic impact interval. d⟨Δv²⟩dt≈8πG²m²nv∫bminbmaxdbb=8πG²m²nvlnΛ Λ≡bmaxbmin, trel≈v³8πG²m²n lnΛ 03Coulomb logarithms and cluster scaling The analogous encounter integral gives the name Coulomb logarithm, although the force here is gravity. Estimate bmin near the large-angle scale Gm/v² and bmax near the system size; the integral has physical cutoffs. v²∼GNmR, tcross∼Rv, trel∼NlnΛtcross Combining the preceding impulse model with a uniform virial sphere gives a coefficient of 1/6. Distribution-averaged coefficients differ; do not mix this estimate with a precision convention. 04Compare half-mass relaxation times Adopt the following conventional equal-mass half-mass relaxation estimate. The coefficient 0.138 and choice ln(0.4N) are supplied conventions, not exact consequences of the uniform-sphere calculation. tdyn≡√(rh³GNm), trh≈0.138Nln(0.4N)tdyn The panel fixes m = 0.5 solar masses, so total mass grows with N. Dynamical time scales as N⁻¹ᐟ² and relaxation approximately as N¹ᐟ²/lnN. Always state which quantities are held fixed. 05Toward segregation and distribution evolution A mass spectrum introduces systematic energy exchange and a tendency for heavier objects to segregate inward. Complete equipartition need not follow. Binaries, strong encounters, tides and stellar evolution also affect long-term evolution. Collecting small mean changes and variances into continuous coefficients leads to the Fokker–Planck equation. This panel recomputes timescale estimates, not an N-body trajectory of a particular cluster. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Raise N from 10⁴ to 10⁵ at fixed stellar mass and half-mass radius. How do dynamical and half-mass relaxation times change? Show the answer and reasoning Dynamical time decreases by √10. Relaxation time changes by √10 ln(4000)/ln(40000) ≈ 2.48. The panel fixes mass per star; fixing total mass instead gives the ratio of N/ln(0.4N). REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. van den Bosch · Astrophysical flows: gravitational encounters and relaxation ↗ Cohn (1979) · Numerical integration of the Fokker–Planck equation ↗ Advanced progress: 0 / 35 ← PreviousSynchrotron radiation and electron coolingNext →Fokker–Planck equation

documents.title: Schwarzschild: clocks, the photon sphere, and the ISCO | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNRead clock rates from the metric, derive an effective potential from conserved quantities, and distinguish the horizon, photon sphere, and ISCO. Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Start from a spacetime ruler A metric specifies how spacetime intervals are measured. Take the Schwarzschild vacuum metric as the supplied solution, then derive consequences using conserved quantities and algebra. The full tensor calculation solving the field equations is outside this lesson. ds²=−A(r)c²dt²+A(r)−1dr²+r²(dθ²+sin²θ dφ²) A(r)=1−2rgr, rg≡GMc², R≡rrg Here r is the areal radius: spheres have area 4πr². It need not equal radial proper distance. Coordinate time t is normalized to a distant static clock. Our gravitational radius is rg = GM/c²; the Schwarzschild radius is twice this value. This is an exterior vacuum solution. A star needs a different interior solution. The exterior can also describe a nonrotating spherical star, but interpret the horizon sketch below as a black-hole exterior. 02Static clocks and light received far away For a clock at fixed spatial coordinates, ds² = −c²dτ². Substitute zero spatial increments into the metric to obtain its proper time τ relative to t. A local clock continues to run normally for an observer beside it. dτdt=√(1−2/R), 1+z=νemν∞=1√(1−2/R) The redshift formula assumes a static emitter and a static receiver at infinity. Moving emitters require additional kinematic effects. Remaining static outside the horizon requires support; a stationary clock cannot be placed on the horizon itself. The panel keeps R strictly greater than two. 03Reduce radial motion using conserved quantities Consider a massive test particle moving freely in the equatorial plane. Time-translation and rotational symmetries supply the following conserved quantities. Neglect the particle’s self-gravity and radiative backreaction. These orbit constants are separate from the mass parameter defining the spacetime. ℰ=A(r)dtdτ, ℓ=r²dφdτ, λ≡ℓcrg, j≡λ² Divide the metric by dτ², set ds²/dτ² = −c², and substitute the constants. Rearranging isolates the radial kinetic term. This is an exact test-particle relation in the supplied metric, rather than an expansion in weak gravity. −c²=−c²ℰ²A+1A(drdτ)²+ℓ²r² 1c²(drdτ)²+U(R)=ℰ² U(R)=(1−2R)(1+jR²)=1−2R+jR²−2jR³ Radial motion requires ℰ² ≥ U. The additional −2j/R³ term changes the inner barrier. U is dimensionless and is compared with squared energy ℰ², not with ℰ. A potential plot alone is not an integration of a chosen trajectory. 04Find circular orbits and test stability For a circular orbit, radial velocity and the potential slope vanish. Differentiate at fixed j and clear denominators. The resulting quadratic exposes both circular branches and the parameter at which they merge. dUdR=2R²−2jR³+6jR⁴=0 R²−jR+3j=0, R±=j ± √(j²−12j)2 j=R²R−3 (R>3) A minimum gives radial stability; a maximum gives instability. Evaluate the second derivative while keeping angular momentum fixed, and then insert the circular-orbit relation. Do not differentiate along a family that changes j. d²UdR²circular=2(R−6)R³(R−3) R>6: stable, 3<R<6: unstable RISCO=6, jISCO=12, ℰISCO=√89 At R = 6 the radial restoring term vanishes: this is the marginal endpoint of the stable circular branch. ISCO does not forbid matter at smaller radii. Infall and accelerated fluid motion are different from stable circular test-particle geodesics. 05The photon sphere and horizon are different radii For light, use ds² = 0. The rest-mass term disappears and the normalized radial potential is W below. Differentiate it to locate the circular null orbit. Its maximum makes that orbit unstable. W(R)=1−2/RR², dWdR=−2R³+6R⁴=0 ⇒ Rph=3 The horizon is at R = 2, the photon sphere at R = 3, and the ISCO at R = 6. They are not three material surfaces. Also distinguish the photon orbit’s areal radius from the impact parameter for capture measured at infinity. Sketch of areal-radius ratios; neither a proper-distance diagram nor an image of the distant shadow. bcrit=rph√A(rph)=3√3 rg Schwarzschild-coordinate coefficients become singular at the horizon, whereas suitable coordinates describe infall across it. This differs from the curvature singularity at r = 0. The panel remains outside and does not draw horizon-crossing trajectories. 06Run clocks and compare circular branches Clock playback advances distant time and computes the proper time of a supported clock at fixed radius. Changing angular momentum compares potential curves; it does not animate a test-particle orbit. The two operations answer different questions. Try j = 16 to compare an unstable circular orbit at R = 4 with a stable one at R = 12. At j = 12 they merge at R = 6; below that value no massive circular geodesic exists. Use the displayed branch labels to connect the graph to the algebra. The solution library compares this exact vacuum solution with fluid equilibria and similarity models. Kerr and Tomimatsu–Sato entries are listed with their lesson availability explicitly distinguished. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Double the mass. How do physical horizon, photon-sphere, and ISCO radii change, and what happens to a static clock rate at fixed r/(GM/c²)? Show the answer and reasoning All three physical radii double because they scale with GM/c². At fixed dimensionless R, the clock factor √(1−2/R) is unchanged; the time unit GM/c³ doubles. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Sedov–Taylor blast waves | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the expansion law, reduce conservation laws to similarity ODEs, and use shock conditions and total energy to determine profiles and normalization. Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01When does a blast wave become simple? Deposit energy E in a small region of a uniform gas of density ρ₀. A spherical blast expands into initially stationary material with negligible upstream pressure compared with the shock pressure. Use an ideal gas with constant heat-capacity ratio γ, neglecting gravity, magnetic forces, and radiative cooling. For a supernova remnant this model mainly applies after the swept-up mass dominates the ejecta and before radiative losses become important. It does not describe the instant of explosion or the later radiative shell stage. 02Obtain the two-fifths exponent from units Write the shock radius as R = C Eᵃρ₀ᵇtᶜ. Since [E] = ML²T⁻² and [ρ₀] = ML⁻³, matching mass, length, and time gives three linear equations for the exponents. a+b = 0, 2a−3b = 1, −2a+c = 0 a = 15, b = −15, c = 25 R = β(Et²ρ₀)1/5, D ≡ dRdt = 2R5t Call the dimensionless coefficient β. The energy estimate E ∼ ρ₀R³D² gives the same exponents, but dimensional analysis cannot determine β. We must solve the interior and normalize its total energy. 03Derive the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions In the shock frame, label upstream and downstream states 1 and 2. Let positive w₁ and w₂ be their speeds through the front. Across a thin, steady front, mass, momentum, and energy fluxes per unit area must match. ρ₁w₁ = ρ₂w₂ p₁+ρ₁w₁² = p₂+ρ₂w₂² w₁²2 + γp₁(γ−1)ρ₁ = w₂²2 + γp₂(γ−1)ρ₂ The last equation is energy flux divided by the common mass flux. Pressure work adds to internal energy to give the specific enthalpy γp/[(γ−1)ρ]. Set χ = ρ₂/ρ₁, so w₂ = w₁/χ. Momentum conservation gives p₂ = p₁ + ρ₁w₁²(1−1/χ). Substitute both into the energy equation and remove the unchanged-flow root χ = 1 to obtain the compressive solution. χ = (γ+1)ℳ₁²(γ−1)ℳ₁²+2, ℳ₁² ≡ ρ₁w₁²γp₁ For a strong shock, ℳ₁ ≫ 1, χ tends to (γ+1)/(γ−1). With stationary upstream gas, w₁ = D and the downstream laboratory speed is u₂ = D − w₂. A monatomic gas with γ = 5/3 gives χ = 4, u₂ = 3D/4, and p₂ = 3ρ₀D²/4. The factor four is the strong-shock limit for an adiabatic monatomic gas converting bulk kinetic energy to heat. Entropy increases across the front; the smooth-flow entropy equation below must not be applied through the discontinuity. 04Combine time and radius into one variable Let u be outward fluid velocity, p pressure, and ρ density. In the smooth interior, spherical mass conservation, momentum balance, and adiabatic evolution hold. A partial derivative ∂ varies one coordinate while holding the other fixed. ∂ρ∂t + 1r²∂∂r(r²ρu) = 0 ∂u∂t + u∂u∂r = −1ρ∂p∂r (∂∂t+u∂∂r) (pργ) = 0 Set x = r/R and scale density by ρ₀, velocity by D, and pressure by ρ₀D². Seek profiles G, V, and Z depending only on x. ρ = ρ₀G(x), u = DV(x), p = ρ₀D²Z(x) ∂x∂r = 1R, ∂x∂t = −DRx For example, ∂ρ/∂t = −ρ₀(D/R)xG′, while the mass-flux derivative is ρ₀(D/R)(G′V + GV′ + 2GV/x). Cancelling the common factor gives the first equation below. 05Similarity ODEs and shock boundaries R ∝ t2/5 implies R(dD/dt)/D² = −3/2. Apply the same chain rule to momentum and adiabatic evolution to reduce the PDEs to three ODEs. Primes now denote x derivatives. (V−x)G′ + G(V′+2V/x) = 0 (V−x)V′ − 32V = −Z′G (V−x)(Z′Z−γG′G) = 3 The shock is at x = 1. Nondimensionalizing the jump conditions supplies the starting values. G(1) = γ+1γ−1, V(1) = 2γ+1, Z(1) = 2γ+1 For γ = 5/3 integrate inward from (4, 3/4, 3/4). The physical branch approaches V → 0, G → 0, and finite Z at the centre. Low density can coexist with finite pressure, unlike a uniformly filled expanding sphere. 06Normalize the total energy to determine β Total energy is kinetic plus internal energy. Their densities are ρu²/2 and p/(γ−1); integrate using the volume element 4πr²dr. I ≡ ∫01 [GV²2+Zγ−1]x²dx E = 4πρ₀R³D²I = 16π25ρ₀R⁵t²I β = (2516πI)1/5 ≈ 1.15167 (γ = 5/3) The panel integrates at fixed γ = 5/3 from x = 1 to 0.05 using Runge–Kutta, evolving logarithms of G and Z to preserve positivity. It approximates the small central thermal-energy contribution with constant Z(0.05); profiles below x = 0.05 are not plotted. The displayed β is a numerical estimate. 07Use conservation laws to challenge the solution The enclosed mass should equal the initially swept volume times density, 4πρ₀R³/3. Thus 3∫Gx²dx = 1 is an independent check. Refine the step and verify convergence of the mass ratio and β. Radius and shock speed imply t = 2R/(5D). With density as well, infer E = ρ₀R⁵/(β⁵t²). Observed gas velocity is not generally the shock-front speed D. Cosmic-ray pressure, particle escape, or a nonuniform medium can change these ideal-gas coefficients and compression ratios. The next chapter begins with acceleration in the limit where energetic particles do not modify the flow. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At the same ambient density and elapsed time, how do radius and speed change if the energy increases by 32? Given a measured shock radius R and shock speed D, what is the model age? Show the answer and reasoning Both R and D scale as E1/5, so both double. Since D = 2R/(5t), the model age is t = 2R/(5D). Using R/D ignores deceleration and overestimates the age by a factor of 5/2. This applies only to an energy-conserving, spherical strong shock in a uniform medium. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Shocks and particle acceleration | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNState the assumptions of diffusive shock acceleration, obtain the relativistic-particle energy slope from compression, and distinguish acceleration time from maximum energy. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A shock can do more than heat gas Shock jump conditions constrain the bulk gas, but particles that repeatedly cross the front can form a high-energy population far from thermal equilibrium. Consider a steady, planar, nonrelativistic shock and particles with speed v ≈ c. In the shock frame let w₁ > w₂ > 0, with compression χ = w₁/w₂. Scattering by magnetic irregularities approximately isotropizes particles in each local fluid frame. Use the test-particle limit, in which accelerated particles do not modify the flow. A static magnetic field does no work on a charge. Energy comes from the bulk flow as particles scatter between moving frames. Significant motion of scattering centres relative to the gas modifies the simple spectral result below. 02Gain and escape in one cycle For a small relative flow speed, changing between fluid frames changes relativistic particle energy by approximately (w₁−w₂)μ/v to first order. Crossing particles are flux-weighted by the direction cosine μ, giving mean μ = (∫₀¹μ²dμ)/(∫₀¹μdμ) = 2/3. Two crossings make a complete cycle. g ≡ ⟨ΔEE⟩cycle ≈ 4(w₁−w₂)3v For downstream particle number density np, the isotropic crossing flux is npv/4. The advective loss flux far downstream is npw₂. Their ratio gives the escape probability per cycle. Pesc ≈ 4w₂v Both are first order in flow speed divided by particle speed. This is the origin of the name first-order Fermi acceleration. This idealization neglects escape through the upstream boundary. 03Eliminate the cycle count to get a power law Start N₀ particles at E₀. After k surviving cycles, Ek = E₀(1+g)k and Nk = N₀(1−Pesc)k. Take logarithms and eliminate k. N(>E)N₀ = (EE₀)ln(1−Pesc)/ln(1+g) N(>E) ∝ E−Pesc/g The second line uses ln(1+g) ≈ g and ln(1−Pesc) ≈ −Pesc for small gains and losses. N(>E) is cumulative. The differential number distribution per energy interval is its negative derivative, adding one to the index. dNdE ∝ E−s, s = 1+Pescg s = 1+3w₂w₁−w₂ = χ+2χ−1 A strong monatomic gas shock has χ = 4, giving s = 2 for relativistic particles per energy interval. A momentum-space distribution function uses dN = 4πp²f(p)dp, so the same solution is written f(p) ∝ p−4. 04A spectral slope does not set the maximum energy Describe scattering by spatial diffusion coefficients κ₁ and κ₂. A residence layer has thickness of order κ/w. Dividing its particle content by crossing flux nv/4 gives tcycle ≈ (4/v)(κ₁/w₁ + κ₂/w₂). Dividing by the gain g gives the local logarithmic acceleration time. tacc(E) ≡ EdE/dt ≈ 3w₁−w₂(κ₁w₁+κ₂w₂) For χ = 4 and κ₁ = κ₂ = κ, tacc = 20κ/w₁². If κ depends on energy, the time from E₀ to E is ∫tacc(E′)dE′/E′, not generally a single value of this local timescale. rL = p|q|B ≲ L ⇒ E ≈ pc ≲ |q|BLc SI units; L is the size of the acceleration region. Confinement, source age, downstream advection, upstream escape, and radiative cooling all matter. The slope derivation does not determine injection efficiency or magnetic turbulence. Propagation also means the cosmic-ray slope measured at Earth need not equal the source slope. After a shock leaves electrons and ions at different temperatures, follow their equilibration in two-temperature plasmas. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For compression χ = 3, what is the index s in dN/dE ∝ E−s? Does confinement alone determine the maximum energy? Show the answer and reasoning s = (χ+2)/(χ−1) = 5/2. Confinement is necessary, but acceleration must also fit within the source age and beat cooling or escape. E−2 is conditional on a strong nonrelativistic shock, a test-particle treatment, relativistic particles, and the stated scattering assumptions. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Strömgren spheres and ionization fronts | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the equilibrium radius from photon and recombination balance, solve volume growth, and explain the neglect of gas motion. Connect to foundations: Atomic light and starlight: why 10.2 eV? ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Count ionizing photons, not just luminosity Hot stars create regions of ionized hydrogen, called H II regions. Ionizing hydrogen requires a photon of at least 13.6 eV, unlike the 10.2 eV Lyα transition. The relevant input is the rate of photons above this threshold, rather than total stellar luminosity alone. S ≡ ∫ν₀∞Lνhνdν, hν₀ = 13.6 eV S has units s−1: divide spectral luminosity by photon energy before integrating. Assume pure hydrogen of uniform nucleus density nH, a constant source S, no dust, and a nearly fully ionized interior. 02Count the recombinations that remove ions Recombination occurs at rate αnenp. Direct recombination to the ground state emits another ionizing photon. In the on-the-spot approximation, that photon is absorbed nearby, so this event does not require a new stellar photon in the net ionization budget. αB(10⁴ K) ≈ 2.6 × 10−13 cm³ s−1 dNrecdt dV = αBnenp ≈ αBnH² The Case B coefficient αB counts recombinations to excited states and is supplied at the assumed temperature. The same photon budget does not apply unchanged to a cloud that leaks ionizing photons or absorbs many of them in dust. 03Balance supply and consumption to find the radius Let the ionized volume be V = 4πR³/3. In equilibrium, the supplied photon rate equals the integrated net recombination rate. At constant density, solving this volume balance gives the radius directly. S = 4π3RS³αBnH² RS = [3S4παBnH²]1/3 For S = 1049 s−1, nH = 100 cm−3, and the stated coefficient, RS is about 3.15 pc. Doubling density quadruples recombinations per unit volume and reduces the radius by 2−2/3. 04Excess photons ionize newly reached gas Start with neutral gas. During growth, some photons replace recombinations in the existing ionized volume, while the remainder ionizes nHdV/dt newly reached atoms. The gas stays fixed; only the ionization boundary advances. nHdVdt = S−αBnH²V dVdt+Vtrec = SnH, trec = 1αBnH Set V = VS + W. Then W′ = −W/trec, so W decays exponentially. Apply V(0) = 0 and take the cube root only after obtaining the volume. V(t) = VS[1−e−t/trec] R(t) = RS[1−e−t/trec]1/3 05An ionization radius versus an expanding H II region In the example, trec is about 1.22 × 10³ yr. At one recombination time, volume is about 63% and radius about 86% of equilibrium. Radius does not advance linearly with time. The circle marks an ionization boundary, not the velocity of all the gas. Extrapolating this instantaneous, nonrelativistic photon budget to t → 0 formally produces infinite front speed. Do not apply it before light-travel times of order R/c or to relativistic fronts. Later, heated gas can expand under pressure and drive shocks; that phase requires gas dynamics. In a clumpy medium, recombinations depend on the average of nenp, not simply the square of mean density. A measured radius alone does not uniquely determine stellar age or photon output without checking leakage, dust, density structure, and dynamical stage. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Multiply the ionizing-photon rate by eight and hydrogen-nucleus density by two. How do equilibrium radius and recombination time change? Show the answer and reasoning RS ∝ (S/nH²)1/3 increases by 21/3, about 1.26. The recombination time 1/(αB nH) halves. This holds at fixed temperature and αB, for fully ionized pure hydrogen with ne = np = nH. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Inverse Compton scattering and the SZ effect | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCompute Compton y from scattering probability and electron temperature, derive the thermal SZ frequency dependence, and explain what the signal measures about cluster electron pressure. Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Use background light to measure a galaxy cluster The cosmic microwave background (CMB) has a nearly blackbody spectrum at 2.7255 K. Hot, diffuse gas fills the space between galaxies in a cluster. Its free electrons scatter passing CMB photons, which on average gain energy through inverse Compton scattering. The resulting small spectral distortion in the cluster direction is the thermal Sunyaev–Zel’dovich (SZ) effect. Thermal SZ is driven by random electron motion. Kinetic SZ, due to the cluster’s bulk line-of-sight motion, is introduced separately in the final extension. This chapter focuses on the connection between cluster gas and observables, taking the scattering collision operator as a physical input. 02Gain per scattering and scattering probability Let ε be photon energy and Te electron temperature. Use nonrelativistic electrons and the Thomson limit: photon energy in the electron rest frame is much smaller than mec². For isotropic photons and electrons, averaging to second order in electron speed gives fractional energy gain (4/3)⟨v²/c²⟩. ⟨v²⟩ = 3kBTeme ⟨Δεε⟩ ≈ 43⟨v²⟩c² = 4θe, θe ≡ kBTemec² The factor 4/3 comes from averaging scattering geometry and Doppler shifts. The recoil term −ε/(mec²) is negligible for CMB photons scattering on hot cluster electrons. The result 4θe is a mean gain per scattering, not the complete SZ spectral shape. For a uniform electron density ne and line-of-sight depth L, the scattering optical depth is τ = neσTL. The probability of at least one scattering is 1 − e−τ, approximately τ when τ ≪ 1. τ = neσTL, y ≡ τθe Mean photon energy gainInitial energy ≈ 4y The final line estimates the ensemble mean energy gain to first order, not the brightness change at every frequency. 03y adds electron pressure along the line of sight If density and temperature vary along the path, add contributions dy = θe neσT dl. Introducing ideal-gas electron pressure Pe = nekBTe makes the observable explicit. y = ∫ kBTemec²neσTdl = σTmec²∫ Pedl σT is an area and Pe dl has units of energy per area, so y is dimensionless. Pe is electron pressure, distinct from total gas pressure including ions. At constant temperature y/τ gives θe, but a thermal SZ signal alone does not separately determine τ and Te. kBTe = 8 keV, ne = 10−3 cm−3, L = 1 Mpc τ ≈ 2.05×10−3, θe ≈ 8511, y ≈ 3.21×10−5 A temperature quoted in keV denotes the thermal energy kBTe. Eight keV corresponds to about 9.3×10⁷ K. Use 1 cm⁻³ = 10⁶ m⁻³ and 1 Mpc ≈ 3.086×10²² m. 04Calculate a distortion of the Planck spectrum Write CMB temperature as T₀ and frequency as ν, and define x = hν/(kBT₀). Express the Planck spectrum using photon occupation N₀ and intensity scale I₀. N₀ is distinct from electron number density ne. N₀(x) = 1ex−1, Bν = I₀x³N₀(x) I₀ = 2(kBT₀)³h²c² For hot nonrelativistic electrons, τ ≪ 1, and y ≪ 1, take the following first-order consequence of the Kompaneets scattering equation as input. It represents repeated small energy changes as diffusion in frequency space. ΔN ≈ yx²ddx(x⁴dN₀dx) Insert dN₀/dx = −eˣ/(eˣ−1)². Apply the product rule to x⁴ and the exponential term, then use ΔIν = I₀x³ΔN. Collecting terms exposes the bracket that controls the sign. ΔIν = I₀y x⁴ex(ex−1)² f(x) f(x) ≡ xex+1ex−1−4 This is a leading nonrelativistic result, not a full relativistic scattering solution. The panel displays the small difference ΔIν. A small-y expansion should not be used to manufacture an exaggerated, highly distorted full CMB spectrum. 05The low-frequency deficit and the approximately 217 GHz null For x ≪ 1, eˣ ≈ 1+x and x(eˣ+1)/(eˣ−1) tends to two. Thus f(x) tends to −2: a low-frequency deficit. Photons have gained energy and been redistributed toward higher frequencies. Brightness differences are often expressed as the temperature change that would produce them in a blackbody. Linearize ΔIν = (∂Bν/∂T)ΔT and differentiate the Planck function: ∂Bν∂T = I₀T₀x⁴ex(ex−1)² ΔTthT₀ = yf(x) → −2y (x ≪ 1) This is a frequency-dependent conversion to CMB thermodynamic temperature, not a claim that the distorted spectrum is a blackbody at a different single temperature. Solving f(x) = 0 gives x ≈ 3.830, or ν ≈ 217.5 GHz at T₀ = 2.7255 K. The thermal signal changes sign across this null. The panel uses the leading nonrelativistic formula, so changing electron temperature does not move its thermal null. Relativistic corrections change the spectral shape and null in reality. Precision analysis of hot clusters requires more than this approximation. 06What does this tell us about a cluster? Measuring y across the sky gives a map of line-of-sight electron pressure. Combine it with other temperature and density measurements to study hot intracluster gas. A pressure-column measurement is not by itself a direct measurement of total cluster mass. The first-order thermal spectrum cannot distinguish hotter, lower-density gas from cooler, denser gas with the same y. Multiple frequencies help isolate its sign-changing spectrum, while dust emission, radio sources, and primary CMB fluctuations must also be considered. 07Extension: distinguish kinetic SZ Bulk motion of cluster gas relative to the CMB creates a Doppler signal distinct from random thermal motion. Take v_∥ positive away from the observer, with small optical depth and |v_∥| ≪ c. ΔTkinT₀ ≈ −τv∥c Receding gas gives a negative signal and approaching gas a positive one. At this order the thermodynamic-temperature shift is independent of frequency and has no thermal-style sign reversal near 217 GHz. The intensity difference still depends on frequency through ∂Bν/∂T. Selecting a velocity in the panel adds kinetic SZ to the thermal intensity difference. For example, τ ≈ 0.00205 and v_∥ = 300 km/s give ΔTkin ≈ −5.60 μK. Kinetic SZ and other emission can remain at the thermal null, so 217 GHz does not isolate the unmodified background. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. In a uniform slab, double the electron temperature, halve its density, and keep its depth fixed. How do τ and y change? Can the first-order nonrelativistic thermal SZ spectra distinguish these cases? What about kinetic SZ? Show the answer and reasoning τ = neσTL halves, while y = τkBTe/(mec²) stays fixed. The first-order thermal spectra used here are identical, so temperature and density cannot be separated. At fixed line-of-sight speed, kinetic SZ halves because it is proportional to τ. Relativistic corrections can carry extra temperature information; this degeneracy belongs to the stated approximation. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Synchrotron radiation and electron cooling | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNRelate magnetic field and electron energy to frequency, derive the spectrum from a power-law electron population, and explain how cooling alters the high-energy emission. Connect to foundations: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A magnetic field bends the electron trajectory Besides thermal blackbody emission, nearly light-speed electrons radiate when bent by magnetic fields. This synchrotron emission can appear from radio to X-rays. Use SI units, with electron charge magnitude e and mass me. γ = 1√(1−v²/c²), E = γmec² rL = γmev⊥eB Here γ is the Lorentz factor, not the gas heat-capacity ratio used in the blast-wave chapter. For γ ≫ 1, total and kinetic energies are nearly equal. The pitch angle ψ is between velocity and magnetic field, with v_⊥ = v sinψ. A static magnetic field changes direction but does no work because its force is perpendicular to velocity. Radiation drains electron kinetic energy; sustaining high energies requires acceleration or replenishment. 02Why does the frequency scale as γ²? Define the nonrelativistic gyrofrequency νB = eB/(2πme). A relativistic electron gyrates more slowly, but its radiation is beamed into an angle of order 1/γ. The observer sees only the short interval when the beam points toward them, further shortened by arrival-time compression. For trajectory curvature radius ρcurv, the emission interval is of order ρcurv/(γc), and arrival-time compression adds another factor of order γ². The characteristic angular frequency is therefore of order γ³c/ρcurv. Using ρcurv ≈ γmec/(eB sinψ) gives γ²B sinψ. Radiation theory supplies the exact critical-frequency normalization below. νc = 3eB4πmeγ² sinψ νc ≈ 4.20 Hz × (B1 μG)γ² sinψ 1 μG = 10⁻¹⁰ T. νc is neither a monochromatic line nor the exact maximum of the single-electron Pν spectrum, which is broad and peaks near 0.29νc. The panel shows the νc scale rather than computing the complete single-electron spectrum. 03The Thomson cross section returns Expressing relativistic radiative power through the Thomson cross section σT connects to the foundation lesson. Use magnetic energy density UB. For one pitch angle, P = 2σTcUBγ²(v/c)²sin²ψ; isotropic directions give ⟨sin²ψ⟩ = 2/3. UB = B²2μ₀, ⟨P⟩ = 43σTcUBγ² (γ ≫ 1) This notation does not mean the electron is Thomson-scattering photons here. The same classical charge–mass combination is expressed using σT; the relativistic radiation formula is a physical input. μ₀ is the vacuum permeability. tsyn ≡ E⟨P⟩ = 3mec4σTUBγ ∝ 1B²γ At fixed B, higher-energy electrons cool faster. At a fixed observing frequency, γ ∝ (ν/B)1/2, so the cooling time scales as B−3/2ν−1/2. 04Convert the electron slope to the light spectrum Let the electron number distribution be N(E)dE = C E−sdE. Assume optically thin emission at fixed magnetic field, away from cooling breaks and energy cutoffs. For the derivation, concentrate each electron’s power near a representative frequency ν ∝ BE². jνdν ∝ N(E)P(E)dE jν ∝ E−s × B²E² × 1BE jν ∝ B(s+1)/2ν−(s−1)/2 The Jacobian dν/dE ∝ BE is essential. Define the emissivity slope by jν ∝ ν−α; then α = (s−1)/2. The preceding chapter’s s = 2 gives α = 1/2. Integrating the full single-electron radiation kernel gives the same slope over a sufficiently broad power-law range. Some references define α with the opposite sign. The photon-number index Γ is also different: dNph/dε ∝ ε−Γ gives Γ = α + 1. Distinguish electron index s, emissivity index α, and photon-number index Γ. 05Solve the cooling equation At fixed magnetic field with ultrarelativistic, isotropically distributed electrons, dγ/dt = −aγ². Here a is a positive cooling coefficient used only in this chapter. Separate variables and integrate from the initial value γ₀. a = 4σTUB3mec 1γ(t) − 1γ₀ = at γ(t) = γ₀1+aγ₀t For steady injection Q(E) ∝ E−s, the cooled high-energy steady distribution follows from number conservation in energy space. Neglect escape and let dot E = −bE²: ddE[ĖN(E)] = Q(E), Ė ≡ dEdt = −bE² N(E) = 1bE²∫E∞Q(E′)dE′ ∝ E−(s+1) (s > 1) The electron index steepens by one, so α steepens by one-half. This cooling break assumes constant field, continuous injection, and radiative-loss dominance. An impulsive population or significant escape need not have the same spectrum. 06Return to observations with the assumptions intact Shock acceleration followed by radiation in a magnetic field produces a continuum that gas temperature alone cannot describe. Higher frequencies probe more energetic electrons, which also cool faster. Self-absorption can alter low frequencies, while maximum electron energy and cooling affect high frequencies. Inverse-Compton and adiabatic losses also matter, so a cooling time is not a unique age measurement. The classical formulas here exclude regimes where quantum effects become important. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed magnetic field, double the electron Lorentz factor. How do characteristic frequency, power, and cooling time change? For an uncooled electron index s = 2, what is the optically thin spectral index α? Show the answer and reasoning In the ultrarelativistic limit, νc ∝ γ², P ∝ γ², and tsyn ∝ γ−1: frequency and power quadruple, while cooling time halves. α = (s−1)/2 = 1/2, giving jν ∝ ν−1/2, away from self-absorption, cooling breaks, and cutoffs. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Tensor virial theorem and Maclaurin/Jacobi sequences | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive tensor virial balance, solve Maclaurin and Jacobi equilibria, and distinguish bifurcation from stability. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Track the second derivative of size along each direction Different directions can require different support even at the same total energy. Differentiate the inertia tensor twice and use continuity and Euler’s equation. For an unmagnetized fluid with zero surface pressure: Iᵢⱼ = ∫ρxᵢxⱼdV, Tᵢⱼ = 12∫ρvᵢvⱼdV 12Ïᵢⱼ = 2Tᵢⱼ+Wᵢⱼ+Πδᵢⱼ Wᵢⱼ = −∫ρxᵢ∂Φ∂xⱼdV, Π=∫PdV Taking the trace recovers the scalar virial theorem. Random orbital stresses enter a stellar system; here Π represents fluid pressure. Do not double count these supports. 02Insert the homogeneous ellipsoid Iᵢᵢ = Maᵢ²5, Wᵢᵢ = −2πGρAᵢIᵢᵢ Φeff = Φ−Ω²2(x²+y²) A uniformly rotating incompressible fluid obeys P/ρ + Φeff = constant in its rotating frame. Zero pressure at the surface requires equal effective potentials at the three axis endpoints. (A₁−ω²/2)a²=(A₂−ω²/2)b²=A₃c², ω² ≡ Ω²πGρ A Jacobi figure rotates in the inertial frame: Ï₁₁ = 2Ω²(I₂₂−I₁₁), rather than zero. Including this term recovers the same surface condition. A fixed shape in a rotating frame need not have fixed inertial tensor components. 03Maclaurin: an axisymmetric sequence For a = b, q = c/a and e = √(1−q²), the two equatorial conditions coincide. Use the previous chapter’s coefficients to obtain angular speed. ω²=2(A₁−q²A₃) = 2√(1−e²)e³[(3−2e²)sin−1e−3e√(1−e²)] At small e, ω² ≈ (8/15)e², so the spherical limit has zero rotation. Angular speed does not grow monotonically forever with flattening; it need not uniquely identify a figure. 04Jacobi: solve a triaxial sequence Set a = 1 and use p = b/a and q = c/a. Eliminate ω² between the equatorial conditions. The panel integrates Aᵢ and bisects for q at each specified p. A₂−A₁p−2−1=A₃q², ω²=2(A₁−A₃q²) As a reference check, Fitzpatrick Table 2.2 gives e₁₃ ≈ 0.85585 and Ω/√(2πGρ) ≈ 0.42827 at e₁₂ = 0.6, or b/a = 0.8. The panel uses Ω²/(πGρ); divide by two and take its square root before comparing to that table. The two controls select independent equilibria, not an equal-angular-momentum pair. These are calculated equilibrium sequences, not a time-dependent transformation from one fluid shape to another. 05Bifurcation and two kinds of instability The Jacobi branch bifurcates near e = 0.81267 and T/|W| = 0.1375. Weak-viscosity secular instability differs from the ideal-fluid dynamical bar instability near e = 0.95289 and T/|W| = 0.2738. These thresholds are supplied perturbation results. T=MΩ²(a²+b²)10, W=−2πGρM5ΣAᵢaᵢ² Solving equilibrium does not prove stability. Compressibility, differential rotation, fields, relativity and collisionless dynamics change the problem. No stability claim is made for the entire Jacobi branch; these plots recompute equilibrium equations, not all paper curves or perturbation eigenvalues. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At e = 0.85 on the homogeneous Maclaurin sequence, distinguish weak-viscosity instability from dynamical instability. Show the answer and reasoning It lies above the secular threshold 0.81267 but below the dynamical bar-mode threshold 0.95289. These are perturbation results for a homogeneous incompressible fluid, not universal rotating-star thresholds. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
