documents.title: Three-body chemistry and molecular hydrogen formation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConserve hydrogen nuclei, solve the molecular fraction, and compare density-dependent chemical and gravitational clocks. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01The third atom carries away energy H + H + H → H₂ + H To form a bound molecule, two hydrogen atoms must transfer excess energy and momentum elsewhere. A third atom provides a collision partner that can carry them away. That partner remains an H atom after the event. This is a three-body chemical reaction, distinct from gravitational encounters involving three stars. This offers an entry to molecular formation in dense primordial gas with little dust. Supply a reaction coefficient and focus on how rapidly composition changes. The microscopic potential and quantum-scattering calculation belong in the reference, rather than becoming a separate subject in this guide. 02Count events separately from consumed atoms Define the event rate per volume and time by R₃ = k₃nH³. The adopted coefficient includes the counting convention; do not append an extra 1/3! factor. Each event makes one molecule and consumes two free atoms net. The third atom is present on both sides of the reaction. dnH₂dt=k₃nH³, dnHdt=−2k₃nH³ nN≡nH+2nH₂ = constant nN is the hydrogen-nucleus density, counting two nuclei inside each molecule. It remains constant in a closed, fixed-volume pure-hydrogen parcel. The sum of atom and molecule counts is not conserved: forming a molecule changes the number of independently moving particles. 03Solve for the fraction of nuclei in molecules x≡2nH₂nN, nH=nN(1−x) dxdt=2k₃nN²(1−x)³ Start with entirely atomic gas, x(0) = 0. Hold temperature and nucleus density fixed so k₃ is constant, then separate variables. Conversion slows as free atoms are depleted. A single initial rate therefore cannot be multiplied by an arbitrarily long time to obtain the final molecular fraction. ∫₀ˣdx′(1−x′)³=2k₃nN²t (1−x)−2−12=2k₃nN²t x=1−(1+4k₃nN²t)−1/2 x(t₅₀)=12 ⇒ t₅₀=34k₃nN² At x = 1/2, half the nuclei reside in molecules, but the molecular number density is nN/4, not nN/2. Keep the nuclei fraction and molecular particle count distinct when interpreting both the equations and the panel. 04Density changes the competition with gravity Use equation (6) of Forrey (2013) as the rate input. TK denotes the numerical temperature in kelvins; k₃ is in cm⁶ s⁻¹. The panel restricts temperature to 600–3000 K. This fit describes the specified reaction and does not replace an entire chemical network. TK≡T1 K, k₃=(6×10−32TK−1/4+2×10−31TK−1/2) cm⁶ s⁻¹ tff=√3π32GmₚnN t₅₀tff∝nN−3/2 (fixed T) Events scale as density cubed, while the rate per atom scales as density squared. This grows faster than the inverse free-fall time, which scales as nN¹ᐟ². High density can therefore make chemistry fast relative to gravity. The displayed tff is a uniform-sphere comparison clock; the chemical parcel itself is not collapsing. 05Molecular formation also affects thermal evolution Using about 4.48 eV for ground-state H₂ binding gives a binding-energy change of 4.48x/2 eV per initial nucleus. Its partition into heat, internal excitation, and later radiation requires additional physics. Since temperature is prescribed here, the panel reports only this energy scale and does not infer a temperature increase. A realistic primordial collapse couples reverse collisional dissociation, H₂ as a third partner, low-density H⁻ pathways, cooling, and compression. Reactions omitted here become especially consequential at high temperature and late conversion. The one-way model cannot determine chemical equilibrium or a self-consistent primordial-star trajectory. Relative to isothermal collapse, this is a small step that relaxes the assumption of fixed composition. A more complete model adds energy and fluid equations to the same nucleus bookkeeping. Identifying the conserved count and the competing clocks is a useful first step before solving that coupled system. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed temperature, increase hydrogen-nucleus density tenfold. How does the ratio of half-conversion time to free-fall time change? Show the answer and reasoning Since t₅₀ ∝ n⁻² and tff ∝ n⁻¹ᐟ², the ratio falls by 10⁻³ᐟ² ≈ 0.0316. Chemistry gains on the gravitational clock at high density; the chemical model itself holds temperature and density fixed. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Tomimatsu–Sato: Ernst potentials and the quadrupole | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive a quadrupole difference at fixed M and J, separating an exact vacuum solution from a regular black hole. Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01An exact solution need not be a regular black hole Stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum solutions need not be Kerr. In the Tomimatsu–Sato family, labelled by an integer δ, δ = 1 is Kerr. Focus on δ = 2 and read physical differences from its supplied Ernst potential. The assumptions differ from black-hole uniqueness theorems requiring a regular horizon. G = c = 1, p²+q² = 1, p > 0, |q| < 1 ρ = κ√[(x²−1)(1−y²)], z = κxy M = 2κ/p, J = M²q Here x > 1 and −1 ≤ y ≤ 1 are prolate spheroidal coordinates; ρ is a cylindrical coordinate, not a material density. M denotes the geometrized mass GM/c². The δ = 2 normalization differs from Kerr’s M = κ/p, so equal x values do not mean equal physical radii. 02Specify the solution with a complex potential Write the stationary axisymmetric vacuum field using the Ernst potential ℰ = f + iψ, where f = −gₜₜ and ψ is the twist potential. Supply the following polynomial solution. Complex arithmetic uses i² = −1; modulus and complex conjugation are not ordinary real squaring. ℰ = (A−B)/(A+B) A = p²(x⁴−1)+q²(y⁴−1)−2ipqxy(x²−y²) B = 2px(x²−1)+2iqy(y²−1) The vacuum equations reduce to the complex PDE below, taken as the supplied field equation. The right side uses complex squares of derivatives, not squared moduli. Numerical checks compare finite-difference residuals away from singularities and f computed from an independent metric representation. Re(ℰ){∂x[(x²−1)∂xℰ]+∂y[(1−y²)∂yℰ]} = (x²−1)(∂xℰ)²+(1−y²)(∂yℰ)² 03Read the quadrupole from axis data On the upper axis y = 1, z = κx. Form ξ = (1−ℰ)/(1+ℰ) = B/A and cancel the common factor. In its asymptotic 1/z expansion, the first three coefficients give M, iJ, and the mass quadrupole Q in this convention. Higher coefficients cannot all be identified directly with relativistic multipoles. ξaxis = 2px/[p²(x²+1)−2ipqx] = 2/(px)+4iq/(p²x²)−[2/p+8q²/p³]/x³+O(x−4) = M/z+iJ/z²+Q/z³+O(z−4) QTS2/M³ = −(1+3q²)/4 QKerr/M³ = −q² (QTS2−QKerr)/M³ = −(1−q²)/4 At fixed M and J, hence fixed q, the quadrupoles differ. Nonrotating TS2 retains Q = −M³/4 and is not spherical. The sign follows Manko’s equation (10). Do not translate this relativistic quadrupole directly into the axis ratio of a homogeneous Newtonian spheroid. 04Locate the ring singularity For 0 < |q| < 1 on y = 0, the condition A+B = 0 locates a ring singularity with x > 1. The polynomial below increases monotonically for x > 1, is −q² at one, and becomes positive at infinity. The panel finds its unique root by bisection. p²x₀⁴+2px₀(x₀²−1)−1 = 0 ρring/M = (p/2)√(x₀²−1) At q = 0 the root retreats to the boundary x = 1; the exterior-ring interpretation no longer applies. TS2 also has causal pathologies including closed timelike curves. It is not automatically an alternative model of an ordinary rotating black hole. This lesson computes the ring location without reconstructing the full causal diagram or all geodesics. 05Compare at fixed mass and spin Multipoles and ring coordinates are recomputed theoretical quantities. A singular ring is neither a black-hole shadow nor a material ring. Spin q is continuous, whereas δ labels integer solution families; parameter comparison is not time evolution. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Does the δ = 2 spacetime become Schwarzschild at q = 0? Show the answer and reasoning No. Q/M³ = −1/4 remains: it is static but nonspherical. At δ = 1, q = 0 instead gives Schwarzschild. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. documents.title: Toomre Q and disk self-gravity | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConstruct the thin-gas-disk dispersion relation, derive Q < 1 and the unstable band by completing the square, and distinguish linear instability from fragmentation. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Rotation also resists long waves in a disk Unlike a uniform three-dimensional Jeans medium, a disk is thin and rotating. A local radial compression involves Coriolis and orbital responses as well as pressure. Use a razor-thin gas disk, a local approximation, axisymmetry, and constant sound speed to examine each wavelength. κ² = 1r³d(r⁴Ω²)dr = 4Ω²+2rΩdΩdr κ is the epicyclic frequency and equals Ω for Keplerian rotation. The density Σ below is mass per disk area, not the three-dimensional density ρ. 02Obtain the gravity of a thin sheet For a surface-density wave δΣ exp(ikx), the potential outside the disk decays vertically as exp(−|kz|). Integrating Poisson’s equation across the sheet equates the jump of the vertical derivative to 4πGδΣ. δΦ(z) = δΦ(0)e−|kz| −2|k|δΦ(0) = 4πGδΣ ⇒ δΦ(0) = −2πGδΣ|k| The wavenumber dependence differs from a uniform three-dimensional medium. This expression assumes zero thickness; a finite disk thickness weakens self-gravity at short wavelengths and requires a modified kernel. 03Linearize mass and two momentum equations Use disturbances exp[i(kx−ωt)], with radial velocity perturbation u and azimuthal perturbation v. Continuity and the two momentum equations let us express surface-density and azimuthal perturbations in terms of u, then eliminate them. −iωδΣ+ikΣu = 0 −iωu−2Ωv = −ik(cs²δΣΣ+δΦ) −iωv+κ²2Ωu = 0 ω² = κ²+cs²k²−2πGΣ|k| The three terms represent rotation, pressure, and self-gravity. Rotation stabilizes long waves, while pressure stabilizes short waves. We now ask whether gravity dominates an intermediate band. 04Complete the square to obtain Q Q ≡ csκπGΣ, x ≡ |k|csκ ω²κ² = 1+x²−2xQ = (x−1Q)²+1−1Q² The minimum is 1−1/Q² at x = 1/Q. All modes have positive ω² when Q > 1. If Q < 1, a band has negative ω². At Q = 1 the mode x = 1 is neutral, with zero exponential growth rate. This is gas Q, with denominator πGΣ. A collisionless stellar disk has a different response involving its velocity distribution; a common stellar Q uses 3.36GΣ. Replacing sound speed with a dispersion is not a derivation of that result. 05The unstable band and fastest-growing mode For Q < 1, solve ω² = 0 to find the band edges and set ω = iσ inside the band. Maximum growth occurs at a finite wavelength between pressure and rotational stabilization, not at the longest possible wave. x± = 1±√(1−Q²)Q, x−<x<x+ kmax = πGΣcs², λmax = 2cs²GΣ σmaxκ = √(1Q²−1) For Q = 0.8, the unstable interval is 0.5 < x < 2, with σ = 0.75κ at x = 1.25. Applying this prediction also requires wavelengths sufficiently small compared with the disk radius for the local approximation. 06Q below one does not guarantee planet formation Compression can heat the gas and increase pressure. With slow radiative cooling, a linearly unstable disk may settle into a heated spiral or gravito-turbulent state rather than fragment. Quantities such as cooling time multiplied by Ω provide additional information about nonlinear outcomes. Cooling thresholds depend on the equation of state, resolution, irradiation, boundary conditions, and other assumptions; there is no single universal number. Use Q as a local axisymmetric linear-stability diagnostic, not a direct assignment of fragment type or mass. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For a gas disk with Q = 0.8, find the unstable interval in x = kcs/κ, the fastest-growing x, and maximum σ/κ. Show the answer and reasoning The unstable band is 0.5 < x < 2, fastest growth is at x = 1.25, and maximum σ/κ = 0.75. The endpoints are neutral. These results assume a local, axisymmetric, razor-thin gas disk and do not guarantee fragmentation into planets or stars. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Two-temperature plasmas and electron–ion relaxation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFollow electron–ion temperature differences using energy conservation, and distinguish exchange and flow times. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A gas need not have just one temperature Temperature measures random particle motion. Electrons and protons can each have a thermal distribution while having different temperatures. A temperature for each species already assumes internal thermalization; it does not require that the two species have finished exchanging energy with each other. A collisionless shock can leave different species with different shares of the thermal energy. Supply the initial ratio β = Tₑ₀/Tᵢ₀ rather than deriving it from the total jump conditions. Then isolate subsequent Coulomb energy exchange from the much more complicated shock heating process. Assume fully ionized pure hydrogen with nₑ = nᵢ = n, nonrelativistic particles, fixed density and volume. Omit external heating, radiation losses, and expansion. 02Energy gained by one species is lost by the other uₑ=32nkBTₑ, uᵢ=32nkBTᵢ Qₑᵢ=32nkBTᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ Qₑᵢ is energy received by electrons per volume per time and is positive when ions are hotter. The ions lose exactly that amount. Equal number densities give equal heat capacities, so the two temperature equations have opposite right-hand sides. Adding them checks conservation before any numerical calculation. dTₑdt=Tᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ, dTᵢdt=−Tᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ Tₑ+Tᵢ=Tₑ₀+Tᵢ₀, T̄=Tₑ₀+Tᵢ₀2 03Exponential relaxation and the factor of two Subtract the electron equation from the ion equation. Cooling of ions and heating of electrons both reduce the difference Δ = Tᵢ−Tₑ. For a constant exchange time τ, separation of variables gives a simple benchmark. dΔdt=−2Δτ ⇒ dΔΔ=−2dtτ Δ=Δ₀e−2t/τ, Tₑ=T̄−Δ2, Tᵢ=T̄+Δ2 Here τ is the exchange time in the electron equation; the difference has an e-folding time τ/2. Holding ions at a prescribed temperature would instead describe an external heat reservoir. Checking which temperatures are allowed to change prevents a factor-of-two error. 04Supply the collision time and follow relaxation Supply the standard exchange time for a weakly coupled classical plasma. In the SI formula below, use density in m⁻³, temperatures in K, and charge in coulombs. Fix the dimensionless Coulomb logarithm at 30 instead of deriving the collision integral. tₑᵢ=3mₑmₚ8√(2π) n [e²/(4πε₀)]² lnΛ (kBTₑmₑ+kBTᵢmₚ)3/2 When the electron thermal-speed term dominates, tₑᵢ scales as Tₑ³ᐟ²/n. Heating electrons then slows exchange, so the panel updates the coefficient rather than using a single exponential. Labels in keV mean kBT, an energy representation of temperature; 1 keV corresponds to about 1.16 × 10⁷ K. Numerically integrate dt/dy = tₑᵢ/2 with y = ln(Δ₀/Δ), then invert the cumulative time. Simpson integration and local bisection give the temperatures while their sum is preserved analytically. The difference stays positive, and equal initial temperatures remain equal. 05Choose the relevant competing clock Compare the flow residence time with the near-equilibrium difference-decay time tₑᵢ(T̄)/2. A long exchange clock permits a difference to survive passage through the region. Since the coefficient changes during relaxation, inspect the trajectory as well as the single clock ratio. The panel is a closed parcel calculation, not a simulated flow. Its residence time is an external comparison scale. Maintaining two temperatures indefinitely requires sources or sinks that distinguish species; exchange alone eventually produces one temperature. Connect to heating in shocks and particle acceleration and electron pressure in the SZ effect. Total pressure is nkB(Tₑ+Tᵢ), whereas the electron pressure is nkBTₑ. Equal total energy therefore does not guarantee equal electron-pressure signals. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For equal electron and proton densities and constant exchange time τ, does the temperature difference fall by e in τ or τ/2? Show the answer and reasoning Both temperatures change, so d(Tᵢ−Tₑ)/dt = −2(Tᵢ−Tₑ)/τ. The difference decays in τ/2, unlike a model with externally fixed ion temperature. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Lynden–Bell–Pringle viscous-disk similarity solutions | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive surface-density diffusion and verify accretion, spreading and angular-momentum conservation in a similarity solution. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From steady disks to evolving disks The alpha chapter examined steady accretion. Now let surface density evolve in a thin Keplerian disk. A fixed central mass dominates; omit winds, external supply and disk self-gravity. Radial velocity is positive outward. ∂Σ∂t+1r∂∂r(rΣvr)=0, j=√(GMr) Subtract j times mass conservation from angular-momentum conservation to eliminate radial advection in favour of a stress gradient. A specified viscosity closes the model. 02Derive surface-density diffusion vr=−3Σr1/2∂∂r(νΣr1/2) ∂Σ∂t=3r∂∂r[r1/2∂∂r(νΣr1/2)] ν represents effective transport, not necessarily molecular viscosity. Prescribe ν = ν₁(r/R₁)ᵞ with γ < 2 and no dependence on time or Σ. This differs from solving temperature and transport together in a general alpha disk. x=rR₁, β=2−γ, ts=R₁²3β²ν₁, T=1+tts 03Substitute a similarity solution Use zero torque at the origin, an infinite outer disk and the smooth initial profile implied below. Differentiating in τ = t/ts and y = xᵝ/T matches the powers of T and x on both sides of the PDE. Σ(r,t)=M₀β2πR₁²x−γT−(5/2−γ)/βexp(−xβT) This is an exact similarity solution for a particular initial profile, not for every disk. It can also provide useful late-time intuition for broader classes of initial data. Md=M₀T−1/(2β), Rc=R₁T1/β Ṁin=M₀2βtsT−(5/2−γ)/β 04Inward accretion and outward spreading vr=3νr[βxβT−12] rturn=R₁[T2β]1/β Flow is inward below rturn and outward above it. The plotted 2πr²Σ/M₀ is mass per log radius normalized to initial mass; colours denote epochs, not tracked particle trajectories. Playback advances t/ts uniformly. Physical R₁ and ν₁ specify ts for conversion; screen seconds are not disk time. 05Account for lost mass and retained angular momentum Substitution y = xᵝ/T gives the disk mass integral. Angular momentum carries an extra √r factor; spreading exactly compensates the decreasing mass. J=2π√(GM)∫0∞Σr3/2dr=constant Maccreted=M₀−Md, −dMddt=Ṁin Accreted material has j → 0 at the origin, leaving angular momentum in the disk. Finite inner radii, stellar spin or winds change the budget. M₀ ≪ M lets us neglect the accreted mass in the central gravitational field. The plots recompute this analytic solution, checked against the PDE and mass/angular-momentum budgets. They do not reproduce all initial profiles or figures in the original paper. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For γ = 1, increase T from 1 to 4. How do disk mass, characteristic radius, central accretion rate and angular momentum change? Show the answer and reasoning Mass halves, characteristic radius grows by four, and central accretion rate falls by eight. Total disk angular momentum stays constant for this infinite outer disk with a zero-torque boundary at the origin. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Zel’dovich approximation and pancakes | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNObtain density from a Lagrangian map’s Jacobian and explain pancakes and shell crossing. Connect to foundations: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Label particles and move their positions Map initial Lagrangian labels q to later comoving positions x. The Zel’dovich approximation keeps the initial displacement direction and multiplies its amplitude by linear growth D. Physical position is r = ax, separating background expansion from peculiar displacement. x(q,t)=q+D(t)s(q), r=a(t)x This is first-order Lagrangian perturbation theory with growing-mode initial data, not an exact general orbit solution. It primarily describes pressureless matter before shell crossing. 02Density follows the volume Jacobian The mass of a labelled element is conserved. A small initial volume d³q maps to d³x = Jd³q; density therefore varies as the inverse determinant. J=det(δᵢⱼ+D∂sᵢ∂qⱼ), ρρ̄=1J For potential displacements, let λᵢ be eigenvalues of −∂sᵢ/∂qⱼ. Each direction has its own compression factor; the largest positive eigenvalue reaches collapse first. ρρ̄=1(1−Dλ₁)(1−Dλ₂)(1−Dλ₃) 03One collapsing direction gives a pancake Simultaneous collapse along three axes requires special symmetry. Compression along one direction first produces a sheet-like structure, hence the name pancake. s(q)=−Aksin(kq), x=q−DAksin(kq) J=1−DAcos(kq), ρρ̄=11−DAcos(kq) The periodic one-dimensional panel uses k = 1. It displays equally spaced particle labels and the density at their mapped Eulerian positions. Playback advances D uniformly, not cosmic time. 04Shell crossing ends the single-stream description At DA = 1 the first zero Jacobian forms a caustic. Collisionless matter can develop multiple streams; gas also needs pressure and shocks. Extending 1/J through negative Jacobians would give an unphysical negative density. Controls stop at DA ≤ 0.95. The panel does not compute post-collapse galaxies, shocks or published N-body results. Even as a peak grows, the mass in one period stays fixed. 05Connect geometry to halo statistics Zel’dovich approximates positions and shapes; Press–Schechter estimates halo statistics from smoothed fluctuations. A spherical-collapse threshold and anisotropic first shell crossing are different criteria. A specified displacement field extends the construction to multiple dimensions, while post-crossing evolution needs methods such as N-body dynamics. Identifying where the approximation fails is part of using it correctly. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. In the one-dimensional sinusoidal model, what is the peak density ratio at DA = 0.8? What fails at DA = 1? Show the answer and reasoning ρ/ρ̄ = 1/(1−DA) = 5, so δ = 4. At DA = 1 the map derivative vanishes and a caustic forms. Multiple streams can then occupy one location, invalidating a single-stream continuation; total particle mass does not become infinite. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. documents.title: Numbers and units for astrophysics | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Home RELATED CHAPTERS 01Start with orders of magnitude Estimating the order of magnitude before calculating helps catch unit errors. This supplement is a reference to use with units, rather than a demand to memorize every digit. c ≈ 3×1010 cm/s, G ≈ 6.7×10−8 cm³ g−1 s−2 1 pc ≈ 3×1018 cm, M☉ ≈ 2×1033 g h ≈ 6.6×10−27 erg s, me ≈ 9.1×10−28 g mec² ≈ 511 keV, α ≈ 1137 The reference values use CODATA 2022 and IAU definitions or nominal conversions, with measurement uncertainties omitted. Distinguish defining values, measurements, astronomical scales, and illustrative choices. Rounded displays do not imply precision beyond their shown digits. c Speed of light in vacuum SI2.997 924 58 × 108 m s−1CGS / related value2.997 924 58 × 1010 cm s−1Exact by definition G Newtonian gravitational constant SI6.674 30 × 10−11 m³ kg−1 s−2CGS / related value6.674 30 × 10−8 cm³ g−1 s−2Measured h Planck constant SI6.626 070 15 × 10−34 J sCGS / related value6.626 070 15 × 10−27 erg sExact by definition ℏ = h/(2π) Reduced Planck constant SI1.054 571 817… × 10−34 J sCGS / related value1.054 571 817… × 10−27 erg sDerived from exact inputs; rounded display mₑ Electron rest mass SI9.109 383 7139 × 10−31 kgCGS / related value9.109 383 7139 × 10−28 gMeasured mₑc² Electron rest energy SI8.187 105 788… × 10−14 JCGS / related value8.187 105 788… × 10−7 erg ≈ 0.510 998 950 69 MeVEnergy, a different dimension from mass kB Boltzmann constant SI1.380 649 × 10−23 J K−1CGS / related value1.380 649 × 10−16 erg K−1Exact by definition e Elementary charge magnitude SI1.602 176 634 × 10−19 CCGS / related value≈ 4.803 204 71 × 10−10 statCExact in SI; Gaussian charge has different dimensions α Fine-structure constant SI7.297 352 5643 × 10−3CGS / related valueSame value α−1 ≈ 137.035 999 177Measured and dimensionless 1 pc Parsec SI≈ 3.085 677 581 49 × 1016 mCGS / related value≈ 3.085 677 581 49 × 1018 cm ≈ 3.261 56 lyDefined as (648000/π) au; rounded display M☉ Solar mass scale SI≈ 1.9884 × 1030 kgCGS / related value≈ 1.9884 × 1033 gNot an exact defining constant H₀ Hubble constant: conversion example SI70 km s−1 Mpc−1CGS / related value≈ 2.2685 × 10−18 s−170 is illustrative, not an exact consensus value 02c, G, and mechanical CGS conversions CGS uses centimetres, grams, and seconds. Convert from SI metres, kilograms, and seconds by tracking each dimensional power. The SI value c = 299792458 m/s is exact; since 1 m = 100 cm, its CGS numerical value is one hundred times larger. 1 erg = 1 g cm² s−2 = 10−7 J 1 dyn = 1 g cm s−2 = 10−5 N 1 g/cm³ = 10³ kg/m³ 1 dyn/cm² = 0.1 Pa, 1 erg/cm³ = 0.1 J/m³ From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G has dimensions length³/(mass × time²). Going from SI to CGS multiplies its numerical value by 100³/1000 = 1000. G ≈ 6.67430×10−11 m³kg s² = 6.67430×10−8 cm³g s² Unlike c or h, G is measured. Its CODATA 2022 relative standard uncertainty is about 2.2×10⁻⁵. A long numerical value is not the same thing as an exact defining value. 03Connect parsecs, light-years, and solar masses The parsec originated with annual parallax and is defined as 1 pc = (648000/π) au. Since one arcsecond is π/648000 radians, this connects to the small-angle relation d ≈ 1 au/p. One au is exactly 149597870700 m. 1 pc ≈ 3.08568×1018 cm ≈ 3.26156 ly 1 kpc = 10³ pc, 1 Mpc = 10⁶ pc 1 ly = c×(365.25×86400 s) ≈ 9.46073×1017 cm The light-year here uses the Julian year of 365.25 days. The solar mass scale, about 2×10³³ g, is useful but is not an exact universal constant in kilograms. Orbital dynamics constrains GM well, and the IAU defines a nominal solar mass parameter. (GM)☉N = 1.3271244×1020 m³ s−2 (GM)☉NG ≈ 1.9884×1030 kg The superscript N denotes a nominal value. Nominal GM is an exact conversion reference, not a claim about the Sun’s instantaneous true GM. Dividing it by measured G introduces G’s uncertainty. 04h versus ℏ, and electron mass versus energy Frequency ν counts cycles per second, while angular frequency ω = 2πν measures phase change per second. Photon energy is hν = ℏω: the same physics with matching frequency conventions. ℏ = h2π, E = hν = ℏω = hcλ hc ≈ 1239.84 eV nm, ℏc ≈ 197.327 MeV fm Electron rest mass is me. The value 511 keV is the rest energy mec²; the mass can be written as 511 keV/c². An electron volt is an energy unit, not a voltage. 1 eV = 1.602176634×10−19 J = 1.602176634×10−12 erg mec² ≈ 8.18711×10−7 erg ≈ 0.510999 MeV The fine-structure constant α is dimensionless and has the same value in SI and Gaussian units. Its vacuum, low-energy value is approximately 1/137. It is distinct from the alpha used for disk transport efficiency. α = eSI²4πε₀ℏc = eG²ℏc ≈ 1137.036 12α²mec² ≈ 13.6 eV The final expression estimates the hydrogen ground-state binding energy with a fixed nucleus. Electron rest energy and α thus connect to atomic photon-energy scales. 05Unpack the Hubble constant’s units H₀ is the present expansion rate inferred from measurements and modelling, not an exact defining universal constant. Use 70 km/s/Mpc as a conversion example, not as a unique answer or a claim of current consensus. H₀ = 70×10⁵ cm/s3.08568×10²⁴ cm ≈ 2.2685×10−18 s−1 H₀−1 ≈ 4.408×1017 s ≈ 13.97 Gyr H₀⁻¹ is the Hubble time, not necessarily the age of the universe. The age depends on a cosmological model and the history of H(t). The dimensionless h in H₀ = 100h km/s/Mpc is also unrelated to Planck’s constant h. 06In Gaussian CGS, convert equations as well as values Electromagnetic CGS conventions include electrostatic, electromagnetic, and Gaussian systems. Here use Gaussian CGS explicitly: charge in statC and magnetic flux density B in gauss (G). Distinguish G as a magnetic unit from G as the gravitational constant. The same physics in matched conventions Quantity / lawSICGS–Gauss Coulomb-force magnitudeF = |q₁q₂|/(4πε₀r²)F = |q₁q₂|/r² Lorentz forceF⃗ = q(E⃗ + v⃗ × B⃗)F⃗ = q(E⃗ + (v⃗/c) × B⃗) Vacuum magnetic energy densityuB = B²/(2μ₀)uB = B²/(8π) Nonrelativistic electron gyrofrequencyωB = eB/mₑωB = eB/(mₑc) Classical electron radiusrₑ = e²/(4πε₀mₑc²)rₑ = e²/(mₑc²) Gaussian Coulomb’s law gives [q]² = [force][length]² = g cm³ s⁻², so charge has dimensions g1/2 cm3/2 s⁻¹. Electric and magnetic fields both have dimensions g1/2 cm−1/2 s⁻¹; v/c in the Lorentz force is dimensionless. 1 G = 10−4 T, 1 μG = 10−10 T 1 statC ≈ 3.33564×10−10 C Match charge and field values together with the equation’s coefficients. Do not insert SI charge numbers into Gaussian equations or simply set ε₀ and μ₀ to one. In the current SI, μ₀ is measured; μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m is an approximation. For B = 1 G, Gaussian uB = 1/(8π) ≈ 0.03979 erg/cm³. Using 10⁻⁴ T in the SI formula gives about 0.003979 J/m³, agreeing after energy-density conversion. 07Try the conversions The field conversion also compares magnetic energy densities. An eV-to-K readout is the equivalent temperature from E = kBT, not an assignment of temperature to every possible particle population. CHECK THE UNITS Calculate with the units When converting 1 pc from metres to centimetres, and electron mass from kilograms to grams, what are the factors? Why is the factor for G not one hundred? Show the answer Length gains a factor 100 and mass a factor 1000. Since G has dimensions length³/mass/time², its factor is 100³/1000 = 1000. Writing dimensions first helps prevent exponent mistakes. REFERENCES & NUMERICAL SOURCES Fundamental values use CODATA 2022. Unit conventions follow NRAO; definitions and nominal scales follow IAU. H₀ = 70 is illustrative. documents.title: Atomic light and starlight: why 10.2 eV? | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate the energy and wavelength of Lyman alpha from hydrogen levels. 01Atoms have discrete energy levels A hydrogen electron cannot have just any bound-state energy. We take the energy-level formula supplied by quantum theory as our starting point. The integer n is 1, 2, 3, …; zero energy corresponds to a separated electron and proton. A level difference becomes photon energyHydrogen emits a 10.2 eV photon when it goes from n = 2 to n = 1. The horizontal lines show state energies, not electron trajectories in space.View larger diagram ↗ En ≈ −13.6 eVn2 A simple hydrogen model, neglecting fine structure and other small corrections. 02What does a 2 → 1 transition emit? Eγ = E2 − E1 = −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV λ = hcEγ ≈ 1240 eV·nm10.2 eV ≈ 121.6 nm This is Lyman alpha (Lyα), an ultraviolet line strongly absorbed by Earth’s atmosphere. It is a valuable tracer of cosmic hydrogen. The 2 → 1 transition is not ionization: removing an electron from the ground state requires about 13.6 eV. 03The same idea as the Rydberg formula 1λ = RH(1nlow2 − 1nhigh2) RH ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. “High” and “low” label the upper and lower levels. Divide the energy difference by hc to obtain this expression. It is the same energy conservation statement written in terms of wavelength. 04Atomic fingerprints on a continuous spectrum Hot, optically thick matter emits a nearly thermal continuum. Foreground gas can absorb photons at selected transition energies, producing absorption lines. Emission from dilute gas can produce bright lines. Line strength depends on temperature, ionization, and radiation transport as well as abundance. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. What energy is emitted in hydrogen’s n = 3 → 2 transition? Is it ultraviolet? Show the answer and reasoning 13.6 × (1/4 − 1/9) ≈ 1.89 eV. Its wavelength is about 656 nm: the red, visible Hα line. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: The Chandrasekhar mass: a white dwarf’s limit | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNExplain why a limiting mass appears by comparing pressure exponents and cancelling radius. 01Electron degeneracy pressure survives cooling A white dwarf is supported mainly by electron degeneracy pressure. The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons from occupying the same full quantum state. A spatial state holds at most two opposite-spin electrons, so packing many electrons fills states up to high momenta. What supports a white dwarf?Left: gravity and electron-pressure support. Each right-hand line represents an example spatial state; arrows indicate two spin states. Higher density requires higher momentum states. The lines are not stellar layers and do not reproduce the actual density of states.View larger diagram ↗ For number density nₑ, a spacing scale is d ∼ nₑ−1/3. Counting quantum states gives a characteristic momentum pF ∼ ℏ/d. Uncertainty offers intuition, but does not by itself derive the exclusion principle. pF ∼ ℏne1/3, ne = ρμemu μₑ is mass per electron in units of mᵤ. It is about 2 for fully ionized carbon or oxygen. 02Nonrelativistic electrons give P ∝ ρ5/3 A pressure scale is number density × momentum × speed: P ∼ nₑpv. At low speeds, v ≈ p/mₑ. Insert p ∼ ℏnₑ1/3. PNR ∼ nepF2me ∼ ℏ2mene5/3 ∝ ρ5/3 With ρ ∼ M/R³, PNR ∝ M5/3/R⁵, whereas PG ∼ GM²/R⁴. Shrinking makes degeneracy pressure grow faster, allowing a new equilibrium radius. At fixed composition, balancing the scalings gives R ∝ M−1/3. 03Relativity changes the exponent E2 = p2c2 + me2c4 This energy–momentum relation is an input from special relativity. At p ≫ mₑc, E ≈ pc and v ≈ c. Momentum keeps increasing while speed approaches c. The pressure scaling changes to: PUR ∼ nepFc ∼ ℏc ne4/3 ∼ ℏc(μemu)4/3M4/3R4 04Cancel radius to expose a mass scale ℏc M4/3(μemu)4/3R4 ∼ GM2R4 M2/3 ∼ ℏcG(μemu)4/3 ⇒ M ∼ (ℏcG)3/21(μemu)2 Divide by M4/3, then raise both sides to the power 3/2. Both pressures scale as R⁻⁴, so changing the radius no longer changes their ratio. This is the central reason a limiting mass appears. 05Where does the coefficient near 1.4 solar masses come from? The estimates above deliberately omitted numerical coefficients. We now use the standard result from a detailed structure calculation for a cold, nonrotating, spherical star with ideal degenerate electrons. MCh ≈ 5.83μe2M☉ ≈ 1.46 (2μe)2M☉ With μₑ defined using the atomic mass constant, this ideal model gives about 1.46 M☉, commonly summarized as “about 1.4 M☉.” Different conventions and corrections also lead to values such as 1.44. Composition, electron capture, nuclear reactions, general relativity, and rotation affect real evolution. Crossing a limiting mass does not guarantee one particular explosion. Composition and accretion history help determine whether thermonuclear runaway, collapse, or another outcome occurs. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. In the ultrarelativistic limit, how do degeneracy and gravitational pressure scales change if radius halves? Show the answer and reasoning Both increase by 16, since both scale as R⁻⁴. Shrinking no longer improves pressure support relative to gravity. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Measuring light, measuring distance | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNExplain how luminosity differs from apparent brightness and how light reveals distance. 01Light carries information Radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, and X-rays are all electromagnetic radiation. In vacuum they travel at c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Wavelength λ and frequency ν obey c = λν. One photon carries E = hν = hc/λ. E[eV] ≈ 1240λ[nm] A 500 nm photon carries about 2.48 eV. Shorter wavelengths mean higher photon energies. 02Spread the light over a sphere Luminosity L is the total energy a star emits per second. If it radiates uniformly, that energy crosses a sphere of area 4πd². The flux f is the power received per square metre. Light spreads over a growing sphereLight from a star of fixed luminosity spreads over spheres. At 2d the area is four times larger, so the flux per receiving area is one quarter. The spheres are schematic.View larger diagram ↗ f = L4πd2 ⇒ d = √(L4πf) This assumes no absorption and isotropic emission. Luminosity is in W; flux in W/m². 03Triangulation for nearby stars As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star shifts against distant background objects. Its annual parallax p corresponds to a baseline of 1 au: half the maximum shift measured six months apart. One parsec is the distance corresponding to one arcsecond. Parallax as a triangleParallax p corresponds to a baseline of 1 au from Sun to Earth. Earth positions six months apart are about 2 au apart, giving a maximum angular shift of about 2p. Angles and body sizes are exaggerated.View larger diagram ↗ d[pc] = 1p[arcsec] A parallax of 0.05 arcseconds gives 20 pc, about 65 light-years. A light-year is a distance. 04A ladder of calibrations Solar-system ranging → stellar parallax → period–luminosity relations such as Cepheids → Type Ia supernovae. Nearby distances calibrate the intrinsic brightness used at the next stage. Type Ia supernovae must be standardized using their light-curve shapes and colours; their luminosities are not identical. v ≈ H0d, z ≈ vc Approximations for the nearby universe at small redshift. H₀ must be calibrated using other distance measurements or a cosmological model. At large redshift, d = cz/H₀ is insufficient. You need the expansion history, a cosmological model, and a specified definition of distance. Continue to cosmic expansion and Hubble’s law → See why uniform fractional growth makes recession speed proportional to distance. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Two stars have equal luminosity. One looks nine times fainter. How much farther away is it? Show the answer and reasoning Three times farther: f ∝ 1/d², so the distance ratio is √9 = 3. Equal luminosity is essential. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: The Eddington limit: when light balances gravity | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNBalance forces and see why r² cancels, giving LEdd = 4πGMc/κ. 01Photons carry momentum as well as energy pγ = Eγc, f = L4πr2 Matter gains momentum by absorbing or scattering radiation. For Thomson scattering, angular averaging lets us use the flux and effective cross section for the net radial momentum transfer. Electric fields couple electrons to ions, so the gas moves together. 02Start with an electron–proton pair Frad = σTL4πr2c, Fgrav ≈ GMmpr2 M is the central mass; the surrounding gas is fully ionized pure hydrogen. Electron mass is negligible compared with proton mass. 03Equate the forces and cancel r² σTL4πr2c = GMmpr2 σTL = 4πGMmpc ⇒ LEdd = 4πGMmpcσT For one solar mass this is approximately 1.26 × 10³¹ W, or 3.3 × 10⁴ L☉, scaling linearly with M. We obtained the coefficient from a force balance without solving a differential equation. 04Use opacity for a different composition arad = κL4πr2c, agrav = GMr2 LEdd = 4πGMcκ This balance assumes spherical symmetry, steady conditions, and a specified effective opacity. Disks, inhomogeneous gas, and transient events can exceed this luminosity. It is not an absolute cap on every astronomical source. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed κ, what happens to LEdd if the central mass grows by ten? What if radius doubles? Show the answer and reasoning Ten times the mass gives ten times the limiting luminosity. Radius cancels because both accelerations fall as 1/r². REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Nucleosynthesis and why helium is about 25% | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNEstimate the helium mass fraction from the neutron-to-proton ratio. 01The hot early universe In the early universe, reactions converted protons and neutrons into one another. Expansion and cooling made those reactions fall behind, and some neutrons decayed. Near the onset of efficient nucleosynthesis, a useful estimate is neutron : proton ≈ 1 : 7. Predicting that ratio requires weak-interaction and expansion calculations. 02Two neutrons and two protons make helium-4 Take 2 neutrons and 14 protons. If almost all neutrons end up in helium-4, one helium nucleus forms and 12 protons remain. Neglecting nucleon mass differences and binding energies, helium contains 4 of the 16 mass units. Yp ≈ 416 = 0.25 Yp is the primordial helium mass fraction in ordinary matter, not 25% of the universe’s total energy. Yp ≈ 2q1+q, q = NnNp Nn neutrons make Nn/2 helium nuclei, containing 2Nn nucleons in total. 03Stars build beyond the primordial elements Primordial nucleosynthesis produced mainly hydrogen and helium, with traces including deuterium, helium-3, and lithium. Stars turn hydrogen into more helium, then later reactions produce carbon and oxygen. Massive-star evolution can build nuclei near the iron group. Elements heavier than iron have several origins, including slow neutron capture in evolved stars and rapid neutron capture in extreme environments such as neutron-star mergers. One kind of supernova does not explain every heavy element. 04Reading light reveals the history of matter Atomic levels produce lines; line ratios and widths reveal temperature, composition, and motion. Luminosity and distance reveal energy output. Gravity and quantum physics set the conditions under which a star can exist. The equations connect different aspects of the same universe. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Start with 2 neutrons and 14 protons and form one helium nucleus. What are helium’s number and mass fractions? Show the answer and reasoning Twelve hydrogen nuclei remain. Helium is 1/(12 + 1) ≈ 7.7% of nuclei by number, but 4/16 = 25% by mass. documents.title: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNObtain v = HD from a scale factor and distinguish redshift, Hubble time, and cosmic age. 01Multiply galaxy separations by a common factor In the standard large-scale model, the universe is approximately homogeneous and isotropic. For points following the cosmic flow, write their same-time proper separation as D(t) = a(t)χ, using an appropriate fixed comoving separation χ. The dimensionless scale factor a(t) is conventionally one today. Galaxy separations grow by the same factorAn example of galaxy separations increasing uniformly by 1.5, with galaxy sizes held fixed. The grid compares distances; it is not a physical framework or a special centre.View larger diagram ↗ D = aχ, D' = a'χ ⇒ D′D = a′a Primes label values at a different time; they do not denote derivatives here. If a grows from 1 to 1.1, separations of points following the cosmic flow grow by 1.1. This does not make galaxies, solar systems, or atoms expand by the same factor: binding forces determine their internal structures. 02Divide the change by time to obtain Hubble’s law During a short interval Δt, let the scale factor increase by Δa. Since χ stays fixed, ΔD = χΔa = DΔa/a. Divide by Δt to find the rate of separation. ΔDΔt = (ΔaaΔt)D Here a and D are evaluated at the start of the interval. For fixed χ this finite-interval equation is an equality. HΔt ≡ ΔaaΔt, vΔt ≡ ΔDΔt ⇒ vΔt = HΔtD For instantaneous rates the relation is vrec = H(t)D. This is the Hubble–Lemaître relation for uniform expansion. H(t) is a fractional growth rate per unit time; H₀ is its present value. The name “Hubble constant” does not make it constant throughout cosmic history. 03Every observer sees more distant points separate faster Imagine A, B, and C on a line with every gap growing by 1% in a short time. If C is twice as far from A as B is, its separation increases twice as much. From B, both sides follow the same rule. This does not identify Earth as a special centre of expansion. vrec is the change of a same-cosmic-time separation to a distant point. At cosmological distances HD can exceed c without an object locally passing an observer faster than light. The local speed limit and this distant-separation rate are different quantities. 04Stretched wavelengths give cosmological redshift z ≡ λobs−λemitλemit ⇒ 1+z = λobsλemit For emission and observation by comoving observers in a homogeneous, isotropic universe, general relativity supplies the following relation. It is an additional result about light propagating through expanding spacetime, not an algebraic consequence of the definition of z alone. 1+z = anowaemit ⇒ aemit = 11+z (anow=1) At z = 1, the emission-era scale factor was 0.5. At high redshift, inserting z into a special-relativistic Doppler formula is not a general way to infer cosmic distance. Observations can also include peculiar velocities and gravitational redshifts. 05Infer distances in the nearby-universe approximation z ≈ vc, v ≈ H0D ⇒ D ≈ czH0 Use H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ as a round teaching example, not a claim that current measurements have settled on a unique value. One megaparsec is about 3.26 million light-years. At 10 Mpc the example gives 700 km/s; at 100 Mpc, 7,000 km/s. For z = 0.005, v ≈ 1,500 km/s and D ≈ 21.4 Mpc. Peculiar motion can substantially affect nearby-galaxy estimates. At large distances the expansion history and the definition of distance matter, so this approximation is insufficient. 061/H₀ is a timescale, not automatically the age H0 ≈ 70 km/s3.086×1019 km ≈ 2.27×10−18 s−1 tH ≡ 1H0 ≈ 4.41×1017 s ≈ 14 billion years The Hubble time for the example H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Dividing the present separation D by the present recession rate H₀D gives 1/H₀. But that separation need not have grown at its present rate throughout the past. Determining the cosmic age requires the expansion history. Accelerated expansion does not necessarily mean an increasing H: H is a fractional rate, not the absolute rate of growth. Hubble’s law describes the expansion pattern; by itself it does not determine how matter, radiation, and dark energy govern the expansion history. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Lyα has a rest wavelength near 121.6 nm. At z = 3, what wavelength do we observe, and how large was the emission-era scale factor relative to today? Show the answer and reasoning λobs = (1 + 3) × 121.6 = 486.4 nm. With anow = 1, aemit = 1/(1 + 3) = 0.25. This alone does not imply an age one quarter of today’s. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNExplain charge cancellation and why gravity adds up. 01Is a cosmic vacuum really empty? Space between stars contains atoms, ions, electrons, dust, and radiation. Even a very dilute medium can absorb or scatter light over a long path. Hot stellar interiors are plasmas: electrons are no longer bound to individual atoms. 02Compare two inverse-square laws FG = Gmp2r2, FE = e24πε0r2 FEFG = e24πε0Gmp2 ≈ 1.2 × 1036 e is the elementary charge, ε₀ the vacuum permittivity, and mₚ the proton mass. This ratio is for two protons. 03Large objects are nearly electrically neutral Nearly equal positive and negative charges largely cancel the long-range electric force. Gravity from ordinary matter adds attractively. This makes gravity central to the global balance of stars, while magnetic fields and electromagnetic forces still matter in many cosmic settings. 04Pressure is force per area P = FA, Pgas = nkBT n is the number of particles per unit volume. The ideal-gas equation describes pressure from particle motion. Pressure itself has no direction. A star is supported by the force imbalance created when pressure is higher inside than outside. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If two protons are separated twice as far, does the ratio of electric to gravitational force change? Show the answer and reasoning No. Both forces scale as 1/r², so the distance cancels in their ratio. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: From Einstein A and B coefficients to Planck’s law | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNSolve detailed balance for uν and identify where the denominator’s −1 comes from. 01Specify the quantity to be found uν is radiation energy density per unit frequency, in J m⁻³ Hz⁻¹. A narrow interval Δν contains approximately uνΔν of energy density. The two levels are separated by hν; n₁ and n₂ are their number densities and g₁ and g₂ their statistical weights. Our B coefficients multiply uν. Coefficients defined to multiply the mean intensity Jν have different numerical values. We assume a narrow line across which uν is nearly constant. 02Write down the three processes Absorption: n₁B₁₂uν. Spontaneous emission: n₂A₂₁. Stimulated emission: n₂B₂₁uν. When atoms and radiation share thermal equilibrium, the upward and downward transition rates balance. n1B12uν = n2A21 + n2B21uν 03Collect the uν terms and divide (n1B12−n2B21)uν = n2A21 uν = A21/B21(n1/n2)(B12/B21)−1 In the second line we divided numerator and denominator by n₂B₂₁. So far this only rearranges the balance condition; it does not yet determine the spectrum. 04Insert the Boltzmann ratio and Einstein relations n1n2 = g1g2ehν/(kBT), g1B12 = g2B21 A21B21 = 8πhν3c3 The B relation reflects microscopic transition symmetry. The A/B ratio is linked to electromagnetic mode counting and can also be fixed by matching the classical Rayleigh–Jeans limit. These are additional physical inputs; detailed balance alone does not determine the factor 8π. 05Arrive at Planck’s law uν(T) = 8πhν3c31exp(hν/kBT)−1 At low frequency, x = hν/(kBT) ≪ 1 and eˣ − 1 ≈ x. Substitution gives uν ≈ 8πν²kBT/c³, the Rayleigh–Jeans result. At high frequency the exponential suppresses the spectrum. Bν = c4πuν For isotropic thermal radiation. Specific intensity Bν, energy density uν, and surface flux have different units. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Which of the three processes produces the “−1” in the final denominator? Show the answer and reasoning Stimulated emission. It comes from the second term in n₁B₁₂ − n₂B₂₁, absorption minus stimulated emission. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish Newtonian estimates from results supplied by general relativity. 01Special relativity: a light clock and Pythagoras Imagine a clock made of light bouncing between mirrors. In its rest frame, a one-way trip covers ℓ in t₀ = ℓ/c. An observer seeing the clock move sideways at speed v sees a diagonal light path. Both measure light speed c. A moving light clock makes a triangleCompare one-way trips between mirrors. The right panel shows the lower mirror at departure and upper mirror at arrival, with horizontal travel vt and mirror spacing ℓ. At the same light speed c, the longer diagonal path takes a longer inertial-frame time t.View larger diagram ↗ (ct)2 = ℓ2 + (vt)2 ⇒ t = t0√(1−v2/c2) For these same two clock events, the inertial-frame interval t exceeds the moving clock’s proper interval t₀. This is special-relativistic time dilation, distinct from gravitational time dilation. 02Estimate escape speed using Newtonian mechanics 12mvesc2 = GMmR ⇒ vesc = √(2GMR) Formally setting vesc = c yields R = 2GM/c². But mv²/2 is not the kinetic energy of a photon. This is a clue to a length scale, not a derivation of a relativistic horizon. 03The relativistic result: Schwarzschild radius rs = 2GMc2 ≈ 2.95 (MM☉) km General relativity describes gravity through spacetime geometry. Its solution for a nonrotating, uncharged, spherical black hole identifies this radius as an event horizon. Future-directed light and matter inside cannot reach the distant exterior. Deriving that spacetime solution is outside our scope. Matching the same radius by substituting c into escape speed does not derive black holes from Newtonian mechanics. The match alone does not establish spacetime’s causal structure. 04Compare stationary clocks in a gravitational field ΔτΔt = √(1−rsr) (r > rs) Δτ is the time recorded by a stationary clock at r; Δt corresponds to a stationary clock far away. This equation is supplied by the relativistic solution. At r = 2rs, the ratio is √(1/2) ≈ 0.707. During an interval corresponding to one hour far away, the stationary local clock advances about 42.4 minutes. A stationary clock cannot be placed at r = rs, and this stationary-clock expression does not apply inside. An infalling observer can cross the horizon in finite proper time. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Would a black hole of one solar mass pull a distant planet more strongly than the Sun? Show the answer and reasoning At the same distant radius in spherical symmetry, the gravity depends on the same mass. What differs is the compactness and the presence of an event horizon. documents.title: The classical electron radius and Thomson scattering | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConnect the scale rₑ to σT and then to opacity κ. 01Compare electric and rest-energy scales Define rₑ as the length at which the electric energy scale e²/(4πε₀r) equals the electron rest energy mₑc². Multiply by r, then divide by mₑc². An accelerated electron scatters lightIn the classical picture of Thomson scattering, the incident electric field accelerates an electron, which radiates. Two outgoing rays illustrate possible directions; they do not imply photon splitting or isotropic scattering.View larger diagram ↗ e24πε0re = mec2 ⇒ re = e24πε0mec2 ≈ 2.82 × 10−15 m This is not a measured physical radius of the electron. It is a length built from electromagnetic constants. A model of a charged sphere would have a self-energy coefficient depending on its charge distribution. 02Light shakes an electron, which radiates Let the incident field be E(t) = E₀ cos(2πνt). A free electron has acceleration amplitude a₀ = eE₀/mₑ. Since the cycle average of cos² is 1/2, ⟨a²⟩ = e²E₀²/(2mₑ²). ⟨P⟩ = e2⟨a2⟩6πε0c3 = e4E0212πε0me2c3 We take the nonrelativistic Larmor radiation law as an input rather than deriving it here. 03Cross section = scattered power / incident flux The mean incident flux is I = ε₀cE₀²/2. A scattering cross section is an effective area: it tells us how much incident power is redirected, rather than measuring a little solid ball. σT = ⟨P⟩I = e46πε02me2c4 = 8π3re2 σT ≈ 6.65 × 10−29 m2 E₀² cancels. In this weak-field limit the cross section depends on neither intensity nor frequency. 04From one electron to one kilogram of gas κe = neσTρ ρ is mass density and nₑ electron number density. Opacity κ has units m²/kg. For fully ionized pure hydrogen, one electron accompanies each proton, so ρ ≈ nₑmₚ and κₑ ≈ σT/mₚ ≈ 0.040 m²/kg. For a hydrogen–helium mixture with hydrogen mass fraction X, κₑ ≈ 0.020(1 + X) m²/kg, or about 0.034 at X ≈ 0.7. Assumptions: nearly stationary free electrons, weak fields, and hν ≪ mₑc² ≈ 511 keV. At higher energies recoil matters; for bound electrons, resonances and absorption matter too. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If the electron mass doubled while other constants stayed fixed, how would σT change? Show the answer and reasoning rₑ would halve. Since σT ∝ rₑ², the cross section would become one quarter as large. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFollow the algebra leading to L ∝ M³ and state its assumptions. 01Estimate the pressure required for support Treat a star of mass M and radius R as a single region, omitting geometric coefficients. A gravitational force scale is GM²/R². Divide by an area of order R² to estimate the supporting pressure. Inside a star, with light escapingTemperature and pressure generally rise toward the centre. The light path is schematic. The circular boundaries are explanatory, not a detailed depiction of stellar layers or convection.View larger diagram ↗ ρ ∼ MR3, Pc ∼ GM2R4 The star needs higher pressure toward its centre. These are representative scale estimates, not a solution for the internal profiles. 02For gas-pressure support, central temperature scales as M/R Pc ∼ ρkBTcμmu ⇒ Tc ∼ μmuGMkBR μ is the mean mass per gas particle in units of the atomic mass constant mᵤ. The right-hand side has units of kelvin. At fixed composition, Tc ∝ M/R. This central temperature is different from the surface effective temperature Teff. The virial theorem chapter obtains the same M/R scaling from the star’s global energy. 03Luminosity from radiative diffusion In a nearly thermal interior, radiation energy density scales as aTc⁴, giving stored radiation energy of order aTc⁴R³. Divide by tdiff ∼ R²/(cℓ) and insert ℓ = 1/(κρ). Here a is the radiation constant. L ∼ acTc4Rℓ ∼ acRTc4κρ ∼ acR4Tc4κM 04The fourth powers of R cancel L ∝ R4(M/R)4κM = M3κ L ∝ M³ assumes fixed composition, nearly constant opacity, important gas-pressure support, and similar radiatively transporting structures. It is not universal: convection in low-mass stars and radiation pressure in very massive stars change the relation. Extension: nuclear temperature sensitivity and stellar radius Approximate energy production per unit mass by ε ∝ ρTcη. Then Lnuc ∼ Mε ∝ Mη + 2/Rη + 3. Equate this to L ∝ M³ in the same constant-opacity model. Rη+3 ∝ Mη−1 ⇒ R ∝ M(η−1)/(η+3) Teff ∝ (LR2)1/4 ∝ M(η+11)/[4(η+3)] For η ≈ 16 this gives R ∝ M0.79 and Teff ∝ M0.355. These are restricted-model scalings, not precision formulas for the whole main sequence. Changing the opacity law requires redoing the derivation. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If L ∝ M³, how do luminosity and fuel lifetime change when mass doubles? Show the answer and reasoning Luminosity rises by 8. If the usable fuel fraction is unchanged, lifetime ∝ M/L drops to 1/4. This neglects evolution and mixing. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Why is the Sun’s surface about 6,000 degrees? | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate effective temperature and distinguish inference from a theoretical prediction. 01Clarify “surface” and “degrees” The Sun has no solid surface. Its photosphere is the layer from which visible light escapes. Its effective temperature is about 5,772 K, or about 5,500°C. “About 6,000 degrees” is a rough statement; 6,000 K and 6,000°C are different. 02Total power = area × power per unit area F = σSBT4, L = 4πR2σSBTeff4 σSB ≈ 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, distinct from σT. Teff = (L4πR2σSB)1/4 Insert L☉ = 3.828 × 10²⁶ W and R☉ = 6.957 × 10⁸ m to obtain about 5,772 K. Effective temperature means the temperature of a blackbody with the same radius and luminosity, even if the actual spectrum is not exactly blackbody. 03How much of “why” have we answered? Measured luminosity and radius determine effective temperature. Predicting luminosity and radius from mass and composition requires a stellar model combining gravity, nuclear reactions, radiation transport, and convection. A mean free path alone cannot select 6,000 degrees. Inside the Sun, absorption, emission, scattering, and energy transport happen repeatedly. It is insufficient to picture a single core photon merely cooling on its way out. Escape becomes likely where the outward optical depth is of order unity. 04A second thermometer: the spectral shape λmaxT ≈ 2.898 × 10−3 m·K Wien’s displacement law for the peak of the wavelength spectrum Bλ. At 5,772 K the Bλ peak is near 502 nm. The Sun emits a broad spectrum, not just green light. Converting the peak of Bν using c/ν does not give the Bλ peak, because the spectral density is defined per a different variable. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At the same radius, how does effective temperature change if luminosity increases by 16? Show the answer and reasoning It doubles: Teff ∝ L1/4, and the fourth root of 16 is 2. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Mean free paths, thermal equilibrium, and Boltzmann factors | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNCalculate a mean free path and follow why a heat bath produces Boltzmann factors. 01The distance between interactions If scatterers have uniform number density n and cross section σ, a narrow path of length x encounters an expected nσx targets. Set nσℓ = 1 to find the mean free path. ℓ = 1nσ = 1κρ, τopt = Rℓ = κρR The second expression is the optical depth of a uniform medium. We write τopt to distinguish it from a lifetime. 02Many scatterings make a random walk After N random steps, the net displacement is roughly √N ℓ. Escaping a region of radius R needs N ∼ (R/ℓ)² steps. Each takes ℓ/c, giving the following diffusion-time estimate. A photon’s random walkOne possible path through many scatterings. Pale circles indicate scatterers and dark dots indicate changes of direction. The step lengths vary; their mean is the mean free path. Distinguish total path length from net displacement.View larger diagram ↗ tdiff ∼ R2cℓ (ℓ ≪ R) Scattering alone need not establish a blackbody photon distribution. Thermalization also needs processes such as sufficient absorption and emission. Dilute gas may not be in local thermodynamic equilibrium. 03An isolated whole, with a subsystem exchanging heat For an isolated “small system + large heat bath,” count the microstates at fixed total energy equally: the microcanonical starting point. The probability that the small system has energy Eᵢ is proportional to the bath’s number of states at Etot − Eᵢ. S = kB ln Ω, ΔSbath ≈ −EiT We use the thermodynamic relation that a large bath losing energy Eᵢ loses approximately Eᵢ/T of entropy while its temperature stays nearly fixed. Divide by kB and exponentiate to obtain the ratio of state counts. pi ∝ gi exp(−EikBT) gᵢ counts states with the same energy: their statistical weight. This is the canonical distribution of the subsystem. 04For two levels, simply take a ratio n2n1 = g2g1exp(−E2−E1kBT) For a 10.2 eV separation at 10⁴ K, kBT ≈ 0.862 eV, giving exp(−11.8) ≈ 7.2 × 10⁻⁶. Thermal excitation is scarce. The overall ionization fraction requires a separate calculation. Extension: entropy maximization with multipliers α and β This optional part uses derivatives, but no differential equations. For classical independent particles with populations nᵢ, Ω = N! ∏gᵢⁿⁱ/nᵢ!. At large populations use Stirling’s approximation: ln n! ≈ n ln n − n. F = ln Ω − α(Σni−N) − β(ΣniEi−U) Maximize lnΩ while keeping Σnᵢ = N and ΣnᵢEᵢ = U fixed. Differentiating with respect to each nᵢ gives −ln(nᵢ/gᵢ) − α − βEᵢ = 0. Exponentiate to solve. ni = gie−αe−βEi, β = 1kBT Identifying β uses the thermodynamic entropy–temperature relation; α normalizes particle number. Applying this classical counting directly to photons does not yield Planck’s law: photons are bosons with nonconserved number. The next chapter uses Einstein coefficients instead. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. What happens to the mean free path when the scatterer density doubles? Show the answer and reasoning It halves: ℓ = 1/(nσ), assuming the interaction cross section remains unchanged. documents.title: A small mathematical toolkit for the universe | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish equalities from estimates and calculate how a quantity scales. 01Start with “by what factor?” A sphere has area A = 4πR². Replace R by 2R to find how the area changes. Ratios like this are one of the most useful tools in astrophysics. A' = 4π(2R)2 = 4 × 4πR2 = 4A The notation a ∝ bⁿ means a = Cbⁿ with the constant C omitted. Check that C stays fixed before using a scaling relation. 02Combine powers and clear denominators R4(MR)4 = R4M4R4 = M4 You may multiply or divide both sides by the same quantity, provided you never divide by zero. A fractional power M1/3 is a cube root; M2/3 is its square. 03Four symbols with different jobs = is an equality within a model; ≈ an approximation; ∼ an order-of-magnitude estimate with coefficients omitted; ∝ a scaling under fixed conditions. An estimate cannot determine an exact coefficient. 04Units are part of the equation We generally use SI: metres, seconds, kilograms, kelvin, joules, and watts (joules per second). Useful reference scales are M☉ ≈ 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg and L☉ ≈ 3.83 × 10²⁶ W. 1 eV = 1.602 × 10−19 J The electronvolt is a unit of energy. Temperature conversions use T[K] = t[°C] + 273.15. exp(x) means eˣ, with e ≈ 2.718. The natural logarithm reverses it: ln(eˣ) = x. If these functions are new to you, start with the numerical examples. 05Keep these constants at hand c: speed of light. G: gravitational constant. h: Planck’s constant, converting photon frequency to energy. ℏ = h/(2π): reduced Planck constant. kB: Boltzmann’s constant, converting temperature to an energy scale. G ≈ 6.674 × 10−11 m3kg−1s−2 h ≈ 6.626 × 10−34 J·s kB ≈ 1.381 × 10−23 J/K ≈ 8.617 × 10−5 eV/K mₑ ≈ 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg is the electron mass; mₚ ≈ 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg is the proton mass; mᵤ ≈ 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg is the atomic mass constant. The elementary charge e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is distinct from the base e of exponential functions; context identifies which is meant. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If a sphere doubles in radius, by what factors do its area and volume change? Show the answer and reasoning Area grows by 2² = 4; volume grows by 2³ = 8. The geometric constants cancel when taking ratios. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. Particle Data Group · Astrophysical constants (2025) ↗ Next →Measuring light, measuring distance

documents.title: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNUse 2K + U = 0 to estimate temperature and track the energy released in contraction. 01Begin with one body in a circular orbit Let a small mass m orbit a dominant mass M in a circle of radius r at speed v. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: mv²/r = GMm/r². Multiply by r to obtain mv² = GMm/r. K = mv22 = GMm2r, U = −GMmr ⇒ 2K + U = 0 K is kinetic energy and U is gravitational potential energy, with zero at infinite separation. For a circular orbit this holds at each instant. Extending it to elliptical orbits and many particles requires averaging and conditions. 02Use the general theorem as a physical input 2⟨K⟩ + ⟨U⟩ = 0 For a gravitationally bound system whose overall extent does not keep growing or shrinking, this relation holds under suitable time averaging. Angle brackets denote time averages. We use the general result as an input, with the circular-orbit example providing intuition. Below we approximate a slowly evolving, quasi-static star by a self-gravitating nonrelativistic monatomic ideal gas. External surface pressure, rotation, magnetic fields, and radiation pressure are neglected, and K is the gas thermal energy. Rapid collapse, degeneracy, or dominant radiation pressure requires a different treatment. 03Estimate an internal temperature from gravity Write the gravitational energy as U ≈ −αGM²/R, with a dimensionless structure coefficient α depending on the density profile. Let N = M/(μmᵤ), and use a mean kinetic energy 3kBT̄/2 per particle. T̄ is a particle-number-weighted mean temperature. 2K = 3NkBT̄ ≈ αGM2R 3MμmukBT̄ ≈ αGM2R ⇒ T̄ ≈ αμmuGM3kBR At fixed composition and structure coefficient, T̄ ∝ M/R: halving the radius approximately doubles the mean temperature. Using the Sun’s M and R, μ ≈ 0.6, and an illustrative α = 1 gives about 4.6 million K. This is an internal temperature scale, not the central temperature or the 5,772 K surface effective temperature. 04Total energy is minus the thermal energy U = −2K ⇒ E = K+U = −K = U2 Watch the signs. A bound star has negative total energy. If it radiates while maintaining this balance at fixed mass and composition, E decreases while K increases. 05Radiating while heating up: negative heat capacity ΔE = −Q ⇒ ΔK = Q, ΔU = −2Q (Q > 0) This describes quasi-static contraction without an energy source such as nuclear burning. Gravitational energy decreases by 2Q: Q raises the thermal energy, and Q escapes as radiation. The half-and-half split follows from the signs in the energy balance. A contracting star can radiate and heat upA schematic quasi-statically contracting star supported by nonrelativistic ideal gas. Particle arrows indicate a thermal-motion scale. The decrease in gravitational energy supplies both heating and radiation.View larger diagram ↗Negative heat capacity here describes the whole self-gravitating system, including structural change. It does not mean a small gas sample has negative heat capacity at fixed volume. The present Sun is powered mainly by nuclear fusion, not contraction. Continue to stellar structure and mass–luminosity scaling → Connect the gravitational temperature scale to the transport of light. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. A star without nuclear burning contracts slowly and radiates Q = 10³⁰ J. In this model, how do K and U change? Show the answer and reasoning ΔE = −Q. Since E = −K, ΔK = +10³⁰ J; since U = −2K, ΔU = −2 × 10³⁰ J. Half the decrease in gravitational energy heats the gas and half is radiated. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics. The explanations and algebra here are written for this guide. documents.title: Why spectral lines have width | Theoretical Astrophysics, Step by Step
documents.text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDistinguish natural and thermal broadening and calculate temperature scaling. 01First define the width We use the full width at half maximum (FWHM): the full separation between the two half-height points. Standard deviations and half-widths have different numerical factors; always specify the convention. 02Finite lifetimes produce natural broadening A wave lasting only a finite time has a spread of frequencies, unlike an endless monochromatic wave. A shorter excited-state lifetime gives a broader natural line. We use the following result from wave analysis. Δνnat,FWHM = 12πτ For a long-lived lower level and negligible additional broadening. The natural profile is Lorentzian. The estimate ΔEΔt ≈ ℏ does not fix the FWHM coefficient. The exact profile convention matters. 03Atoms move toward and away from us Δνν0 ≈ vlosc, σv = √(kBTm) vlos is positive toward the observer; σv is the one-dimensional velocity standard deviation. We assume |v| ≪ c. Δνth,FWHM = ν0c√(8 ln 2 · kBTm) A Gaussian distribution of line-of-sight thermal velocities gives a Gaussian frequency profile. Its FWHM is 2√(2 ln 2) ≈ 2.355 times the standard deviation. 04Compare the widths for hydrogen at 10,000 K Hydrogen has σᵥ ≈ 9.1 km/s and a thermal FWHM of about 21 km/s. At Lyα, ν₀ ≈ 2.47 × 10¹⁵ Hz, so Δνth ≈ 1.8 × 10¹¹ Hz. A 2p lifetime of about 1.6 ns gives a natural width near 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz. Thermal broadening dominates the core in this example, but Lorentzian wings decline slowly and can still matter far from line centre. Combining the two gives a Voigt profile. Collisions, turbulence, rotation, and instruments can add further broadening. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. If the temperature of hydrogen gas quadruples, what happens to its thermal line width? Show the answer and reasoning It doubles: thermal width scales as √(T/m). At the same temperature, heavier atoms have narrower thermal lines. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics.
