documents.title: Biological model equations and numerical verification · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Biological model equations and numerical verification This survey selects 22 biological and biologically motivated model families, from population growth to stochastic gene regulation and fluid–structure coupling. It expands the equation map beyond conservation-law CFD. All 22 entries are literature and proposed benchmark designs; this addition implements no biological solver and reports no simulated biological result. The equations below use conventional simplified or normalized forms. A source identifies the model lineage, not a claim that every coefficient and variable matches that paper. The structured catalog retains references, numerical issues, verification targets and scope for each entry. The selection emphasizes numerical variety, rather than a comprehensive review of present-day mathematical biology. Sources checked on 6 November 2026. Which biological questions exercise which algorithms# Population growth and ecology: logistic, predator–prey, Fisher fronts, cross-diffusion and replicator dynamics test positive states, invariant sets, long-time behavior and spatial invasion. Demography and epidemics: age transport and compartment models test renewal boundaries, balances, nonnegative compartments and thresholds. Biochemistry and metabolism: enzyme kinetics and Monod growth connect stiff ODEs, conservation laws and reduced models. Morphogenesis: Turing analysis, Gierer–Meinhardt, Schnakenberg and Gray–Scott separate physical instability from numerical pattern selection. Excitation: Hodgkin–Huxley, FitzHugh–Nagumo and Aliev–Panfilov connect stiff reactions to pulse conduction, refractoriness and spiral waves. Gene regulation and noise: delayed feedback, toggles, repressilators and the chemical master equation need history interpolation, bifurcation analysis or jump-process simulation. Biomechanics: a fluid–elastic structure requires constitutive forces and a coupling discretization in addition to fluid equations. Existing diffusion and elliptic methods, FEM, sparse/Newton methods, stiff integrators and incompressible projection supply useful numerical building blocks. Their current tests do not verify these new biological systems. Historical model catalog# Dates identify an early source or a selected development, not an exclusive priority claim. Later spatial extensions, reductions and translations are identified with their individual entries. 01 · 1838 · Logistic population growth# Population and ecology · Survey only. Density-limited growth with carrying capacity K. It is the simplest biological ODE baseline. N˙=rN(1−N/K).N˙=rN(1−N/K). Numerical issue. Positivity, preservation of equilibria and overshoot of K; an accurate-looking curve can still violate the invariant interval. Proposed verification. Compare with N(t)=K/[1+(K/N0−1)exp(−rt)] for N0>0; measure temporal order and behavior near 0 and K. Model convention. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map. Sources: Verhulst, Pierre-François (1847). 02 · 1913 · Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics# Biochemical reactions · Survey only. Enzyme saturation; the full mass-action system resolves the transient complex C, while the rate law eliminates a fast variable. E+S⇌k−1k1C⟶k2E+P,v=Vmax⁡S/(KM+S).E+S⇌k−1​k1​​C⟶k2​E+P,v=Vmax​S/(KM​+S). Numerical issue. Fast initial layers and stiffness; full and reduced models have different validity regimes. Under the usual quasi-steady approximation KM=(k−1+k2)/k1. Proposed verification. Check E+C and S+C+P conservation in the closed mechanism. Compare reduced and full systems as enzyme/substrate scales vary, rather than calling the reduction exact. Model convention. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct. Sources: Michaelis–Menten (1913; via the 2011 translation), Briggs, George E. and Haldane, J. B. S. (1925), Johnson, Kenneth A. and Goody, Roger S. (2011). 03 · 1920 · Lotka–Volterra predator–prey# Population and ecology · Survey only. Coupled prey growth and predation; a phase-plane and long-time integration test. x˙=αx−βxy,y˙=δxy−γy.x˙=αx−βxy,y˙​=δxy−γy. Numerical issue. Positive states and artificial damping or growth of closed orbits. Periodic orbits of this idealized system are not attracting limit cycles. Proposed verification. Monitor H=δx−γ ln(x)+βy−α ln(y) for positive x,y, and compare orbit drift under step refinement. Sources: Lotka, Alfred J. (1920), Volterra, Vito (1926). 04 · 1926 · McKendrick age-structured population# Structured population transport · Survey only. Individuals move through age a at unit speed; newborns enter through a nonlocal renewal boundary. ∂tn+∂an=−μ(a)n,n(0,t)=∫0∞b(a)n(a,t) da.∂t​n+∂a​n=−μ(a)n,n(0,t)=∫0∞​b(a)n(a,t)da. Numerical issue. Upwind/FV transport in age, birth-boundary quadrature and truncation of the infinite age interval. Proposed verification. Use characteristic survival along cohorts and check d∫n da/dt=births−deaths, including any artificial oldest-age outflow. Model convention. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance. Sources: McKendrick, A. G. (1926). 05 · 1927 · SIR and SEIR compartment models# Epidemic compartments · Survey only. Closed, well-mixed normalized population fractions. SEIR adds an exposed compartment and a progression rate. s˙=−βsi,i˙=βsi−γi,r˙=γi,s+i+r=1.s˙=−βsi,i˙=βsi−γi,r˙=γi,s+i+r=1. Numerical issue. Nonnegative compartments, invariant total population and correct resolution of epidemic peak times. Proposed verification. Check total 1 and i+s−(γ/β)ln(s) for β>0,s>0; compare early growth rate βs0−γ and final-size relation in the closed SIR specialization. Model convention. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions. Sources: Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927). 06 · 1937 · Fisher–KPP invasion front# Population and ecology · Survey only. Spatial spread of an invading population or advantageous allele, represented by a reaction–diffusion front. ut=DΔu+ru(1−u),0≤u≤1.ut​=DΔu+ru(1−u),0≤u≤1. Numerical issue. Spatial and temporal front-speed errors; leading-edge resolution, positivity and finite-domain boundary contamination. Proposed verification. Use the Ablowitz–Zeppetella exact front at c=5√(Dr/6), or test the minimal speed 2√(Dr) only with the appropriate steep initial-data regime on a sufficiently large domain. Model convention. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed. Sources: Fisher, R. A. (1937), Ablowitz, Mark J. and Zeppetella, Anthony (1979). 07 · 1949 · Monod growth and chemostat# Biochemical reactions · Survey only. Nutrient-limited biomass X, substrate S, yield Y and chemostat dilution d; d=0 gives a closed batch model. μ(S)=μmax⁡SKS+S,X˙=(μ(S)−d)X,S˙=d(Sin−S)−μ(S)X/Y.μ(S)=μmax​KS​+SS​,X˙=(μ(S)−d)X,S˙=d(Sin​−S)−μ(S)X/Y. Numerical issue. Washout near a threshold, disparate resource/growth scales, positivity and the distinction between yield and rate constants. Proposed verification. For d=0 check S+X/Y. For d>0 use d(S+X/Y)/dt=d[Sin−(S+X/Y)] and verify the washout equilibrium. Model convention. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model. Sources: Monod, Jacques (1949). 08 · 1952 · Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics# Excitable systems · Survey only. Voltage and gating variables z=m,h,n describe an ionic excitable membrane. A cable extension adds spatial axial current. CmV˙=Iapp−gˉNam3h(V−ENa)−gˉKn4(V−EK)−gL(V−EL),z˙=αz(V)(1−z)−βz(V)z.Cm​V˙=Iapp​−gˉ​Na​m3h(V−ENa​)−gˉ​K​n4(V−EK​)−gL​(V−EL​),z˙=αz​(V)(1−z)−βz​(V)z. Numerical issue. Stiff gates, removable singularities in rate formulas, gating bounds, voltage/current sign and temperature conventions. Proposed verification. Select an explicitly versioned CellML/reference convention, verify resting equilibrium and gate relaxation at clamped voltage, then refine spike time and waveform. Model convention. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey. Sources: Hodgkin, A. L. and Huxley, A. F. (1952). 09 · 1952 · Turing reaction–diffusion framework# Pattern formation · Survey only. A framework for diffusion-driven pattern onset around a homogeneous reaction equilibrium, not a unique choice of f and g. ut=DuΔu+f(u,v),vt=DvΔv+g(u,v).ut​=Du​Δu+f(u,v),vt​=Dv​Δv+g(u,v). Numerical issue. Physical versus numerical instability, domain eigenmodes and errors in the discrete Laplacian dispersion relation. Proposed verification. For a selected kinetic law compare eigenvalues of J−k²diag(Du,Dv) with early-time Fourier-mode growth. Show that the k=0 reaction equilibrium is stable before asserting diffusion-driven instability. Model convention. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes. Sources: Turing, Alan M. (1952). 10 · 1961 · FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery# Excitable systems · Survey only. A normalized fast excitation/slow recovery model for pulses, refractoriness and spiral waves when extended in space. vt=DΔv+v−v3/3−w+I,wt=ϵ(v+a−bw).vt​=DΔv+v−v3/3−w+I,wt​=ϵ(v+a−bw). Numerical issue. Stiff time-scale separation, splitting error, wave-speed convergence and numerical wave breakup. Proposed verification. Check ODE fixed points/nullclines and small-perturbation eigenvalues first; then refine a 1D pulse before a 2D spiral movie. Model convention. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations. Sources: FitzHugh, Richard (1961), Nagumo, Jinichi and Arimoto, Suguru and Yoshizawa, Shuji (1962). 11 · 1970 · Keller–Segel chemotaxis# Chemotaxis · Survey only. Cell density n drifts up a chemoattractant gradient; τc=0 gives an elliptic chemical subproblem. nt=DnΔn−χ∇⋅(n∇c),τcct=DcΔc+αn−λc.nt​=Dn​Δn−χ∇⋅(n∇c),τc​ct​=Dc​Δc+αn−λc. Numerical issue. Cross-coupled flux, positivity, mass conservation and concentrated peaks; spurious undershoots must not be mistaken for physical aggregation or blowup. Proposed verification. With zero total cell flux check ∫n conservation, homogeneous equilibria and linear growth; refine the peak and domain before discussing singularity. Use manufactured smooth solutions before aggregation cases. Model convention. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics. Sources: Keller, Evelyn F. and Segel, Lee A. (1970). 12 · 1972 · Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor# Pattern formation · Survey only. A representative simplified short-range activation/long-range inhibition model. at=DaΔa+ρa2/h−μa+σa,ht=DhΔh+ρha2−νh.at​=Da​Δa+ρa2/h−μa+σa​,ht​=Dh​Δh+ρh​a2−νh. Numerical issue. The inhibitor denominator can become singular; positive h, narrow peaks and reaction stiffness require explicit treatment. Proposed verification. Choose a positive homogeneous equilibrium, check its dispersion relation and inhibitor positivity, then refine spike width and pattern wavelength. Model convention. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant. Sources: Gierer, Alfred and Meinhardt, Hans (1972). 13 · 1972 · Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries# Biomechanics · Survey only. Fluid coupled to a deformable structure; biological examples include valves and membranes, once a force/constitutive law is supplied. ρ(ut+u⋅∇u)=−∇p+μΔu+f,∇⋅u=0,Xt=u(X,t).ρ(ut​+u⋅∇u)=−∇p+μΔu+f,∇⋅u=0,Xt​=u(X,t). Numerical issue. Stiff elastic forces, pressure projection, Eulerian–Lagrangian interpolation/spreading and volume leakage. Proposed verification. Specify elastic energy and force before solving. Check force transfer, adjoint interpolation/spreading, fluid divergence and enclosed-volume drift on a simple relaxing boundary. Model convention. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling. Sources: Peskin, Charles S. (1972). 14 · 1977 · Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA# Stochastic reaction networks · Survey only. Integer molecule counts, reaction jumps νj and propensities aj; SSA samples paths of this continuous-time Markov model. ∂tP(n,t)=∑j[aj(n−νj)P(n−νj,t)−aj(n)P(n,t)].∂t​P(n,t)=j∑​[aj​(n−νj​)P(n−νj​,t)−aj​(n)P(n,t)]. Numerical issue. Correct combinatorial propensities, event ordering, absorbing states and statistical error; tau-leaping is a separate approximation. Proposed verification. Use immigration–death reactions ∅→X at constant rate k and X→∅ at rate γn: stationary counts are Poisson(k/γ). Compare ensemble mean, variance and distribution with confidence intervals. Model convention. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation. Sources: Gillespie, Daniel T. (1977). 15 · 1977 · Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback# Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Delayed feedback in a normalized physiological control model; delay can change stability and oscillatory behavior. x˙(t)=βx(t−τ)1+x(t−τ)p−γx(t).x˙(t)=1+x(t−τ)pβx(t−τ)​−γx(t). Numerical issue. A history function over [−τ,0], delayed interpolation, propagated derivative discontinuities and delay-aware adaptive stepping. Proposed verification. Check the τ=0 ODE limit, a constant equilibrium history and a manufactured forced solution. Compare long-time statistics rather than expecting chaotic trajectories to match pointwise indefinitely. Model convention. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model. Sources: Mackey, Michael C. and Glass, Leon (1977). 16 · 1978 · Replicator evolutionary game dynamics# Evolutionary dynamics · Survey only. Strategy fractions reproduce according to relative payoff in a specified matrix game. x˙i=xi[(Ax)i−xTAx],xi≥0,∑ixi=1.x˙i​=xi​[(Ax)i​−xTAx],xi​≥0,i∑​xi​=1. Numerical issue. Preserving the probability simplex, behavior near extinction boundaries, neutral cycles versus attracting equilibria. Proposed verification. Check simplex conservation, exact invariant faces and an analytically chosen game equilibrium; use the appropriate game-specific invariant or Lyapunov function. Model convention. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed. Sources: Taylor, Peter D. and Jonker, Leo B. (1978). 17 · 1979 · Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion# Pattern formation · Survey only. A simple autocatalytic kinetic law extended in space, useful for reproducible Turing-onset tests. ut=DuΔu+a−u+u2v,vt=DvΔv+b−u2v.ut​=Du​Δu+a−u+u2v,vt​=Dv​Δv+b−u2v. Numerical issue. Reaction stiffness, positive concentrations and the distinction between kinetic Hopf and spatial Turing instabilities. Proposed verification. Check u*=a+b, v*=b/(a+b)², then compare mode-growth rates with the linearized discrete and continuum operators under fixed boundaries. Model convention. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue. Sources: Schnakenberg, Jürgen (1979). 18 · 1979 · Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion# Population and ecology · Survey only. Competition with density-dependent self- and cross-dispersal can produce spatial segregation. ut=Δ[(d1+α11u+α12v)u]+u(a1−b1u−c1v),vt=Δ[(d2+α21u+α22v)v]+v(a2−b2u−c2v).ut​=Δ[(d1​+α11​u+α12​v)u]+u(a1​−b1​u−c1​v),vt​=Δ[(d2​+α21​u+α22​v)v]+v(a2​−b2​u−c2​v). Numerical issue. A coupled nonlinear diffusion matrix, loss of simple scalar maximum-principle arguments, positivity and entropy-compatible discretization. Proposed verification. Start with manufactured smooth solutions and constant-state equilibria. With reactions removed and no normal flux, conserve each species mass; check coefficient assumptions before claiming an entropy law. Model convention. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations. Sources: Shigesada, Nanako and Kawasaki, Kohkichi and Teramoto, Ei (1979). 19 · 1983 · Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis# Pattern formation · Survey only. A chemical feed/decay model whose spatial extension supports diverse spot and wave patterns. ut=DuΔu−uv2+F(1−u),vt=DvΔv+uv2−(F+k)v.ut​=Du​Δu−uv2+F(1−u),vt​=Dv​Δv+uv2−(F+k)v. Numerical issue. Sensitivity to F,k, diffusion, domain and finite-amplitude initial perturbations; grid-scale patterns and floating-point variation can affect long-time morphology. Proposed verification. Record every parameter and the perturbation seed. Verify the homogeneous (1,0) state and early perturbation response, then perform grid/time refinement of quantitative observables. Model convention. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability. Sources: Gray, Peter and Scott, Stephen K. (1983), Pearson, John E. (1993). 20 · 1996 · Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation# Excitable systems · Survey only. A reduced phenomenological excitation/recovery model for cardiac waves and restitution. ut=DΔu−ku(u−a)(u−1)−uv,vt=(ϵ0+μ1vu+μ2)[−v−ku(u−b−1)].ut​=DΔu−ku(u−a)(u−1)−uv,vt​=(ϵ0​+u+μ2​μ1​v​)[−v−ku(u−b−1)]. Numerical issue. Stiff recovery, denominator behavior and sensitivity of wave speed/restitution to resolution and time splitting. Proposed verification. Select a specific model encoding and parameters; establish single-cell and 1D conduction convergence before 2D reentry. Compare a restitution curve, not only a spiral image. Model convention. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model. Sources: Aliev, R. R. and Panfilov, A. V. (1996). 21 · 2000 · Repressilator mRNA–protein network# Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Three repressing genes form a cyclic network; retaining mRNA and protein gives six state variables. m˙i=α1+pi−1n+α0−mi,p˙i=β(mi−pi),i=1,2,3 cyclic.m˙i​=1+pi−1n​α​+α0​−mi​,p˙​i​=β(mi​−pi​),i=1,2,3 cyclic. Numerical issue. Multiple degradation scales, oscillation onset, phase error and differences between deterministic cycles and noisy individual-cell behavior. Proposed verification. Check the symmetric equilibrium and its linear stability. Compare period and amplitude under time refinement after a stated transient. Model convention. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent. Sources: Elowitz, Michael B. and Leibler, Stanislas (2000). 22 · 2000 · Genetic toggle switch# Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Mutual repression produces a possible bistable genetic switch in a normalized model. u˙=α11+vp−u,v˙=α21+uq−v.u˙=1+vpα1​​−u,v˙=1+uqα2​​−v. Numerical issue. Parameter-dependent bistability, saddle separatrices, continuation and sensitivity to perturbations near basin boundaries. Proposed verification. Find all positive equilibria and their Jacobian eigenvalues; verify hysteresis with sufficiently slow continuation and multiple initial conditions. Model convention. Bistability is not guaranteed for arbitrary Hill exponents or production rates. Induction, mRNA dynamics and noise are additional model choices. Sources: Gardner, Timothy S. and Cantor, Charles R. and Collins, James J. (2000). A verification path before attractive movies# A practical first sequence is logistic/SIR → full enzyme kinetics → Fisher front → FitzHugh–Nagumo pulse → Schnakenberg modes → Keller–Segel aggregation. Predator–prey can run alongside the Hamiltonian notebook as a long-time invariant test, while a birth–death SSA provides the first stochastic branch. Gray–Scott is a later visually useful chemical exhibit, with explicit feed rates, spatial scales, initial perturbation and source attribution. This order is an implementation proposal, separate from the historical order. An exact nonlinear front# For the scaled Fisher equation, the special front of Ablowitz–Zeppetella (1979) gives a particularly useful deterministic reference: u(x,t)=[1+exp⁡(r6D(x−ct−x0))]−2,c=5Dr6.u(x,t)=[1+exp(6Dr​​(x−ct−x0​))]−2,c=56Dr​​. A finite interval should use matching time-dependent analytic boundary data, or put boundaries far enough away and quantify the truncation effect. Compare front location, profile norms and temporal/spatial refinement separately. The special explicit front travels faster than the minimal-speed front; confusing these two reference problems would produce a false solver error. Pattern onset is a quantitative test# For a chosen two-species reaction equilibrium, form its Jacobian J. On the continuum, a Fourier mode with wavevector k evolves under L(k)=J−∣k∣2diag⁡(Du,Dv).L(k)=J−∣k∣2diag(Du​,Dv​). On a uniform square grid with a centered Laplacian, replace |k|² by κh2=4h2[sin⁡2(kxh/2)+sin⁡2(kyh/2)].κh2​=h24​[sin2(kx​h/2)+sin2(ky​h/2)]. Seed one small eigenmode, measure its early exponential growth and compare both dispersion relations. A stable k=0 reaction system and an unstable nonzero mode diagnose the selected diffusion-driven instability; nonlinear late-time spots alone do not. Schnakenberg supplies a simple kinetic law for this exercise; it should not be silently substituted for Turing's own example. Periodic and zero-flux boundaries admit different mode sets. Preserve the model before judging the method# Each future run should specify dimensional or normalized variables, the full parameter set, boundary/initial conditions, units, random seed where relevant, model version and source. Balances include boundary flux and source terms: not every biological reaction–diffusion problem conserves each species mass. Positivity fixes that clip values may change totals and extinction thresholds. An implicit diffusion step alone does not prove positivity of a split update. For stochastic networks, distinguish discretization/model approximation from finite-ensemble sampling uncertainty. For nonlinear reaction networks the ODE solution need not equal the exact stochastic mean. For delayed equations, record the history function and interpolation rule. For biochemical reductions, measure the model-reduction error separately from integration error. Sources and further branches# Murray's third-edition introduction (2002) provides a broad reading route across these branches. Physiome's Hodgkin–Huxley workspace and Aliev–Panfilov encoding are model-version references to inspect before choosing implementation parameters, rather than independent validation data. Separate follow-up surveys could cover neural population fields, spatial stochastic reaction–diffusion, intracellular polarity and mass-conserving reaction networks, cell-cycle size structure, vertex/phase-field cell mechanics, tumor/nutrient free boundaries, and population genetics with drift. These are additional branches, not a claim that the current 22 entries exhaust biological modeling. Numerical verification against a stated equation is also different from validation against organism- or experiment-specific data. documents.title: The carbuncle phenomenon · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data The carbuncle phenomenon A strong shock can develop a spurious bulge, streaks, or alternating transverse states when captured by a multidimensional numerical scheme. This carbuncle instability is a property of the discretized flow problem; a sharp-looking shock alone does not establish accuracy. Grid-aligned shocks are a particularly revealing setting. Quirk (1994) documents failures of Godunov-type solvers and motivates switching between complementary fluxes. Pandolfi and D’Ambrosio (2001) analyze shock-related instabilities and localized remedies. Their analyses motivate the diagnostic questions below; this chapter does not claim a universal mechanism or a new stability proof. Why a one-dimensional flux can fail in two dimensions# A face-normal Roe flux has the form F^n=12(Fn(UL)+Fn(UR))−12∑k∣λ~k∣ αkr~k.Fn​=21​(Fn​(UL​)+Fn​(UR​))−21​k∑​∣λk​∣αk​rk​. Its characteristic decomposition gives different dissipation to acoustic, contact, and shear waves. Near a stationary, grid-aligned shock, disturbances in neighboring rows can interact with weakly damped transverse modes and the discrete shock structure. Resolving contacts accurately and stabilizing every strong multidimensional shock are separate design demands. The entire scheme matters: reconstruction, flux, time integration, mesh, and boundaries. Odd–even decoupling describes alternating neighboring-row behavior and is a useful shock-instability diagnostic. It is related to carbuncle studies, but the terms do not identify one identical test in every paper. The familiar blunt-body shock bulge and a perturbed planar-shock experiment have different geometries and boundary conditions. Three different questions# Entropy correction: a transonic rarefaction can be represented by an inadmissible expansion shock. Smoothing a small acoustic eigenvalue addresses this sonic-wave issue. It does not by itself certify multidimensional strong-shock stability. Positivity: density and pressure must remain admissible. Wave-speed bounds, a suitable CFL restriction, and positivity-preserving reconstruction address this question. Positive states can still contain a carbuncle. Transverse shock robustness: perturbations along the shock must not grow into a grid-dependent artifact. This requires its own multidimensional evidence. The library’s 1D Roe entropy smoothing belongs to the first category. Passing Sod or the double-rarefaction test does not answer the third. Remedies and their tradeoffs# A two-wave HLL/HLLE flux or Rusanov flux usually adds more dissipation to contact and shear information than a contact-resolving solver. A shock sensor can blend a sharper flux with a more dissipative one locally. Rotated or multidimensional flux constructions seek dissipation in directions that a strictly face-normal treatment can miss. See Nishikawa and Kitamura (2008) for a rotated-hybrid approach. These are design directions, not interchangeable guarantees. A sensor may also damp a physical shear layer; excessive dissipation can conceal an instability while losing the feature of interest. State the actual wave-speed estimate: this atlas’s 2D baseline uses HLL with Davis-type bounds, not an implementation of every Einfeldt HLLE variant. What an honest comparison must measure# Use a perturbed planar strong shock, then a blunt-body flow on a controlled grid sequence. Fix the shock Mach number, shock location relative to cell faces, perturbation amplitude and wavelength, boundary conditions, reconstruction, CFL, and final time. Compare Roe, HLL/HLLE, and a proposed hybrid under matched settings. Repeat with shifted or rotated meshes. For periodic transverse rows, one possible alternating-density diagnostic at a selected shock-normal station is Aπ(i,t)=∣1Ny∑j=0Ny−1(−1)j(ρi,j(t)−ρ‾i(t))∣.Aπ​(i,t)=​Ny​1​j=0∑Ny​−1​(−1)j(ρi,j​(t)−ρ​i​(t))​. Record its time history and the maximum over the shock neighborhood, together with shock position, transverse velocity, pressure, and positivity. For a moving shock, track the shock neighborhood rather than a single fixed column. Other wavelengths need their own diagnostics. A small final residual or a visually smooth contour is insufficient evidence. Status in this edition# The Double Mach Reflection exhibit is an actual first-order HLL computation of an oblique shock interaction. It is not a controlled Roe-versus-HLL carbuncle experiment and supplies no carbuncle-free certification. The planar-shock section below adds a controlled row-perturbation diagnostic; a separate stage adds conforming-grid cylinder-forebody snapshots and controls. The physical cylindrical viscous stress and numerical shock dissipation also represent different operators. Continue with Roe’s legacy, the flux benchmarks, and the implementation roadmap. Computed planar odd–even diagnostic# Open the controlled comparison. This independent test uses a stationary Mach-6 normal shock in [0,1] × [0,0.25], γ=1.4, upstream (ρ,u,v,p)=(1.4,6,0,1), and exact normal-shock downstream states. Both x boundaries are fixed, y is periodic, and cells are square. Compare 64 × 16 and 128 × 32 at t=0.2 using first-order space, SSPRK2 and CFL 0.3. The shock is either at x=0.5, aligned with a face, or half a cell farther right. Initial conservative means integrate a row-dependent front displacement of ±10⁻⁴Δx exactly. Each configuration has an unperturbed control. Compare raw Roe, Roe with acoustic smoothing δ=0.1c̃, Davis HLL, Einfeldt-type HLLE, a pressure-sensor Roe/HLLE blend, and the common-sound-speed cubic-pressure AUSM baseline. All runs use the same spatial/time settings; their step counts and costs need not match. The blend uses S=max_neighbors |p_neighbor−p|/min(p_neighbor,p), θ=clip((S−0.05)/0.2,0,1), and the maximum adjacent cell θ at each face. F=(1−θ)F_Roe_fixed+θF_HLLE. The x-pressure jump can therefore activate HLLE on nearby transverse faces. This is an explicit educational sensor, not the published rotated-hybrid construction or a universal cure. Measure max_i Aπ over |x−xshock|<0.1, pressure/density admissibility, retry counts, transverse velocity and each row's integrated mass-deficit position. The latter is not a pointwise detected front location. Density maps subtract the transverse row mean, using one signed color range per comparison. The history's logarithmic display floors values at 10⁻¹⁶; raw values remain in the download. No state clipping or hidden flux replacement is used. Face-aligned Roe runs amplify the chosen row mode; shifting the shock half a cell changes the response substantially. The entropy correction does not remove this position sensitivity. HLL/HLLE and the other fluxes must be judged from these stated runs, rather than their names. The special Nyquist seed preserves a symmetry with zero transverse velocity even as density rows separate, so this experiment does not probe general transverse motion. Reproduce with python scripts/build_shock_robustness.py. Download all perturbed/control histories, definitions and source hashes and final conservative fields. This is not the original Quirk moving-shock/perturbed-grid duct or a blunt-body carbuncle bulge. Cylinder-forebody cases are now a separate computed stage. Other wavelengths, mesh rotations and broader CFL/strength sweeps remain required work; no carbuncle-free claim is made. See Property U for the separate single-jump algebra. Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport Chapman–Enskog（チャップマン–エンスコッグ）expansion separates kinetic relaxation from slowly varying hydrodynamic fields. The classical kinetic theory is treated by Chapman and Cowling's The Mathematical Theory of Non-Uniform Gases (first edition 1939; third edition 1970). The book's date is not the invention date of the expansion. This chapter gives an independent, unforced, isothermal lattice-BGK derivation at low Mach number. A small parameter and solvability# Introduce a bookkeeping parameter ε for slow variation: fq=fq(0)+ϵfq(1)+ϵ2fq(2)+⋯ ,∂t=ϵ∂t1+ϵ2∂t2,∇=ϵ∇1.fq​=fq(0)​+ϵfq(1)​+ϵ2fq(2)​+⋯,∂t​=ϵ∂t1​​+ϵ2∂t2​​,∇=ϵ∇1​. Conserved moments are carried by the local equilibrium, so higher-order corrections have zero mass and momentum moments: ∑qfq(k)=0,∑qcqfq(k)=0(k≥1).q∑​fq(k)​=0,q∑​cq​fq(k)​=0(k≥1). These are constraints on the expansion, not instructions to erase the nonequilibrium stress. The stress moment of f^(1) produces viscous transport. Keep the discrete-time Taylor term# For lattice BGK, expand the streaming side with D_q=∂t+c_q·∇. In lattice time units the Taylor series starts as D_q f_q + D_q² f_q/2. At successive orders, fq(0)=fqeq,fq(1)=−τD1qfqeq,fq(0)​=fqeq​,fq(1)​=−τD1q​fqeq​, ∂t2fqeq+(1−12τ)D1qfq(1)=−fq(2)τ.∂t2​​fqeq​+(1−2τ1​)D1q​fq(1)​=−τfq(2)​​. The first-order mass and momentum moments give the continuity and Euler parts. The second-order stress correction supplies the Newtonian viscous part. D2Q9 equilibrium isotropy, the low-Mach approximation, and the preceding factor give the shear viscosity ν=cs2(τ−12)Δt.ν=cs2​(τ−21​)Δt. Here τ is the dimensionless number of lattice time steps used for relaxation, with physical τ_relax=τΔt. Continuous-time BGK instead gives ν=c_s²τ_relax for the corresponding isothermal model; there is no streaming Taylor half-step in that continuous equation. Mixing those definitions yields a wrong viscosity. What this derivation does and does not establish# The D2Q9 experiment measures shear damping rather than only substituting this formula. Qian et al. (1992) is the lattice-model source; the BGK source concerns continuous kinetic relaxation. Guo et al. (2002) treats the force discretization separately; the unforced algebra above does not derive its source term. This is a formal near-equilibrium asymptotic expansion, with small gradients and small Mach number for the truncated isothermal equilibrium. It does not prove stability near shocks, justify arbitrary relaxation times, recover an energy equation, or make this model a general rarefied-gas Boltzmann solver. Burnett-order transport and thermal collision models require additional moments and analysis. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Chebyshev approximation | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Chebyshev approximation Chebyshev approximation uses endpoint-clustered nodes and a connection with trigonometric functions. Interpolation, weighted projection and best uniform approximation are distinct constructions. Problem and representative equations Set Tₖ(cosθ)=cos(kθ) and approximate f on [−1,1] by ΣaₖTₖ. Lobatto nodes xⱼ=cos(jπ/n) allow interpolation coefficients to be computed by a discrete cosine transform. Orthogonality uses weight (1−x²)⁻¹/², not the unit weight of Legendre polynomials. T0(x)=1,T1(x)=x,Tk+1(x)=2xTk(x)−Tk−1(x),xj=cos⁡(jπ/n).T0​(x)=1,T1​(x)=x,Tk+1​(x)=2xTk​(x)−Tk−1​(x),xj​=cos(jπ/n). Algorithm Map the physical interval, sample the nodes, compute coefficients and evaluate the series by recurrence. Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature integrates the interpolant; its nodes and exactness properties are not identical to Gaussian quadrature. Conditions and pitfalls Analytic functions can give rapid coefficient decay, while jumps cause Gibbs oscillations and finite smoothness slows decay. Differentiation amplifies coefficient errors. A small coefficient tail alone cannot rule out unresolved features between sampling nodes. What to check Test reproduction of Tₖ, nodal interpolation and approximation of exp(x), then compare convergence for an absolute value or jump. Measure errors off the interpolation grid and verify derivative scaling under interval maps. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Chebyshev approximation Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. C. W. Clenshaw and A. R. Curtis (1960). A method for numerical integration on an automatic computer. Numerische Mathematik Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Bibliography checked · Consulted record Bibliographic identity checked against the DOI registration on 2026-11-22. Relevant abstracts or selected passages are separately identified in the detailed-reading source notes; this is not a claim of a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. F. W. J. Olver and A. B. Olde Daalhuis and D. W. Lozier and B. I. Schneider and R. F. Boisvert and C. W. Clark and B. R. Miller and B. V. Saunders and H. S. Cohl and M. A. McClain (eds.) (2010). NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions. Official reference documentation · Selected source passages consulted · Consulted record Living official reference, not the original discovery papers. Sections 3.5 and 18.2/18.3/18.9 supply quadrature and orthogonal-polynomial conventions. The year is initial release, not a claim that the current version dates from 2010. Citation and reuse

documents.title: CIP: carry the value and the gradient · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data CIP: carry the value and the gradient The original cubic-interpolated pseudo-particle (CIP) idea stores a field and its spatial derivative, then reconstructs an upwind cubic profile. The broader family is also called constrained interpolation profile. The CIP notebook implements the original polynomial construction for constant-speed periodic scalar advection. It compares value-only linear interpolation with CIP and checks diffusion, gradient transport, oscillations, refinement, and conservation. Historical references are Takewaki–Nishiguchi–Yabe (1985) and Yabe–Aoki (1991). The accessible Saito–Obase–Abe-Ouchi (2020) paper describes CIP-family value/gradient evolution and a rational variant; its ice-sheet application and RCIP algorithm are separate from this polynomial example. Characteristics and an additional unknown# For constant velocity a, ft+afx=0,g=fx,gt+agx=0.ft​+afx​=0,g=fx​,gt​+agx​=0. At a receiving point x_i, trace backward to x_d=x_i−a dt. Interpolate both f and g from the old upwind interval at that departure point. The evolved g is an independent state variable; it is not replaced after each step by a finite difference of the updated f. For N nodes, CIP therefore stores 2N scalar unknowns, while the linear comparison stores N. For variable velocity the gradient equation instead includes stretching: gt+agx=−axg.gt​+agx​=−ax​g. Source terms, velocity variation, and compressibility require additional updates and characteristic treatment. A transported tracer f_t+a f_x=0 and a conserved density f_t+(af)_x=0 also differ when a_x is nonzero. This edition uses constant a only, where the two PDE forms coincide. Four endpoint constraints determine a cubic# On an interval of width h, with normalized coordinate s∈[0,1], the cubic is P(s)=H00(s)fL+hH10(s)gL+H01(s)fR+hH11(s)gR,P(s)=H00​(s)fL​+hH10​(s)gL​+H01​(s)fR​+hH11​(s)gR​, H00=2s3−3s2+1,H10=s3−2s2+s,H01=−2s3+3s2,H11=s3−s2.H00​H01​​=2s3−3s2+1,=−2s3+3s2,​H10​H11​​=s3−2s2+s,=s3−s2.​ The endpoint values and physical derivatives are reproduced, and the new states are f_i=P(s_d) and g_i=P′(s_d)/h. Here P′ differentiates with respect to s. For positive a, the interval is [x_{i−1},x_i] and s_d=1−a dt/h; for negative a it is [x_i,x_{i+1}] and s_d=−a dt/h. The implementation restricts |a|dt/h≤1 to keep the departure point in this adjacent interval. The case |a|dt/h=1 shifts both arrays by one node exactly. This is a complete characteristic/remapping update for this constant-speed problem, rather than a spatial RHS subsequently advanced by an arbitrary RK method. It belongs beside the RK family, not inside its list of time-integration tableaus. More general semi-Lagrangian schemes can cross multiple cells; that capability is outside this adjacent-cell example. Reproducible scalar tests# The domain is periodic [0,1], with N=128 point nodes x_i=i/N. Notebook choices are a=±1, Courant magnitudes 0.25, 0.6, or 1, and final times 0.25 or 1. The last step is shortened. Every configuration is solved independently to its selected final time, without interpolation between saved solutions. The smooth profile is 1+0.2 sin(2πx). Initial g is either its analytic derivative or the centered periodic difference. The square pulse is one on [0.2,0.4) and zero elsewhere. Its initial slopes are either zero or centered differences. Zero is an explicit convention at a sampled discontinuity, not an analytic derivative there. Consequently there is no square-pulse exact gradient error displayed. The reference f is exact translated point samples. These are not the cell-average references used in the finite-volume limiter notebook. Reported L1 means the average absolute point error. Initial-gradient choice can materially affect sharp features. The basic cubic has no TVD, monotonicity, or positivity limiter, and the square test shows overshoot and undershoot. The linear interpolation comparison is the same signed-characteristic point-value update, algebraically first-order upwind for |C|≤1. Smooth refinement uses N=32,64,128,256, a=1, Courant=0.6, and T=0.37. The computed value errors approach order three for both gradient initializations; the gradient errors are recorded separately. A cubic interpolant alone is not a fourth-order global-accuracy claim after repeated remapping. Integer Courant shifts are a special exact-translation case, so they are not used to infer a generic refinement order. No equal-cost ranking is made between the N-state linear method and the 2N-state CIP method. Why a sine wave is not a conservation proof# The exact integral of the periodic piecewise-Hermite reconstruction is M=∑i[h2(fi+fi+1)+h212(gi−gi+1)]=h∑ifi.M=i∑​[2h​(fi​+fi+1​)+12h2​(gi​−gi+1​)]=hi∑​fi​. For uniform constant-speed remapping with fraction s, its one-step change is ΔM=h2 [H10(s)+H11(s)]∑igi.ΔM=h2[H10​(s)+H11​(s)]i∑​gi​. The initial analytic sine slopes and centered differences sum to zero, so the displayed scalar runs can conserve this integral to roundoff even though the method has no universal conservative remapping property. The separate counterexample uses N=32 and a valid periodic C1 Hermite field with f_i=1 and g_i=1 at every node. This is not a constant function: each interval contains a small cubic ripple, and its derivative varies between the nodes. Its exact integral is 1. Exact translation preserves that integral, while one CIP remapping step at C=0.35 gives s=0.65,ΔM=h s(1−s)(1−2s)=−0.0021328125.s=0.65,ΔM=hs(1−s)(1−2s)=−0.0021328125. The plot shows the exact shifted original reconstruction and the reconstructed CIP field over the first four intervals. This is an intentionally constructed grid-scale test of a claimed property, not a prediction of the mass error for every smooth flow. Integrals are evaluated analytically, not by coarse quadrature. Small errors in an easy test cannot establish a stronger guarantee. Conservative and shape-preserving branches# CIP–CSL (Yabe et al., 2001) introduces an integral constraint and conservative semi-Lagrangian transport. Rational CIP / RCIP changes the reconstruction, and variants apply additional shape constraints. Conservation and boundedness require their own definitions and tests; neither follows solely from the CIP name. This edition implements the original 1D cubic only. CIP–CSL2/CSL4, RCIP, fluid advection/non-advection splitting, multidimensional mixed derivatives, and complete compressible or multiphase solvers are reading context. The existing Euler shock-tube solvers retain their documented reconstruction and flux choices. Reproduce# from numart.cip import solve_advection, mass_counterexample wave = solve_advection(profile="sine", speed=-1., cfl=0.6) pulse = solve_advection(profile="square", gradient="centered") print(mass_counterexample()["mass_after"]) python scripts/build_cip.py python scripts/sync_web_content.py docs/figures/cip.json records 48 paired CIP/linear configurations, derivative arrays, diagnostics, three refinement series, the conservation counterexample, and source hashes. The browser selects these Python-computed results. Tests check exact cubic reconstruction and derivatives, both directions, one-cell shifts, constant preservation, smooth refinement, oscillations, and the analytic mass-change identity. documents.title: Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity The formulas below use physical components in the orthonormal basis (e_r,e_phi,e_z), with cylindrical coordinates (r,phi,z), phi in radians, and r > 0. A planar polar field is obtained by setting u_z = 0 and all z derivatives to zero. Coordinate-basis tensor components have different metric factors; mixing the conventions creates incorrect viscous forces. For a reference derivation of cylindrical fluid equations, see Richard Fitzpatrick’s lecture notes. This chapter states a general bulk-viscosity convention explicitly and checks it with analytic fields. Velocity gradient: differentiate the basis too# Let L_ij = e_i · ((e_j · grad)u). Its rows are velocity components and columns are differentiation directions: L=(∂rur(∂ϕur−uϕ)/r∂zur∂ruϕ(∂ϕuϕ+ur)/r∂zuϕ∂ruz(∂ϕuz)/r∂zuz).L=​∂r​ur​∂r​uϕ​∂r​uz​​(∂ϕ​ur​−uϕ​)/r(∂ϕ​uϕ​+ur​)/r(∂ϕ​uz​)/r​∂z​ur​∂z​uϕ​∂z​uz​​​. The terms −u_phi/r and +u_r/r arise from rotation of the basis. Define D = (L+L^T)/2 and theta = tr(L): θ=∇⋅u=∂rur+urr+∂ϕuϕr+∂zuz.θ=∇⋅u=∂r​ur​+rur​​+r∂ϕ​uϕ​​+∂z​uz​. The input partials[...,i,j] in numart.coordinates means the plain coordinate derivative of physical velocity component i with respect to coordinate j = (r,phi,z). Supply the phi derivative itself, not a derivative already divided by r. Newtonian stress: all six independent components# With total stress sigma = −p I + tau, dynamic shear viscosity mu, and bulk viscosity zeta, the three-dimensional constitutive law is τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−23μ.τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−32​μ. Stokes’ hypothesis sets zeta = 0. It is a material assumption, distinct from imposing incompressibility theta = 0. Positive mu and nonnegative zeta ensure nonnegative viscous dissipation. τrr=2μ ∂rur+λθ,τϕϕ=2μr(ur+∂ϕuϕ)+λθ,τzz=2μ ∂zuz+λθ,τrϕ=μ(∂ruϕ−uϕr+∂ϕurr),τrz=μ(∂zur+∂ruz),τϕz=μ(∂zuϕ+∂ϕuzr).τrr​τϕϕ​τzz​τrϕ​τrz​τϕz​​=2μ∂r​ur​+λθ,=r2μ​(ur​+∂ϕ​uϕ​)+λθ,=2μ∂z​uz​+λθ,=μ(∂r​uϕ​−ruϕ​​+r∂ϕ​ur​​),=μ(∂z​ur​+∂r​uz​),=μ(∂z​uϕ​+r∂ϕ​uz​​).​ The lower indices here label physical components, not covariant coordinate-basis components. Off-diagonal engineering shear rates are twice the corresponding D component; applying another factor of two to the formulas above would be an error. Stress divergence: the viscous force per volume# For a symmetric physical stress tensor, f = div(tau) has components fr=∂rτrr+1r∂ϕτrϕ+∂zτrz+τrr−τϕϕr,fϕ=∂rτrϕ+1r∂ϕτϕϕ+∂zτϕz+2τrϕr,fz=∂rτrz+1r∂ϕτϕz+∂zτzz+τrzr.fr​fϕ​fz​​=∂r​τrr​+r1​∂ϕ​τrϕ​+∂z​τrz​+rτrr​−τϕϕ​​,=∂r​τrϕ​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕϕ​+∂z​τϕz​+r2τrϕ​​,=∂r​τrz​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕz​+∂z​τzz​+rτrz​​.​ The acceleration contribution is f/rho. Pressure contributes −grad(p) separately. These divergence formulas allow spatially variable mu and zeta when stress derivatives include their variation. In the Python routine, partials[...,i,j,k] is the coordinate derivative k of physical stress component (i,j). Constant viscosity and the vector Laplacian# Only for constant mu and lambda can the force be simplified to f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ.f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ. For a scalar g, let Δsg=1r∂r(r∂rg)+1r2∂ϕ2g+∂z2g.Δs​g=r1​∂r​(r∂r​g)+r21​∂ϕ2​g+∂z2​g. The physical components of the vector Laplacian are (∇2u)r=Δsur−urr2−2r2∂ϕuϕ,(∇2u)ϕ=Δsuϕ−uϕr2+2r2∂ϕur,(∇2u)z=Δsuz.(∇2u)r​(∇2u)ϕ​(∇2u)z​​=Δs​ur​−r2ur​​−r22​∂ϕ​uϕ​,=Δs​uϕ​−r2uϕ​​+r22​∂ϕ​ur​,=Δs​uz​.​ For incompressible constant-viscosity flow, theta vanishes, but the radial and azimuthal vector-Laplacian metric terms remain. For variable coefficients, pulling mu outside derivatives omits terms 2D·grad(mu) and theta grad(lambda). Evaluate the full stress divergence instead. Axisymmetry, polar slices, and material acceleration# Axisymmetry removes phi derivatives, not the terms u_r/r, −u_phi/r, or the stress-divergence metric terms. Axisymmetric flow may still have swirl. For a planar polar slice of a three-dimensional Newtonian fluid, retain the 2mu/3 bulk correction and tau_zz = lambda theta. A genuinely two-dimensional constitutive model uses a different deviatoric trace subtraction and must be declared separately. The scalar advective derivative is D_s/Dt = partial_t + u_r partial_r + (u_phi/r) partial_phi + u_z partial_z. Vector material acceleration has extra radial and azimuthal terms: ar=DsurDt−uϕ2r,aϕ=DsuϕDt+uruϕr,az=DsuzDt.ar​=DtDs​ur​​−ruϕ2​​,aϕ​=DtDs​uϕ​​+rur​uϕ​​,az​=DtDs​uz​​. These inertial terms are different from viscous metric terms. Coordinate-basis tensors and transformations# The cylindrical coordinate basis is (partial_r,partial_phi,partial_z) = (e_r,r e_phi,e_z), with metric diag(1,r²,1). Thus physical u_phi = r u^phi, and physical tau_phi,phi = r² tau^{phi,phi} = tau_{phi,phi}^{coordinate}/r². Covariant, contravariant, and physical arrays cannot be substituted for one another without these factors. Nonzero Christoffel symbols include Gamma^r_phi,phi = −r and Gamma^phi_r,phi = Gamma^phi_phi,r = 1/r. Covariant differentiation accounts for the same basis changes included explicitly above. The Cartesian transformation uses the orthogonal matrix Q with columns e_r, e_phi, e_z: L_cart = Q L_cyl Q^T and tau_cart = Q tau_cyl Q^T. Analytic checks and the axis# Rigid rotation: u_phi = Omega r gives antisymmetric L, D = 0, and zero viscous stress. Using partial_r u_phi alone would incorrectly create shear. Pipe Poiseuille flow: u_z = Umax(1−r²/R²) gives tau_rz = −2 mu Umax r/R² and f_z = −4 mu Umax/R². Steady axial momentum requires dp/dz = f_z. Circular Couette flow: u_phi = A r+B/r gives tau_rphi = −2 mu B/r² and zero azimuthal viscous-force divergence away from boundaries. Cartesian affine fields: random constant Cartesian velocity gradients are transformed into cylindrical data and back. Constant Cartesian stresses have zero divergence after angular basis derivatives are included. The tests also verify the dissipation identity τ:D=2μDdev:Ddev+ζθ2≥0.τ:D=2μDdev​:Ddev​+ζθ2≥0. These routines require r > 0. At the axis, use regularity and analytic limits rather than replacing r by a small arbitrary number. For a smooth axisymmetric field, u_r and u_phi are O(r), and u_z = u_z(0)+O(r²). Then the axial scalar radial Laplacian tends to 2 partial_r² u_z. Nonaxisymmetric regular Cartesian fields have different component limits; even uniform Cartesian translation need not have u_r = O(r). import numpy as np from numart.coordinates import cylindrical_velocity_gradient, newtonian_stress r, omega = 0.7, 2.0 u = np.array([0., omega*r, 0.]) du = np.zeros((3,3)); du[1,0] = omega L = cylindrical_velocity_gradient(r, u, du) assert np.allclose(newtonian_stress(L), 0.) The code checks tensor identities at supplied points. A cylindrical Navier–Stokes PDE solver, axis boundary scheme, and spherical-coordinate implementation remain future work. documents.title: Differential-algebraic equations / DAE | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Differential-algebraic equations / DAE A DAE combines differential evolution with algebraic constraints. An implicit ODE is not necessarily a DAE; singular dependence on derivatives is central to the distinction. Problem and representative equations Use F(t,y,ẏ)=0. A semi-explicit system ẋ=f(x,z,t), 0=g(x,z,t) with invertible g_z is a representative locally eliminable index-1 case. Several index definitions exist; differentiation index concerns differentiating constraints to obtain an explicit ODE. F(t,y,y˙)=0,y˙n+1≈α0yn+1+∑j=1kαjyn+1−jΔt,JN=Fy+α0ΔtFy˙.F(t,y,y˙​)=0,y˙​n+1​≈Δtα0​yn+1​+∑j=1k​αj​yn+1−j​​,JN​=Fy​+Δtα0​​Fy˙​​. Algorithm BDF methods approximate ẏ from the state history and solve F=0 using Newton iterations. The Newton matrix includes F_y+α₀F_ẏ/Δt. Initial values and derivatives must be consistent with both algebraic constraints and F(t₀,y₀,ẏ₀)=0. Conditions and pitfalls Higher-index systems can contain hidden constraints, drift and degraded error control, requiring index reduction or projection formulations. Smaller ODE time steps alone do not fix these issues. Scale tolerances separately for differential and algebraic variables and their units. What to check For an index-1 system with known solution, measure state error, F residual, algebraic-constraint violation and initialization consistency. Vary steps, nonlinear tolerances and initial perturbations; record constraint drift and termination reasons. documents.title: Double Mach Reflection · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Double Mach Reflection This exhibit computes a Mach-10 shock reflecting from a wall using the two-dimensional ideal-gas Euler equations. The benchmark is associated with Woodward and Colella (1984). NASA’s LAVA tutorial is a modern implementation reference. Equations and initial states# Use gamma = 1.4 on [0,4] × [0,1], with conserved state U = (rho, rho u, rho v, E) and E = p/(gamma−1) + rho(u²+v²)/2. The initial shock intersects the bottom wall at x = 1/6 and makes a 60-degree angle with it: xs(y,0)=16+y3.xs​(y,0)=61​+3​y​. The post-shock state to its left is (rho,u,v,p) = (8, 8.25 sqrt(3)/2, −4.125, 116.5). The ambient state to its right is (1.4,0,0,1). The upstream sound speed is one, so the shock-normal propagation speed of ten corresponds to Mach 10. Initial cell states are assigned by the cell-center side of the shock; cut-cell averages are not integrated exactly. The moving incident-shock line is xs(y,t)=16+y+20t3.xs​(y,t)=61​+3​y+20t​. These states satisfy the moving Rankine–Hugoniot relation in the shock-normal direction; the automated check uses normal (sqrt(3)/2,−1/2) and speed 10. Boundary conditions and discretization# The left boundary supplies the post-shock state. The right boundary uses zero-gradient outflow. At the bottom, x < 1/6 supplies post-shock data; the remaining wall reflects normal momentum. The top boundary assigns the two states using x_s(1,t). SSPRK2 stages evaluate this boundary at their corresponding stage times. The calculation uses piecewise-constant finite volumes, a two-wave HLL flux with Davis-type minimum/maximum acoustic speeds, and an unsplit flux divergence. The step is bounded by Δt=C[max⁡(∣u∣+c)Δx+max⁡(∣v∣+c)Δy]−1.Δt=C[Δxmax(∣u∣+c)​+Δymax(∣v∣+c)​]−1. The displayed run has Nx = 256, Ny = 64, delta x = delta y = 1/64, C = 0.4, final time 0.2, and 811 steps. Its minimum final density is 1.4 and minimum final pressure is 1.0. These are measured diagnostics for this run, not a general positivity theorem. Reproduce and inspect# python -m numart.cli run double-mach --n 64 --cfl 0.4 --output outputs/double-mach Here --n sets Ny and Nx = 4 Ny. The command saves solution.npz, run.json, and double-mach.png. The gallery snapshot includes its run manifest and conserved-state arrays. Array q has shape (Nx,Ny,4); x and y are cell-center coordinates. The manifest records source hashes and the working-tree state at generation time. What the figure establishes# The image shows a computed incident/reflected shock pattern, with density and thirty density contours. First-order spatial reconstruction is deliberately diffusive. This grid does not resolve the fine wall jet and roll-up of high-resolution PPM or adaptive calculations. There is no exact final-time solution, grid-convergence study, or digitized original-paper comparison in this exhibit. Tests check equal-state flux consistency, a periodic uniform state, the incident-shock jump relation, moving-top and reflecting-wall data, and admissible states in a small-grid run. They do not establish convergence of the full reflection pattern. Further work should add higher-order reconstruction, refinement, and independent reference-code comparisons. For strong-shock instability diagnostics, continue to the carbuncle phenomenon. This HLL image is not a demonstration that a Roe implementation is stable or unstable. Watch the reflection evolve# The saved-state movie shows density and pressure from the same 256 × 64 calculation. It includes actual physical times, solver steps, fixed scales, frame inspection, and MP4 export. Read the sampling definitions. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: DSMC and kinetic transport | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: DSMC and kinetic transport DSMC approximates dilute-gas Boltzmann collisions by stochastic collisions between computational particles. It differs from deterministic pair-potential molecular dynamics and from self-consistent plasma PIC fields. Problem and representative equations Consider Boltzmann f with molecular velocity v, acceleration a and collision operator Q. A simulator particle represents F_N physical molecules. In a cell of volume V_c, sample pair collisions according to total cross section σ_T and relative speed g. State the phase-space number-density normalization of f. ∂tf+v⋅∇xf+a⋅∇vf=Q(f,f),Ppair∼FNσTg ΔtVc.∂t​f+v⋅∇x​f+a⋅∇v​f=Q(f,f),Ppair​∼Vc​FN​σT​gΔt​. Algorithm Move particles, apply wall/boundary interactions and sample collisions within cells. A representative no-time-counter algorithm uses a bound on gσ_T for candidate selection and acceptance. Specify hard-sphere, VHS or another collision model, distinguishing Bird’s early construction from later algorithms. Conditions and pitfalls DSMC uses dilute-gas and molecular-chaos assumptions. Compare cell size with mean free path and step size with mean collision time; adequate resolution is problem dependent. In low-speed flow, the macroscopic signal can be buried in thermal noise, and longer averaging does not remove discretization bias. What to check Test homogeneous velocity relaxation, Maxwellian equilibrium, wall-driven Couette flow or a rarefied shock. Check collision-level momentum/energy conservation, cell/step/particle-count sensitivity and uncertainty accounting for correlated samples. documents.title: Krylov eigenvalue solvers | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Krylov eigenvalue solvers Krylov eigensolvers approximate a few eigenpairs through a small subspace instead of diagonalizing a large matrix in full. Arnoldi, symmetric Lanczos and shift-invert require different assumptions. Problem and representative equations Build Kₘ(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Aᵐ⁻¹v}. Arnoldi gives an orthonormal Vₘ and upper-Hessenberg Hₘ. Solve Hₘy=θy and set x=Vₘy. The last Arnoldi vector and hₘ₊₁,ₘ give the Ritz residual. AVm=VmHm+hm+1,mvm+1emT,∥Ax−θx∥2=∣hm+1,memTy∣(∥y∥2=1).AVm​=Vm​Hm​+hm+1,m​vm+1​emT​,∥Ax−θx∥2​=∣hm+1,m​emT​y∣(∥y∥2​=1). Algorithm Expand the basis using matrix-vector products and orthogonalization, solve the projected eigenproblem and restart when needed. Hermitian matrices permit a Lanczos three-term recurrence. Shift-invert targets interior eigenvalues but each inverse action requires a linear solve. Conditions and pitfalls Finite-precision loss of orthogonality can create ghost duplicates. For nonnormal matrices, a small residual need not imply a comparably small eigenvalue error. State B and the inner product in generalized problems Ax=λBx, and assess inner-solve tolerances for shift-invert. What to check Check scaled residuals ∥Ax−θx∥/(∥A∥+|θ|), orthogonality, known eigenpairs and clustered/repeated eigenvalues. For symmetric cases compare Rayleigh quotients, and record restarts and initial-vector sensitivity. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. documents.title: Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration Parabolic problems: evolving diffusion# Solve u_t=νu_xx on [0,1] with zero Dirichlet boundaries and initial data sin(πx). The reference solution is u=exp(-νπ²t)sin(πx). numart.linear.diffusion_1d returns interior nodes. Second-order centered differences and the θ method give (I−θνΔtDxx)un+1=(I+(1−θ)νΔtDxx)un.(I−θνΔtDxx​)un+1=(I+(1−θ)νΔtDxx​)un. θ=0: FTCS, requiring r=νΔt/h²≤1/2. θ=1: backward Euler, first order in time and unconditionally stable for linear diffusion. θ=1/2: Crank–Nicolson, second order in time and A-stable for linear diffusion. The Fourier amplification factor is G=[1-4(1-θ)r sin²(ξ/2)]/[1+4θr sin²(ξ/2)]. For large r, Crank–Nicolson can have negative G: high-frequency modes alternate sign while remaining stable. Stability, positivity, monotonicity, and temporal resolution need separate checks. Crank–Nicolson (1947). spectral_diffusion solves a separate periodic problem by multiplying each Fourier coefficient by exp(-νk²t). Accuracy comparisons with the Dirichlet finite-difference problem must account for their different boundaries. Thomas elimination: from implicit steps to tridiagonal systems# For subdiagonal a, diagonal b, and superdiagonal c, forward elimination uses m_i=a_i/b'_{i-1}, b'_i=b_i-m_i c_{i-1}, and d'_i=d_i-m_i d'_{i-1}. Back substitution uses x_i=(d'_i-c_i x_{i+1})/b'_i. Both work and storage are O(N). thomas preserves its inputs and raises an error for a small pivot. It uses elimination without pivoting, so it is not safe for every tridiagonal matrix. The diffusion matrices used here are strictly diagonally dominant. The original 1949 Thomas report has not been inspected; the historical citation and the verification of this modern implementation are separate claims. Elliptic problems: the Poisson equation# The sign convention is -Δu=f. In 1D, use a tridiagonal system and Thomas elimination; in 2D, use a five-point stencil with matrix-free conjugate gradients or multigrid. Default manufactured solutions are sin(πx) in 1D and sin(πx)sin(πy) in 2D. Check the linear-system residual separately from the discretization error relative to the continuous solution. Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundaries# Dirichlet specifies u=g_D; Neumann specifies the outward normal derivative ∂u/∂n=g_N; Robin specifies αu+β∂u/∂n=g. The normal derivative is -u_x at the left end and +u_x at the right. Outward conductive heat flux is -k∂u/∂n, so both the specified quantity and its sign matter. Pass Boundary.dirichlet(value), Boundary.neumann(value), or Boundary(alpha,beta,value) to poisson_boundary_1d. Robin and Neumann conditions eliminate ghost points and use half weights at the endpoints. The time-dependent diffusion_1d currently supports zero Dirichlet boundaries. A pure-Neumann Poisson solution is determined only up to an additive constant. The divergence theorem requires ∫Ωf dV=−∫∂ΩgN dS.∫Ω​fdV=−∫∂Ω​gN​dS. The implementation checks the discrete compatibility condition corresponding to trapezoidal quadrature and fixes the constant with a prescribed mean, defaulting to zero. Some Robin coefficients also lead to a loss of uniqueness. Periodic Poisson problems similarly need zero-mode compatibility and a mean constraint, with the endpoints identified. Spectral radius of the iteration matrix# For a stationary iteration x^{k+1}=T x^k+c solving Ax=b, errors satisfy e^{k+1}=T e^k. In finite dimensions, convergence for every initial error is equivalent to ρ(T)<1, where ρ(T)=max |λ_i(T)|. This differs from the radius of convergence of a power series, R=1/limsup |a_n|^{1/n}, and from a Newton iteration's basin of convergence. With A=D+L+U, Jacobi has T=-D^{-1}(L+U), Gauss–Seidel has T=-(D+L)^{-1}U, and SOR has T=(D+ωL)^{-1}[(1-ω)D-ωU]. iteration_matrix and spectral_radius support small-matrix demonstrations. Nonnormal matrices can exhibit transient error growth even when ρ<1. The system condition number κ(A) and iteration spectral radius ρ(T) measure different properties. Netlib Templates. Red-black Gauss–Seidel and SOR# Color the five-point grid with (i+j) mod 2. Updates of one color depend only on the other color; update red, then black. Set ω=1 for Gauss–Seidel and use 0<ω<2 for SOR relaxation. This interval alone does not guarantee convergence for arbitrary nonsymmetric systems. The implementation targets symmetric positive-definite Dirichlet Poisson problems. Geometric multigrid V-cycle# Apply three red-black Gauss–Seidel sweeps on the fine grid. Compute r_h=f_h-A_h u_h. Restrict the residual by full weighting. Solve the coarse-grid error equation recursively. Prolongate the correction bilinearly. Apply three more fine-grid sweeps. Each side has N=2^k-1 interior nodes. Coarse grids use rediscretized five-point operators, and the one-unknown coarsest problem is solved directly. Tests check interpolation, restriction, grid spacing, and boundary consistency. Variable coefficients, anisotropy, curved grids, AMG, and FAS are outside this edition. Fedorenko (1961), Brandt (1977). For a teaching path, start with Briggs–Henson–McCormick, A Multigrid Tutorial, second edition (2000), then use Trottenberg–Oosterlee–Schüller, Multigrid for local Fourier analysis, algorithm design and advanced applications. The textbook guide explains where each book fits. Their broader scope includes methods beyond the geometric V-cycle implemented here. Particle and disk gravity# The new particle-gravity chapter connects PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid. Gravity boundary kernels adds Hockney–Eastwood isolated convolution and Koyama–Ostriker slab Fourier kernels. The existing multigrid example retains its 2D zero-Dirichlet operator; it is not a 3D open-boundary gravity solver. Further routes to diffusion and elliptic problems# See continuous P1 FEM for weak-form assembly, GMRES/ILU and nonlinear solves for nonsymmetric systems, and Nishikawa hyperbolic diffusion for auxiliary-gradient pseudo-time iteration. The equation gallery separately shows physical-time heat diffusion. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Same-system Poisson comparison# Open the Poisson solver notebook. All 2D methods solve one constant-coefficient five-point SPD system on the unit square with zero Dirichlet boundaries. N=31,63,127 counts interior nodes per side, hence N² unknowns. Every iterative method starts from zero. The common stopping criterion uses the explicitly recomputed true residual, including for CG: (Ahu)ij=4uij−ui−1,j−ui+1,j−ui,j−1−ui,j+1h2,h=1N+1,∥f−Ahu∥2∥f∥2≤10−8.(Ah​u)ij​=h24uij​−ui−1,j​−ui+1,j​−ui,j−1​−ui,j+1​​,h=N+11​,∥f∥2​∥f−Ah​u∥2​​≤10−8. Forcing choices are a broad smooth manufactured field and two localized opposite-sign sources. The manufactured solution is u=x(1−x)e^(2x)y(1−y)e^(−1.5y), with f=−Δu differentiated analytically. The localized forcing is 100exp(−[(x−0.28)²+(y−0.35)²]/0.006) −60exp(−[(x−0.70)²+(y−0.65)²]/0.012), with no continuous exact solution supplied. Algebraic error is nodal RMS against the FFT/DST discrete solution; continuous nodal RMS for the manufactured field measures discretization error. Neither is a continuous integral L2 norm. Tight residuals do not remove second-order discretization error. The separate N=31 single-sine diagnostic uses u=sin(πx)sin(πy) and f=2π²u. It is one eigenvector of this discrete matrix: exact-arithmetic CG requires one iteration from zero. It is therefore unsuitable as the sole general solver benchmark. Broad forcing avoids this shortcut. The compared configurations are Jacobi, weighted Jacobi (ω=2/3), red-black Gauss–Seidel, red-black SOR, unpreconditioned CG, the existing geometric multigrid V-cycle, DST+Thomas and FFT/DST direct elimination. SOR uses ω=2/[1+sin(π/(N+1))] for this model and ordering. This is not a generally optimal setting for arbitrary meshes/operators. A sweep, CG iteration and V-cycle are different work units. Multigrid has three pre/post RBGS sweeps at every level and additional coarse-grid work. Its cycle count is not a fine-grid sweep count. Netlib's SOR discussion provides the method context. The FFT route uses an orthonormal DST-I computed with an odd extension and NumPy FFT, following the DST-I definition. The 1D eigenvalues of the difference operator are λk=4h⁻²sin²[kπ/(2(N+1))]; in 2D divide by λk+λl. This solves the same discrete operator, rather than substituting continuum wave numbers k². Zero Dirichlet boundaries are not periodic boundaries. No SciPy dependency is required by the implementation. Plain Thomas solves 1D tridiagonal systems. The 2D separable direct route transforms y, solves N shifted tridiagonal x systems with Thomas, then applies the inverse transform. It is labeled DST+Thomas, not a generic 2D Thomas solver. Both FFT/DST routes rely on constant coefficients, a rectangular uniform mesh and separable boundary conditions. A separate 1D table compares plain Thomas with FFT/DST at N=63,255,1023 for u=x(1−x)e^(2x). Timing protocol and downloadable evidence# Each configuration is run three times after a small N=7 code-path warmup. The reported median trial supplies its own convergence history. Wall time includes solver setup, allocations, per-unit true-residual checks and logging; it excludes imports, problem/reference generation, file I/O and plotting. No cached factorization/eigenvalues are reused between trials. The 1D timings also include their final residual check. Hardware/software metadata and all three times are saved. Python loops and compiled NumPy kernels have different costs; these measurements rank these diagnostic implementations on one host, not algorithms independently of implementation or hardware. Direct solvers have only a completed-solve endpoint marker. The chart samples long histories and floors displayed residuals at 10⁻¹⁴; full values are in the table and download. The NPZ retains every selected-trial residual/timestamp and final fields. CG's recursive residual chooses directions, but its true residual decides convergence. Residual histories need not be monotone. Reproduce with python scripts/build_poisson_comparison.py. Download settings, sampled histories, timings and source hashes and fields and full selected histories. Tests independently check DST against a dense sine matrix, direct solves against dense linear systems, common true residuals, all method solutions, zero forcing and manufactured second-order refinement. Variable coefficients, anisotropy, irregular meshes, periodic/pure-Neumann nullspaces and parallel scaling require separate comparisons. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm The local Web edition provides an Equations gallery with saved profiles, physical-time controls, fixed plot ranges, initial/boundary conditions, characteristic speeds and links back to methods and papers. It contains nine cases across seven equation families. Data are generated by python scripts/build_equation_gallery.py, not invented animation curves. Translation and diffusion# Linear advection u_t+u_x=0 moves a periodic sine wave. First-order upwind with forward Euler is compared with exact translated cell averages. Heat diffusion u_t=0.02u_xx damps the same Fourier mode; centered spatial differences and forward Euler use νΔt/Δx²≤0.4. Their discrete means are conserved. Burgers: shocks and fans# Burgers (1948) is the classical model reference; this exhibit uses its inviscid scalar conservation law: ut+(u2/2)x=0,f′(u)=u.ut​+(u2/2)x​=0,f′(u)=u. A decreasing jump forms a shock traveling at (u_L+u_R)/2. An increasing jump forms a rarefaction fan, with u=x/t in coordinates centered on the initial jump. Exact Godunov flux selects the entropy solution, including zero flux inside a transonic Burgers fan. The plotted exact curves are cell integrals, so a shock cutting a cell is not treated as a point sample. Traffic: a jam can move against the cars# Lighthill–Whitham (1955) and Richards (1956) are the independent classical traffic references. This exhibit chooses a normalized quadratic fundamental diagram, rather than asserting that every traffic model has it: ρt+[ρ(1−ρ)]x=0,0≤ρ≤1.ρt​+[ρ(1−ρ)]x​=0,0≤ρ≤1. Vehicles move at 1−ρ, while small density disturbances move at 1−2ρ. A jump from 0.3 to 0.9 shocks at speed −0.2, despite positive vehicle speeds. The opposite ordering creates a clearing fan because the flux is concave. Both Burgers and traffic use MUSCL minmod, Godunov flux, SSPRK3 and CFL≤0.4. Density bounds are checked; the solver does not silently clip them. Fluid systems and kinetic methods# The existing Euler Sod, wet shallow-water dam-break and isothermal density-jump solvers are connected as additional cases. All three now overlay conserved cell means from semi-analytic Riemann references: known wave fronts split Gauss quadrature, and the 24/48-point difference estimates integration convergence. The reference library explains the formulas, root residuals and point-versus-mean convention. Dry-bed reference formulas do not extend the positive-state numerical solver to dry states. Those models and positive-depth limits are defined in the benchmark guide. LBM, Chapman–Enskog expansion, periodic incompressible flow, and hyperbolic diffusion have separate computed exhibits. An equation, a kinetic model and a discretization are different choices. Saved times and reproducibility# Scalar snapshots observe completed solver steps: their actual times can differ slightly from the requested display times. Output requests leave the trajectory unchanged. The existing 1D system baseline has no snapshot API; its displayed fluid times are explicitly labeled independent solves, each ending at the shown time. Playback links those runs and does not imply identical intermediate steps. Outflow mean changes include boundary flux and are not labeled mass loss. Download profiles and source hashes. Additional convergence evidence keeps these new experiments separate from the atlas's original validation manifest. Additional equation maps# The biological survey catalogs 22 model families with original references and proposed verification, without adding biological simulations. The Arakawa grid chapter adds computed A/B/C Fourier-symbol comparisons for linear rotating shallow water, rather than another fluid movie. These statuses remain distinct from the nine precomputed cases above. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Ewald summation | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Ewald summation Ewald summation evaluates periodic Coulomb interactions through complementary real- and reciprocal-space sums. It defines a different boundary-value problem from simply truncating 1/r at a finite radius. Problem and representative equations Consider point charges qᵢ in a neutral, triply periodic cell. Set rᵢⱼₙ=rᵢ−rⱼ+n, cell volume V, splitting parameter α>0 and reciprocal vector k. S(k) is the charge structure factor. The energy below uses unit Coulomb prefactor, omits k=0 and assumes a conducting macroscopic boundary. The prime excludes only i=j,n=0. S(k)=∑jqjeik⋅rj,E=12∑i,j,n′qiqjerfc⁡(αrijn)rijn+2πV∑k≠0e−k2/(4α2)k2∣S(k)∣2−απ∑iqi2.S(k)E​=j∑​qj​eik⋅rj​,=21​i,j,n∑′​qi​qj​rijn​erfc(αrijn​)​+V2π​k=0∑​k2e−k2/(4α2)​∣S(k)∣2−π​α​i∑​qi2​.​ Algorithm Accumulate screened real-space pairs and Gaussian-damped reciprocal modes, then subtract the self energy. Restore the same Coulomb prefactor to every term in dimensional units. Changing α redistributes work between sums but cannot change their converged total. Derive forces from the same energy convention. Conditions and pitfalls A net-charged cell requires an additional convention such as a compensating background. Specify potential gauge, surface term, periodic self images and molecular exclusions separately. A periodic gravitational Poisson solve changes the kernel/sign and mean-density treatment; it is not the same calculation. What to check For a small neutral configuration, increase both cutoffs independently and test α independence. Compare forces with finite differences of energy, and check translation invariance and net force. Agreement between two unconverged sums is not independent validation. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Ewald summation Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. Ewald, P. P. (1921). Die Berechnung optischer und elektrostatischer Gitterpotentiale. Annalen der Physik Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Bibliography checked · Consulted record Reviewed as a source for priority-method metadata. The individual method records distinguish reference roles, relevant full-text passages, abstracts and bibliographic checks; this does not imply a new numerical validation. Hockney, R. W. and Eastwood, J. W. (1981). Computer Simulation Using Particles. McGraw-Hill Author monograph / supporting reference · Bibliography checked · Consulted record Original book date is 1981, as cited by Barnes and Hut (1986); DOI identifies a later Taylor & Francis reissue. Reference for particle-mesh methods and isolated doubled-domain convolution; the self-cell kernel convention is stated separately in our code. Citation and reuse
