documents.title: Interactive experiment guide · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Interactive experiment guide The basis notebook adds computed reference-element algebra: Legendre and Lagrange shapes, exact versus GLL-quadrature matrices, smooth/jump approximation, and triangular P2 functions. Its saved arrays and source hashes come from scripts/build_basis.py; it does not introduce a new PDE evolution solver. The web edition now includes a stability laboratory and a convergence notebook. The laboratory computes in the browser; the convergence notebook displays measurements from the original gallery manifest. These are distinct sources of evidence. Periodic advection in the browser# The model is ut+aux=0,x∈[0,1],u(x+1,t)=u(x,t).ut​+aux​=0,x∈[0,1],u(x+1,t)=u(x,t). Use 64 cell-centered sample points, h=1/64, velocity a=+1 or a=-1, and Δt=|C|h. The signed Courant number is C=aΔt/h. The controls expose 0.05≤|C|≤1.5 and 0–100 time steps. The exact comparison samples the continuous translated profile u(x-at,0) at the same grid points. Initial data can be a sine wave, a square pulse equal to one on [0.25,0.65) and zero elsewhere, or a sine wave with small high-frequency perturbations: u(x,0)=sin⁡(2πx)+10−3[sin⁡(2π(N/2)x)+cos⁡(2π(N/4)x)].u(x,0)=sin(2πx)+10−3[sin(2π(N/2)x)+cos(2π(N/4)x)]. The ripple seeds both Nyquist and shorter resolved grid-scale modes. It makes unstable growth visible without relying on machine roundoff. The square pulse illustrates smearing and dispersive oscillations; it is not a smooth convergence test. Four discrete updates# numart.advection.difference_step and the browser implement FTCS, upwind, classical Lax–Friedrichs, and Lax–Wendroff. Upwind switches stencil with the velocity sign. The stability chapter develops their context. For FTCS, ujn+1=ujn−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n),G(θ)=1−iCsin⁡θ.ujn+1​=ujn​−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​),G(θ)=1−iCsinθ. Its squared amplification is 1+C²sin²θ. Consequently, nonzero C produces growing modes even when the necessary domain-of-dependence bound |C|≤1 is met. Upwind, LF, and LW satisfy the Fourier stability criterion for this periodic constant-coefficient problem when |C|≤1. The solution plot updates alongside |G(θ)|. The reported maximum samples all distinct real-data Fourier wavenumbers of the 64-point grid. The dashed threshold marks |G|=1. When the solution grows, its vertical scale expands rather than clipping the computed values. Pointwise L1 error, maximum amplitude, and arithmetic mean drift are reported separately. These properties concern this linear periodic model. They do not transfer automatically to nonlinear systems, other boundaries, or a different time integrator. With unstable growth, cancellation and floating-point rounding can also corrupt the measured mean. Reproducibility and export# The browser kernels are compared with 24 reference cases generated from the Python implementation: four methods, six signed Courant numbers, and twelve updates per case. Tests compare complete sample arrays and complex Fourier amplification factors. Separate tests check exact one-cell translation at unit CFL, direction reversal, periodic wrapping, and observed-order arithmetic. The fixture records the SHA-256 of numart/advection.py; a source mismatch fails the browser numerical tests until the reference export is refreshed. The experiment download contains settings, grid coordinates, initial, computed, and exact samples, diagnostics, and the Python reference hash. It records a calculation performed in JavaScript, rather than claiming that Python runs in the browser. To apply the same stencil from Python: import numpy as np from numart.advection import difference_step n, courant, steps = 64, 0.8, 40 x = (np.arange(n) + 0.5) / n q = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) for _ in range(steps): q = difference_step(q, courant, "lax-wendroff") exact = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (x - courant * steps / n)) print("pointwise L1 error:", np.mean(abs(q - exact))) Reading a refinement study# The notebook uses the first-edition docs/figures/validation.json measurements. The original manifest, including source hashes and runtime versions, is available for download. These data predate the browser laboratory and are not new wall-clock measurements. For successive meshes, the displayed observed order is pobs=log⁡(Ecoarse/Efine)log⁡(Nfine/Ncoarse).pobs​=log(Nfine​/Ncoarse​)log(Ecoarse​/Efine​)​. DG advection: periodic scalar transport, final time 0.2, CFL 0.2, N=8,16,32,64, modal Legendre P0/P1/P2, and SSPRK3. The error is RMS sampled at the implementation's quadrature points. It is not a separately integrated L2 norm. Pp stores N(p+1) scalar unknowns. Toggle the horizontal axis between elements and unknowns; the data remain unchanged. Spatial orders 1, 2, and 3 and SSPRK3's time order three explain the expected smooth behavior. Euler entropy wave: final time 1, CFL 0.3, N=40,80,160, primitive minmod MUSCL or componentwise FD WENO5-JS with SSPRK3. The error is pointwise density L1. WENO's fifth-order spatial reconstruction does not remove the third-order time error, so slopes from this finite sequence do not guarantee asymptotic fifth-order fully discrete convergence. Euler stores three scalar state components per point or cell; equal counts do not imply equal computational cost or identical approximation spaces. A decreasing error, an observed slope, a positivity test, a small divergence, and a performance comparison answer different questions. The notebook keeps those distinctions explicit. See the benchmark definitions and the implementation roadmap for the remaining checks. Temporal trajectories and mesh connectivity# The time integration notebook selects Python-computed y′ = i y trajectories for twelve temporal methods, with fixed final time 20. It exposes step size, leapfrog startup perturbation, two characteristic roots, sampled error, and amplitude. These are precomputed ODE results, unlike the browser-computed spatial stability laboratory. Read the time integration definitions. The mesh explorer displays three explicit vertex/cell datasets. Selection highlights face-sharing neighbors; the cell dropdown and keyboard-accessible polygons provide equivalent controls. Geometry is fixed, and no flow is integrated. Read mesh definitions, ALE, and SPH. Both notebooks expose foundations.json, generated by scripts/sync_web_content.py, with source SHA-256 hashes for the temporal and geometry modules. Their Python tests check refinement orders, leapfrog modes, midpoint amplitude, kernel normalization, mesh topology, and moving-volume uniform-state preservation. Hamiltonian maps# The Hamiltonian notebook loads 30 Python-computed cases on demand. It compares energy errors at a shared fixed step, then lets readers inspect one map’s phase-space orbit or square-boundary image. Analytic local Jacobian diagnostics distinguish symplectic structure from energy preservation. Read the definitions. Regenerate the dataset and figure with python scripts/build_hamiltonian.py. Nonsteady movie and KEEP exhibits# The motion gallery presents actual saved solver states and explicit physical timestamps, with fixed color scales and MP4 export. KEEP is evaluated on a smooth exact-reference vortex, with separate spatial/time-refinement and entropy diagnostics. No shock-capturing claim follows from that smooth computation. Slope limiters and advanced reconstruction# The limiter notebook loads 45 Python-computed curves on demand, together with six smooth-refinement studies and three constructed Euler reconstruction failures. Select minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, or clipped van Albada, inspect scalar periodic TV and mass, and compare Sod with the same HLLC flux. Scalar errors use exact cell averages; Sod retains its pointwise reference convention. First-order and unlimited baselines apply only to scalar advection. The advanced controls select TVB M=0,10,50 and demonstrate conservative positive-state scaling. Read slope definitions and the advanced assumptions. python scripts/build_limiters.py generates docs/figures/limiters.json with source hashes; the standard sync copies it to the web edition. Neither the scalar TVB example nor the positive reconstruction helper confers a fully discrete Euler positivity guarantee. Runge–Kutta family notebook# The family notebook compares nine fixed-step explicit RK tableaus. Three RK2 methods share a linear stability polynomial but differ on the nonlinear y′=−y² test. Select a one-step size, inspect actual RHS-stage predictors, and compare sampled stability contours and final-time refinement. Formal order, stage count, nonlinear SSP coefficient, and RHS work are displayed separately. Read the RK chapter for all definitions and conditional SSP assumptions. python scripts/build_runge_kutta.py creates the plotted data and source manifest. The existing oscillator notebook now offers twelve temporal methods; its implicit options remain scalar linear models. CIP value and gradient transport# The CIP notebook compares original cubic-Hermite CIP with linear point interpolation on uniform periodic scalar advection. It displays the independently transported gradient, derivative-initialization choices, smooth refinement, overshoot on a square pulse, and an analytic conservation counterexample. Read the definitions; point samples and finite-volume averages are not interchangeable. Rebuild with python scripts/build_cip.py before syncing. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Yee finite-difference time-domain method | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Yee finite-difference time-domain method Yee FDTD advances Maxwell curl equations on a lattice staggered in both space and time. It is a specific arrangement, not simply centered differences with electric and magnetic fields collocated. Problem and representative equations In a linear isotropic nondispersive medium with constant ε and μ, c=1/√(εμ). Store E at integer times and B at half times, with H=B/μ. curlₕ denotes the discrete curl compatible with the chosen spatial placement; J is electric current density. Bn+1/2=Bn−1/2−Δt curl⁡hEn,En+1=En+Δtϵ(curl⁡hHn+1/2−Jn+1/2).Bn+1/2En+1​=Bn−1/2−Δtcurlh​En,=En+ϵΔt​(curlh​Hn+1/2−Jn+1/2).​ Algorithm Update magnetic flux from electric circulation, then advance E from magnetic circulation and current. Initialize fields and boundaries at their staggered times. The compatible divₕ curlₕ identity helps preserve a magnetic constraint; electric charge conservation also requires a compatible current update. Conditions and pitfalls For the standard uniform Cartesian constant-medium scheme, cΔt√(Δx⁻²+Δy⁻²+Δz⁻²)≤1. Dispersive materials, absorption layers and conduction terms need their own analysis. Stability does not eliminate phase error or staircase geometry error, and a PML setting does not imply zero reflection. What to check Compare periodic-wave phase speed and grid convergence, conducting-cavity frequencies and interface reflection/transmission with analytic results. Track energy balance, magnetic divergence and Gauss-law residuals separately. Similarities with MHD constrained transport do not make their equations identical. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Numerical solution of initial boundary value problems involving maxwell's equations in isotropic media. documents.title: Continuous finite elements: from weak form to sparse assembly · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Continuous finite elements: from weak form to sparse assembly Implemented: continuous P1 elements on intervals and affine triangles, Poisson with Dirichlet data, consistent mass matrices, and quadrature error norms. This is distinct from the atlas's discontinuous Galerkin advection example. The basis-function chapter and notebook connect these nodal shapes to Legendre modes, GLL nodes, exact and quadrature mass matrices, and triangular P2 functions. The assembler in this FEM chapter remains P1. 1943: a variational route# Courant (1943) is a foundational variational reference. This chapter's small implementation is an independent modern P1 demonstration, rather than a reproduction of his examples. For −Δu=f, prescribe u=g on the boundary. Multiplication by a test function that vanishes there and integration by parts give ∫Ω∇uh⋅∇vh dΩ=∫Ωfvh dΩ.∫Ω​∇uh​⋅∇vh​dΩ=∫Ω​fvh​dΩ. Write u_h as nodal coefficients times continuous piecewise linear basis functions. On a triangle K, the shape gradients are constant: KijK=∣K∣∇ϕi⋅∇ϕj,MijK=∣K∣12(1+δij).KijK​=∣K∣∇ϕi​⋅∇ϕj​,MijK​=12∣K∣​(1+δij​). Shared nodes accumulate element contributions into CSR storage. Nonzero Dirichlet values move to the right-hand side before symmetric row/column elimination. Treating only rows would destroy the symmetry relevant to CG. The example uses ILU-preconditioned GMRES. Inspect the evidence# The manufactured solution is sin(πx)sin(πy) on the unit square. L2 and H1 seminorm errors are integrated inside elements, not measured only at nodes. The expected smooth-solution orders are two and one. Tests also cover affine patches, nonzero boundary data, constant null vectors before boundary elimination, and total consistent mass. from numart.fem import poisson_2d result = poisson_2d(16) print(result.residual, result.u.shape) Reproduce with python scripts/build_equation_gallery.py. The dedicated manifest records errors and source hashes. Mixed velocity–pressure elements, inf–sup conditions, curved meshes, general Neumann/Robin assembly and adaptive refinement remain future work. The current projection example uses a staggered finite-difference grid. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids A/B/C names specify where different variables live on a mesh. They are not an accuracy order, a mesh shape, or a time-stepping family. A structured rectangular mesh may use any of these staggerings. The conventional comparison is described by Arakawa–Lamb (1977), with a useful agency exposition in the ECMWF numerical-methods notes. Implemented here: spherical mesh geometry diagrams, plus placement diagrams and tested Fourier symbols for a linear periodic f-plane shallow-water system. This is not an A/B/C nonlinear weather or ocean model, and it introduces no new full flow simulation. A sphere needs several charts# Mesh geometry and variable staggering are separate choices. A cubed sphere can carry a C-grid arrangement; a triangular mesh can also store edge-normal velocities. A/B/C labels alone do not specify spherical connectivity or metrics. On a sphere of radius R, with latitude φ and longitude λ, ds2=R2(dφ2+cos⁡2φ dλ2),Δsλ≃Rcos⁡φ Δλ.ds2=R2(dφ2+cos2φdλ2),Δsλ​≃RcosφΔλ. Geographic poles are regular physical locations. Longitude becomes undefined there, while equal longitude increments become very short near them. An explicit wave/advection CFL bound can therefore become restrictive. Pole filters, reduced grids and spectral methods are other responses; replacing the mesh is not the only option. The three constructions below avoid the single latitude–longitude chart's polar convergence, while introducing other coupling and metric questions. None is automatically equal-area. Yin–Yang: two overlapping low-latitude patches# Kageyama–Sato (2004) combine two identical latitude–longitude patches. In each patch's own coordinates, ∣φ∣≤π/4+δ,∣λ∣≤3π/4+δ,xYang=(−100001010)xYin.∣φ∣≤π/4+δ,∣λ∣≤3π/4+δ,xYang=​−100​001​010​​xYin. The rotation puts each chart's poles inside the other chart's low-latitude region. The figure uses δ=3°; purple marks overlap, not a third patch. Each component retains orthogonal latitude–longitude coordinates and familiar metrics. Boundary data must be transferred through the overlap. Interpolating scalar values alone does not guarantee a globally conservative mass budget; overlap ownership/weights and conservative coupling need explicit design. Velocity components must also rotate between local tangent bases. These transfers are explained here, but no overset transport solver is implemented. Cubed sphere: six connected panels# The six-face construction is associated with Ronchi–Iacono–Paolucci (1996). Our diagram chooses equiangular gnomonic coordinates. For an orthonormal face frame with outward normal n and tangent directions e₁,e₂, x(ξ,η)=R n+tan⁡ξ e1+tan⁡η e2∥n+tan⁡ξ e1+tan⁡η e2∥,−π/4≤ξ,η≤π/4.x(ξ,η)=R∥n+tanξe1​+tanηe2​∥n+tanξe1​+tanηe2​​,−π/4≤ξ,η≤π/4. The picture has 8×8 cells per panel. Adjacent panel boundaries match; three panels meet at each cube corner. This mapping avoids a latitude–longitude pole but is generally nonorthogonal inside a face, and cell areas and metric factors vary. Other cubed-sphere projections have different properties. Neighbor indices, vector components and numerical fluxes must agree across seams. A continuous-looking diagram is not a test of those operators. Icosahedral triangles and their dual# Start with 20 triangular faces, split each triangle into four using edge midpoints, and project new vertices radially onto the sphere. At level L, F=20 4L,E=30 4L,V=10 4L+2,V−E+F=2.F=204L,E=304L,V=104L+2,V−E+F=2. Level 2 has 320 triangles, 480 edges and 162 vertices. Twelve vertices have five neighbors; the others have six. Connecting neighboring face centers through shared edge midpoints produces a dual with twelve pentagons and otherwise hexagons. Here the centers are normalized triangle centroids: this is a barycentric dual, not a claim of a Voronoi/Delaunay orthogonal pair. For this unoptimized sample, the largest triangle area is about 1.275 times the smallest, so quasi-uniform does not mean equal-area. The connectivity formulas apply to this regular refinement, not every possible spherical unstructured mesh. The ICON model description is a useful example of triangular mesh geometry combined with C-type staggering. Our illustration is not the optimized ICON mesh or its dynamical core. Accurate divergence, gradient, vorticity and wave dispersion still depend on compatible discrete operators. Interfaces, vectors and what the figures verify# A physical tangent velocity is one vector, even when its components differ between charts. If E_A and E_B have orthonormal tangent basis vectors as columns in one common Cartesian frame, then v=EAuA=EBuB,uB=EBTEAuA.v=EA​uA​=EB​uB​,uB​=EBT​EA​uA​. This formula uses orthonormal physical components. Covariant or contravariant components in nonorthogonal coordinates require the corresponding metric and dual basis. Copying two component arrays across a seam is insufficient. For finite volumes, a shared interface needs the same integrated flux with opposite signs in neighboring cell budgets. Overset grids additionally need a well-defined accounting of overlap; summing both full patches counts some area twice. The geometry tests check unit radii, matching cube-panel boundary nodes, icosahedral edge incidence and valence, Euler's identity, and total spherical triangle area 4π. A deterministic equal-area sample checks Yin–Yang coverage and overlap; this sampled check is not a formal coverage proof. Reproduce both figures with python scripts/build_spherical_meshes.py; the geometry manifest records construction choices, area statistics and source/artifact hashes. These checks do not establish transport accuracy, seam conservation or geophysical wave convergence. Useful next tests would rotate a smooth tracer across every seam and monitor global mass, then compare balanced shallow-water waves under refinement. A, B and C specify relative placement# Take free-surface perturbation η at scalar cell centers (i+1/2,j+1/2), with square cell size Δ. Define u as the x velocity and v as the y velocity. A grid: η, u and v are all at the same center. B grid: η is at the center; both u and v are at vertices (i,j). C grid: η is at the center; u is at x-normal faces (i,j+1/2), and v is at y-normal faces (i+1/2,j). Choosing vertices rather than centers as the origin reverses some diagram conventions without changing the relative placement. Plot the locations and component directions before comparing array indices between models. On a C grid, normal face velocities naturally supply cell divergence, and center-to-center scalar differences give face pressure gradients. That is the placement already used by the atlas's periodic MAC projection. The relationship concerns spatial location; MAC and an ocean C-grid dynamical core need not share their Coriolis, advection, boundary or time algorithms. The official MITgcm staggering description shows this face-normal arrangement in three dimensions. Rotation and gravity waves make the difference visible# For constant mean depth H and constant Coriolis parameter f, ut−fv=−gηx,vt+fu=−gηy,ηt+H(ux+vy)=0.ut​−fv=−gηx​,vt​+fu=−gηy​,ηt​+H(ux​+vy​)=0. The continuum has a zero-frequency geostrophic branch and gravity branches ω2=f2+c2(k2+ℓ2),c=gH,LD=c/∣f∣.ω2=f2+c2(k2+ℓ2),c=gH​,LD​=c/∣f∣. A discrete dispersion relation depends on the operators and the locations. Here each grid uses centered second-order pressure/divergence; C-grid Coriolis uses the symmetric four-point interpolation between u and v locations. With the physical staggering phases removed, the effective wavenumbers are A:k~=sin⁡(kΔ)/Δ,ℓ~=sin⁡(ℓΔ)/Δ,fh=f,B:k~=2sin⁡(kΔ/2)cos⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ~=2cos⁡(kΔ/2)sin⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,fh=f,C:k~=2sin⁡(kΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ~=2sin⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,fh=fcos⁡(kΔ/2)cos⁡(ℓΔ/2).A:B:C:​k=sin(kΔ)/Δ,k=2sin(kΔ/2)cos(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,k=2sin(kΔ/2)/Δ,​ℓ=sin(ℓΔ)/Δ,ℓ=2cos(kΔ/2)sin(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ=2sin(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,​fh​=f,fh​=f,fh​=fcos(kΔ/2)cos(ℓΔ/2).​ The computed baseline has ω_h²=f_h²+c²(k̃²+ℓ̃²). For the energy-scaled state (u,v,cη/H), the full 3×3 Fourier generator is skew-Hermitian: its eigenvalues are 0 and ±iω_h. This is a semi-discrete result. A time integrator can add phase error, damping or instability even when the spatial generator conserves this linear energy. Checkerboards and an unresolved deformation radius# A centered A-grid pressure gradient cannot see the shortest alternating height mode in a coordinate direction. The B-grid baseline removes that axis-only null mode but retains a diagonal height checkerboard. The C-grid pressure-gradient/divergence pair couples that mode; however, its simple Coriolis average vanishes at certain shortest waves. These are distinct operator effects, not one universal checkerboard diagnosis. The figure compares both axial and diagonal waves at L_D/Δ=0.25 and 2. A and B overlap on the diagonal for these square-grid operators, while their axial curves differ. When the deformation radius is unresolved, Coriolis averaging can strongly distort the C-grid near-inertial branches. Thus “C is always best” is not a valid conclusion. Resolved gravity waves, coarse-grid geostrophic adjustment and directional errors are different tests. Different Coriolis discretizations can change the comparison without changing the C placement itself. D and E, vertical staggering and magnetic grids# The D grid interchanges the face locations of u and v relative to C: u lies at the y-normal face location and v at the x-normal face location. The arrows still denote physical x and y components, so a D diagram is not obtained by merely renaming the C velocity arrays. The E grid is commonly viewed as a B arrangement rotated by 45 degrees; its indexing and resolvable wavevector set must be treated consistently. They are described here but have no implemented symbols in this addition. Horizontal Arakawa staggering is separate from Lorenz versus Charney–Phillips vertical staggering. Likewise, MHD constrained transport uses face/edge placement to enforce a magnetic-divergence identity; it is not synonymous with an Arakawa C-grid shallow-water algorithm. Each needs its own compatible discrete operators. Evidence and the next geophysical benchmarks# numart.geophysical_grids supplies the A/B/C symbols. Tests compare them with independently applied physical-grid finite-difference stencils on Fourier waves, check skew-Hermitian energy structure and the geostrophic zero branch, verify long-wave second-order convergence, and expose the distinct short-wave null modes. Reproduce the figure with python scripts/build_geophysical_grids.py; the manifest records assumptions, sampled frequencies and source hashes. A sensible next flow sequence is geostrophic adjustment, inertia–gravity waves, a coastal Kelvin wave, and a beta-plane Rossby wave, followed by potential-vorticity and nonlinear energy/enstrophy budgets. The present constant-f symbols do not verify beta-plane Rossby propagation, coastlines, spherical metrics, topography or wetting/drying. A nonlinear Arakawa Jacobian or energy/enstrophy-conserving shallow-water flux is another algorithmic choice; selecting A, B or C placement alone does not provide those invariants. documents.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab The boundary condition is part of a Poisson solver’s definition. A finite isolated mass, a fully periodic density contrast, and a horizontally periodic disk with vacuum above and below have different Green functions. Padding an array does not by itself choose the right one. The isolated construction here follows the Hockney–Eastwood doubled-domain convolution idea in Computer Simulation Using Particles. The disk reference is Koyama and Ostriker (2009), ApJ 693, 1316–1345, §2.3 and Appendix A (author preprint). It uses horizontal periodicity, vertical domain doubling, and mode-dependent image corrections. Below we derive and test kernels with our own explicit transform normalization; the finite sampled DFT and the continuum Fourier coefficient are distinguished. Isolated gravity: linear convolution on a doubled grid# With G = 1, the three-dimensional isolated potential is ϕ(x)=−∫ρ(x′)∣x−x′∣ d3x′.ϕ(x)=−∫∣x−x′∣ρ(x′)​d3x′. For a source grid Nx × Ny × Nz, pad the density with zeros to 2Nx × 2Ny × 2Nz. Build a kernel using signed grid lags on that doubled domain, multiply its FFT by the padded density FFT, invert, and retain the original physical block: ϕphysical=ΔV R IFFT⁡[FFT⁡(ρpadded)FFT⁡(Kdoubled)].ϕphysical​=ΔVRIFFT[FFT(ρpadded​)FFT(Kdoubled​)]. Source–target separations inside the retained block are less than the original domain length in each direction. The doubled cyclic convolution therefore equals the desired nonperiodic discrete convolution. This is stronger than merely moving periodic images farther away. Replacing K by the usual periodic symbol −4 pi/k² would solve a different problem. The singular grid-origin kernel must be declared. isolated_potential assigns an explicit self_kernel, default zero, and uses −1/r elsewhere. It does not integrate the kernel over a finite source cell. Its roundoff-level agreement with a direct grid sum verifies convolution and padding, not high-order continuum accuracy or a uniquely correct self-cell prescription. A fully isolated finite mass can have phi tending to zero at infinity; a slab with nonzero surface density generally cannot. Horizontal Fourier transform of a slab# Take x and y periodic and let the density vanish outside a vertical interval of length Lz. With horizontal wavevector k_perp, use the convention ρ^k(z)=1LxLy∫ρ(x,y,z)e−i(kxx+kyy) dx dy,k=kx2+ky2.ρ​k​(z)=Lx​Ly​1​∫ρ(x,y,z)e−i(kx​x+ky​y)dxdy,k=kx2​+ky2​​. Poisson’s equation becomes (partial_z²−k²) phi_hat = 4 pi G rho_hat. The full gravitational kernel, including 4 pi G, is Gk(s)={−2πGke−k∣s∣,k>0,2πG∣s∣,k=0,ϕ^k(z)=∫Gk(z−z′)ρ^k(z′) dz′.Gk​(s)=⎩⎨⎧​−k2πG​e−k∣s∣,2πG∣s∣,​k>0,k=0,​ϕ​k​(z)=∫Gk​(z−z′)ρ​k​(z′)dz′. Our sign convention includes the gravitational prefactor in the kernel; some references factor it out. The derivative jump at s = 0 gives 4 pi G, which checks both sign and normalization. Nonzero horizontal modes decay into the exterior. The zero mode is the horizontally averaged mass sheet, with a finite exterior force rather than a decaying potential. The vertical Fourier coefficient and the image factor# Only separations |s| < Lz are required. Extend the kernel periodically over a separation interval of length 2Lz and set k_z,ell = pi ell/Lz. For k > 0 the continuous integral is G~k,ℓ=∫−LzLzGk(s)e−ikz,ℓs ds=−4πGk2+kz,ℓ2[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz].G​k,ℓ​=∫−Lz​Lz​​Gk​(s)e−ikz,ℓ​sds=−k2+kz,ℓ2​4πG​[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz​]. It follows by integrating the even exponential against a cosine. The square-bracket factor distinguishes the slab kernel from the ordinary fully periodic Poisson multiplier. Equivalently, doubling z and adding a negative image density at displacement Lz with horizontal-mode factor exp(−k Lz) produces this factor before applying the ordinary nonzero Poisson multiplier. For the k = 0 horizontal mode, the continuous coefficient is G~0,ℓ={2πGLz2,ℓ=0,4πG[(−1)ℓ−1]kz,ℓ2,ℓ≠0.G​0,ℓ​=⎩⎨⎧​2πGLz2​,kz,ℓ2​4πG[(−1)ℓ−1]​,​ℓ=0,ℓ=0.​ The all-zero coefficient fixes an additive potential constant in this convention. Other constant gauges give the same force. Dropping the entire horizontal k = 0 mode, however, removes the physical mean sheet and is incorrect. Our slab solver does not subtract the mean density. A sampled DFT is a different numerical object# Let dz = Lz/Nz and s_j be the 2Nz signed vertical lags. The multiplier for the discrete quadrature is G~k,ℓsampled=Δz∑j=02Nz−1Gk(sj)e−2πijℓ/(2Nz).G​k,ℓsampled​=Δzj=0∑2Nz​−1​Gk​(sj​)e−2πijℓ/(2Nz​). This is exactly dz times the DFT of the sampled kernel. It is not, at finite Nz, identical to the continuous integral above. For k > 0 its real value can also be evaluated by the geometric series G~k,ℓsampled=−2πGΔzksinh⁡(kΔz)cosh⁡(kΔz)−cos⁡(πℓ/Nz)[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz].G​k,ℓsampled​=−k2πGΔz​cosh(kΔz)−cos(πℓ/Nz​)sinh(kΔz)​[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz​]. Use a separate k = 0 branch to avoid cancellation and division by zero. Expanding sinh, cosh, and cos recovers the continuous coefficient for fixed resolved modes as dz tends to zero. Tests measure this convergence. The distinction prevents labeling a continuum coefficient as the exact finite sum of sampled values. slab_green_transform exposes both sampled and continuum representations. slab_potential defaults to the sampled kernel, so its FFT result matches an independent direct vertical quadrature. The continuum option applies the analytic coefficient instead. This is a small independently written kernel laboratory, not a reproduction of all numerical choices or the interstellar-medium simulations in the paper. Check the boundary physics before a galaxy calculation# import numpy as np from numart.gravity_boundaries import isolated_potential, slab_potential rho = np.ones((8,8,16)) phi_slab = slab_potential(rho) # horizontal mean mode retained phi_isolated = isolated_potential(rho, spacing=(1/8,1/8,1/16)) These two arrays describe different boundary problems. Tests compare isolated FFT convolution with a direct nonperiodic grid sum, including a source near a boundary; verify the mean plane’s quadratic potential and linear interior acceleration; and recover the exponential field of a sinusoidal sheet. For a sheet of surface density Sigma, the mean potential is 2 pi G Sigma |z−z0| and the nonzero mode decays as exp(−k|z−z0|). The kernel verification manifest records source hashes and measured errors for the displayed checks. The implementation uses ordinary horizontal periodicity, not shear-periodic remapping. Mass assignment, self-cell integration, vertical quadrature accuracy, force differentiation, and gravity–hydrodynamics coupling require further checks before production use. Continue with particle gravity, multigrid, and Hamiltonian maps. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH) · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Godunov smoothed particle hydrodynamics (GSPH) Status: source-based reading notes and an implementation plan. The existing SPH example reconstructs fields; it does not advance a GSPH fluid. No GSPH benchmark result is claimed here. Inutsuka's formulation# Inutsuka (2002) derives particle evolution from convolutions of the fluid equations. Pairwise Riemann problems supply pressure and velocity for the interactions, replacing a separately prescribed shock artificial viscosity. Riemann dissipation still remains. The author's preprint, sections 2–3 is the equation reference. It also cites the earlier Godunov-type SPH contribution (1994); that original report has not been inspected here. For a common Gaussian smoothing length, a linear approximation to specific volume V = 1/rho gives the overlap coefficient (equations 48–52) Cij=Vi−Vj∣xi−xj∣,Dij=Vi+Vj2,Vij2(h)=Dij2+h2Cij24.Cij​=∣xi​−xj​∣Vi​−Vj​​,Dij​=2Vi​+Vj​​,Vij2​(h)=Dij2​+4h2Cij2​​. Equation 65 then uses the pair pressure in the momentum update: dvidt=−2∑jmjPij∗Vij2(h)∇iW(xi−xj,2h).dtdvi​​=−2j∑​mj​Pij∗​Vij2​(h)∇i​W(xi​−xj​,2​h). This is the common-h Gaussian form. The paper's variable-h expressions and time-centered internal-energy update are needed for its conservation argument. Changing only the pressure in an existing SPH force is not that derivation. Connecting the existing exhibits# The implementation path joins particle kernels, Euler Riemann solvers, and moving-particle time integration. The current interpolation uses a compact cubic kernel; the derivation above uses a Gaussian and its overlap. Their kernel-width conventions must be kept explicit. The existing fixed-grid flux returns F(U), whereas a GSPH pair update needs a consistently oriented star pressure and velocity. Reusing a flux function alone does not provide a complete particle interaction. A staged verification plan# Check kernel overlaps, specific-volume reconstruction, pair orientation, equal and unequal masses, and uniform-pressure consistency. Advance pair forces and internal energy with a matched time update; measure momentum and total-energy drift before adding adaptive smoothing lengths. Run a smooth acoustic wave and an advected contact with controlled particle spacing and smoothing scale. Separate interpolation and time-step refinement. Compare the paper's first shock tube (equation 89, Figure 2) with its exact Euler solution, then add the shared Sod and Shu–Osher tests. Record particle masses, spacing, neighbors, boundary reservoirs, and reconstruction choices. For that first published shock tube, the primitive left/right states are (rho, v, p) = (1, 0, 1) and (0.5, 0, 0.2), gamma = 1.4, at t = 0.2. It differs from the standard Sod parameters used elsewhere in this atlas. These are proposed verification targets, not computed GSPH results. The MHD branch# Iwasaki and Inutsuka (2011) extend the particle approach: compressive interactions use a nonlinear Riemann problem with magnetic pressure, while Alfvén waves use characteristics. Their paper includes Alfvén, shock-tube, Orszag–Tang, rotor, and magnetized-blast tests. This is a separate GSPMHD implementation direction; the atlas's existing grid-based CT/GLM does not implement it. Particle magnetic-divergence and tensile-instability treatments would require their own verification. Special-relativistic continuation# Kitajima, Inutsuka, and Seno (2026) develop SRGSPH with a relativistic Riemann solver, unequal particle baryon numbers, and variable smoothing lengths. The preprint dates to 2025; the journal issue is 2026. This is special relativity, not a general-relativistic fluid solver. Continue with the SRHD/GRHD development review. documents.title: Historical atlas · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Historical atlas Dates refer to original publication years, with translations, reprints, and online publication dates distinguished where relevant. This atlas offers a reading path through representative sources. It does not settle every claim of invention or priority. The reference catalog records the relationship between each source and the implementation, including open questions. Classical foundations: equations, differences, and iteration# Begin with forward, backward, and centered differences, Euler time integration, Fourier expansions, heat conduction, and the Laplace and Poisson equations. Distinguish boundary values from boundary fluxes before introducing Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions. The mathematical origins of these ideas precede their later use in computational fluid dynamics. 1928: CFL and domains of dependence# Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy compares the continuous domain of dependence with the reach of a discrete stencil. Vary C=a Δt/Δx in linear advection to distinguish necessary conditions from sufficient ones. Original CFL paper, derivations and experiments. 1939–1943: kinetic asymptotics and variational assembly# Chapman–Cowling's kinetic-theory book appeared in 1939; this is a book date, not the invention date of the Chapman–Enskog expansion. Courant (1943) connects variational problems to piecewise representations. The P1 FEM exhibit implements independent sparse Poisson examples. 1947–1950: diffusion, implicit methods, and linear stability# Crank–Nicolson (1947); Thomas tridiagonal elimination, commonly cited to a 1949 report whose original text has not been inspected here; and stability analysis in Charney–Fjørtoft–von Neumann's numerical forecasting work (1950). The 1950 paper is historical context, rather than a claim that von Neumann analysis originated in that paper alone. Connect the diffusion number r=ν Δt/Δx² with A-stability, monotonicity, and implicit linear systems. Diffusion and linear solvers. Burgers (1948) supplies a parallel nonlinear model branch. The equation gallery uses the inviscid shock/fan problem, rather than reproducing its turbulence analysis. 1954–1961: Lax, Godunov, and conservation form# Lax (1954), Lax–Richtmyer (1956), Godunov (1959), Lax–Wendroff (1960), and Rusanov (1961) lead into weak solutions, numerical fluxes, shock speeds, numerical viscosity, and dispersion. The Lax–Richtmyer linear convergence theorem and Lax–Wendroff-type results about weak limits of nonlinear conservative approximations have different hypotheses. Here, method="godunov" denotes a Godunov-type finite-volume method with approximate Riemann fluxes, rather than a complete reproduction of the original exact-flux algorithm. BGK (1954) provides a kinetic relaxation model. Lighthill–Whitham (1955) and Richards (1956) connect conservation laws to traffic waves. These separate branches meet in the gallery through explicit equations and references, not a single invention chronology. 1961–1977: relaxation, multigrid, and local and global bases# Fedorenko (1961), Reed–Hill (1973), Gottlieb–Orszag (1977), and Brandt (1977). Split Poisson iteration into smoothing of high-frequency errors and coarse-grid correction of smooth errors. DG uses elementwise polynomials joined by boundary fluxes; spectral methods use global bases. Earlier Galerkin and Fourier ideas provide the mathematical background to these developments. Poisson and multigrid, numart.advection.dg_advection. Chorin (1968) leads to incompressible projection. Alexander (1977) supplies the SDIRK branch; source treatment and adaptive error control remain distinct from a method's linear stability function. 1978–1983: shared benchmarks and high-resolution fluxes# Sod (1978), van Leer's MUSCL (1979), Orszag–Tang (1979), Roe (1981), and Harten–Lax–van Leer (1983). Compare contact and acoustic-wave resolution on the same Sod problem. The first-edition MUSCL implementation uses minmod and the method of lines; van Leer's original Lagrangian/remap construction is different. The original incompressible Orszag–Tang study and the normalization of today's compressible test are also distinguished. Benchmark definitions, MHD. 1984–1989: TVD slopes and TVB extrema relaxation# Sweby (1984) organizes scalar flux-limiter bounds. Cockburn–Shu (1989) develops the TVB RKDG framework. Compare five slope limiters, then inspect the separate TVB and positive-state scaling building blocks. The latter also links the positivity framework of Zhang–Shu (2010), with its required flux, quadrature, CFL, and SSP conditions. 1985–1991: cubic profiles and transported gradients# Takewaki–Nishiguchi–Yabe (1985) and Yabe–Aoki (1991) develop the CIP line of cubic value/gradient transport. The CIP chapter computes a constant-speed scalar example and distinguishes later conservative and rational branches. Its constructed Hermite-field test separates low diffusion from a mass-conservation guarantee. 1987–1989: higher order, preconditioning, and magnetic constraints# ENO by Harten and colleagues (1987), Turkel's low-speed preconditioning (1987), Einfeldt (1988), Evans–Hawley CT (1988), Shu–Osher (1988, 1989), and Cockburn–Shu RKDG (1989). High-order interpolation alone does not ensure robust shock capture. Entropy fixes and positivity require separate attention. The Shu–Osher test combines a shock with a smooth density wave. 1991–1996: unsteady iteration, low densities, HLLC, and WENO# Einfeldt and colleagues (1991), Jameson (1991), Toro–Spruce–Speares (1994), Liu–Osher–Chan (1994), and Jiang–Shu (1996). Study physical and pseudo-time, low-density failure, contact restoration, and nonlinear WENO weights. The origin of WENO in 1994 is distinguished from WENO5-JS (1996), which is the variant implemented in this edition. Preconditioning and dual time stepping. 2000–2008: multidimensional robustness and constraints# Tóth (2000), Dedner and colleagues (2002), Abgrall's residual-distribution review (2006), and Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008). Follow discrete CT/GLM operators, conservative residual distribution, rotated-hybrid fluxes, and the carbuncle instability. The 2006 date identifies the RD review, rather than the invention of residual distribution. Inutsuka (2002) adds a parallel particle branch: convolution-based SPH evolution with pairwise Riemann problems. The GSPH chapter distinguishes its 1994 precursor from the detailed 2002 formulation and the later MHD extension by Iwasaki–Inutsuka (2011). These are source notes and planned fluid solvers, rather than the existing static SPH reconstruction. 2001–2009: SSP inheritance and additional Runge–Kutta stages# Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor (2001), Spiteri–Ruuth (2002), and Gottlieb–Ketcheson–Shu (2009) distinguish scalar linear stability from conditional nonlinear stability inheritance. These are developments in the SSP branch, not the origin of Runge–Kutta methods. The RK family chapter compares RK2 variants, RK4, and SSPRK(s,p), with actual nonlinear stages and refinement. Relativistic branch: 1972–2026# The SRHD/GRHD/GRMHD review connects Wilson's Kerr-background calculation (1972), exact SR Riemann solutions (1994), Valencia (1997), local-frame solvers (1998), relativistic magnetic constraints, HARM (2003), dynamical spacetime, and nonlinear primitive recovery. Later branches include radiation, DG–FD hybrids, physical-state constraints, and GPU-oriented merger codes. SRGSPH (2026) connects back to Inutsuka's particle formulation. The review records source and publication status as checked on 6 November 2026; it adds no relativistic solver. Toward modern verification and validation# The NASA 2D case catalog introduces the distinction between numerical verification and physical validation against experiments. Each future exhibit should connect its original source, current data access point, implementation status, and verification evidence. Moving meshes, particles, and temporal modes# The fixed-grid history has parallel branches. Hirt, Amsden, and Cook (1974) provide a classical ALE framework; Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977) are independent early SPH sources. The new ALE, particle, and mesh chapters connect their different representations of geometry and motion. The code implements small reconstruction and geometric-conservation examples, rather than those original flow calculations. The time integration chapter gives the two-step leapfrog recurrence and its computational root. Its discussion of time filtering points to a later modification by Williams (2009), without assigning the invention of leapfrog to that paper. The Double Mach Reflection exhibit adds a computed two-dimensional shock interaction. Quirk (1994) and Pandolfi and D’Ambrosio (2001) lead into the separate carbuncle reading notes. Finally, Remembering Philip L. Roe records the university’s 2026 memorial and returns to his 1981 contribution. Particle fields and canonical time maps# Hockney’s P³M account (1981), Barnes–Hut (1986), and Greengard–Rokhlin (1987) connect mesh, tree, and expansion-based field calculations. Yoshida (1990) provides a route to high-order symplectic compositions. The new gravity and Hamiltonian-map chapters make their different roles explicit. Koyama–Ostriker (2009) supplies the disk-potential FFT reference in the boundary-kernel chapter. Smooth-flow structure and honest test selection# Kuya, Totani, and Kawai (2018) introduce the KEEP line of compressible-flow discretizations. The KEEP chapter implements the original second-order Cartesian form and distinguishes later entropy, pressure-equilibrium, and temporal extensions. Its smooth-vortex refinement and saved-state movie are separate from shock-capturing benchmarks; neither kinetic-energy consistency nor a visually smooth movie is a universal stability guarantee. Parallel solver branches: 1986–2010# GMRES (1986) and BiCGSTAB (1992) provide nonsymmetric sparse-system solvers. Qian et al. (1992) and Guo et al. (2002) lead to the lattice-BGK and forcing exhibits. Nishikawa (2007) develops the first-order hyperbolic diffusion system, with an advection–diffusion extension published in 2010. The reading room distinguishes that system's original second-order RD scheme from our first-order FV baseline. Biological and geophysical branches# The biological equation survey follows population growth through Lotka/Volterra, age structure and SIR, then Fisher fronts, Turing morphogenesis, excitable membranes, chemotaxis, stochastic reaction networks and synthetic gene circuits. Original, translated and reduced model forms have separate source notes. All 22 biological entries are survey-only. Arakawa–Lamb (1977) connects variable placement to geophysical waves. The A/B/C chapter adds independent centered f-plane symbol comparisons; the horizontal grid classification is separate from vertical staggering and nonlinear invariant conservation. Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Nishikawa's hyperbolic diffusion: iterate a first-order system Hiroaki Nishikawa (2007) introduces the first-order hyperbolic-system approach to steady diffusion, including second-order residual-distribution schemes. The 2010 extension unifies advection and diffusion. The date is the journal publication year, not the DOI's year. Implemented here: a periodic 1D, first-order upwind finite-volume baseline with SSPRK2. It demonstrates equivalent steady equations; it does not implement the original paper's second-order multidimensional RD constructions. Evolve the solution and its gradient# For the steady problem −νu_xx=f, introduce p and pseudo-time τ: ∂τu−ν∂xp=f,∂τp−1Tr∂xu=−pTr.∂τ​u−ν∂x​p=f,∂τ​p−Tr​1​∂x​u=−Tr​p​. At convergence, p=u_x, recovering the original steady diffusion equation. The homogeneous flux Jacobian has eigenvalues λ±=±ν/Tr.λ±​=±ν/Tr​​. The relaxation time T_r is a numerical parameter controlling pseudo-time propagation and damping. It is not the physical diffusivity. A hyperbolic Courant restriction scales with h for fixed T_r; an explicit source treatment also has a relaxation restriction. The demonstration therefore uses Δτ=Ca/h+1/Tr,a=ν/Tr,C≤12.Δτ=a/h+1/Tr​C​,a=ν/Tr​​,C≤21​. A physical heat equation is not recovered at every finite pseudo-time. Replacing the heat gallery's physical-time curve by this iteration history would change the problem. Time-accurate extensions require additional analysis. Residual convergence and discretization error# The manufactured steady reference is sin(2πx), with zero mean on the periodic unit interval and forcing ν(2π)²sin(2πx). The initial mean fixes the constant null mode. Both equation residuals are measured; the gradient residual is scaled by 2π in the combined RMS diagnostic. A small residual does not eliminate the first-order upwind spatial error. N=32,64,128 checks that error separately. The manifest records steps and pseudo-time sizes, without a matched-cost speedup claim. Compare Thomas and multigrid, sparse preconditioning, and the physical diffusion gallery. Anisotropic diffusion, high-order face reconstruction, viscous Navier–Stokes coupling and the complete RD formulation are future extensions. Publisher records and abstracts were checked; full original-paper reproductions are not claimed. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Incompressible flow: project with compatible discrete operators Implemented: unit-density periodic 2D Navier–Stokes on a MAC grid, centered convection and viscosity, projected SSPRK2, and discrete-FFT Poisson inversion. 1968: the projection branch# Chorin (1968) is the original projection reference. Our periodic RK model illustrates the principle; it does not reproduce his boundary treatments or original time step. Velocity components live on different faces; pressure lives at cell centers. Choose divergence D and gradient G so that D=−Gᵀ under the periodic grid inner product. Then DGϕ=Du∗,u=u∗−Gϕ,Du=0.DGϕ=Du∗,u=u∗−Gϕ,Du=0. The FFT must invert the symbol of DG, not continuum −|k|²: λh=−4h2[sin⁡2(kxh/2)+sin⁡2(kyh/2)].λh​=−h24​[sin2(kx​h/2)+sin2(ky​h/2)]. The pressure constant is undetermined. Set its mean to zero; subtract the mean from the Poisson source for periodic compatibility. Tests check the adjoint identity, projection idempotence, energy contraction and divergence removal. Taylor–Green verification# On [0,2π)² with viscosity ν, use u=sin⁡xcos⁡y e−2νt,v=−cos⁡xsin⁡y e−2νt.u=sinxcosye−2νt,v=−cosxsinye−2νt. The velocity error refines at second order for N=16,32,64 at T=0.5, ν=0.1. Mean kinetic energy is e^(−4νt)/4. Stage projection multipliers are not silently labeled physical pressure; a final pressure estimate is reconstructed from the momentum RHS, without a claimed pressure-order verification. Reproducible measurements include maximum absolute discrete divergence. The explicit step retains both advective and viscous restrictions. No-slip cavity boundaries, SIMPLE/PISO, cylinder wakes, mixed FEM, turbulence models and experimental validation are not implemented by this periodic test. Compare the separate low-Mach LBM model. The Arakawa A/B/C comparison places this MAC arrangement in a geophysical context. Matching face locations does not automatically supply a Coriolis or potential-vorticity algorithm. documents.title: KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data KEEP schemes: preserve the smooth-flow balance, test the limits KEEP stands for kinetic-energy and entropy preserving. The work of Yuichi Kuya, Kosuke Totani, and Soshi Kawai at Tohoku University seeks a low-dissipation balance between the conservative equations of compressible flow. The original 2018 paper is the starting point. The authors’ 2022 conference explanation, especially §2.2 and Eq. (9), states the Cartesian flux implemented here. This exhibit implements the original second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian flux, with periodic boundaries and classical RK4. It does not implement every later scheme named KEEP. Watch its smooth-vortex evolution. Which quantities should be preserved?# In a smooth periodic inviscid flow, mass, momentum, and total energy are conservative. The total kinetic energy alone is generally not constant in compressible flow: pressure work exchanges kinetic and internal energy. With K = integral rho |u|²/2, dKdt=∫p ∇⋅u dV.dtdK​=∫p∇⋅udV. A kinetic-energy-consistent convective discretization should not create a spurious kinetic-energy source through an inconsistent mass/momentum product rule. This is different from imposing dK/dt = 0 on a compressible vortex. We measure the dimensionless entropy proxy S∗=∫ρlog⁡(pργ)dV.S∗​=∫ρlog(ργp​)dV. For a fixed ideal-gas composition this differs from physical entropy only by fixed factors and an additive mass term. Its change per initial mass is useful when initial isentropic data give S_* approximately zero; dividing by initial S_* would be ill-conditioned. For the grid update formula, see the semidiscrete update and two-point flux. The semidiscrete update and two-point flux# Let an overbar denote the arithmetic mean of left and right values, u_n the velocity normal to a Cartesian face, and e = p/[rho(gamma−1)]. The baseline flux is C=ρ‾ u‾n,Fρui=C u‾i+p‾ δin,FE=C[12uL⋅uR+e‾]+12(un,LpR+un,RpL).CFρui​​FE​​=ρ​un​,=Cui​+p​δin​,=C[21​uL​⋅uR​+e]+21​(un,L​pR​+un,R​pL​).​ The mass flux is C. The cross-velocity kinetic term and cross-pressure work are deliberate; replacing them by a convenient average of the full physical flux changes the discrete energy exchange. The implementation is a central two-point flux-difference method of second spatial order. It has no Riemann-solver dissipation. 1. Distinguish the two discrete operators# Work first in one space dimension on a periodic uniform grid of spacing h, with positive density. The left and right states at a face are the two neighboring nodal values. A bar is their arithmetic mean and a jump is right minus left. D differences a face flux; D₀ is the centered derivative of a nodal field. aˉi+1/2=ai+ai+12,[a]i+1/2=ai+1−ai,(DF)i=Fi+1/2−Fi−1/2h,(D0a)i=ai+1−ai−12h.aˉi+1/2​(DF)i​(D0​a)i​​=2ai​+ai+1​​,[a]i+1/2​=ai+1​−ai​,=hFi+1/2​−Fi−1/2​​,=2hai+1​−ai−1​​.​ Two exact algebraic identities explain why the particular averages matter: [ab]=aˉ[b]+bˉ[a],ab‾=aˉ bˉ+14[a][b].[ab]=aˉ[b]+bˉ[a],ab=aˉbˉ+41​[a][b]. For example, averaging ρu is different from multiplying the separate means of ρ and u. They agree for equal states and to first order about a constant state, but their nonlinear jump terms differ. KEEP chooses the products of means to make the equations exchange energy consistently. Conservation of the summed total energy alone would not determine these products. 2. Derive kinetic energy from mass and momentum# Let m denote momentum per unit volume. Use the mass flux C and momentum flux M below; each face has one shared flux. The full two-dimensional flux was given above. Here the velocity is a scalar to expose the cancellation. mi=ρiui,ρ˙i=−(DC)i,m˙i=−(DM)i,C=ρˉ uˉ,M=Cuˉ+pˉ.mi​C​=ρi​ui​,ρ˙​i​=−(DC)i​,m˙i​=−(DM)i​,=ρˉ​uˉ,M=Cuˉ+pˉ​.​ Time is still continuous, so the ordinary chain rule applies to K=m²/(2ρ). Substituting the two conservative equations gives a kinetic-energy flux 𝒦 and a pressure-gradient term: Ki=mi22ρi=12ρiui2,K˙i=uim˙i−12ui2ρ˙i=−(DK)i−ui(D0p)i,Ki+1/2=12Ci+1/2uiui+1.Ki​K˙i​Ki+1/2​​=2ρi​mi2​​=21​ρi​ui2​,=ui​m˙i​−21​ui2​ρ˙​i​=−(DK)i​−ui​(D0​p)i​,=21​Ci+1/2​ui​ui+1​.​ The advective cancellation at the right face is explicit: ui(Ci+1/2ui+ui+12)−12ui2Ci+1/2=12uiui+1Ci+1/2.ui​(Ci+1/2​2ui​+ui+1​​)−21​ui2​Ci+1/2​=21​ui​ui+1​Ci+1/2​. The left face cancels in the same way. Also D applied to the face mean of p is D₀p. Summing over the periodic grid cancels all shared kinetic-energy fluxes; discrete summation by parts then gives ddt(h∑iKi)=−h∑iui(D0p)i=h∑ipi(D0u)i.dtd​(hi∑​Ki​)=−hi∑​ui​(D0​p)i​=hi∑​pi​(D0​u)i​. The sign is positive in the last expression: pressure dilatation transfers energy between kinetic and internal energy. Thus compressible-flow kinetic energy is generally not constant. The identity excludes a spurious advective source while retaining that physical exchange. In multiple dimensions, replace uLuR by the velocity dot product and sum the directional pressure work. 3. Recover the internal-energy pressure work# Choose the pressure contribution P to the total-energy flux as a cross product of left and right values. Expanding its face difference gives an exact discrete product rule: Pi+1/2=12(uipi+1+ui+1pi),(DP)i=ui(pi+1−pi−1)+pi(ui+1−ui−1)2h=ui(D0p)i+pi(D0u)i.Pi+1/2​(DP)i​​=21​(ui​pi+1​+ui+1​pi​),=2hui​(pi+1​−pi−1​)+pi​(ui+1​−ui−1​)​=ui​(D0​p)i​+pi​(D0​u)i​.​ Use the same mass flux to transport the arithmetic mean of the specific internal energy. Subtracting the derived kinetic-energy equation from the total-energy equation then yields Ii=ρiei=Ei−Ki,ei=piρi(γ−1),Ii+1/2=Ci+1/2eˉi+1/2,FE=K+I+P,E˙i+(DFE)i=0⟹I˙i+(DI)i+pi(D0u)i=0.Ii​Ii+1/2​E˙i​+(DFE)i​​=ρi​ei​=Ei​−Ki​,ei​=ρi​(γ−1)pi​​,=Ci+1/2​eˉi+1/2​,FE=K+I+P,=0⟹I˙i​+(DI)i​+pi​(D0​u)i​=0.​ The unwanted uD₀p terms cancel, leaving the internal-energy pressure work pD₀u with the required sign. This explains the cross-pressure term and the cross-velocity kinetic term in the implemented flux. They are not an arbitrary average of the physical energy flux. These are independent algebraic steps for the published implementation, corresponding to the second-order formulation in §2.2, Eqs. (8)–(12). This derivation does not prove roundoff-exact entropy conservation. Entropy also involves nonlinear thermodynamic chain rules. The arithmetic-mean 2018 baseline preserves the balances above but retains entropy-conservation error; later KEEP variants and logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative fluxes have different definitions. The next formula returns to the actual two-dimensional update used by the code. 4. The implemented two-dimensional update Evaluate this two-point flux between neighboring grid nodes, then take the right-minus-left flux difference to update the conserved state. Written in the two-dimensional notation of this implementation, Kuya and Kawai (2022), §2.2, Eqs. (1), (8) and (9) give the following semidiscrete system: space is discrete while time remains continuous. E is total energy per unit volume. qi,j=(ρ,ρu,ρv,E)i,jT,dqi,jdt=−F^i+1/2,j x−F^i−1/2,j xΔx−F^i,j+1/2 y−F^i,j−1/2 yΔy,F^i+1/2,j x=F(x)(qi,j,qi+1,j),F^i,j+1/2 y=F(y)(qi,j,qi,j+1).qi,j​dtdqi,j​​Fi+1/2,jx​Fi,j+1/2y​​=(ρ,ρu,ρv,E)i,jT​,=−ΔxFi+1/2,jx​−Fi−1/2,jx​​−ΔyFi,j+1/2y​−Fi,j−1/2y​​,=F(x)(qi,j​,qi+1,j​),=F(y)(qi,j​,qi,j+1​).​ Here F(x) and F(y) are the two-point flux above with normal velocity u and v, respectively. In the public numart/keep.py, rhs() forms the right flux with keep_flux(q, np.roll(q, -1, axis=axis), axis) and subtracts the left flux obtained with np.roll(flux, 1, axis=axis). The implementation uses a square periodic uniform grid with Δx = Δy = L/N. This is a nearest-neighbor, second-order central spatial operator; higher-order multi-point assembly and curvilinear forms are not implemented. Both neighboring nodes share the same face flux. Its differences telescope when summed over the periodic grid, conserving total mass, momentum and total energy. RK4 retains these linear conservation laws, apart from roundoff. Kinetic-energy pressure-work balance and entropy involve nonlinear relations: this spatial formula alone does not guarantee their exact preservation after time discretization. Tests verify equal-state consistency, left/right symmetry, periodic conservation of the primary variables, and the semidiscrete kinetic-energy pressure-work identity. RK4 adds temporal truncation error and does not inherit every semidiscrete identity exactly. Non-dissipative does not mean dispersion-free# Dissipation changes amplitude; dispersion changes phase speed. A spatial operator can avoid artificial damping and still move different wavelengths at incorrect speeds. To isolate that distinction, linearize the symmetric, consistent two-point flux about one uniform state q₀. Symmetry and F(q,q)=f(q) give equal left and right Jacobians. For a scalar characteristic wave with speed a, the result is the centered advection equation: The von Neumann foundations explain the general procedure for reading dissipation and dispersion from an amplification factor’s magnitude and argument. Here that procedure is applied to KEEP linearized about a uniform state. ∂1F(q0,q0)=∂2F(q0,q0)=12A,A=f′(q0),v˙i=−avi+1−vi−12h.∂1​F(q0​,q0​)v˙i​​=∂2​F(q0​,q0​)=21​A,A=f′(q0​),=−a2hvi+1​−vi−1​​.​ For an individual Fourier mode, with θ=kh, substitution gives vi(t)=v^ ei(kih−ωht),θ=kh,λh=−i asin⁡θh,ωh=asin⁡θh.vi​(t)λh​​=vei(kih−ωh​t),θ=kh,=−iahsinθ​,ωh​=ahsinθ​.​ The eigenvalue is purely imaginary, so this semidiscrete linear mode has no amplitude decay. Its phase and group velocities are nevertheless cpha=ωhak=sin⁡θθ,cga=1adωhdk=cos⁡θ,sin⁡θθ=1−θ26+O(θ4).acph​​acg​​θsinθ​​=akωh​​=θsinθ​,=a1​dkdωh​​=cosθ,=1−6θ2​+O(θ4).​ The ratio at θ=0 is understood by continuity. At four grid points per wavelength, θ=π/2, the second-order phase speed is only 2/π≈0.637 times a. At θ=π the centered derivative vanishes on the alternating grid mode; that is a resolution failure, not accurate transport. Underresolved wave packets can also have an incorrect group velocity. The speed ratios assume a≠0. When a=0, this linearization has ωh=0 and the mode is stationary. The sine relation is not a general nonlinear KEEP dispersion law. Finite-amplitude products couple modes and introduce aliasing questions. Kuya and Kawai’s 2022 split-form analysis treats that different problem: its nonlinear modified wavenumber cannot be replaced by this linearized example, and a finite-difference split form does not automatically remove aliasing. The authors also identify dispersion-error reduction as a reason for higher-order KEEP formulations (§2.4). The figure compares the analytical spatial ratios for this uniform-state linear example. It is separate from the nonlinear saved vortex calculation below. Spatial dispersion of the uniform-state linearization. Speed ratios approach one at low wavenumber; short waves have phase and group errors. What changes when RK4 advances time?# The displayed solver uses classical four-stage RK4. For a frozen linear mode with eigenvalue −iωh, one step multiplies the amplitude by G. This follows directly from the RK4 stages; it is an analysis of the integrator used here, not of a later fully conservative temporal KEEP scheme. vn+1=Gvn,G=R(−iξ),ξ=ωhΔt,R(z)=1+z+z22+z36+z424.vn+1R(z)​=Gvn,G=R(−iξ),ξ=ωh​Δt,=1+z+2z2​+6z3​+24z4​.​ Its squared amplitude gain is exactly ∣G∣2=1−ξ672+ξ8576,∣G∣≤1 ⟺ ∣ξ∣≤22(ξ∈R).∣G∣2=1−72ξ6​+576ξ8​,∣G∣≤1 ⟺ ∣ξ∣≤22​(ξ∈R).​ Strictly inside this interval, a nonzero ξ gives |G| smaller than one. Thus RK4 damps this otherwise undamped spatial mode. Gain is one at ξ=0 and at the two endpoints; beyond them it exceeds one. This pure-imaginary linear-mode stability limit is not a global CFL or positivity guarantee for the nonlinear, variable-state, two-dimensional solver. Phase must also be checked. Define arg₀ by continuous continuation from ξ=0 rather than by a wrapped principal angle. The fully discrete frequency Ω and the amplitude after n equal steps satisfy ΩΔt=−arg⁡0R(−iξ),∣vn∣=∣G∣n∣v0∣,ΩΔt=ξ−ξ5120+O(ξ7).ΩΔtΩΔt​=−arg0​R(−iξ),∣vn∣=∣G∣n∣v0∣,=ξ−120ξ5​+O(ξ7).​ For small ξ the leading amplitude defect and the combined spatial/temporal phase-speed ratio are log⁡∣G∣=−ξ6144+O(ξ8),ΩΔtakΔt=sin⁡θθ −arg⁡0R(−iξ)ξ.log∣G∣akΔtΩΔt​​=−144ξ6​+O(ξ8),=θsinθ​ξ−arg0​R(−iξ)​.​ For θ=π/2 and aΔt/h=0.5, the spatial phase-speed ratio is about 0.636620; including RK4 gives about 0.636317. The RK4 gain is about 0.999894878 per step and 0.989542 after 100 steps. These are calculations for one linear mode. The small-ξ expansion shows phase lag near zero, but RK4 does not lag throughout its stable interval. At ξ=2, for example, its continuous phase is about 2.0344, ahead of the exact value 2. The first factor in the last expression is spatial dispersion. The second is the additional RK4 phase error, with its limit taken at ξ=0. The accompanying response plot is for the scalar linear test equation; its amplitude is not a measured entropy error of the vortex. There is no contradiction with conservation of the summed primary variables. If the discrete right-hand side has zero summed mass, momentum and total-energy residual at every stage, RK4 preserves those linear sums, apart from roundoff. K=m²/(2ρ), entropy, wave amplitudes and phases are nonlinear or more detailed properties; preserving the sums does not fix them. See the Runge–Kutta chapter for the stages and stability-function context. RK4 amplitude and phase response for a pure-imaginary eigenvalue. Outside the dashed stability boundary this linear test equation is unstable. Read the diagnostics separately# At fixed grid spacing, reduce Δt. Changes in amplitude and phase expose temporal error; the spatial dispersion remains. Refine the grid as well, with sufficiently small temporal error. Refinement at fixed CFL changes both h and Δt, so it alone does not separate their contributions. For small perturbations of a uniform state, compare one mode with its exact amplitude and phase. For a nonlinear vortex, compare fields and pressure-work/entropy diagnostics instead of applying the scalar sine relation to the whole flow. Track primary conservation, kinetic-energy pressure-work balance, entropy-proxy change, density/pressure positivity, and field error separately. A dispersive oscillation is not automatically growing instability; conversely, actual growth cannot be dismissed as harmless dispersion. The two response figures are analytical diagnostics, not additional atlas test problems. They do not change the published solver, fixed inputs, saved vortex results or code-edition ZIP. The existing vortex study below supplies the separate finite-grid evidence. Recompute the figures and data Save the analysis script and requirements in one folder, then run with Python 3.9 or later. Choose a new output directory. See the instructions and scope and script license. python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python analyse-keep.py --output generated Spatial dispersion CSV · RK4 response CSV · Results and fixed inputs JSON · File hashes JSON · Editable prose and LaTeX JSON Appropriate first test: smooth isentropic vortex advection# Use gamma = 1.4 on a periodic [−10,10]² square, background velocity (1,0.5), and vortex strength beta = 3. Relative to its translating center, write X, Y and r² = X²+Y². The reference is u=1−βY2πe(1−r2)/2,v=0.5+βX2πe(1−r2)/2,T=1−(γ−1)β28γπ2e1−r2,ρ=T1/(γ−1),p=ργ.uT​=1−2πβY​e(1−r2)/2,=1−8γπ2(γ−1)β2​e1−r2,​vρ​=0.5+2πβX​e(1−r2)/2,=T1/(γ−1),p=ργ.​ The whole-plane vortex translates analytically. Minimum-image coordinates in a box of length 20 leave its boundary tails below floating-point significance for these parameters, avoiding an appreciable periodic boundary jump. Positivity of the analytic temperature is checked explicitly. The static study runs 48², 96², and 192² cells to t = 1 at CFL 0.25. It reports pointwise density L1 error, primary-conservation drift, and the change in S_* per mass. A separate 96² run halves the CFL to assess the time-step contribution. The measurement manifest states the actual errors; the expected smooth spatial order is two. The movie instead runs 96² to t = 4 and is a qualitative time-history exhibit, not a substitute for refinement. Appropriate next tests# A compressible inviscid 3D Taylor–Green vortex is a primary KEEP benchmark. Fix the periodic box [0,2 pi]³, reference density, gamma, initial Mach number, velocity amplitude, initial pressure perturbation, and temporal scheme. Track total energy, kinetic energy, pressure dilatation, entropy, density/temperature RMS fluctuations, and resolved spectra under grid and time refinement. Pressure-work exchange must be separated from numerical dissipation. The original paper also examines inviscid isotropic turbulence. These 3D computations are not implemented in this edition; a 2D slice is not a replacement for the three-dimensional vortex-stretching dynamics. A smooth constant-pressure density wave tests preservation of pressure/velocity equilibrium. It is a useful additional diagnostic, but that property depends on the flux variant. Our original arithmetic-mean flux produces a nonzero semidiscrete pressure residual for this data; a test records that limitation instead of claiming it passes. Shima et al. (2021) study pressure-equilibrium-preserving split forms. Caveats: entropy, shocks, and the scheme version# Preserving is not a roundoff-exact entropy guarantee. The authors explicitly distinguish improved entropy behavior from exact conservation in their 2022 explanation. Tamaki, Kuya, and Kawai (2022) analyze remaining entropy errors and redefine KEEP variants with tunable approximation order. Our code does not implement that redefinition or an exact logarithmic-mean entropy-conservative flux. A shock requires entropy production. A bare non-dissipative central flux supplies no general mechanism to select a non-oscillatory admissible shock solution. Sod, Shu–Osher, and Double Mach Reflection are not acceptance tests for the unstabilized baseline demonstrated here. A shock-tube run can still be a deliberate limitation/oscillation diagnostic; it should not be advertised as a validated shock-capturing result. It is inaccurate to turn this into a universal statement that every KEEP-based method is unable to solve any shock tube. Shock stabilization changes the method. A sensor, artificial viscosity, upwind blending, filtering, or another entropy-stable construction needs its own definition and tests. Record shock/contact thickness, oscillations, positivity, and added dissipation; keep separate results for the smooth base scheme and stabilized extension. No such extension is implemented here. No positivity theorem is supplied. Positive density and pressure in the displayed smooth runs do not establish robustness near vacuum or under arbitrary under-resolution. The code stops on nonphysical states rather than silently clipping them. Time integration and boundaries matter. Asada, Maruyama, and Kawai (2024) address temporal preservation. Our RK4, periodic uniform-grid experiment does not implement their method, high-order/curvilinear KEEP, hanging-node treatments, wall models, or a production LES solver. Reproduce# python scripts/build_keep.py python -m pip install '.[movies]' python scripts/build_movies.py The first command creates the smooth-error figure and its source manifest. The second build adds the KEEP vortex to the motion gallery. Continue with shock benchmarks, carbuncle caveats, and the distinction from symplectic Hamiltonian maps: KEEP’s fluid energy/entropy consistency and symplecticity of a mechanical time map are different properties. documents.title: Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Lattice Boltzmann: collide, stream, recover fluid motion Implemented: low-Mach, isothermal D2Q9–BGK, Guo body forcing, periodic boundaries and stationary half-way bounce-back walls. Lattice units use Δx=Δt=ρ_ref=1, c_s²=1/3. 1954 → 1992 → 2002# The relaxation model of Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (1954) precedes lattice BGK. Qian–d'Humières–Lallemand (1992) is the lattice-BGK reference. Guo–Zheng–Shi (2002) supplies the force discretization used here. These are distinct developments. D2Q9 has one resting population, four axial directions and four diagonals. Weights are 4/9, 1/9 and 1/36 for those groups. The equilibrium is fqeq=wqρ[1+3cq⋅u+92(cq⋅u)2−32∣u∣2].fqeq​=wq​ρ[1+3cq​⋅u+29​(cq​⋅u)2−23​∣u∣2]. Collision relaxes populations, then streaming shifts each by its integer lattice velocity: fq(x+cq,t+1)=fq(x,t)−fq−fqeqτ+Sq.fq​(x+cq​,t+1)=fq​(x,t)−τfq​−fqeq​​+Sq​. For a force density F, Guo forcing uses Sq=wq(1−12τ)[3(cq−u)+9(cq⋅u)cq]⋅F,ρu=∑qfqcq+F2.Sq​=wq​(1−2τ1​)[3(cq​−u)+9(cq​⋅u)cq​]⋅F,ρu=q∑​fq​cq​+2F​. Density is the population sum, pressure is c_s²ρ, and viscosity is ν=c_s²(τ−1/2). The Chapman–Enskog derivation explains the discrete-time half-step correction. τ>1/2 makes this viscosity positive; it is not a universal nonlinear stability certificate. Two independent tests# A transverse periodic shear wave decays as exp(−νk²t), allowing an independent viscosity measurement. Force-driven Poiseuille flow has exact profile u_x=F_x y(H−y)/(2ρ_refν). The walls sit half a lattice spacing beyond the outer fluid nodes, not at those node centers. Fixed τ=0.8, peak velocity 0.01, and Ny=8,16,32 test wall placement and refinement. Startup runs for twelve slowest viscous decay times; finite-time and spatial errors remain distinct. The data manifest records channel errors, Mach numbers, force settings and step counts. Unit tests also verify periodic mass/momentum conservation and equilibrium moments. BGK is a single-relaxation baseline: MRT/TRT, entropic and cumulant collisions, thermal/compressible LBM, moving walls and multiphase models remain extensions. Projection flow solves a different discrete system and provides another route to incompressibility. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Slope limiters: minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, and van Albada Limiters trade linear high-order reconstruction for a nonlinear choice of local slope. Open the limiter notebook to compare five choices on identical grids and time integrators, together with first-order and unlimited scalar baselines. Reconstruction and the ratio convention# For uniform cells, let the backward and forward increments be ai=uˉi−uˉi−1,bi=uˉi+1−uˉi,ri=ai/bi,si=ϕ(ri)bi.ai​=uˉi​−uˉi−1​,bi​=uˉi+1​−uˉi​,ri​=ai​/bi​,si​=ϕ(ri​)bi​. The two states reconstructed from cell i are ui+1/2L=uˉi+12si,ui−1/2R=uˉi−12si.ui+1/2L​=uˉi​+21​si​,ui−1/2R​=uˉi​−21​si​. The implementation works directly with a and b, so a zero denominator at a plateau requires neither a numerical epsilon nor an arbitrary ratio. Opposite signs or either zero increment give zero limited slope. These are increments; divide by cell width only if a derivative is required. Five limiter functions# Each function below is zero for r ≤ 0. For r > 0: ϕminmod(r)=min⁡(1,r),ϕSuperbee(r)=max⁡{min⁡(2r,1),min⁡(r,2)},ϕMC(r)=min⁡{2r,(1+r)/2,2},ϕvan Leer(r)=2r/(1+r),ϕvan Albada(r)=(r2+r)/(r2+1).ϕminmod​(r)ϕSuperbee​(r)ϕMC​(r)ϕvan Leer​(r)ϕvan Albada​(r)​=min(1,r),=max{min(2r,1),min(r,2)},=min{2r,(1+r)/2,2},=2r/(1+r),=(r2+r)/(r2+1).​ This is the clipped, symmetric van Albada form, without an epsilon regularization; other variants differ near extrema. MC means monotonized central. All five satisfy phi(1)=1 and the plotted scalar bounds 0 ≤ phi(r) ≤ min(2r,2). See Sweby (1984) for the scalar flux-limiter framework and Roe's compressive construction, and the Clawpack limiter documentation and MPI-AMRVAC slope-limiter notes for implementation conventions. Names shared by different codes do not settle which variables, time integrator, or epsilon are used. Minmod chooses the smaller same-sign increment. Superbee takes a more compressive slope and can sharpen a smooth feature into a plateau. MC and van Leer retain more slope than minmod in many monotone regions. The notebook lets the error, variation, and overshoot measurements qualify those tendencies; no limiter wins every problem. Computed comparisons# The scalar equation is u_t + a u_x = 0 on [0,1], with periodic boundaries. All runs use conservative finite volumes, upwind interface fluxes, SSPRK(3,3), N=200, |a| dt/dx ≤ 0.3, and final time 1. The last step is shortened. Both directions a=±1 are computed. The two profiles are a unit square pulse on [0.2,0.4] and sin(2πx). Initial and reference values are exact cell averages, including partially covered square-pulse cells and the sine's sinc factor. Displayed L1 errors use those cell averages. Periodic total variation includes the last-to-first cell jump; mass is dx times the sum. Maximum TV uses every saved full-step diagnostic, including the initial state. The first-order comparison has zero slope. The unlimited comparison uses the centered slope (a+b)/2 with the same flux and SSPRK3; it can produce oscillations. It is not the Lax–Wendroff fully discrete method. The separate Sod comparison uses the existing ideal-gas setup, gamma=1.4, N=200, t=0.2, HLLC, primitive-variable reconstruction, and SSPRK3 at CFL=0.3. Only the slope choice changes. Its density error is pointwise, following the existing Sod convention; it is not an exact cell-average error. Outflow boundaries mean that the periodic scalar mass/TV diagnostics are not applied to this panel. Smooth sine refinement at N=40,80,160 and t=0.2 reports measured L1 errors and orders. A second-order label describes smooth-region consistency, not uniform pointwise accuracy at extrema or a second-order error on discontinuities. TVD is a property of the complete scalar update# For this scalar MUSCL operator, the stated slope bounds together with |a| dt/dx ≤ 1/2 give a TVD forward-Euler building block; SSPRK3 preserves its convex stability property under that bound. The executable solver restricts CFL to this range. Tests check both signs, periodic conservation, full-step variation, bounds, and a forward-Euler random-data case at CFL=1/2. The same function applied componentwise to Euler primitive variables is not a general system TVD theorem, entropy condition, or guarantee of positive cell averages. Characteristic reconstruction and a fully discrete positivity construction are separate extensions. See advanced limiters for TVB extrema relaxation and conservative positive-state scaling. Reproduce and inspect# python -m numart.cli run sod --method muscl --riemann hllc --limiter superbee --n 200 python scripts/build_limiters.py python scripts/sync_web_content.py from numart import get_problem, solve from numart.tvd import solve_advection sod = solve(get_problem("sod"), limiter="mc") pulse = solve_advection(profile="square", limiter="van-leer", speed=-1.) docs/figures/limiters.json records all plotted arrays, refinement results, diagnostics, and source hashes. The browser selects these Python-computed curves; it does not run another implementation of the PDE solver. Default MUSCL remains minmod. The limiter option does not apply to WENO5 or the 2D Euler/MHD baselines. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE
