documents.title: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes Separate acoustic/convective preconditioning from transonic numerical-viscosity corrections. Connect a concrete Γ, a linear eigenvalue model, Mach cutoffs and dual time stepping with explicit variable conventions. Matrix-solve and PDE preconditioning Left preconditioning P⁻¹Ax=P⁻¹b assists an iterative linear solve. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning instead changes pseudo-time mass matrices or characteristic numerical dissipation. Papers may use P for both; identify the operator being modified first. At low Mach number, |u_n±a| is large compared with convection |u_n|, affecting steady iteration and low-speed flux accuracy. This is a different limit from a transonic characteristic u_n±a=0. Place Γ on pseudo time Distinguish conservative U from primitive q and pseudo time τ from physical time t. Steady problems omit the physical-time term. Unsteady dual-time iterations retain the physically discretized term, such as BDF2, throughout the inner solve. Γ is not the same matrix as U_q. For nonsingular Γ and unchanged R, a converged steady pseudo-time solve still satisfies R=0. Preconditioning spatial dissipation additionally changes the discrete residual construction. Indiscriminately preconditioning physical time changes the unsteady solution, including acoustics. Γ(q)∂q∂τ+∂U(q)∂t+R(U(q))=0,q=(p,u,v,w,T)T.Γ(q)∂τ∂q​+∂t∂U(q)​+R(U(q))=0,q=(p,u,v,w,T)T. A concrete Weiss–Smith-type matrix For a calorically perfect ideal gas, use q=(p,u,v,w,T), total specific enthalpy H=c_pT+(u²+v²+w²)/2, constant c_p, ρ_T=(∂ρ/∂T)_p and physical sound speed a. Θ replaces the usual pressure-density derivative. This ideal-gas specialization is not a general real-fluid formula. Setting U_ref=a gives Θ=ρ/p and recovers the physical Jacobian U_q in this ordering. Reducing U_ref toward a convective scale changes pseudo-acoustic scales. Γ, its inverse and a conservative-variable P are not numerically identical matrices. Γ=(Θ000ρTΘuρ00ρTuΘv0ρ0ρTvΘw00ρρTwΘH−1ρuρvρwρTH+ρcp),Θ=1Uref2−ρTρcp,ρT=−ρT.Γ=​ΘΘuΘvΘwΘH−1​0ρ00ρu​00ρ0ρv​000ρρw​ρT​ρT​uρT​vρT​wρT​H+ρcp​​​,Θ=Uref2​1​−ρcp​ρT​​,ρT​=−Tρ​. Stagnation singularities and a Mach cutoff A representative bounded parameter is shown below. Positive M_cut prevents U_ref=0 at stagnation; the upper bound recovers the physical system at supersonic speed. This is an illustrative choice, not a universal prescription: viscous, unsteady and boundary-aware variants use other reference scales. The cutoff avoids degeneracy of the preconditioner near zero velocity; it does not remove physical Mach-1 flow from the domain. Too large a cutoff weakens low-Mach benefits; too small a value can impair robustness or boundary behavior. M=∥u∥a,β=min⁡(1,max⁡(M,Mcut)),Uref=βa,0<Mcut≤1.M=a∥u∥​,β=min(1,max(M,Mcut​)),Uref​=βa,0<Mcut​≤1. How characteristic eigenvalues change To expose the effect, linearize about constant density/sound speed and use pressure perturbation divided by ρ₀a, normal/tangential velocities and an advected entropy variable with fixed scaling. The following P is an illustrative pressure-row scaling, not the nonlinear Γ above. For nonzero β comparable with Mach number, pseudo-acoustic eigenvalues become convective in scale. However, a matrix 2-norm condition number is a singular-value ratio, not generally an absolute-eigenvalue ratio. Examine normality, variable scaling, boundaries and discretization as well. A=(una00aun0000un0000un),P=diag⁡(β2,1,1,1),qτ+PAqx=0.A=​un​a00​aun​00​00un​0​000un​​​,P=diag(β2,1,1,1),qτ​+PAqx​=0. λ±=(1+β2)un±(1−β2)2un2+4β2a22,λ0=un (twice),λ+λ−=β2(un2−a2).λ±​=2(1+β2)un​±(1−β2)2un2​+4β2a2​​,λ0​=un​ (twice),λ+​λ−​=β2(un2​−a2). κ2(A)=σmax⁡(A)/σmin⁡(A),χλ(A)=max⁡i∣λi∣/min⁡λi≠0∣λi∣.κ2​(A)=σmax​(A)/σmin​(A),χλ​(A)=imax​∣λi​∣/λi​=0min​∣λi​∣. Preconditioning does not remove a physical sonic zero The model has zero acoustic eigenvalue product when u_n²=a². More generally, multiplication by an invertible P cannot remove singularity of A. Do not claim that a preconditioning matrix eliminates physical sonic points. Sonic singularities of particular attempts at isotropic acoustic preconditioning also require formulation-specific discussion. det⁡(PA)=det⁡(P)det⁡(A),P nonsingular.det(PA)=det(P)det(A),P nonsingular. Transonic rarefaction and an entropy fix A Roe linearization can produce an unphysical expansion shock when a characteristic crosses zero through a rarefaction. A representative smoothing replaces |λ| in the numerical dissipation as below. δ has speed units; state-aware choices and fixed fractional cutoffs are different variants. This modifies numerical viscosity rather than deleting the physical characteristic. The published acoustic quadratic smoothing is not claimed as a faithful reproduction of every Harten–Hyman construction. Entropy correction, HLLE low-density robustness, carbuncle control and low-Mach preconditioning address different problems. ψδ(λ)={∣λ∣,∣λ∣≥δ,(λ2+δ2)/(2δ),∣λ∣<δ,δ>0.ψδ​(λ)={∣λ∣,(λ2+δ2)/(2δ),​∣λ∣≥δ,∣λ∣<δ,​δ>0. Checks that keep the mechanisms separate Test spectra, recovery at β→1, low-Mach scaling and near-stagnation invertibility on small linear problems. Measure pseudo-time convergence separately from solution error due to changed spatial fluxes. Interior eigenvalue analysis alone cannot assess boundary reflection. Use transonic Burgers/Euler rarefactions to examine expansion shocks, refinement and δ sensitivity. For unsteady problems separate physical-time convergence from inner pseudo-residual convergence. Low-Mach checks here are proposed work; existing Jacobi scaling or dual-time examples do not validate a dedicated low-Mach flow solver. Publication scope and related entries Low-Mach PDE preconditioning is reading-only, without dedicated code or numerical verification. Existing educational acoustic Roe smoothing does not implement Γ or the Weiss–Smith method. Dated verification records are unchanged, and proposed preconditioning checks are not presented as executed results. Preconditioned methods for solving the incompressible and low speed compressible equations. documents.title: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Markov-chain Monte Carlo / MCMC MCMC constructs a Markov chain with a chosen invariant distribution when direct independent sampling is difficult. Invariance and adequate exploration in a finite run are separate requirements. Problem and representative equations For an unnormalized target π and proposal q(y|x), use the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability. Unknown target normalization cancels. Proposal factors cancel only for symmetric proposals; omitting them for an asymmetric proposal changes the target. a(x,y)=min⁡ ⁣(1,π(y)q(x∣y)π(x)q(y∣x)),Neff≈N1+2∑k≥1ρk.a(x,y)=min(1,π(x)q(y∣x)π(y)q(x∣y)​),Neff​≈1+2∑k≥1​ρk​N​. Algorithm Propose y, accept or retain x, and keep rejected repetitions as samples. Assess initial transients and use dispersed initial states across chains. Interpret autocorrelation-based effective sample size only when stationarity and autocorrelation estimation are credible. Conditions and pitfalls Detailed balance alone does not establish irreducibility or aperiodicity. Multimodality, correlations and boundaries can slow mixing. High acceptance can simply reflect tiny moves. Thinning is not a general way to increase information for a fixed computational budget. What to check Check means, variances and quantiles for known targets, including asymmetric proposals and rejections. For multimodal cases report between-chain comparisons, autocorrelations, effective sample sizes and uncertainty; visually flat traces alone are not proof of convergence. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. documents.title: Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Structured, unstructured, and triangular meshes A mesh describes geometry and connectivity. Cell shape and indexing are different choices: triangles may be obtained by splitting a structured lattice, or connected in an irregular unstructured triangulation. The mesh explorer makes this distinction visible. The element-basis chapter supplies the other half of the representation: Legendre modes, nodal Lagrange functions, quadrature and mass matrices, quadrilateral tensor products, and triangular P1/P2 shape functions. The basis notebook shows these functions inside a reference cell. Structured meshes# A logically rectangular mesh admits indices (i,j) and predictable neighboring indices. Cartesian rectangles are the simplest example, but a body-fitted curvilinear mesh may retain structured indexing. Metric terms, face normals, and cell volumes then come from its geometry. Multiblock grids join several such index spaces. The explorer’s first example has 8 × 6 rectangular cells on the unit square. Connectivity is still exported explicitly so that the same inspection code can handle every example. Triangles and unstructured connectivity# Splitting each rectangle into two triangles changes the cell shape while preserving an underlying lattice pattern. The third example instead triangulates deterministic irregular interior points and a fixed square boundary. It uses Matplotlib’s Delaunay triangulation, not a call to the Triangle package. Shewchuk’s Triangle paper is a historical and algorithmic reading reference. An unstructured solver normally stores vertices, cells, faces, and owner/neighbor relationships. Boundary faces have one adjacent cell; interior faces have two. The explorer highlights face-sharing neighbors, not every cell that merely touches a vertex. Labels are vertex-average cell centers; for triangles these equal the area centroids. Conservation is a face contract# For a finite volume K with area |K|, ddt(∣K∣U‾K)=−∑f⊂∂K∣f∣ F^(UK,UKf;nK,f).dtd​(∣K∣UK​)=−f⊂∂K∑​∣f∣F(UK​,UKf​​;nK,f​). An interior face contributes equal and opposite fluxes to its two cells. This cancellation is independent of whether K is a quadrilateral or triangle. With counterclockwise vertices, an edge displacement (dx,dy) has outward unit normal (dy,−dx)/length. Signed polygon areas detect reversed or degenerate cells. Quality and implementation scope# Small angles, skewness, aspect ratio, nonorthogonality, and volume variation influence reconstruction and stability differently. Delaunay connectivity alone does not guarantee adequate boundary-layer resolution or a suitable minimum angle for arbitrary point sets. No mesh-quality optimization is performed here. numart.geometry.example_meshes supplies the three examples. Tests verify positive cell areas, unit total area, connected face-neighbor graphs, reciprocal adjacency, and the planar Euler relation V−E+F_cells = 1 for these simply connected domains. The explorer is a geometry/connectivity demonstration; an unstructured Euler or viscous flow solver remains future work. Continue with ALE moving cells, SPH particles, and cylindrical metrics and tensors. Variable staggering is another choice# Arakawa A/B/C placement specifies which variables occupy centers, corners and faces on a given mesh. It is independent of structured versus unstructured connectivity and of temporal order. The new chapter connects the existing MAC layout to rotating shallow-water waves, with explicit Coriolis averaging and tested Fourier symbols. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data MHD: constrained transport and divergence cleaning The GSPH/GSPMHD notes describe a separate particle branch. The relativistic development review follows SRMHD and GRMHD, including CT, primitive recovery, and evolving spacetime. Neither branch is implemented by the Newtonian planar model below. Problem and units# The original Orszag–Tang baseline is planar 2D ideal MHD with γ=5/3, μ0=1, and vz=Bz=0 on the periodic unit square. Arrays are indexed [x,y,variable], with state q=(ρ,mx,my,E,Bx,By,ψ) and E=p/(γ-1)+ρ(vx²+vy²)/2+(Bx²+By²)/2. The Orszag–Tang initial condition is ρ=2536π,p=512π,v=(−sin⁡2πy,sin⁡2πx),B=14π(−sin⁡2πy,sin⁡4πx).ρ=36π25​,p=12π5​,v=(−sin2πy,sin2πx),B=4π​1​(−sin2πy,sin4πx). This is a widely used compressible-test normalization, rather than a complete reproduction of the original incompressible MHD study by Orszag–Tang (1979). The MASCLET paper is one reference for this compressible normalization. CT: share the same edge electric field# Store normal magnetic components on cell faces and update both directions with a shared corner Ez: for example, Bx <- Bx - Δt D_y Ez and By <- By + Δt D_x Ez. The corresponding divergence update contains -D_xD_y Ez+D_yD_x Ez=0, preserving the matching discrete divergence. This edition uses a simple flux-CT construction with arithmetic averages of electric fields from Rusanov face fluxes. Face Riemann problems use a single normal magnetic field; interface energy is adjusted to preserve primitive pressure. After each update, cell-centered fields are averaged from faces. Total energy is not reset nonconservatively. This implementation does not reproduce every coordinate-system detail of Evans–Hawley or Athena's upwind CT. Evans–Hawley (1988), Tóth (2000). GLM: transport and damp divergence errors# With cell-centered B and an auxiliary variable ψ, solve ∂tB+∇⋅(vB−Bv)+∇ψ=0,∂tψ+ch2∇⋅B=−αψ.∂t​B+∇⋅(vB−Bv)+∇ψ=0,∂t​ψ+ch2​∇⋅B=−αψ. The induction flux components are F_i(B_j)=v_i B_j-B_i v_j+δij ψ. This edition fixes ch=3 and uses α=damping*ch/h, with damping=0.18. Linear ψ damping is split off and integrated exponentially; the remaining update uses first-order Rusanov fluxes and forward Euler. The energy variable is conventional MHD energy without a ψ² contribution. This educational Dedner-type model covers a subset of GLM/EGLM formulations. Dedner et al. (2002). Measuring ∇·B# CT uses face-field differences; GLM uses centered differences of cell-centered B. Records include the operator name, because values from different discrete divergences cannot directly rank methods. With the fixed, relatively dissipative GLM wave speed and symmetric OT data, centered divergence can remain extremely small. OT alone therefore gives incomplete evidence about cleaning performance. A separate diagnostic injects Bx += 0.01sin(2πx) with magnetic_error=0.01, adjusting energy to preserve initial gas pressure. This is not the standard OT problem. It examines divergence-wave transport and damping while distinguishing damping from error reduction by numerical viscosity. CT preserves an initial discrete constraint; it does not automatically remove an existing magnetic-monopole error. Verification scope# Tests check periodic mass and total energy, density and pressure positivity on selected cases, CT divergence preservation, and GLM injected-error cleaning. The HLLD section below adds Brio–Wu, Alfvén-wave refinement and field loops. External reference-code comparisons remain future work. The low-resolution, first-order OT figures are introductory demonstrations of magnetic-constraint handling. Time evolution# The motion gallery now includes separate 64² Orszag–Tang CT and GLM movies. Their actual adaptive-CFL snapshot times and native divergence diagnostics differ. Playback does not supply an equal-accuracy ranking. HLLD and standard wave tests# Open the HLLD test comparisons. These new full-vector ideal-MHD runs retain all three velocity and magnetic components, unlike the planar Orszag–Tang baseline above. With μ0 = 1, q = (ρ,ρvx,ρvy,ρvz,E,Bx,By,Bz) and E = p/(γ−1) + ρ|v|²/2 + |B|²/2. The HLLD fan resolves the contact and two rotational waves between its outer fast-wave bounds. Intermediate star/double-star states use one shared normal magnetic field. Invalid intermediate states fall back to HLLE and each face fallback is counted. Miyoshi–Kusano (2005) is the original bibliographic source; the accessible Athena++ HLLD implementation was used to cross-check the equations. This is an independent educational implementation, not an Athena++ run or full reproduction of the paper. All three tests use primitive MC slopes and SSPRK2 with face positivity scaling. Step retries and HLLE fallbacks are recorded; no conserved mean is clipped. Selected physical states staying positive is not a general robustness proof. Brio–Wu: γ = 2 on [0,1], initial discontinuity at x = 0.5, (ρ,p,By)L = (1,1,1), (ρ,p,By)R = (0.125,0.1,−1), Bx = 0.75, all velocities and Bz zero, open ends, t = 0.1, CFL 0.35. Compare HLLE/HLLD at 400 cells and HLLD at 800. Profiles are numerical grid comparisons, not exact-solution overlays or a universal uniqueness claim. Brio–Wu (1988). Circular Alfvén wave: γ = 5/3, ρ = 1, p = 0.1, Bx = 1, (By,Bz) = 0.1(cos(2πx),sin(2πx)), (vy,vz) = −(By,Bz), vx = 0, periodic unit interval, one period t = 1, CFL 0.35. Exact conservative cell averages include sinc-averaged transverse fields and constant total energy; energy is not reconstructed from squares of averaged fields. HLLE and HLLD use 32, 64, 128 and 256 cells. The finest measured orders for the mean absolute transverse-field error are both approximately 1.98. Weak magnetic loop: γ = 5/3, ρ = p = 1, v = (2,1,0), Az = 10⁻³ max(0.3−r,0) on a periodic 2 × 1 box, t = 1, CFL 0.3, 64 × 32 and 128 × 64 cells. Compare HLLE/HLLD with each of CT and GLM. Finite-field translation is a diagnostic, not an exact solution: magnetic forces are small, not zero. CT-Contact and GLM scope in the loop test# CT initializes face B from a corner-potential curl. A contact-upwinded corner EMF uses the face mass-flux sign for transverse electric-field derivatives (CT-Contact in Mignone–Del Zanna (2021), equations 20–22). It reduces to the face induction flux in a grid-aligned 1D limit. This is not the UCT-HLLD construction. The shared curl preserves the native face divergence at each SSPRK stage; cell B is averaged from faces and total energy is not reset. GLM initializes cell B from a centered curl of cell Az. At each face, the longitudinal subsystem is solved first: Bn∗=Bn,L+Bn,R2−ψR−ψL2ch,ψ∗=ψL+ψR2−ch(Bn,R−Bn,L)2.Bn∗​=2Bn,L​+Bn,R​​−2ch​ψR​−ψL​​,ψ∗=2ψL​+ψR​​−2ch​(Bn,R​−Bn,L​)​. HLLD/HLLE then receives common Bn*, preserving interface primitive pressure; fluxes of Bn and ψ are ψ* and ch²Bn*. Set ch = 4 and use exponential ψ half-step damping with rate 0.18ch/h before/after SSPRK2. E has no ψ energy. This is a conservative GLM model inspired by the longitudinal solve in Mignone–Tzeferacos (2010), not their CTU integrator or EGLM variant. The fixed cleaning speed also changes the step count. The initial magnetic discretizations and native divergence operators differ. Energy fractions are normalized by each run's own initial cell-field energy. Do not infer an equal-accuracy or matched-cost CT/GLM ranking. At 128 × 64, CT preserves native maximum divergence below 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ in these runs; GLM's centered maximum is about 3.7 × 10⁻⁴. These operator-dependent numbers have units of B/length. All published loop runs have zero HLLE fallbacks and zero retries. External reference-code comparisons, stronger-field loop tests and UCT-HLLD remain future work. Reproduce with python scripts/build_mhd_tests.py. Download definitions, diagnostics and hashes and computed conservative arrays. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Monte Carlo integration | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Monte Carlo integration Monte Carlo integration estimates an integral as an expectation. Accuracy depends on the sampling distribution, weights and variance, not merely on using random numbers. Problem and representative equations Draw independent samples Xᵢ from a density p covering the support of f and average Yᵢ=f(Xᵢ)/p(Xᵢ). With finite second moment, estimate standard error by s_Y/√N. Uniform sampling requires the domain-volume factor. I=∫f(x) dx=Ep ⁣[f(X)p(X)],I^N=1N∑i=1Nf(Xi)p(Xi),SE⁡^=sY/N.I=∫f(x)dx=Ep​[p(X)f(X)​],IN​=N1​i=1∑N​p(Xi​)f(Xi​)​,SE=sY​/N​. Algorithm Specify the distribution and random generator, draw samples and compute the weighted mean and variance. Importance sampling concentrates p where contributions matter, while monitoring heavy tails of f/p. Record generator/version, seed and sample count for reproducibility. Conditions and pitfalls The N⁻¹/² scale is statistical and conditional on assumptions such as independence and finite variance; it is not a deterministic bound for each run. Rare events and missed peaks can make variance estimates misleading. Correlated MCMC samples need a different uncertainty calculation. What to check Use repeated independent runs on known integrals to examine N scaling and interval coverage. Record actual mean error separately from estimated uncertainty, and verify that changes in importance density preserve the target integral. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Monte Carlo integration Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. Nicholas Metropolis and S. Ulam (1949). The Monte Carlo Method. Journal of the American Statistical Association Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Abstract and bibliography checked · Consulted record Publisher abstract and bibliographic identity; independent-sample estimator shown in modern notation. documents.title: Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Time-dependent tests: movies and saved states Open the motion gallery. Use movies when the evolution is part of the question: a shock reflecting, a vortex advecting, or magnetic structures forming. Steady solutions, manufactured equilibrium profiles, and final elliptic fields remain still figures. A solver residual versus iteration is an algorithmic history, not a physical-time flow movie. Five computed movies# Double Mach Reflection: Mach-10 2D Euler reflection on 256 × 64 cells, t = 0 to 0.2, first-order HLL with SSPRK2 and CFL 0.4. The fine wall jet is not resolved. Read the setup. Orszag–Tang with CT: 64² periodic planar ideal MHD, t = 0 to 0.5, first-order Rusanov with forward Euler and CFL 0.3. Magnetic divergence uses the staggered face operator. Orszag–Tang with GLM: the same resolution and physical interval, with fixed cleaning speed 3 and damping 0.18. Its native divergence uses the cell-centered central operator. The CT and GLM plots do not form an equal-accuracy ranking. Read the MHD definitions. Smooth isentropic vortex with original KEEP: 96² periodic Euler on [−10,10]², t = 0 to 4, the second-order arithmetic-mean Cartesian KEEP flux and classical RK4, CFL 0.25. No shock stabilization, pressure-equilibrium-preserving extension, or exact entropy claim is included. Read the KEEP chapter. Mach-3 forward-facing step: 240 × 80 cells, t = 0 to 4, first-order HLL and SSPRK2 with CFL 0.4. Grid-aligned blocked cells represent a step at x = 0.6 of height 0.2. Standard reflection is applied without an entropy/enthalpy corner reset. Diagnostics exclude solid cells. This is a classical inviscid benchmark, not a NASA experimental validation. See the shock-case definitions. Density and pressure appear together in every movie. These are rendered numerical states from the repository solvers, not interpolated illustrations or reproductions of original-paper movies. Actual physical times, unchanged time steps# Each movie requests 81 output times, including the initial and final times. The recorder saves the first completed solver state at or after each request. It does not shorten a numerical step to hit a requested time and does not interpolate the solution. If a coarse step crosses several requests, one state represents them. Actual times and solver step counts accompany every frame. The production movies have 81 distinct states each. The MHD CT and GLM solvers choose different time steps, so similarly numbered frames need not have identical intermediate physical times. Read the timestamps before comparing them. Snapshot tests verify that enabling output leaves the final state and numerical history unchanged. Fixed scales and explicit playback# Each density and pressure color scale is fixed across its entire run using that run’s extrema over the saved states. Colors must not be interpreted as identical values across different movies unless their scale labels agree. The minima and maxima listed beside the player are measurements of the currently displayed state; they do not establish a positivity theorem. Playback starts only after pressing Play. Pause, first/last, previous/next, a saved-frame slider, speed selection, and an optional loop support inspection. Speed is presentation speed, not a change to the simulation. At the nominal rate, 81 saved frames at 12 frames per second make a 6.75-second clip. All physical times remain printed inside the images. A native MP4 player and MP4/frame downloads are also available. MP4 uses H.264 video with no audio; the inspectable image frames are lossless WebP. Video compression is a presentation step and never feeds back into the computation. Reproduce and verify# python -m pip install '.[movies]' python scripts/build_movies.py python scripts/check_movies.py The builder writes the published frames, MP4 files, and movie catalog into website/public/assets/movies. It also saves full numerical snapshots as compressed NumPy arrays in the ignored outputs/movies directory for local inspection. Source hashes, image/video hashes, numerical-state hashes, software versions, methods, boundary conditions, physical scales, and per-frame diagnostics are recorded in the catalog. The fifth movie is built by python scripts/build_shock_gallery.py and has a separate shock catalog; the player combines both catalogs. Its full saved states are in outputs/shock-gallery. The checker validates hashes and metadata, opens each saved image, and decodes each MP4 to verify its dimensions, playback rate, and complete frame count. A short small-grid build can be made with --quick --output <directory>; its catalog is marked as a quick check and is not the published production run. Multidimensional still fields# The numerical gallery opens with 2D/3D spatial fields, including the five movie entry points above. Dimension and subject filters can be combined; all dimensions also includes the 1D comparisons and algorithmic diagnostic figures. Three additional still figures expose fields from existing solvers: 2D triangular P1 Poisson: 24 × 24 split squares (1152 triangles), zero Dirichlet data and exact solution sin(πx)sin(πy). The second panel is nodal error; continuous L2/H1 errors are measured separately inside elements. 2D periodic Taylor–Green: 64 × 64 MAC cells, viscosity 0.1, t = 0.5. Speed/arrows average face velocities to cell centers only for visualization; velocity RMS and divergence diagnostics use the native MAC arrays. 3D periodic Poisson: a 32³ FFT solve with density 1 + 0.3 cos(2πx)cos(4πy)cos(2πz), G = 1 and zero-mean potential. Three orthogonal slices at coordinate 0.5 use the same color limits. This is a static 3D field checked against one exact Fourier mode, not a 3D fluid or particle-evolution simulation. Reproduce these still fields with python scripts/build_multidimensional_gallery.py. Download the definitions, diagnostics and source hashes and computed arrays. These views add no new solver or convergence study; the existing FEM and MAC refinement tests remain separate evidence. What a movie does not establish# A visually smooth evolution does not establish mesh convergence, an entropy inequality, shock robustness, long-time turbulent accuracy, or agreement with experiments. The KEEP vortex refinement supplies separate smooth-error measurements. The carbuncle chapter explains why a shock movie alone cannot certify multidimensional stability. Reconstruction comparison clips# The Euler comparison page adds paired first-order/minmod/MC clips of the same forward-step case, with shared color scales and 81 output states per method. Read actual timestamps in the frames: adaptive solver steps need not land on identical intermediate times. These compare reconstructions; they do not add physical cases to the five-case movie catalog. python scripts/build_euler_comparison.py builds them and decodes each MP4 to check its frame count. documents.title: NASA 2D verification and validation case catalog · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data NASA 2D verification and validation case catalog Start with the official NPARC Verification and Validation Archive, CFL3D test cases, and Turbulence Modeling Resource. NASA's TMR information page describes the resource's move to GitHub in February 2026. The two 15-degree wedge flows are now computed educational Euler baselines. The remaining NASA entries below are cataloged candidates. These independent calculations are not Wind-US output, experimental validations or reproductions of NASA's complete solver/grid comparison. A classical Mach-3 forward-facing step and Double Mach Reflection complement the NASA cases. Computed shock tests# Open the shock-containing fields in the gallery. Both wedges start from uniform freestream with gamma 1.4, density 1 and sound speed 1. The independent body-fitted mesh spans x = −0.5 to 1, the lower wall y = max(x,0) tan(15°), and the upper boundary y = 1.2. The higher farfield keeps the Mach-2 weak shock below that boundary at the outlet; it differs from the height 1 of NASA's Mach-2.5 domain. Inlet and upper-boundary states are fixed at freestream, the outlet is extrapolated and the lower wall reflects normal momentum. Shared oriented face fluxes conserve the cell totals; cell areas and face normals come from the actual quadrilaterals. NASA wedge, Mach 2.0: Mach and pressure maps on 240 × 80 cells at t = 3, with the theoretical weak-shock line. A 120 × 40 run supplies a second grid. NASA setup. NASA wedge, Mach 2.5: the same independent meshes and terminal time. The reference shock angle is approximately 36.94490°, pressure ratio 2.467500, and downstream Mach number 1.873526. The theta–beta–Mach root and normal-shock relations supply the reference, with a numerical Rankine–Hugoniot check. NASA analytical comparison. Classical Mach-3 forward-facing step: a 3 × 1 tunnel with the step at x = 0.6 and height 0.2, uniform inflow (density 1.4, pressure 1, velocity 3), reflecting walls and an extrapolated exit. A 240 × 80 grid reaches t = 4, with 81 saved states and an MP4. Watch the shock reflections. This is the classical Emery/Woodward–Colella benchmark, not a NASA-originated experiment. The corner treatment differs from the corrected PPM comparison in Woodward–Colella §VI.b: this baseline applies plain reflection and does not reset entropy or enthalpy near the step corner. Corner artifacts and smeared slip lines may remain. These use first-order HLL finite volumes and SSPRK2, with CFL 0.4. Wedges have no imposed analytical shock in their initial state. Their normalized L1 density errors compare conservative cell averages with an exactly clipped piecewise-constant oblique-shock reference. Wall-pressure medians use the first fluid row over 0.5 < x < 0.9; a density-gradient fit over 0.35 < x < 0.85 estimates the shock angle. Mach-2 MC still has local time variation at t = 3 (maximum conserved update rate approximately 6.08 in the published run); it is not a converged steady solution. This residual is exposed alongside the sharper density error. Two grids at one finite terminal time do not establish general asymptotic order or complete steady convergence. The step has no exact overlay and only one published grid; t = 4 is an unsteady snapshot. Reproduce with python scripts/build_shock_gallery.py; --reuse renders cached, source-checked trajectories. Download run definitions, diagnostics and hashes, final numerical fields, and the step movie manifest. Shock-containing NASA cases still to implement# The Mach-5 shock/boundary-layer interaction, Mach-7 laminar ramp, Sajben diffuser and RAE 2822 are later candidates. Their viscous, turbulence or gas-model requirements are part of each case; an inviscid wedge image is not a substitute for those validations. These cases have no computed exhibit here. Starting with Euler and analytical references# 15° wedge, Mach 2.0 — computed baseline: oblique shock and wall pressure with two grids. Roe/HLLE method comparisons remain future work. NASA case. 15° wedge, Mach 2.5 — computed baseline: shock angle and downstream-state reference. Pair this compression case with the planned expansion corner below. NASA case. Prandtl–Meyer 15° expansion, Mach 2.5: expansion-fan structure and analytical Mach/pressure relations. Official archive. Laminar flow, unsteadiness, and pressure Poisson problems# Driven cavity: centerline velocities, primary vortex, and corner vortices in a square. NASA uses low-Mach calculations to approximate incompressible flow and compares with Ghia and colleagues. NASA case. Blasius laminar flat plate: boundary-layer profiles, skin friction, and wall-normal mesh resolution. NASA case. Unsteady laminar circular cylinder: vortex shedding, drag/lift histories, and temporal accuracy; a candidate after dual time stepping. NASA case. Turbulence models, separation, and airfoils# Zero-pressure-gradient turbulent flat plate: skin friction, turbulence-model implementation verification, and grid convergence. TMR verification. 2D bump-in-channel: curved-wall pressure and friction, with comparisons between codes using the same turbulence model. TMR verification. Driver–Seegmiller backward-facing step: separation, reattachment, Cp/Cf, and velocity profiles. Fix the dataset version, including Reynolds-number definitions and corrections. TMR validation, NPARC. Sajben transonic diffuser: internal shocks, back pressure, and shock/boundary-layer interaction. NASA case. RAE 2822 transonic airfoil: surface Cp, shocks, and boundary layers. State the case number and corrected Mach number and angle of attack. NASA case. NACA 0012: surface pressure, lift/drag, and sensitivity to grids, far-field boundaries, and turbulence models. TMR validation. NACA 4412 trailing-edge separation: adverse pressure gradients and trailing-edge separation. TMR validation. NASA wall-mounted hump: wall-induced separation and reattachment. Record the applicability of 2D calculations to experiments containing three-dimensional effects. TMR validation. 2D mixing layer: free-shear-layer growth, velocity, and turbulence quantities. TMR validation. 2D airfoil near-wake: wake velocity deficit and recovery. TMR validation. Other classical 2D benchmarks# Double Mach Reflection, the Mach 3 forward-facing step, 2D Riemann configurations, the isentropic vortex, and odd-even shock/carbuncle tests are also useful flux demonstrations. The first two have a representative source in Woodward–Colella (1984). Our Double Mach Reflection exhibit and the forward step above are implemented first-order HLL baselines. Riemann configurations and controlled odd-even/carbuncle comparisons remain future work; the smooth KEEP vortex is computed. See the separate carbuncle notes for the required stability comparisons. Do not label all of these as NASA-originated problems. ONERA M6 is a 3D wing; axisymmetric bump and jet cases are also different from planar 2D cases and are excluded from the main list. Information to fix for each implementation# Record the original source, case number, geometry, nondimensionalization, Mach/Reynolds numbers, angle of attack, wall/far-field/inlet/outlet boundaries, grid sequence, exact turbulence-model variant, convergence residuals, time steps, and definitions of Cp/Cf/Cl/Cd. A decreasing residual alone establishes neither grid convergence nor agreement with experiments. Add the original measurement papers at implementation time rather than citing only NASA's resource pages. MUSCL reconstruction comparisons# Compare first order, minmod and MC. The new runs keep acoustic HLL, SSPRK2 and nominal CFL 0.4 fixed. Primitive variables are reconstructed from physical gradients at quadrilateral area centroids to face midpoints. On the body-fitted grid, x secants account for the accompanying physical y displacement. A shared face flux updates both neighbors. The limiter choices are minmod(a,b) and MC(a,b) = minmod(2a,(a+b)/2,2b); see the limiter definitions. Boundary reconstruction excludes solid neighbors and reflects fluid-side states. One cellwise factor scales reconstructed deviations when a face would have nonpositive density or pressure. Failed SSPRK2 steps halve the step size and retry; these events are recorded. Conserved means are not clipped. This is a tested safeguard, not a general positivity theorem for this solver. Both NASA wedges have all three reconstructions on 120 × 40 and 240 × 80 meshes at t = 3. Wall pressure, fitted shock angle and integrated density errors use the definitions above. A separate periodic entropy wave uses velocity (0.7,0.3), pressure 1 and density 1 + 0.2 sin(2πx) sin(2πy), initialized and compared as exact cell averages. Grids 16², 32², 64² and 128² reach t = 0.5. Observed orders are printed in the comparison page; MC approaches second order on this smooth test. Limiter activation at extrema affects the measured minmod order. Shock errors have a different convergence regime and do not establish smooth second order. The forward-step comparison adds minmod and MC stills and 81-state clips on the same 240 × 80 mesh. All three clips share density/pressure scales and requested output times, but actual intermediate timestamps can differ by one adaptive solver step. Nominal CFL and grids do not imply equal computational cost. These are three reconstructions of one physical case; the original first-order movie remains available. The corner treatment is unchanged and the t = 4 flow is unsteady. Reproduce with python scripts/build_euler_comparison.py. Download the comparison definitions, diagnostics and hashes and final conservative arrays. Full trajectories are cached locally under outputs/euler-comparison. documents.title: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization Gradient methods use first derivatives; quasi-Newton methods infer curvature from gradient differences. This introduction treats smooth unconstrained minimization, separately from constrained optimality conditions. Problem and representative equations Let gₖ=∇f(xₖ), Hₖ approximate the inverse Hessian and pₖ=−Hₖgₖ. In BFGS, s=xₖ₊₁−xₖ, y=gₖ₊₁−gₖ and ρ=1/(yᵀs). Hₖ=I gives steepest descent in the chosen coordinates, so units and scaling matter. xk+1=xk−αkHkgk,Hk+1=(I−ρsyT)Hk(I−ρysT)+ρssT.xk+1​=xk​−αk​Hk​gk​,Hk+1​=(I−ρsyT)Hk​(I−ρysT)+ρssT. Algorithm Evaluate gradients, select a step length using a line search and update curvature. BFGS enforces Hₖ₊₁y=s with a symmetric update. Positive-definite Hₖ and yᵀs>0 preserve positive definiteness. Poor curvature requires an explicit policy such as skipping or damping the update. Conditions and pitfalls For nonconvex problems, finding a local stationary point is different from finding a global optimum. Noisy gradients, nonsmooth objectives and inaccurate inner PDE solves can corrupt curvature. Do not stop on relative objective change alone: inspect gradient norms, step sizes, limits and termination reasons. What to check Vary conditioning on positive-definite quadratics with known minima and check gradients by directional differences. On curved valleys vary initialization, scaling and line searches. Decreasing an objective does not validate physical assumptions or constraints. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. R. Fletcher (1970). A new approach to variable metric algorithms. The Computer Journal Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Bibliography checked · Consulted record Bibliographic identity checked against the DOI registration on 2026-11-22. Relevant abstracts or selected passages are separately identified in the detailed-reading source notes; this is not a claim of a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Citation and reuse

documents.title: Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Particle gravity: PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid Poisson solvers and particle force algorithms answer related questions with different representations. Begin by fixing the Green function, boundary conditions, mass assignment, softening, and force operator. A periodic PM field and an isolated direct-sum field solve different problems, so their raw difference is not a force-accuracy measurement. Particle–mesh: mass to potential to force# In a three-dimensional periodic cube, ∇2ϕ=4πG(ρ−ρ‾),ϕ^(k)=−4πG∣k∣2ρ^(k)(k≠0),ϕ^(0)=0.∇2ϕ=4πG(ρ−ρ​),ϕ​(k)=−∣k∣24πG​ρ​(k)(k=0),ϕ​(0)=0. Subtracting the mean supplies the periodic compatibility condition; setting the potential’s zero mode fixes its gauge. This choice differs from an isolated sheet, whose horizontal mean produces a real vertical force. PM deposits particle masses onto a grid, solves the mesh Poisson equation, differentiates the potential, and interpolates acceleration back to particles. The example uses cloud-in-cell (CIC) weights on eight neighboring mesh nodes in 3D, a continuum Fourier Laplacian symbol, and spectral force derivatives. An even-grid derivative sets its unpaired Nyquist mode to zero. Matched CIC deposition/interpolation and an odd force operator yield zero total internal force to roundoff in the tested periodic example. Assignment and interpolation smooth the force. The mesh Green function, discrete derivative, aliasing, grid anisotropy, and any deconvolution all influence the effective particle interaction. Accurate solution of a manufactured mesh mode does not establish accurate close-pair forces. P³M: correct the near field without counting it twice# Particle–particle/particle–mesh adds a short-range correction to the mesh force: ai=aiPM+∑j∈Ni(aijtarget−aijmesh,near).ai​=aiPM​+j∈Ni​∑​(aijtarget​−aijmesh,near​). The subtracted term must correspond to the chosen PM assignment and force operator, or to a consistently designed force split. Adding an unmodified Newtonian pair force to an already complete PM force counts part of the interaction twice. Neighbor lists and clustering determine short-range work. See Hockney’s original P³M code description. A production P³M solver, matching correction table, and adaptive refinements are not implemented here. Barnes–Hut Tree: open the nearby cells# Barnes and Hut (1986) organize particles into an octree. A distant cell is approximated by its mass distribution moments; nearby cells are opened recursively. Our geometric acceptance test is s/d < theta, with cell side s and distance d to its center of mass. A node containing the target is always opened, and direct leaves exclude self-interaction. The implemented isolated reference uses G = 1 and Plummer softening: ai=−∑j≠imjxi−xj(∣xi−xj∣2+ϵ2)3/2.ai​=−j=i∑​mj​(∣xi​−xj​∣2+ϵ2)3/2xi​−xj​​. The Tree and direct sum use identical particles, masses, and epsilon. Smaller theta usually trades more interactions for lower error, but individual-particle errors need not decrease monotonically. The familiar O(N log N) description is a typical algorithmic scaling under suitable distributions, not a timing result or worst-case guarantee for this Python example. Multipole expansion: monopole and second moments# Let R point from a cell’s center of mass to the target, delta_a be source offsets, M be total mass, and S = sum m_a delta_a delta_a^T. The center-of-mass dipole vanishes. With s² = R²+epsilon², a Taylor expansion of the same softened kernel gives ϕ(R)≈−G[Ms+3RTSR2s5−tr⁡S2s3].ϕ(R)≈−G[sM​+2s53RTSR​−2s3trS​]. The code differentiates this potential analytically. It retains the full second moment, including its trace; silently substituting an unsoftened traceless quadrupole formula would change the approximation. The gallery compares monopole and second-moment errors against the same direct force sum. A fast multipole method also forms and translates local expansions, reusing cell-to-cell interactions. It is more than adding a quadrupole to Barnes–Hut. Greengard and Rokhlin (1987) are the original FMM reading reference; FMM translations are not implemented here. TreePM: a different near-field evaluator# TreePM combines a mesh long-range field with a short-range Tree field. A representative Gaussian potential split has ϕ^long=ϕ^ e−k2rs2,ϕshort(r)=−Gmrerfc⁡(r2rs).ϕ​long​=ϕ​e−k2rs2​,ϕshort​(r)=−rGm​erfc(2rs​r​). The short-range force is the derivative of this potential, not merely Newton’s force times erfc. Cutoffs, periodicity, and softening must match the split. Springel’s GADGET-2 paper provides a primary example. The two independent PM and Tree examples here do not constitute an implemented TreePM solver. Where multigrid belongs# Multigrid solves a discretized elliptic equation rather than directly summing particle pairs. A smoother reduces oscillatory error; restriction, a coarse solve, prolongation, and correction address smoother error components. It can replace the grid Poisson solve inside a particle–mesh pipeline, provided its operator, boundary treatment, and particle coupling are specified. The existing multigrid implementation solves a 2D five-point negative-Laplacian problem with zero Dirichlet boundaries. It is not yet the isolated 3D particle-gravity solver. Boundary values for an isolated finite mesh may be supplied by multipoles or another open-boundary construction; setting phi = 0 at a nearby box face generally does not reproduce phi tending to zero at infinity. Reproduce the static checks# python scripts/build_particle_gravity.py This creates the figure and measurement manifest. The Tree experiment uses 192 equal-mass particles, seed 17, epsilon = 0.03, five opening angles, and both moment orders. Its error is ||a_tree−a_direct||₂ / ||a_direct||₂. Counts of accepted nodes and direct pairs are reported; their operation costs differ, so their sum is not a timing comparison. The PM test uses a 24³ periodic mesh. A separate density 1+0.2 cos(2 pi x) has potential −0.2 cos(2 pi x)/pi for G = 1. Tests cover CIC mass conservation, periodic wrapping, constant interpolation, self-force, net force, the manufactured Poisson mode, exact Tree opening at theta = 0, and selected force-error refinements. A target-by-target approximate Tree need not preserve pairwise momentum exactly; the manifest records a net-force diagnostic. Continue with isolated FFT and slab Green functions, and the symplectic map chapter for the additional requirements on force consistency and time integration. documents.title: Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Particle methods and smoothed particle hydrodynamics Lagrangian particles carry quantities while moving with a flow. SPH replaces a field value or derivative by a local kernel-weighted particle sum. The independent early papers by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977) are historical starting points. The static reconstruction below does not reproduce their stellar calculations. From an integral to particles# A smoothed field is approximated by fh(x)=∫f(x′)W(x−x′,h) dx′≈∑bmbρbfbW(x−xb,h).fh​(x)=∫f(x′)W(x−x′,h)dx′≈b∑​ρb​mb​​fb​W(x−xb​,h). The volume weight m_b/rho_b matters. Smoothing length h is a kernel scale, not necessarily the particle spacing. Compact support defines the neighbor search; it does not impose a fixed mesh connectivity. Our one-dimensional example uses the normalized cubic spline, with q = |x|/h: W(x,h)=23h{1−32q2+34q3,0≤q<1,14(2−q)3,1≤q<2,0,q≥2.W(x,h)=3h2​⎩⎨⎧​1−23​q2+43​q3,41​(2−q)3,0,​0≤q<1,1≤q<2,q≥2.​ This prefactor is one-dimensional. Two- and three-dimensional kernels require different normalization constants. Partition of unity and correction# The raw sum of particle volumes times W need not equal one on a discrete particle set. A Shepard-normalized interpolant divides by that sum. It reproduces a constant wherever the denominator is nonzero, but this interpolation correction alone does not establish conservative dynamics, linear consistency, or stable pressure forces. import numpy as np from numart.geometry import sph_reconstruct p = (np.arange(64) + 0.5) / 64 x = np.linspace(0, 1, 201) f, partition = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04) f_corrected, _ = sph_reconstruct(x, p, np.sin(2*np.pi*p), h=0.04, normalize=True) The routine uses periodic minimum-image distances on [0,1] and equal volume weights 1/N. It requires 0 < h < 1/4 so the support fits the minimum-image convention. It does not infer physical density from arbitrary unequal particle spacings. What a fluid solver would additionally need# Density estimation or a continuity update, a consistent pressure force, momentum and energy evolution, boundary particles, time stepping, neighbor-search updates, and treatment of shocks or tensile/pairing instabilities are additional modeling decisions. Artificial viscosity used in shock-capturing SPH must be distinguished from the physical Newtonian viscous stress tensor. Tests check the continuous kernel’s normalization and discrete constant reproduction after normalization. This edition implements kernel reconstruction only, not an SPH flow solver. See time integration for why a particle kick–drift leapfrog and a two-step first-order ODE leapfrog should not be conflated. Particle gravity is a separate operator# PM, P³M, Tree, and multipole methods compute gravitational fields; SPH kernels reconstruct fluid quantities and their derivatives. Read particle gravity, isolated and slab boundary kernels, and symplectic time integration to connect these different parts of a self-gravitating particle model. Godunov SPH: the Riemann-solver branch# Inutsuka's GSPH connects particle hydrodynamics with pairwise Riemann problems. The chapter follows the 2002 convolution-based derivation, identifies its 1994 precursor, and links the 2011 MHD extension by Iwasaki and Inutsuka. It is a reading and implementation plan; the kernel reconstruction above is not a GSPH fluid calculation. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Particle-in-cell / PIC | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Particle-in-cell / PIC Plasma PIC represents a distribution by computational particles and self-consistent fields by a mesh. Its smoothing, collisionality and sampling error differ from direct all-pairs Coulomb dynamics. Problem and representative equations Start with nonrelativistic electrostatic Vlasov–Poisson. Computational particle p has weight wₚ, charge qₚ and position xₚ. Dimensionless shape weights Sᵢ sum to one, and Vᵢ is cell volume. Deposit ρ, solve Poisson with the stated boundary conditions, and use E=−∇φ. ρi=1Vi∑pwpqpSi(xp),−∇h2ϕi=ρi/ϵ0,v˙p=(qp/mp)Eh(xp).ρi​=Vi​1​p∑​wp​qp​Si​(xp​),−∇h2​ϕi​=ρi​/ϵ0​,v˙p​=(qp​/mp​)Eh​(xp​). Algorithm Repeat charge deposition, field solution, particle gathering and particle pushing; include background ions in ρ. Electromagnetic PIC additionally needs current deposition and Maxwell updates consistent with discrete continuity. Dawson’s sheet model is a historical particle-plasma example, not the definition of every PIC discretization. Conditions and pitfalls Explicit electrostatic PIC must examine plasma-frequency time scales and Debye-length resolution. Exact restrictions depend on the particle pusher, shape and field solver. Separate sampling convergence in particle count from grid/time convergence, and check self-force and finite-grid heating. What to check Begin with single-particle self-force, a uniform neutral distribution, and small-amplitude plasma oscillations or Landau damping. Report charge, energy drift, particle-count dependence and independent random realizations. Compare damping rates only within the linear-amplitude regime used by the theory. documents.title: PINNs and neural operators | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: PINNs and neural operators A PINN fits a neural representation of a particular solution; a neural operator learns a map from input functions such as coefficients or initial data to solution functions. Their targets and validation protocols differ. Problem and representative equations A PINN minimizes an empirical weighted loss of PDE, boundary and data residuals. N and B are differential/boundary operators and f,g are prescribed data. A representative FNO layer combines a Fourier-parameterized integral operator K with a local map W acting on feature functions v. L(θ)=λr⟨∣N[uθ]−f∣2⟩r+λb⟨∣B[uθ]−g∣2⟩b+λd⟨∣uθ−uobs∣2⟩d.L(θ)=λr​⟨∣N[uθ​]−f∣2⟩r​+λb​⟨∣B[uθ​]−g∣2⟩b​+λd​⟨∣uθ​−uobs​∣2⟩d​. vℓ+1=σ ⁣(Wℓvℓ+F−1[Kℓ Fvℓ]).vℓ+1​=σ(Wℓ​vℓ​+F−1[Kℓ​Fvℓ​]). Algorithm For a PINN, scale coordinates/units, differentiate residuals, specify collocation points and boundary enforcement, and optimize. FNO trains an operator on input/reference-solution pairs and truncates Fourier modes. Cite the PINN and FNO papers as separate proposals. Conditions and pitfalls Small training loss is not a bound on global solution error or conservation. Examine residual imbalance, shocks, stiff scales and out-of-distribution inputs. Transfer between discretizations is not a guarantee of physical correctness at arbitrary resolution. What to check Compare against analytic or independently converged conventional solutions. Measure off-training L1/L2/L∞ errors, boundaries, conservation and multiple seeds. Split operator data by independent problems rather than nearby time slices alone, and report distribution-shift tests separately. documents.text: Particle mesh Ewald / PME PME transfers the reciprocal Ewald calculation to a mesh and uses FFTs. Distinguish the original Lagrange-interpolation PME from the later B-spline construction of SPME. Problem and representative equations For a neutral triply periodic Coulomb system, Qₘ is charge assigned to mesh point xₘ using weights Wₘ. The reciprocal operator Ĝₕ includes Ewald screening, mesh conventions and interpolation corrections. This schematic describes only the reciprocal contribution; real-space and self terms remain necessary. Qm=∑iqiWm(ri),ϕh=Fh−1 ⁣[G^h FhQ].Qm​=i∑​qi​Wm​(ri​),ϕh​=Fh−1​[Gh​Fh​Q]. Algorithm Assign charges with local Lagrange polynomials, transform the mesh, apply the reciprocal convolution and transform back. Specify the differentiation and particle-gather rules together. A mesh-interpolated field and the derivative of the discrete energy need not give identical forces. Conditions and pitfalls Separate mesh resolution, interpolation order, Ewald cutoffs and force differentiation in error studies. State FFT normalization, k=0 treatment and units. The usual O(N log N) description assumes an appropriate mesh-growth regime and is not an accuracy guarantee. What to check Use a converged direct Ewald calculation for the identical neutral cell. Vary mesh size, interpolation order and screening; measure RMS/maximum energy and force errors and sensitivity to common translations. A gravity-PM test does not validate PME. documents.title: QR, SVD and least squares | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: QR, SVD and least squares Least squares, low-rank approximation and conditioning call for different matrix decompositions. QR reduces a problem to orthogonal transformations and a triangular solve; SVD exposes singular values and resolvable directions. Problem and representative equations For a real m×n matrix with m≥n, thin QR has QᵀQ=I and upper triangular R. Full column rank gives the least-squares solve Rx=Qᵀb. SVD has nonnegative singular values σᵢ. Truncating small σᵢ in a pseudoinverse regularizes the problem and can change the solution being sought. A=QR=UΣVT,min⁡x∥Ax−b∥2,A+b=∑σi>τuiTbσivi(truncated).A=QR=UΣVT,xmin​∥Ax−b∥2​,A+b=σi​>τ∑​σi​uiT​b​vi​(truncated). Algorithm Householder QR eliminates subdiagonal entries with reflections and generally maintains orthogonality better than classical Gram–Schmidt. Consider column pivoting or SVD for rank diagnosis. Classical SVD algorithms reduce to bidiagonal form using orthogonal transformations rather than explicitly forming normal equations. Conditions and pitfalls For full column rank, κ₂(AᵀA)=κ₂(A)². A small residual can coexist with uncertain coefficients under ill-conditioning or noise. Choose a numerical-rank threshold relative to scale, rounding and measurement uncertainty, and consider column scaling when variables have different units. What to check Check relative factorization residuals, orthogonality and Aᵀ(Ax−b). Test prescribed singular values and rank-deficient cases, and compare solution changes under controlled data perturbations. documents.title: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature Gaussian quadrature selects nodes and weights for a measure to integrate polynomials efficiently. Adaptive integration separately allocates function evaluations using local error estimates. Problem and representative equations For a positive measure, an n-point Gaussian rule is exact through degree 2n−1 when the required moments exist. The Jacobi matrix J of orthogonal-polynomial recurrence coefficients has quadrature nodes as eigenvalues. Weights are μ₀ times squared first components of normalized eigenvectors, with μ₀=∫w. ∫abf(x)w(x) dx≈∑j=1nωjf(xj),Jvj=xjvj,ωj=μ0(vj)12.∫ab​f(x)w(x)dx≈j=1∑n​ωj​f(xj​),Jvj​=xj​vj​,ωj​=μ0​(vj​)12​. Algorithm Golub–Welsch solves this symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem. Adaptive Gauss–Kronrod-type integration uses differences between nested rules to estimate local errors, subdivides intervals and checks absolute/relative tolerances. The rule difference is not an unconditional error bound. Conditions and pitfalls Singularities, jumps, rapid oscillations and narrow peaks can be missed by sampled nodes. Split at known discontinuities and consider transformations or matched weighted rules. Relative tolerance alone is unsuitable when the integral is close to zero. What to check Verify degree of exactness on monomials, then test nonpolynomials with known integrals, singularities and narrow peaks. Record estimated versus true error, evaluation count and termination caused by subdivision limits. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. documents.text: ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE · QUANTUM CHEMISTRY · DFT Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations From Schrödinger, HF and DFT to bases, SCF and correlation, including space groups, little-group irreps, SOC and time reversal in band calculations. Bilingual reading for 18 entries and 28 primary publications. Runnable code and numerical validation cover two hydrogenic/He problem families. Molecular and periodic examples remain under construction. Three choices to keep separate Physical model and approximation HF, KS-DFT, MP2, CI or CC: which many-electron states and energies are approximated? Representation and discretization Basis, grid, pseudopotential and k sampling: how is the model made finite? Equation solver Eigensolvers, SCF, mixing and DIIS: how accurately is the chosen discrete problem solved? SCF convergence, basis convergence and physical adequacy are distinct checks. Representative equations use atomic units (ℏ = m_e = e = 4πε₀ = 1). Finite molecules and periodic solids also require different boundaries. Schrodinger eigenproblems The common starting point is a many-electron eigenproblem at fixed nuclear positions. We use nonrelativistic Born–Oppenheimer theory and atomic units, separating electronic energy E_el from nuclear repulsion E_NN. R_A and Z_A denote nuclear positions and charges; r_ij is an electron–electron distance. For one electron the pair-repulsion sum vanishes; hydrogenic energies E_n = −Z²/(2n²) provide references. The many-electron wavefunction depends on all electronic coordinates and spins, unlike the individual three-dimensional orbitals in HF or KS. Uniform radial-grid tests of isolated hydrogenic 1s, 2s, 2p and 3d states; not a direct general many-electron Schrödinger solver. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks H^el=−12∑i∇i2−∑iAZA∣ri−RA∣+∑i<j1rijH^el​=−21​i∑​∇i2​−iA∑​∣ri​−RA​∣ZA​​+i<j∑​rij​1​H^elΨ=EelΨ,Etot=Eel+∑A<BZAZBRABH^el​Ψ=Eel​Ψ,Etot​=Eel​+A<B∑​RAB​ZA​ZB​​ Long equations scroll horizontally. Nuclear dynamics, relativity, spin–orbit coupling and external fields are outside this representative Hamiltonian. A small eigenpair residual does not establish domain or basis convergence. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Schrödinger, E. (1926) Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951) Hartree–Fock HF makes the energy stationary within single antisymmetric Slater determinants. Exchange follows from the determinant; electron correlation relative to the HF reference is absent. Closed-shell RHF builds its Fock operator from doubly occupied spatial orbitals. J_j is a Coulomb operator and K_j is generally nonlocal exchange. Open-shell choices include UHF and ROHF, with spin contamination and symmetry breaking requiring explicit diagnostics. Only spherical helium with one doubly occupied 1s spatial orbital; the local HF exchange reduction is specific to this two-electron problem. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks F^=h^+∑j∈occ(2J^j−K^j),F^ϕi=εiϕiF^=h^+j∈occ∑​(2J^j​−K^j​),F^ϕi​=εi​ϕi​FC=SCε,C†SC=IFC=SCε,C†SC=I Long equations scroll horizontally. HF solutions need not be unique. SCF termination does not prove basis convergence, orbital stability or the desired electronic state. Bond dissociation can expose single-reference limitations. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951) Kohn–Sham density functional theory / DFT Here DFT means density functional theory, rather than the discrete Fourier transform. Within the Hohenberg–Kohn ground-state framework, Kohn–Sham theory represents the density using auxiliary noninteracting orbitals. State the spin convention for occupations f_i and enforce their sum N. T_s is the auxiliary kinetic energy and E_H the classical Coulomb energy. E_xc includes exchange, correlation and the difference between interacting kinetic energy and T_s. Updating density to potential and orbitals back to density produces the nonlinear SCF problem. The representative local KS equation below assumes a differentiable density functional. Distinguish generalized KS treatments of nonlocal hybrid exchange and orbital-dependent meta-GGAs. Spin-unpolarized exchange-only Dirac LDA for spherical helium; correlation, GGA, hybrids, molecules, periodic systems and excitations are not implemented. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks E[n]=Ts[n]+∫vextn dr+EH[n]+Exc[n]+ENNE[n]=Ts​[n]+∫vext​ndr+EH​[n]+Exc​[n]+ENN​[−12∇2+vext+vH+vxc]ϕi=εiϕi[−21​∇2+vext​+vH​+vxc​]ϕi​=εi​ϕi​n(r)=∑ifi∣ϕi(r)∣2,∫n dr=N,vxc=δExcδnn(r)=i∑​fi​∣ϕi​(r)∣2,∫ndr=N,vxc​=δnδExc​​ Long equations scroll horizontally. Distinguish exact-functional theory from calculations with approximate functionals. KS eigenvalues are not generally excitation energies; ground-state DFT alone does not guarantee excited-state accuracy. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Hohenberg, P.; Kohn, W. (1964) Kohn, W.; Sham, L. J. (1965) Electronic-structure basis sets The same HF or DFT model can use Gaussian or Slater atomic orbitals, plane waves, or a real-space grid. Nonorthogonal bases retain an overlap matrix S and require a generalized eigenproblem. Vary basis size, polarization and diffuse functions for atomic orbitals; cutoff and cell size for plane waves; spacing and domain for real-space grids. Boys provides an original entry point for Gaussian integral methods. ϕi=∑μCμiχμ,Sμν=⟨χμ∣χν⟩ϕi​=μ∑​Cμi​χμ​,Sμν​=⟨χμ​∣χν​⟩FC=SCεFC=SCε Changing the basis is different from changing electron correlation or the functional. Check near-linear dependence, basis-set superposition error and pseudopotential compatibility. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Boys, S. F. (1950) Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951) Self-consistent field iteration / SCF SCF is an iteration for self-consistency in HF or KS, rather than a physical model. The map M builds a potential from the input density, solves for orbitals and constructs an output density. Save density differences, electron number and eigenpair or orbital-gradient residuals as well as energy changes. Record mixing, initial density, occupations, iteration limits and an explicit nonconvergence termination reason. Helium linear density mixing with density/energy/orbital-residual checks, alternative starts/mixing and explicit failure; no DIIS. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks nk+1=(1−α)nk+αM[nk],0<α≤1nk+1​=(1−α)nk​+αM[nk​],0<α≤1Tr(PS)=N,R=FPS−SPFTr(PS)=N,R=FPS−SPF Long equations scroll horizontally. A small energy change alone is insufficient. Convergence also does not establish the lowest-energy stable electronic solution. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Roothaan, C. C. J. (1951) Pulay, P. (1980) Pulay / DIIS acceleration DIIS determines extrapolation coefficients from stored iterates and error vectors. Its basic form minimizes the extrapolated error norm subject to coefficients summing to one. SCF commonly uses Fock matrices and an overlap-consistent commutator residual. It changes the nonlinear solution strategy rather than the physical approximation. Compare against damping using the same initial state and stopping rules; record history length and treatment of singular history matrices. min⁡{cj}∥∑jcjej∥2,∑jcj=1{cj​}min​​j∑​cj​ej​​2,j∑​cj​=1 Extrapolation guarantees neither convergence nor monotonic energy decrease. Investigate initial-state dependence and unstable stationary solutions even when a residual appears small. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Pulay, P. (1980) Coulomb and Hartree potentials With n defined as positive electron number density, the Hartree potential is the positive Coulomb integral below. Its sign differs from charge density ρ_charge = −n. Distinguish v_H in the electronic energy from electrostatic potential generated by charge. Isolated systems require far-field conditions. Periodic systems require a stated G=0 convention, neutrality, compensating background when used, and potential reference. Existing Poisson, FFT and particle-force methods must be matched to these signs and boundaries. Cumulative Coulomb quadrature for isolated spherical densities, checked against analytic exponential densities; not a general 3D or periodic Poisson implementation. Check the Poisson residual, integrated electron number, far-field behavior and the one-half double-counting factor separately. A charged periodic cell does not directly give an isolated-system energy. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Hartree, D. R. (1928) Kohn, W.; Sham, L. J. (1965) LDA, GGA and hybrid functionals LDA depends on local density, GGA on density and its gradient, and meta-GGA on quantities such as orbital kinetic-energy density. Hybrids mix in HF-type exchange. PBE, SCAN, B3 variants and PBE0 are approximation choices rather than a universal ranking. The formula below is spin-unpolarized Dirac exchange only. Distinguish it from LDA including correlation. State functional components, parameters, library/version and the density integration grid. Only spin-unpolarized Dirac exchange energy and its functional derivative are verified; LDA correlation, GGA, meta-GGA and hybrids remain reading-only. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks ExLDA[n]=−34(3π)1/3∫n4/3 drExLDA​[n]=−43​(π3​)1/3∫n4/3drvxLDA=−(3nπ)1/3vxLDA​=−(π3n​)1/3 Basis, grid and SCF convergence do not remove functional error. Assess self-interaction, charge transfer, strong correlation and dispersion for the chosen system and approximation. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Dirac, P. A. M. (1930) Perdew, J. P.; Burke, K.; Ernzerhof, M. (1996) Sun, J.; Ruzsinszky, A.; Perdew, J. P. (2015) Becke, A. D. (1993) Adamo, C.; Barone, V. (1999) Pseudopotentials and PAW Pseudopotentials represent core effects effectively while focusing on valence electrons. Distinguish norm-conserving, ultrasoft and PAW approaches. PAW uses a transformation and reconstruction; describing it as only a smooth local replacement is inadequate. Save the element, valence configuration, generating functional, relativistic treatment, dataset version and cutoff guidance. Compare against all-electron calculations under matched physical conditions and observables. Do not compare absolute energy zeroes across different pseudopotentials without alignment. Cutoff convergence alone does not establish transferability. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Hamann, D. R.; Schlüter, M.; Chiang, C. (1979) Vanderbilt, D. (1990) Blöchl, P. E. (1994) Periodic electronic structure and k-point sampling For a periodic potential, Bloch orbitals reduce Brillouin-zone integrals to weighted k-point sums. u_nk is lattice periodic. Monkhorst–Pack supplies an original entry point for special-point integration. Save k-mesh density and shift, symmetry, occupations/smearing, cell and basis cutoff. A molecule in a large periodic cell must also be distinguished from an isolated-boundary calculation. ψnk(r)=eik⋅runk(r),∫BZg(k) dk≈∑νwνg(kν)ψnk​(r)=eik⋅runk​(r),∫BZ​g(k)dk≈ν∑​wν​g(kν​) Long equations scroll horizontally. Distinguish metallic occupation/smearing dependence, finite-temperature free energy and zero-temperature energy. Whether Γ-only sampling is adequate depends on the system and cell. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Monkhorst, H. J.; Pack, J. D. (1976) Band symmetry groups and irreducible representations A structural space group includes translations, rotations, mirrors, inversion and their combinations. Band classification must use the symmetries actually preserved by the Hamiltonian, including magnetic order, spin–orbit coupling (SOC) and external fields. A Seitz operation g = {R|τ} maps position to Rr + τ. With lattice translations T as a normal subgroup, G/T is the crystal point group. At each k, the little group G_k retains operations taking Rk back to k modulo a reciprocal vector K. Its little co-group G_k/T is distinct from the full crystal point group. g={R∣τ}: r↦Rr+τ,P=G/Tg={R∣τ}: r↦Rr+τ,P=G/TGk={{R∣τ}∈G: Rk=k+K, K∈L∗}Gk​={{R∣τ}∈G: Rk=k+K, K∈L∗} Long equations scroll horizontally. Read little-group irreps and degeneracies Symmetries act within the Bloch-state space associated with k. Irreducible small representations classify bands. Their dimensions constrain symmetry-required multiplicities; accidental coincidence and antiunitary pairing are additional possibilities. Nearly equal energies alone do not identify an irrep. Little groups change between high-symmetry points, lines and planes. Compatibility relations track representation branching and band connectivity. For a simple symmorphic mirror line without SOC, mirror eigenvalues +1 and −1 label distinct sectors that cannot hybridize while that symmetry is preserved. Screw axes, glide planes and nonsymmorphic groups Screw and glide operations include fractional translations. Bloch phases matter, particularly at zone boundaries, so ordinary crystal-point-group character tables are insufficient. Use little-group small representations or equivalent projective little-co-group representations with their factor systems. Nonsymmorphic symmetry can constrain degeneracies and connectivity. It does not imply that every band is degenerate at every k: specify the group, k, spin and time-reversal conditions. ψnk(r+a)=eik⋅aψnk(r),a∈Lψnk​(r+a)=eik⋅aψnk​(r),a∈L SOC, double groups, time reversal and Kramers pairs Spin-1/2 SOC requires spinors that change sign under a 2π rotation, hence double-valued representations of double groups. Time reversal Θ is antiunitary with Θ² = −1 for electrons. Time reversal alone generally pairs k with −k; Kramers degeneracy at the same k is guaranteed at time-reversal-invariant momenta (TRIM), where 2k is reciprocal. In the usual nonmagnetic spin-1/2 setting with both inversion P and time reversal Θ, PΘ preserves each k and squares to −1, producing double degeneracy at each k. This conclusion cannot be transferred unchanged to a noncentrosymmetric system. Spinless Θ² = +1 models also do not satisfy these Kramers assumptions. Magnetic order may break time reversal or retain only its combination with a spatial operation. Magnetic space groups and antiunitary corepresentations require separate treatment. Reassess symmetry settings whenever SOC or magnetic state changes. ΘH(k)Θ−1=H(−k),Θ2=−1ΘH(k)Θ−1=H(−k),Θ2=−1kTRIM=−kTRIM+K,K∈L∗kTRIM​=−kTRIM​+K,K∈L∗ Distinguish plotted paths from irreducible-zone integration Labels such as Γ, X, L and K and the chosen path depend on lattice, standardized cell and reciprocal-coordinate conventions. A plotted high-symmetry path is not an integration mesh. Band extrema may lie off the path, so it alone does not establish the global band gap. Irreducible integration points and weights use the actual Hamiltonian symmetries and valid time reversal. Save lattice, positions/species, primitive/conventional-cell transformations, symmetry tolerances, SOC, magnetic and time-reversal settings, path/weights and software versions. Check sensitivity to structural rounding. Bilbao supplies little-group representations; SeeK-path provides crystallographic paths; Quantum ESPRESSO bands.x documents lsym classification by little-group irreps. These links do not represent an atlas-verified band calculation or irrep assignment. This is an introduction to concepts, conditions and their computational use. (2007) MP2 perturbation theory MP2 is a second-order perturbative correction to an HF reference. The representative expression uses canonical HF spin orbitals, occupied i,j, virtual a,b and antisymmetrized two-electron integrals. Coefficients and index conventions differ for restricted spatial-orbital formulas. Match the basis, frozen core, reference orbitals, spin and nuclear geometry in comparisons. Save the correlation correction separately from total energy. EMP2(2)=14∑ijocc∑abvirt∣⟨ij∥ab⟩∣2εi+εj−εa−εbEMP2(2)​=41​ij∑occ​ab∑virt​εi​+εj​−εa​−εb​∣⟨ij∥ab⟩∣2​ Long equations scroll horizontally. Small denominators and strong static correlation can invalidate low-order perturbation. An energy below HF is not by itself evidence of improvement toward the exact value. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Møller, C.; Plesset, M. S. (1934) Configuration interaction / CI CI diagonalizes the many-electron Hamiltonian in a space of determinants or configuration state functions. FCI spans the full chosen finite one-electron basis, electron number and symmetry sector; CISD truncates to single and double excitations from a reference. Use FCI as a reference only with its finite-basis scope stated. Determinant spaces grow rapidly, motivating small validation systems such as H₂. ∣Ψ⟩=∑IcI∣ΦI⟩,∑JHIJcJ=EcI∣Ψ⟩=I∑​cI​∣ΦI​⟩,J∑​HIJ​cJ​=EcI​ Finite-basis FCI is not the exact continuum solution. Check size consistency of truncated CI and the assumptions behind variational bounds. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Knowles, P. J.; Handy, N. C. (1984) Coupled cluster / CCSD(T) Coupled cluster represents the wavefunction using an exponential excitation operator. CCSD iterates T₁+T₂; CCSD(T) conventionally adds a noniterative perturbative triples correction. It is distinct from CCSDT. Assess whether a single determinant is adequate, using amplitude and reference diagnostics. Match frozen core, basis and reference state when comparing weakly correlated single-reference systems. ∣ΨCC⟩=eT^∣Φ0⟩,T^=T^1+T^2+⋯∣ΨCC​⟩=eT^∣Φ0​⟩,T^=T^1​+T^2​+⋯ Conventional projected CC energies are not variational upper bounds. CCSD(T) is not a universal standard for bond breaking or strong correlation. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Raghavachari, K.; Trucks, G. W.; Pople, J. A.; Head-Gordon, M. (1989) CASSCF and multireference methods CASSCF optimizes configuration coefficients and orbitals within a selected active space. Record CAS(n_e,n_o), specifying electrons and spatial orbitals, their character, spin and any state averaging. It addresses static correlation, but does not automatically recover adequate dynamic correlation outside the active space. Subsequent methods such as CASPT2 and NEVPT2 are separate future extensions. ∣ΨCAS⟩=∑I∈CAS⁡(ne,no)cI∣ΦI⟩∣ΨCAS​⟩=I∈CAS(ne​,no​)∑​cI​∣ΦI​⟩ Active-space dependence is distinct from grid error. Track orbital character across geometries rather than only orbital indices. Assumptions, implementation status and JSON Roos, B. O.; Taylor, P. R.; Siegbahn, P. E. M. (1980) Time-dependent density functional theory / TDDFT TDDFT concerns time-dependent densities. The local time-dependent KS equation shown is representative; initial-state dependence and exchange-correlation memory can remain. Distinguish real-time propagation from linear response around a ground state. For response calculations save excitation energies and oscillator strengths. For real time save the field, step size, propagation length and spectrum-transform settings. The adiabatic approximation concerns functional time dependence. i∂tϕi(r,t)=[−12∇2+vs[n](r,t)]ϕi(r,t)i∂t​ϕi​(r,t)=[−21​∇2+vs​[n](r,t)]ϕi​(r,t) Bare ground-state KS eigenvalue differences are not TDDFT excitation energies. When using a fixed-node treatment of the fermion sign problem, identify its systematic bias. Record random streams, autocorrelation-aware statistical uncertainty, time step, walker population, trial state and finite size. (1980) DMRG and tensor networks Quantum-chemical DMRG treats orbitals as sites and approximates many-electron states with representations such as matrix product states (MPS). Increasing bond dimension increases expressiveness; requirements also depend on orbital ordering and entanglement. Record the active orbitals, ordering, bond dimension, sweeps, truncation measures and energy convergence.
