documents.title: Radiation transport and moment methods | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Radiation transport and moment methods Radiation transport resolves intensity in space, direction and frequency. Moment methods reduce the angular dimension but require closure for information removed by integration. Problem and representative equations Use frequency-integrated grey intensity I in a static medium, with isotropic emissivity η and absorption coefficient κ of inverse-length units; omit scattering here. Define E=(1/c)∫I dΩ, F=∫nI dΩ and P=(1/c)∫nnI dΩ. Moment equations for E and F require a prescription for P. 1c∂tI+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂tE+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂tF+∇⋅P=−κF/c.c1​∂t​I+n⋅∇I=η−κI,∂t​E+∇⋅F=4πη−cκE,c−2∂t​F+∇⋅P=−κF/c. Algorithm Discrete ordinates discretizes angle directly; moment methods close P=D E. M1 obtains D locally from E and F, while flux-limited diffusion instead approximates F from the gradient of E. Check optically thick and free-streaming limits and couple matter exchange through a consistent energy balance. Conditions and pitfalls M1 generally cannot propagate crossing beams independently. FLD ties flux to the energy gradient, limiting shadows and strongly anisotropic fields. A reduced light speed changes transport/relaxation scales and must be justified against the physical time scales of interest. What to check Test exponential absorption, isotropic diffusion, free streaming/shadows and crossing beams separately. Check E≥0, |F|≤cE, matter-plus-radiation energy and angular/spatial/time convergence. Distinguish closure error from discretization error. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Radiation transport and moment methods Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. C.D. Levermore (1984). Relating Eddington factors to flux limiters. Journal of Quantitative Spectroscopy and Radiative Transfer Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Abstract and bibliography checked · Consulted record Publisher abstract for distinctions between Eddington closure and flux limiting. documents.title: Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Euler reconstruction: PPM, characteristics, WENO-Z and AUSM Open the computed comparison. This 1D experiment separates reconstruction choices from numerical-flux choices. It extends the original componentwise MUSCL/WENO baseline; previous exhibits are retained. What is compared# The reconstruction view compares conservative-component and characteristic MUSCL/MC, limited parabolic finite volumes, and finite-difference WENO5-JS/Z. FV uses HLLC; FD uses global Lax–Friedrichs flux splitting. Both use SSPRK3, nominal CFL 0.3 and the same number of grid locations. Their representations, fluxes and error norms differ: this is not an isolated reconstruction or matched-cost ranking. Within each method, changing only the basis is a controlled component/characteristic comparison. The separate flux view fixes conservative characteristic MUSCL/MC and SSPRK3, then switches HLLC, acoustic-smoothed Roe, Einfeldt-type HLLE and the explicitly defined AUSM baseline below. It does not change the spatial reconstruction. Limited parabolic finite volumes# Following the reconstruction idea of Colella–Woodward (1984), form a parabola in each cell from its mean and two edges. The inspected public 1982 author preprint is an earlier version, not the final journal layout. This implementation includes limited edge interpolation and monotonicity constraints, coupled by method of lines to SSPRK3. It excludes original PPM wave tracing, contact steepening, shock flattening, Lagrangian evolution and remap. Direct-Eulerian tracing, contact steepening and flattening are now available in the second computed stage; Lagrangian evolution and remap remain future work. For a cell mean Q and edges L,R, use the local coordinate ξ in [0,1]: q(ξ)=L+ξ[R−L+q6(1−ξ)],q6=6Q−3(L+R).q(ξ)=L+ξ[R−L+q6​(1−ξ)],q6​=6Q−3(L+R). The integral is exactly Q. Limit initial edge interpolation between adjacent means; flatten a parabolic extremum and apply the usual curvature bounds. Characteristic projection freezes a local conservative eigenbasis in each cell, limits projected deviations, then transforms back. Components are conservative variables, not primitive variables. Reconstructed left/mid/right states share one affine positivity scaling about Q if needed. Their Simpson mean remains Q; no conserved mean is clipped. Inadmissible RK stages retry with a halved time step. These safeguards do not prove fully discrete positivity. Characteristic finite-difference WENO-Z# For each face freeze a Roe-averaged conservative eigenbasis. Project the positive and negative global-LF split flux stencils, reconstruct each characteristic component, and transform the resulting face flux back. FD evolves point values; it is not FV state reconstruction. Shared flux differences conserve the discrete sum on a periodic grid. The Z variant uses the JS smoothness indicators with τ5=∣β0−β2∣,αkZ=dk[1+(τ5βk+ϵ)2],ωkZ=αkZ∑lαlZ,(d0,d1,d2)=(0.1,0.6,0.3).τ5​=∣β0​−β2​∣,αkZ​=dk​[1+(βk​+ϵτ5​​)2],ωkZ​=∑l​αlZ​αkZ​​,(d0​,d1​,d2​)=(0.1,0.6,0.3). Here ε = 10⁻⁶ is fixed and the Z exponent is 2. These choices must accompany comparisons; the regularization and normalization of the characteristics affect the weights. Borges, Carmona, Costa and Don (2008) is the original bibliographic reference. Publisher metadata and the public earlier three-author manuscript were inspected; that manuscript has different weight conventions. The formula above, its exponent and the executable checks define this edition's variant; no final-paper figure is reproduced. AUSM: keep the variant explicit# Liou–Steffen (1993) introduced AUSM. The local baseline uses a common interface sound speed a = (aL+aR)/2, Mach polynomials M± = ±(M±1)²/4 in the subsonic interval, and the cubic pressure fractions P± = (M±1)²(2∓M)/4. Supersonic branches use signed upwind Mach and pressure fractions. These formulas were cross-checked against the official FEST-3D AUSM source. This is an independently implemented, specified AUSM-family variant, not FEST-3D output or a reproduction of every 1993 sound-speed/pressure option. Let Mf = M+(uL/a)+M−(uR/a). Upwind the advected vector (ρ,ρu,ρv,ρH) using a max(Mf,0) on the left and a min(Mf,0) on the right, and add pL P+(uL/a)+pR P−(uR/a) to normal momentum only. Energy transports total enthalpy. Tests include uniform states, both supersonic directions, Mach ±1 branch limits, stationary/moving contacts and the computed Euler problems. AUSM+ (1996) and AUSM+-up (2006) are separately defined in the new traced-PPM comparison. The current baseline has no all-speed correction or low-Mach verification. None of these names implies universal shock stability; inspect the separate odd–even comparison. Problems, references and accuracy# Sod: N=200, x∈[0,1], t=0.2, standard states, extrapolated ends. Moving contact: N=200, periodic [0,1], u=p=1, density 1 on the first half and 2 on the second; one crossing t=1. Shu–Osher: N=240, x∈[−5,5], t=1.8, fixed end states, shock at −4, left (ρ,u,p)=(3.857143,2.629369,10.33333), right density 1+0.2sin(5x), u=0,p=1. The dashed curve is our internal characteristic FD WENO-Z N=960 run, not an exact solution or an external-code validation. FV initialization integrates conserved quantities. Sod final density errors use 128-node Gauss quadrature of the analytic Riemann solution; the saved 64/128-node discrepancy estimates quadrature sensitivity across discontinuities. FD errors are pointwise. Derived FV primitive curves are primitive variables of conserved means, not exact primitive means. No exact Shu–Osher error is reported. A separate smooth periodic entropy wave uses N=32,64,128 at t=0.2 and CFL = 0.25(32/N)^(2/3). This reduces dt proportional to dx^(5/3), making the SSPRK3 time error O(dx⁵). Measured WENO orders are about five on this smooth case; limited PPM is about two on this sequence because of extremum limiting. This is not a global fifth-order guarantee at shocks or arbitrary critical points. Reproduce with python scripts/build_reconstruction.py. Download profiles, diagnostics and source hashes and conserved arrays. The final arrays, positive-state checks and retry counts apply only to the stated tests. documents.title: Exact and reference solutions · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Exact and reference solutions A verification library should say what its answer means. The reference explorer contains 18 cases with formulas, assumptions, source links, point values and, for one-dimensional cases, cell means. It evaluates references; it does not advance a numerical PDE solution. Four different reference categories# Analytic: explicit formulas, including scalar entropy waves, sine translation/decay, dry-bed and vacuum fans, channel profiles and Taylor–Green flow. Floating-point evaluation still has rounding error. Semi-analytic: Euler, wet shallow-water and isothermal Riemann solutions. The wave curves are analytic, but matching the middle state requires a numerical scalar root solve. Manufactured: prescribe a smooth field and derive the forcing and boundary conditions. The Poisson sine case tests a forced problem chosen for that field. Numerical reference: a refined numerical computation. It retains discretization, boundary and time-integration errors. Existing high-resolution atlas comparisons belong here when explicitly identified; they are not additional analytic cases in this library. Agreement with a reference verifies a particular setup. It does not validate a physical model against experiments or certify every boundary treatment. Included fields and assumptions# The scalar cases are periodic sine advection and heat decay, Burgers shock/fan and quadratic traffic shock/fan. Euler includes Sod, Lax, a double rarefaction and a generated vacuum, all for an ideal gas with gamma 1.4. Shallow water includes a wet dam break, expansion into a dry bed and a dry middle state, with a flat bottom and gravity 1. Isothermal Euler uses constant sound speed 1 and strictly positive initial density; it has no energy equation and no finite vacuum state. The viscous cases are planar steady Couette and Poiseuille profiles in a unit channel and a periodic two-dimensional Taylor–Green vortex. Channel profiles are velocity fields, not compressible conserved states. Taylor–Green returns velocity and pressure with a fixed zero-mean pressure gauge. The Poisson manufactured sine returns both the field and its forcing. These are canonical, nondimensional setups. Dry-bed/vacuum support in the reference evaluator does not add that capability to the existing positive-state finite-volume solver. Topography, viscosity in Riemann problems, arbitrary equations of state and multidimensional shock interactions are outside this first library. Point values and finite-volume means# For a conserved state, a finite-volume comparison uses U‾i(t)=1xi+1/2−xi−1/2∫xi−1/2xi+1/2U(x,t) dx.Ui​(t)=xi+1/2​−xi−1/2​1​∫xi−1/2​xi+1/2​​U(x,t)dx. The library integrates density, momentum and total energy for Euler, and depth/density and momentum for shallow-water/isothermal flow. Converting a mean conserved state to primitive variables is generally different from averaging primitive variables. A shock cutting a cell makes a center sample particularly misleading. Known shocks, contacts and both edges of rarefaction fans split each integral into smooth pieces. Gauss–Legendre quadrature uses 24 and 48 points per piece; saved means use the 48-point result. The maximum difference between the two orders is a convergence estimate, not a rigorous error bound. This convention also applies to analytic cases: their saved cell means use finite-order quadrature rather than symbolic integration. For a nonuniform mesh, the reported error norms are normalized by total domain length: L1=∑iΔxi∣ei∣∑iΔxi,L2=(∑iΔxiei2∑iΔxi)1/2,L∞=max⁡i∣ei∣.L1​=∑i​Δxi​∑i​Δxi​∣ei​∣​,L2​=(∑i​Δxi​∑i​Δxi​ei2​​)1/2,L∞​=imax​∣ei​∣. Each component is reported separately. The Euler/SWE/isothermal equation gallery now uses these conserved cell means. Its saved physical times still come from independent final-time numerical solves. Riemann construction and tolerances# The self-similar solution uses xi=(x−x0)/t. For Euler the matched unknown is pressure; for shallow water it is depth; for isothermal flow it is density. The implementation brackets a monotone wave-matching residual in the logarithm of that positive unknown, then bisects. The target logarithmic bracket width is 2e−13, with at most 160 bisections and a final residual check of 2e−10 times a characteristic velocity scale. An exact zero residual can terminate earlier. Iterations, final bracket width and residual are saved alongside each case. Separating Euler or shallow-water fans can create a middle vacuum/dry region. Those cases bypass the positive-state root solve. Conserved variables vanish there. Velocity is physically undefined in vacuum; the low-level conversion displays zero by convention. Isothermal expansion approaches arbitrarily small positive density instead of a finite vacuum. States outside the supported float64 range raise an error rather than silently clipping the reference. The Clawpack Euler chapter and shallow-water chapter describe the wave construction and dry/vacuum cases. Bhat and Fetecau's author manuscript gives the isothermal wave curves for the original Euler system in its Riemann-problem discussion; this library uses that original system, not the paper's regularized model. Viscous and manufactured formulas# For a unit-height channel, unit density and viscosity nu, the steady profiles are uCouette(y)=y,uPoiseuille(y)=G2νy(1−y),G=1,ν=0.1.uCouette​(y)=y,uPoiseuille​(y)=2νG​y(1−y),G=1,ν=0.1. Couette has wall speeds 0 and 1 with zero pressure gradient. Poiseuille has stationary no-slip walls; G is either the negative pressure gradient per unit density or an equivalent body acceleration. These are fully developed planar flows, not pipe flow. For Taylor–Green on the periodic square [0,2pi]², with nu=0.1 and unit density, u=sin⁡xcos⁡y e−2νt,v=−cos⁡xsin⁡y e−2νt,p=cos⁡(2x)+cos⁡(2y)4e−4νt.u=sinxcosye−2νt,v=−cosxsinye−2νt,p=4cos(2x)+cos(2y)​e−4νt. The Web explorer displays an x-slice at y=pi/4, not two-dimensional area means. The Python evaluator accepts full 2D coordinates and smooth rectangular box averages. Related methods are in the viscous-flow chapter. The manufactured case prescribes u=sin(pi x), giving −u_xx=f=pi² sin(pi x) with homogeneous Dirichlet endpoints. Its source is available through the same object; it is not an arbitrary-source Poisson solver. Reuse and reproduce# import numpy as np from numart.reference_solutions import get_reference, riemann_reference ref = get_reference('euler-sod') edges = np.array([0., .15, .42, .51, .7, 1.]) points = ref.point((edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2, t=.2) report = ref.cell_average_report(edges, t=.2) means = report['values'] # columns: rho, rho*u, E # With actual numerical conserved means q of the same shape: # errors = ref.compare_means(q, edges, t=.2) custom = riemann_reference('shallow-water', (2., 0.), (1., 0.), parameter=9.81) tg = get_reference('taylor-green') box_mean = tg.box_average([0., 0.], [.2, .3], t=.5) Rebuild the saved profiles and figure with MPLCONFIGDIR=.mplconfig python scripts/build_reference_solutions.py. Download the data and numerical source hashes. Python tests compare Euler with an existing independent implementation, check Rankine–Hugoniot jumps and Lax inequalities, rarefaction PDE residuals and invariants, global balances, known integrals, manufactured forcing and Taylor–Green momentum/divergence residuals. The Web build checks the saved schema, wave locations, source hashes and averaging conventions. Blasius, Sedov, Noh and additional multidimensional references remain future extensions. LANL ExactPack is an independent source collection to consult for those additions; it is not a dependency or a claim of cross-validation for the cases above. documents.title: References by original publication year · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data References by original publication year Original papers and books are distinguished from sources used to check the implementations. A DOI does not imply that the full text has been inspected or its figures reproduced. Each note identifies publicly available originals, later expositions, and original sources that still need verification. NASA case resources appear in the 2D case catalog. This file and references.bib are generated from catalog/references.json by python scripts/build_references.py. 1847 · verhulst1847# Verhulst, Pierre-François. Sur la loi d’accroissement de la population (Deuxième mémoire). Mémoires de l’Académie royale de Belgique. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original archival text and metadata available. This is the later 1847 memoir, read in 1846; it must not be labeled the original 1838 logistic note. The early note is not audited in this survey. 1913 · michaelis1913# Michaelis, Leonor and Menten, Maud L.. Die Kinetik der Invertinwirkung. Biochemische Zeitschrift. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original 1913 bibliographic identification through the explicitly labeled Johnson–Goody 2011 translation. This URL identifies the translation, not a 1913 DOI. Original German text not audited; rapid-equilibrium and later quasi-steady-state interpretations are distinguished. 1920 · lotka1920# Lotka, Alfred J.. Analytical Note on Certain Rhythmic Relations in Organic Systems. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original bibliographic record checked. Early rhythmic organic-system model, before the 1925 book and independent Volterra 1926 source. The survey gives a conventional normalized predator–prey system, not a reproduction of the original figures. 1925 · briggs1925# Briggs, George E. and Haldane, J. B. S.. A Note on the Kinetics of Enzyme Action. Biochemical Journal. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original bibliographic record and original-paper search excerpt checked. Quasi-steady-state enzyme-kinetics reference; not conflated with the original rapid-equilibrium interpretation. 1926 · mckendrick1926# McKendrick, A. G.. Applications of Mathematics to Medical Problems. Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original first-page text checked: read January 1926, received August 1926, in the 1925–26 session volume. Not dated to the much later online digitization. A later von Foerster lineage is not assigned to this author alone. 1926 · volterra1926# Volterra, Vito. Fluctuations in the Abundance of a Species considered Mathematically. Nature. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher record and abstract checked. Independent ecological interaction source; Lotka’s earlier publications are cited separately. 1927 · kermack1927# Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G.. A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publication identified separately from the 1991 reprint. The survey uses the closed homogeneous SIR specialization; it does not reproduce the original general infection-age formulation. 1928 · cfl1928# Courant, Richard and Friedrichs, Kurt and Lewy, Hans. Über die partiellen Differenzengleichungen der mathematischen Physik. Mathematische Annalen. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Originally published in 1928; the linked source is a later English translation. Background on domains of dependence and the CFL condition. 1937 · fisher1937# Fisher, R. A.. The wave of advance of advantageous genes. Annals of Eugenics. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher metadata and original-text excerpt checked. Population-genetic front source. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original is not audited here. 1939 · chapman1939# Chapman, Sydney and Cowling, T. G.. The Mathematical Theory of Non-Uniform Gases. Cambridge University Press. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original-edition bibliographic preview checked; the 1939 book is not assigned as the invention date of Chapman-Enskog expansion. Third edition appeared in 1970. The atlas gives its own formal unforced isothermal lattice-BGK expansion, not a full audit of this book. 1943 · courant1943# Courant, Richard. Variational methods for the solution of problems of equilibrium and vibrations. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original variational reference. The atlas implements an independent continuous P1 Poisson example; it does not reproduce the original numerical examples. 1947 · crank1947# Crank, John and Nicolson, Phyllis. A practical method for numerical evaluation of solutions of partial differential equations of the heat-conduction type. Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Originally published in 1947; the linked source is a 1996 reprint. This edition implements the theta method for linear diffusion, rather than reproducing the original nonlinear problem. 1948 · burgers1948# Burgers, Johannes M.. A mathematical model illustrating the theory of turbulence. Advances in Applied Mechanics. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Publisher metadata and summary checked. Classical model reference; the gallery implements the inviscid scalar Riemann problem, not viscous Burgers turbulence or original-paper figures. 1949 · monod1949# Monod, Jacques. The Growth of Bacterial Cultures. Annual Review of Microbiology. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher metadata checked and university-hosted original identified. Historical microbial-growth review; the proposed batch/chemostat benchmark specifies its own yield and feed assumptions. 1949 · thomas1949# Thomas, Llewellyn Hilleth. Elliptic problems in linear difference equations over a network. Watson Scientific Computing Laboratory, Columbia University. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference The original report and a holding URL have not been verified. This provisional record follows the historical citation in Netlib and does not imply direct inspection of the original. 1950 · charney1950# Charney, Jule G. and Fjørtoft, Ragnar and von Neumann, John. Numerical Integration of the Barotropic Vorticity Equation. Tellus. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Publicly accessible original paper. Historical context for stability analysis; the numerical weather forecast is not implemented here. 1952 · hodgkin1952# Hodgkin, A. L. and Huxley, A. F.. A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve. The Journal of Physiology. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher metadata and the existence of its 2019 modern-convention supplement checked. Physiome CellML encoding identified separately. Voltage offsets, current signs and temperature conventions require an explicitly selected version before implementation. 1952 · turing1952# Turing, Alan M.. The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference University-hosted original text inspected for the model setting and instability premise. The survey’s general two-species reaction–diffusion form is a framework, not one uniquely specified Turing kinetic law. 1954 · bgk1954# Bhatnagar, P. L. and Gross, E. P. and Krook, M.. A Model for Collision Processes in Gases. I. Small Amplitude Processes in Charged and Neutral One-Component Systems. Physical Review. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher record checked. Continuous kinetic relaxation source, distinguished from later lattice BGK and its discrete-time viscosity correction. No full-paper numerical reproduction. 1954 · lax1954# Lax, Peter D.. Weak solutions of nonlinear hyperbolic equations and their numerical computation. Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Publisher bibliographic record and abstract. Background on weak solutions and Lax-type differences. The Lax shock-tube parameters have not been matched directly to the original table. 1955 · lighthill1955# Lighthill, M. J. and Whitham, G. B.. On kinematic waves. II. A theory of traffic flow on long crowded roads. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original bibliographic record and publisher-supplied abstract checked. LWR traffic source; the atlas independently chooses a normalized quadratic fundamental diagram. Full original text was not audited. 1956 · lax1956# Lax, Peter D. and Richtmyer, Robert D.. Survey of the stability of linear finite difference equations. Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Publicly accessible original paper. The equivalence theorem assumes a well-posed linear initial-value problem and a consistent linear approximation. 1956 · richards1956# Richards, Paul I.. Shock Waves on the Highway. Operations Research. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher record checked. Independent classical traffic-wave source; the atlas uses exact entropy Riemann solutions for its chosen quadratic flux. 1959 · godunov1959# Godunov, Sergei K.. A difference method for numerical calculation of discontinuous solutions of the equations of hydrodynamics. Matematicheskii Sbornik. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publication in 1959, accepted in 1956. The godunov option in this edition is a Godunov-type finite-volume method with approximate fluxes. 1960 · lax1960# Lax, Peter D. and Wendroff, Burton. Systems of conservation laws. Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Publisher bibliographic record. Background for linear-advection Lax–Wendroff and systems of conservation laws. 1961 · fedorenko1961# Fedorenko, Radii P.. A relaxation method for solving elliptic difference equations. Zhurnal Vychislitelnoi Matematiki i Matematicheskoi Fiziki. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publication in 1961; English translation in 1962. A historical entry point to multigrid. 1961 · fitzhugh1961# FitzHugh, Richard. Impulses and Physiological States in Theoretical Models of Nerve Membrane. Biophysical Journal. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original bibliographic record and abstract checked. Two-state excitable/oscillatory model; the survey writes a conventional normalized FitzHugh–Nagumo form, not a claim of identical coefficients or signs across variants. 1961 · rusanov1961# Rusanov, Vladimir V.. The calculation of the interaction of non-stationary shock waves with barriers. Zhurnal Vychislitelnoi Matematiki i Matematicheskoi Fiziki. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Russian original in 1961; English translation in 1962. This edition uses a modern local Lax–Friedrichs/Rusanov flux. 1962 · nagumo1962# Nagumo, Jinichi and Arimoto, Suguru and Yoshizawa, Shuji. An Active Pulse Transmission Line Simulating Nerve Axon. Proceedings of the IRE. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Bibliographic cross-check only; full original not inspected. Independent electrical pulse-line contribution cited alongside FitzHugh rather than silently assigning both developments to a single paper. 1963 · dahlquist1963# Dahlquist, Germund G.. A special stability problem for linear multistep methods. BIT. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher metadata and abstract checked. Foundational A-stability reference in the linear-multistep setting; full text not audited. The atlas distinguishes one-step stability functions, multistep root conditions, stiff damping and spatial error norms. 1968 · chorin1968# Chorin, Alexandre Joel. Numerical solution of the Navier-Stokes equations. Mathematics of Computation. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher record and author-hosted original checked. Projection source; the independent periodic MAC/SSPRK2 demonstration is not the original boundary/time algorithm. 1970 · keller1970# Keller, Evelyn F. and Segel, Lee A.. Initiation of Slime Mold Aggregation Viewed as an Instability. Journal of Theoretical Biology. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference University-hosted original formulation inspected. It includes more biochemical species than the common two-field Keller–Segel reduction used in the survey. No universal critical mass or original-figure reproduction is asserted. 1972 · gierer1972# Gierer, Alfred and Meinhardt, Hans. A theory of biological pattern formation. Kybernetik. Original bibliographic record · Full text or implementation reference Original publisher metadata and abstract checked. Short-range activation/long-range inhibition source. documents.title: Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Relativistic hydrodynamics: SRHD, GRHD, and GRMHD Literature review, checked 6 November 2026. These methods are not implemented in the atlas's Newtonian Euler library. The development has several interacting branches: conservative shock capture, curved and evolving geometry, magnetic constraints, physical-state recovery, high-order methods, radiation, and portable parallel computation. Dates below distinguish publication from preprint and acceptance dates. This is a selected reading path, not an exhaustive review or a ranking of codes. What changes from the existing Euler examples?# SRHD evolves relativistic matter in flat spacetime. GRHD includes a curved metric, which may be prescribed or evolved with Einstein's equations. GRMHD also evolves the electromagnetic contribution. A Kerr-background accretion calculation and a binary-neutron-star calculation with dynamical spacetime therefore test different systems. With c = G = 1 and metric signature (-,+,+,+), ideal-fluid equations are ∇μ(ρ0uμ)=0,∇μTμν=0,Tμν=ρ0huμuν+pgμν,h=1+ϵ+pρ0.∇μ​(ρ0​uμ)=0,∇μ​Tμν=0,Tμν=ρ0​huμuν+pgμν,h=1+ϵ+ρ0​p​. Here rho0 is rest-mass density and epsilon is specific internal energy. In Cartesian SRHD, a common conservative state is W=(1−v2)−1/2,D=ρ0W,Si=ρ0hW2vi,τ=ρ0hW2−p−D.W=(1−v2)−1/2,D=ρ0​W,Si​=ρ0​hW2vi​,τ=ρ0​hW2−p−D. It differs from the Newtonian state in the existing benchmarks. Primitive recovery is nonlinear. One-dimensional acoustic speeds with zero transverse velocity are (v +/- cs)/(1 +/- v cs), not v +/- cs. In a 3+1 GR formulation, lapse, shift, spatial volume factors, and metric derivatives enter the fluxes and sources. These are structural changes, not a different value of gamma. Font (2008) is the formulation review used here; the original Valencia reference is below. 1972–1998: from curved-background flows to conservative HRSC# Wilson (1972) is an early numerical study of gas falling into a Kerr black hole. It provides historical context for relativistic fluid computation, rather than a claim that fixed-background hydrodynamics solves the full evolving Einstein system. The high-resolution shock-capturing (HRSC) branch brings the characteristic and conservative methods of classical CFD into relativity. Martí and Müller (1994) give an exact SR Riemann solution for flow normal to the initial discontinuity. That scope matters when selecting multidimensional tests with transverse velocities; the original normal-flow reference is not a general transverse Riemann solution. Banyuls et al. (1997) present the 3+1 local characteristic formulation commonly called Valencia. Its conservative state, characteristic information, and geometric source terms make modern shock capture applicable in GR. It is a central reference, not a claim that all earlier relativistic methods were nonconservative. Pons et al. (1998) connect GRHD to SR Riemann solvers through a local coordinate transformation. Curvature and coordinate effects still have to be accounted for outside that local solve. 1999–2006: magnetic constraints and dynamical spacetime# Komissarov (1999) develops a multidimensional Godunov-type relativistic MHD scheme with magnetic flux conservation. HARM, Gammie–McKinney–Tóth (2003) combines conservative GRMHD, HLL fluxes, and a Tóth-type CT construction, with black-hole torus calculations among its examples. Its original formulation must be distinguished from later dynamical-spacetime frameworks. Duez et al. (2005) evolve the coupled Einstein–Maxwell–MHD system, using BSSN for spacetime and conservative shock capture for the matter. This is the additional step needed when matter and geometry affect one another dynamically. Conservation variables do not remove the need to recover physical fluid states. Noble et al. (2006) compare nonlinear recovery algorithms, including reductions to one or two unknowns. Recovery failure, atmosphere floors, and repairs must be tracked separately from truncation error and conserved-variable residuals. 2011–2026: the particle branch from GSPH# Inutsuka's original GSPH connects to Iwasaki–Inutsuka (2011), a Newtonian particle MHD method using Riemann problems and Alfvén characteristics. It is not itself relativistic. Kitajima–Inutsuka–Seno (2026) then formulate special relativistic Godunov SPH (SRGSPH). The paper addresses convolution-based interactions, unequal baryon numbers, and variable smoothing lengths, with shock-tube and Kelvin–Helmholtz examples. It is a direct bridge between the requested particle and relativistic branches. The preprint is from October 2025; the journal issue is January 2026, despite the DOI's 2025 identifier. It should not be described as a GRHD implementation. 2013 onward: radiation and microphysics add stiff systems# Sądowski et al. (2013) describe KORAL's covariant M1 radiation moments with semi-implicit interaction sources. This connects relativistic fluid methods to the atlas's planned implicit and IMEX chapters. M1 closes angular moments; it does not solve the full radiation distribution without approximation. For neutron-star mergers, Foucart (2023) reviews leakage, moment, and Monte Carlo neutrino transport and the remaining interaction-modeling limitations. Tabulated finite-temperature equations of state, composition, transport, and their uncertainties are separate advances from the choice of a Riemann flux. Ideal relativistic hydrodynamics also does not automatically supply a causal relativistic viscous theory. A parallel 1979–2019 branch: causal viscous fluid theory# The Newtonian viscous stress cannot simply be inserted into relativistic Euler equations without examining causality and the initial-value problem. Israel–Stewart (1979) provides a central reference for transient dissipative theories with additional relaxation variables. Bemfica–Disconzi–Noronha (2019) and Kovtun (2019) develop a different line: appropriate first-gradient constitutive choices and hydrodynamic frames can support causal or stable formulations under specified conditions. The former paper addresses nonlinear causality without extra extended variables; the latter examines stable first-order frames. Their results should not be merged into an unconditional claim for every equation of state or transport choice. Physical causality, PDE well-posedness, and stability of a discrete time step are separate checks. This branch is theory and reading context in the atlas, not an implemented viscous relativistic solver. 2022–2025: high order with shocks, surfaces, and physical constraints# Deppe et al. (2022) develop a DG–finite difference hybrid: attempt a high-order DG update and recompute inadmissible regions with robust FD. The 2021 preprint and 2022 publication dates should remain distinct. Their binary-neutron-star study (2024 preprint) extends the hybrid approach to dynamical spacetime and merger calculations. The latter is cited here as a preprint; a separate journal record has not been verified in this review. Cao–Peng–Wu (2025) study physical-constraint-preserving, oscillation-eliminating DG for GRHD, including positive thermodynamic states and subluminal velocity under their stated scheme assumptions. Their results are not a guarantee for arbitrary limiters, fluxes, EOS, or spacetime discretizations. A theorem for a selected GRHD formulation and an astrophysical merger-code demonstration are different types of evidence. 2025–2026: portable GPU computation of the coupled system# AthenaK, Fields et al. (2025) demonstrates dynamical-spacetime GRMHD and binary-neutron-star mergers on GPUs, with CT and first-order flux correction among its numerical ingredients. Its preprint is from 2024; the journal reference is ApJS 276, 35 (2025). AsterX, Kalinani et al. (2025 issue) provides another open GPU-oriented GRMHD framework, based on Valencia and Z4c. Its online publication was December 2024. Refinement infrastructure is part of those source codes; implementing AMR in this atlas remains deferred. GRACE, Musolino et al. was accepted by Physical Review D on 2 November 2026, as checked on 6 November. Its July 2026 preprint describes Kokkos-based portability, CT, Z4c coupling, and neutron-star merger examples. Acceptance is not a verified final volume/page citation. These papers establish examples of portable implementations; they do not establish a universal speed or accuracy ranking across hardware and physics. What the atlas can reproduce in stages# The following is an implementation proposal, not a result of this review: SRHD: primitive/conservative round trips, characteristic speeds, smooth waves, shock tubes, reflection, and transverse-velocity cases. Check EOS validity, rho and pressure positivity, and speeds below c. SRMHD: add relativistic Alfvén waves, magnetic shock tubes, and a rotor; specify the magnetic-divergence operator and every repair/floor. Fixed-metric GR: metric-aware flat-space limits, Michel/Bondi accretion, equilibrium stars, and torus configurations, with geometric source balance. Dynamical GR: couple a separately verified spacetime evolution; monitor Einstein constraints, baryon conservation, stellar oscillations, and waveform convergence before attempting mergers. Radiation or SRGSPH: keep each branch's state, boundary, conservation, transport closure, and reference tests explicit. Reuse the Newtonian examples as comparisons, not as evidence that a relativistic solver already exists. The historical conclusion is that progress comes from the combination of these layers. A new high-order reconstruction or a larger GPU run alone does not resolve primitive recovery, surface/atmosphere handling, constraint errors, or microphysical uncertainty. documents.title: v0.1.0 — First edition · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data v0.1.0 — First edition The first edition of The Art of Numerical Algorithms connects historical papers with equations, executable educational implementations, benchmark figures, and numerical verification. Included# An English historical atlas and method notes covering conservation laws, stability, diffusion, boundary conditions, iterative solvers, DG, spectral methods, and MHD. A Python library and CLI for Euler, shallow-water, isothermal, linear-advection, diffusion, Poisson, and planar ideal-MHD examples. Godunov-type and MUSCL finite volumes, Rusanov/HLL/HLLE/HLLC/Roe fluxes, FD WENO5-JS, modal DG, and Fourier propagation. Thomas elimination, matrix-free conjugate gradients, red-black relaxation, and geometric multigrid. Minimal dual-time, matrix-scaling, and scalar residual-distribution examples. CT and GLM magnetic-constraint demonstrations with distinct divergence diagnostics. A 39-entry bibliography with English source notes, generated Markdown and BibTeX, plus a NASA 2D case catalog for future work. Automated numerical checks and a gallery-generation workflow for Python 3.9 and 3.12. Install and run# Requires Python 3.9 or later. From the repository root: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install '.[test]' python -m pytest -q python -m numart.cli gallery --output outputs/gallery Start with the reading guide and benchmark definitions. Scope of this edition# The examples are independently implemented educational models. Their figures do not claim to reproduce the original papers' figures. Verification covers selected configurations and does not prove general nonlinear stability or positivity. Finite-volume and finite-difference errors are identified as pointwise comparisons, and CT/GLM divergence measurements name their operators. NASA flow cases, multidimensional Euler rotated-hybrid fluxes, low-Mach PDE preconditioning, Euler/MHD DG, and multidimensional residual distribution remain future work. See the roadmap for next steps and the reference notes for unverified original-source details. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Implementation roadmap Editorial scope The focus is mathematical methods, formulations, applicability and verification. AMR (adaptive mesh refinement), parallelization and mixed-precision techniques for computational efficiency are outside the scope of dedicated coverage and development. Ordinary roundoff and numerical stability remain foundational topics. Current development plan and published examples Help people and AI check conditions and evidence, then use public code, inputs and results. Improve the existing foundation and complete execution and validation paths through representative examples. Prioritize the P0 shared foundation and existing examples. P1 additions are conditional on established validation and the progress of earlier work. Do not promise exhaustive method coverage or completion of unverified calculations. Update status after checking publication. Target milestones and review gates End of November: shared registry and three example entries Check shared paths from the published Barnes–Hut, hydrogenic and helium examples to inputs, execution, results and citation. This does not mean completing every implementation candidate. Additions conditional on validation and progress (P1) A small Ewald validation example and PME/SPME reading Conditional candidate A conditional addition after the shared registry and representative examples. Fix self and zero-mode terms, boundaries and units for a neutral 3D periodic system, then compare energies, forces and convergence with an independent reference. Provide at least original sources, formulations and validation specifications for PME/SPME. Keep entries as reading or planned if the comparison is not established. An H₂ example using external electronic-structure software Conditional candidate A candidate using existing public software with fixed geometry, basis, spin, functional, quadrature and SCF settings to compare RHF, specified DFT and finite-basis FCI. Do not call reruns in the same software independent-implementation validation or describe the example as an atlas-built general molecular solver. Periodic band calculations are a separate task. Representative examples and reading already available Barnes–Hut fixed inputs and direct-sum comparison Scoped verified example published Published code, inputs and JSON/CSV compare isolated softened gravity for 192 particles with an identical-kernel direct sum. This is a static-force comparison, not a complete orbital integrator, FMM or TreePM solver. Inputs, results and reproduction Quantum chemistry and DFT: map and formulations Reading published Bilingual introductions to 18 entries, representative equations and primary references. A separate chapter supplies scoped hydrogenic/He runs; other dedicated implementations remain future work. Representative runnable quantum-chemistry and DFT checks Scoped verified examples published Published fixed inputs, code, results and independent references for executed hydrogenic atoms and spherical-helium closed-shell HF / exchange-only LDA. This does not verify general molecular, periodic or correlation-inclusive DFT. An H₂ addition is conditional; periodic numerical validation is a separate task. Runnable hydrogenic / helium checks Goals for 2027 or later Atlas-based specialist AI and model research 2027 or later A goal for 2027 or later: investigate retrieval plus execution, verified training examples and held-out evaluation. This is not a commitment to deliver an independently pretrained foundation model. Current work queue / JSON Development history and field-specific validation candidates The sections below retain earlier development records and field-specific validation candidates. They are not the current priority order or a commitment to implement every item this year. Existing section links are preserved. Earlier priority: shock methods# At that stage, shock-method expansion took priority over relativity and new subject areas. The first published stage adds limited parabolic FV, characteristics, WENO-Z and an AUSM baseline, Roe's Property U with numerical counterexamples, and controlled planar odd–even diagnostics. The second computed stage adds direct-Eulerian traced PPM with independent steepening/flattening switches, specified AUSM+/AUSM+-up fluxes, and conforming-grid cylinder-forebody tests including a directional HLLE/Roe experiment. The recorded strong-jump AUSM+ failure, finite-time bow-shock behavior and unresolved verification are explicit. Lagrange/remap, optimized original Rotated-RHLL, broader strength/rotation studies and external-code comparisons remain future work. First edition: executable foundations# Version 0.1.0 brings together an educational Python library, a historical atlas, English method notes, a bibliographic catalog, comparison figures, and automated numerical checks. The repository is the first-edition distribution; the reading guide in the README connects the material. The NASA case catalog includes computed 15-degree wedge baselines and remaining implementation candidates. A separate conforming-grid forebody diagnostic now includes a directional hybrid; catalog inclusion alone still does not indicate an implemented simulation. Earlier validation candidates# Strengthen links between run manifests and saved arrays; report grid and time refinement together with wall-clock costs. Add finite-volume cell-average initialization and integrated references, characteristic WENO, positivity limiters, and stronger shock tests. Added shallow-water and isothermal Riemann references; topography, well balancing, and numerical dry-bed evolution remain separate implementation steps. Extend the new HLLD standard tests with UCT-HLLD, stronger-field cases and external reference-code comparisons. Explore nonlinear Fourier methods and dealiasing, Euler DG with limiting, and multidimensional residual distribution. Implement low-Mach PDE preconditioning and extend the directional 2D Euler hybrid beyond its stated forebody tests; test entropy correction, positivity, and carbuncle resistance separately. Extend elliptic solvers to variable coefficients, anisotropy, line smoothing, FAS, AMG, and 2D mixed boundaries. Earlier suggested order for NASA cases# Start with wedge and expansion flows to verify 2D Euler fluxes and wall boundaries. Use the cavity and Blasius cases to establish viscous, pressure, and boundary treatments, then the cylinder to examine unsteady accuracy. For RANS, verify model implementations on flat-plate and bump cases before moving to airfoils, steps, diffusers, and humps. This order follows dependencies and difficulty and complements the atlas's publication chronology. Shock gallery: NASA wedges and a forward-facing step# Computed the NASA 15-degree wedges at Mach 2.0 and 2.5 with independent body-fitted first-order HLL / SSPRK2 finite volumes, two grids and oblique-shock references. Added the classical Mach-3 forward step on a 240 × 80 blocked-cell mesh, 81 saved states to t = 4 and an MP4, bringing the movie catalog to five. The step uses plain reflecting corners, not the entropy/enthalpy reset of the original PPM comparison. These are educational inviscid baselines, not Wind-US outputs or viscous experimental validations. Setup and limits. Mach-5 shock/boundary-layer interaction, Mach-7 viscous ramps and the existing transonic diffuser/airfoil cases remain implementation candidates. Web edition# The public web edition organizes the first-edition library as a historical atlas, method reading room, computed gallery, and searchable reference library. Each exhibit connects literature, equations, execution, figures, and verification scope. The interactive Sod comparison switches between four precomputed MUSCL density curves from the Python library. Figures and the original gallery validation manifest remain available alongside the complete source edition. Future exhibits should continue to distinguish tested educational examples, original-figure reproductions, prototypes, literature-only entries, and planned work. First expansion: interactive numerical notebooks# The stability laboratory runs periodic FTCS, upwind, classical LF, and LW updates in the browser, with both velocity signs, Fourier amplification, pointwise error, and downloadable experiment snapshots. Its numerical kernels are checked against the Python implementation across 24 reference cases. The convergence notebook makes the existing DG and Euler entropy-wave gallery measurements inspectable, including observed slopes and scalar-unknown counts. It introduces no new wall-clock ranking or general nonlinear stability claim. The experiment guide records definitions and provenance. Second expansion: geometry, time, and multidimensional shocks# Added seven scalar ODE integrators with a temporal notebook; three mesh-connectivity examples with an explorer; 1D SPH kernel reconstruction; a 1D ALE geometric-conservation check; and cylindrical gradient, Newtonian stress, and stress-divergence operators verified against analytic fields. The coordinate and viscosity chapter distinguishes physical components from coordinate-basis tensors. The 2D Double Mach Reflection baseline now computes an actual Mach-10 interaction with first-order HLL and SSPRK2. Higher-order reconstruction, full grid refinement, and resolution of the fine wall jet remain future work. The NASA wedge baselines were added later; the cataloged viscous and turbulence cases remain unimplemented. Blunt-body carbuncle comparisons beyond the new planar diagnostic, a complete SPH fluid solver, unstructured flow fluxes, and a complete ALE Euler solver also remain future work. The Roe memorial is sourced from official university records. Third expansion: Hamiltonian maps and particle gravity# Added fixed-step canonical maps and a notebook for harmonic/quartic oscillators; periodic 3D CIC/FFT PM; an isolated softened octree with monopole/full second moments; isolated doubled-grid convolution; and sampled/continuum slab Green-transform options. Figures have dedicated source manifests. P³M corrections, a coupled TreePM solver, FMM translations, cosmological expansion, shear-periodic remapping, and a gravity-coupled SPH fluid integrator remain future work. Fourth expansion: nonsteady movies and smooth KEEP# Added saved-state output that leaves solver time steps unchanged, four numerical movies with frame inspection and MP4 export, and the original second-order Cartesian KEEP flux with smooth-vortex refinement. Steady fields retain still images. The KEEP implementation excludes shock stabilization, later PEP/redefined variants, high-order curvilinear forms, and the 3D TGV/LES examples discussed in the reading guide. Fifth expansion: limiters, RK families, and CIP# Added selectable MUSCL slopes, TVB modified-minmod and positive-reconstruction building blocks, nine explicit RK tableaus with nonlinear stage verification, twelve oscillator methods, and original cubic-Hermite CIP with a conservation counterexample. Full Euler-update positivity is still a separate extension. Sixth expansion: equations, sparse systems and kinetic transport# Added nine saved-profile cases across seven equation families, including Burgers and LWR traffic. Scalar exact cell averages and conserved cell means of semi-analytic Euler/shallow-water/isothermal Riemann references are distinguished. The reference library adds 18 formula-based cases, including vacuum/dry fans, viscous profiles and a manufactured Poisson field. The new continuous P1 FEM, sparse/nonlinear solvers, stiff ODE integrators, periodic MAC projection, D2Q9–BGK, and first-order hyperbolic diffusion baseline have dedicated numerical checks, figures and source-hashed manifests. Chapman–Enskog expansion is a formal derivation linked to the measured shear viscosity. These educational additions are included in the published atlas at https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/ . Their implementation limits and remaining verification work are stated in each chapter. Earlier implementation candidates and progress# Added — Roe's Property U: original four conditions, parameter-vector derivation, jump/consistency/eigenbasis checks and an expansion-discontinuity counterexample; see the explanation. Inutsuka's GSPH: Gaussian convolution and specific-volume reconstruction, oriented pair Riemann states, a matched conservative energy update, and smooth/contact/shock-tube verification before variable smoothing lengths. The Iwasaki–Inutsuka GSPMHD extension is a later, separately verified stage; see the source notes and staged plan. Relativistic hydrodynamics is a source-based extension plan: SRHD recovery and characteristic tests before SRMHD, fixed-metric GR, and independently verified Einstein–matter coupling. Radiation and SRGSPH are separate branches; see the development review checked in November 2026. First stage added: limited parabolic FV, conservative characteristics and FD WENO-Z with Sod/contact/Shu–Osher comparisons. Direct-Eulerian tracing/steepening/flattening are now added in the second stage; Lagrange/remap remain separate. AUSM common-sound-speed baseline retained; specified AUSM+ and AUSM+-up fluxes, matched traced-PPM cases and a recorded admissibility failure are added in the second stage. Completed web stage: HLLD with Brio–Wu, Alfvén-wave refinement and weak field-loop CT-Contact/GLM comparisons; see the MHD tests. Planned — electromagnetic FDTD (finite-difference time-domain): Yee-grid placement, leapfrog Maxwell updates, CFL limits and numerical dispersion; start with vacuum-wave and conducting-cavity tests, then absorbing boundaries and PML reflection checks. Implementation and dedicated verification are pending. Planned — plasma PIC (Particle-in-Cell): start with electrostatic particle–Poisson coupling, then electromagnetic particle–Maxwell coupling. Cover particle shapes, deposition/gather, Boris pushing, charge-conserving current deposition and Gauss-law diagnostics. Plan plasma-oscillation, two-stream and Landau-damping tests, with energy, noise and grid/time/particle refinement checks. Existing gravitational PM is a separate scoped example. The WarpX PIC theory notes are a starting reference; no plasma PIC solver is implemented here yet. Stiff integration: higher-order IMEX, embedded DIRK, variable-step BDF and operator splitting beyond the implemented BE/BDF2/SDIRK2/IMEX-Euler models. Sparse/nonlinear solvers: matrix-free Newton–Krylov, robust reorderings/fill, flexible preconditioning and broader nonlinear benchmarks beyond the implemented fixed-right GMRES/BiCGSTAB and ILU(0). Viscous/incompressible flow: wall projection, SIMPLE/PISO, cavity and cylinder-wake validation beyond periodic Taylor–Green. FEM: mixed velocity–pressure pairs, inf–sup checks, curved/irregular meshes and natural/mixed boundary assembly. LBM: MRT/TRT/cumulant collisions, thermal and multiphase models beyond low-Mach isothermal D2Q9–BGK. Hyperbolic diffusion: full second-order RD, anisotropy and unified advection/viscous systems beyond the periodic first-order baseline. AMR is outside the editorial scope. Biological and geophysical survey additions# The biological catalog contains 22 survey-only model families, with equations, source conventions and proposed verification. A practical implementation sequence is logistic/SIR and enzyme kinetics, then Fisher fronts, FitzHugh–Nagumo, Schnakenberg and Keller–Segel, with a birth–death SSA as a separate stochastic branch. No biological solver or biological validation is added by the survey. Arakawa A/B/C has variable-location diagrams and tested semi-discrete f-plane Fourier symbols. D/E, vertical staggering, nonlinear potential-vorticity schemes, Kelvin/Rossby waves and coastlines remain additional work. This is not a full geophysical dynamical core. Longer-term candidates: machine-learning numerics# Status: revision candidates; the dedicated explanations, implementations and verification below have not been added. Start with stable function evaluation, automatic differentiation and optimization as shared foundations for Volume 1. Scientific machine-learning applications are later candidates. These plans do not add to implemented-method counts, and no release date is assigned. Mixed-precision arithmetic and the design of low-precision GPU computations are outside the current scope. Ordinary floating-point roundoff and stable function evaluation remain part of the shared foundations. Softmax and log-sum-exp: maximum shifting, log-softmax, exponential overflow and underflow. Plan checks for large inputs, invariance under constant shifts, probability sums and derivative consistency. See the SciPy softmax notes. Cross-entropy and stable loss evaluation: compute directly from logits, connect to log-sum-exp, and cover sigmoid and binary cross-entropy. Check finite values and analytic gradients for extreme inputs. Start from the PyTorch cross-entropy documentation. Automatic differentiation and backpropagation: forward/reverse modes, the chain rule, Jacobian–vector products (JVPs), vector–Jacobian products (VJPs) and Hessian–vector products. Distinguish symbolic and finite-difference derivatives; cover roundoff, nondifferentiable points and intermediate-storage costs. Use the JAX autodiff guide and plan analytic/directional derivative comparisons. Implicit differentiation, adjoints and differentiable solvers: sensitivities through linear solves, converged nonlinear systems and time evolution. Distinguish unrolling iterations from differentiating the defining equations; state Jacobian invertibility, solve tolerances and gradient checks. The implicit-differentiation paper is a starting reference. Machine-learning optimization: gradient descent/SGD, momentum, Adam, L-BFGS and Gauss–Newton/Levenberg–Marquardt. Distinguish objective minimization from the existing Newton root solves; compare scaling, conditioning, learning rates and gradient norms. Do not claim universal convergence or a universal ranking. Application candidate — PINNs and inverse problems: separate PDE, initial/boundary and observation losses; compare with conventional finite differences/FEM using shared error measures. A lower training loss alone is not a PDE-error guarantee. See the authors' PINN notes and failure-mode study. Application candidate — neural operators/Fourier neural operators: connect learned function-to-solution maps with the existing Fourier bases and spectral methods. Plan separate checks of out-of-distribution behavior, grid changes, discretization and aliasing errors; changing grid resolution alone does not guarantee accuracy. See the neural-operator paper. Application candidate — symbolic regression and equation discovery: search for explicit expressions from data or learned models, separately from automatic derivative evaluation. Assess noise, dimensions/symmetries, expression complexity and independent-data checks. Consider the study on extracting symbolic models from deep learning. Electronic structure: published examples and remaining work Introductions, representative formulas and primary references are available for 18 entries. Hydrogenic/He examples supply fixed inputs, code and independent reference comparisons. H₂ is a conditional addition; periodic numerical validation is a separate task. Bilingual overview, runnable examples and next plans Verified Euler and MHD comparisons# Added 2D primitive MUSCL with minmod/MC, exact-cell-average smooth refinement, NASA wedge first/second-order comparisons on two grids, and three forward-step reconstruction clips. The comparison page fixes HLL/SSPRK2 and exposes diagnostics. Added full-vector HLLD, Brio–Wu, four-grid circular Alfvén waves and weak magnetic loops on two grids with HLLE/HLLD × CT-Contact/GLM. Source/artifact hashes, conservative arrays, positivity/retry/fallback diagnostics and bilingual scope notes accompany the MHD page. These complete the agreed three web stages; books remain deferred. Same-system Poisson solvers# The comparison notebook adds Jacobi, weighted Jacobi, red-black GS/SOR, CG, V-cycles, FFT/DST and separable DST+Thomas under one residual target. Two broad-source problems, a single-eigenmode diagnostic, three timing trials and a separate 1D Thomas table expose the differences. Definitions and limits. documents.title: Remembering Philip L. Roe · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Remembering Philip L. Roe Philip Lawrence Roe died on April 26, 2026, aged 87. The University of Michigan’s memorial by Ken Powell records his contributions to aerospace engineering, numerical methods, teaching, and the computational fluid dynamics community. This atlas remembers him through a question that remains central to its subject: how can a numerical method preserve the wave structure of the equations while making the computation practical? A career in computational fluid dynamics# Roe worked at the Royal Aircraft Establishment from 1962 to 1984, became a professor at Cranfield, and joined the University of Michigan in 1990. He retired in 2021. Michigan’s official retirement memoir documents this chronology and his 2015 AIAA Fluid Dynamics Award. The university memorial also recalls his role with Bram van Leer and Ken Powell in establishing the Keck CFD laboratory. The 1981 idea, still executable# In Approximate Riemann solvers, parameter vectors, and difference schemes, Roe developed a way to replace a nonlinear interface problem with a carefully constructed linearized system. A defining condition is A~(UL,UR)(UR−UL)=F(UR)−F(UL).A(UL​,UR​)(UR​−UL​)=F(UR​)−F(UL​). Together with consistency and a usable characteristic decomposition, this connects a conservative flux difference to recognizable waves. The Sod comparison and the atlas home-page selector let readers inspect one educational 1D Euler implementation of this idea alongside HLL, HLLC, and Rusanov. Our code uses acoustic entropy smoothing. It is an independent teaching implementation, not Roe’s original software. His name identifies a much broader body of work than this one exhibit. Precision as a form of respect# The same wave resolution that makes an approximate solver useful invites careful questions about entropy, low densities, and multidimensional shocks. The carbuncle chapter treats these as separate numerical issues and points to later research. Studying such limits is part of understanding the method’s contribution. Roe’s later interests included Active Flux; the Michigan MICDE profile provides an institutional starting point. Active Flux is a reading direction here, not an implemented solver. We dedicate this reading room’s Roe notes to his memory: an invitation to read the original work, examine the equations, and keep testing the computation. documents.title: Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver Rotated Riemann methods construct dissipation using directions beyond the face normal. Ren’s rotated Roe method (2003) and Nishikawa–Kitamura’s rotated-hybrid method (2008) are related but distinct. Problem and representative equations For 2D Euler states U_L,U_R and unit face normal n, resolve n into orthogonal unit directions n₁,n₂ with weights αᵢ=n·nᵢ. The formula below defines this atlas’s educational HLLE/Roe experiment, not the optimized dissipation formula in the 2008 paper. n=α1n1+α2n2,F^(n)=α1F^HLLE(n1)+α2F^Roe(n2).n=α1​n1​+α2​n2​,F(n)=α1​FHLLE​(n1​)+α2​FRoe​(n2​). Algorithm The implementation aligns n₁ with the velocity jump, orienting directions to have nonnegative projections on the face normal. A tiny jump falls back to the face tangent. Rotate the same states into each frame, evaluate HLLE/Roe, rotate momentum fluxes back and combine. This differs from a pressure-sensor flux blend. Conditions and pitfalls Roe (1981) supplies the component approximate solver. The 2003 rotated-method paper is by Y.-X. Ren; the 2008 rotated-hybrid paper is by Hiroaki Nishikawa and Keiichi Kitamura. Roe, Nishikawa, Ismail and Scalabrin (2005) is related carbuncle research, not the authorship/date of that 2008 paper. No universal carbuncle or positivity guarantee is claimed here. What to check Check constant states, flux reversal under state/normal exchange and rotational covariance. Separate normal compression from pure tangential shear, then compare perturbed planar shocks and blunt-body cases under fixed conditions. Link the dated package’s actual tests/results without claiming a new reproduction of the papers. Publication scope and related entries Links lead to existing educational code and dated verification records. This reading/translation update changes no scientific code or historical measurements and does not claim reproduction of an entire paper. documents.title: Runge–Kutta families: stages, order, stability, and SSP · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Runge–Kutta families: stages, order, stability, and SSP RK2 and RK4 denote orders, while SSP describes a stability-inheritance property. These labels answer different questions. The Runge–Kutta family notebook compares nine explicit methods, their full stage coefficients, nonlinear predictors, linear stability contours, and measured refinement orders. One step, several right-hand-side evaluations# An explicit s-stage Runge–Kutta method for y′=f(t,y) is Yi=yn+h∑j<iaijkj,ki=f(tn+cih,Yi),yn+1=yn+h∑i=1sbiki,ci=∑j<iaij.Yi​=yn​+hj<i∑​aij​kj​,ki​=f(tn​+ci​h,Yi​),yn+1​=yn​+hi=1∑s​bi​ki​,ci​=j<i∑​aij​. The Butcher tableau arranges c, A, and b into one coefficient diagram. The number of stages s counts RHS evaluations in this implementation. Order p means a global error of O(h^p) under the required smoothness, stability, and fixed-interval assumptions. Stage predictors Y_i are generally not accurate solutions at intermediate times. Stage times can go backward: SSPRK(4,3) evaluates at c=(0,1/2,1,1/2). Time-dependent forcing and boundary data must use the correct c_i, not just the next chronological fraction of a step. RK2 is a family# The two-stage, second-order family can be written k1=f(tn,yn),k2=f(tn+αh,yn+αhk1),yn+1=yn+h[(1−12α)k1+12αk2].k1​=f(tn​,yn​),k2​=f(tn​+αh,yn​+αhk1​),yn+1​=yn​+h[(1−2α1​)k1​+2α1​k2​]. Heun / explicit trapezoid takes alpha=1; explicit midpoint takes alpha=1/2; Ralston takes alpha=2/3. Heun is also SSPRK(2,2). For the full nonlinear methods here, their SSP coefficients are respectively 1, 0, and 1/2, as checked from the absolute-monotonicity inequalities for the complete tableau. All three have the same scalar linear stability polynomial R(z)=1+z+12z2,z=hλ.R(z)=1+z+21​z2,z=hλ. Consequently their trajectories on y′=lambda y coincide in exact arithmetic. Their nonlinear stages and errors need not coincide. The notebook therefore also computes y′=−y², y(0)=1, whose exact solution is 1/(1+t). This separates methods that an oscillator alone cannot distinguish. One benchmark does not establish a universally best RK2 variant. RK3, classical RK4, and SSP stage counts# The implemented third-order group contains Kutta's classical three-stage method, SSPRK(3,3), and SSPRK(4,3). The first two share R(z)=1+z+z²/2+z³/6, but their nonlinear SSP coefficients differ: 0 and 1. SSPRK(4,3) uses a fourth RHS evaluation, has C=2, and adds z⁴/48 to that polynomial. Four stages do not make it fourth order. Classical four-stage RK4 uses weights (1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6). Its stability polynomial adds z⁴/24 instead, and it is fourth order. Its general nonlinear SSP coefficient is zero. This does not say that every RK4 computation oscillates; it says the generic forward-Euler SSP inheritance guarantee is unavailable. The Numipedia RK4 record lists its tableau and scalar stability properties. For comparison, the notebook implements the five-stage fourth-order Spiteri–Ruuth SSP method, labeled SSPRK(5,4). Its full coefficients are given in section 3.1 of the Gottlieb–Ketcheson–Shu review. The implementation converts that decimal Shu–Osher form to a Butcher tableau; representing increments relative to y_n avoids drift from rounded affine weights. It uses the conservative rounded bound C=1.508, rather than claiming an exact rational coefficient. Order conditions and nonlinear refinement are checked at the supplied coefficient precision. For standard explicit RK methods with a positive general nonlinear SSP coefficient, the order is at most four. A four-stage fourth-order explicit method cannot have C>0; fourth-order SSP therefore needs additional stages. SSPRK(5,4) is one example, not a claim that every five-stage fourth-order method is SSP. See Spiteri–Ruuth (2002) and Gottlieb–Ketcheson–Shu (2009). What SSP preserves# Suppose a particular semidiscrete spatial operator L satisfies a convex stability property under forward Euler for h ≤ h_FE. An SSP method with coefficient C inherits that property under h≤ChFE.h≤ChFE​. The premise might concern total variation, a norm, or an admissible convex set, provided the actual operator and its stage treatment satisfy the premise. SSP does not create a TVD spatial discretization, cure an inappropriate boundary condition, or supply missing positive Euler states. The SSP review by Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor (2001) develops this viewpoint. Compare it with the separate slope-limiter and positive-reconstruction requirements. The family labels are SSPRK(s,p): stages first, order second. In this edition, Heun / SSPRK(2,2) has C=1, SSPRK(3,3) has C=1, SSPRK(4,3) has C=2, and SSPRK(5,4) has C=1.508 as a rounded bound. The SSP step bound per RHS evaluation, C/s, is useful context but is not a wall-clock performance ranking. Memory traffic, storage, spatial accuracy, and other stability constraints can decide the actual cost. Linear stability is a separate picture# For y′=lambda y, one step multiplies y by R(z)=1+z bT(I−zA)−11.R(z)=1+zbT(I−zA)−11. The region |R(z)|≤1 is the scalar absolute-stability region. Its boundary is sampled on a 401×401 grid over Re(z)∈[−6,2], Im(z)∈[−4,4]. The curves in the notebook are approximate contours, not rigorous boundary locations. An eigenvalue of a normal linear spatial operator suggests where to evaluate R; eigenvalues alone may miss transient growth for a nonnormal operator. For the undamped oscillator, RK2 has no nonzero imaginary-axis stability interval, while SSPRK(3,3) and classical RK4 do. This concerns the scalar linear problem; it does not contradict Heun's SSP property, because forward Euler itself has no nonzero stable step on that oscillator. Other branches of the time-integration family# Embedded RK pairs, such as Dormand–Prince 5(4), use two orders to estimate error and select a step. Here those parentheses describe the embedded orders, unlike the stage/order pair in SSPRK(s,p). No embedded error estimator, adaptive controller, dense output, or FSAL optimization runs in this edition. Low-storage RK methods reorganize stage calculations to reduce stored arrays; they are not automatically SSP. Implicit RK families include midpoint and Gauss/Radau/SDIRK methods, with nonlinear solves and their own stability properties. IMEX pairs split explicit and implicit operators. These are reading context, except for the existing scalar linear backward-Euler and implicit-midpoint demonstrations. The generic rk_step below supports the nine explicit tableaus only. Leapfrog is a multistep recurrence; mechanical Verlet and the symplectic maps form another distinct branch. Reproduction and verification# from numart.runge_kutta import rk_step, nonlinear_trajectory value, stages = rk_step(lambda t, y: -y*y, 0., 1., 0.5, method="ssprk43", return_stages=True) t, y = nonlinear_trajectory("ssprk54", steps=40) python scripts/build_runge_kutta.py python scripts/sync_web_content.py The JSON records all tableaus, contours, 27 one-step stage cases (h=0.25,0.5,1), and nine refinement studies (N=10,20,40,80, T=1), plus source hashes. Errors use the exact nonlinear solution; stages are actual RHS evaluations. Tests check all order conditions through order four, a nonlinear manufactured time-dependent equation, complex linear stability factors, full-tableau SSP inequalities at the stated C, and scalar MUSCL conservation/TVD under the inherited step restriction. These do not turn the existing Euler/WENO solvers into selectable-RK or fully positivity-preserving implementations. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Stochastic differential equations | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Stochastic differential equations Brownian increments in an SDE scale as √Δt. Adding random numbers to an ODE solver does not by itself specify the stochastic interpretation or convergence order. Problem and representative equations The formula uses a scalar Itô SDE. a is drift, b is diffusion and ΔWₙ are independent Gaussian increments with mean zero and variance Δt. Euler–Maruyama evaluates both coefficients at n. Converting a Stratonovich equation requires the appropriate drift correction. dX=a(X,t) dt+b(X,t) dW,Xn+1=Xn+a(Xn,tn)Δt+b(Xn,tn)ΔWn.dX=a(X,t)dt+b(X,t)dW,Xn+1​=Xn​+a(Xn​,tn​)Δt+b(Xn​,tn​)ΔWn​. Algorithm Generate Wiener increments and advance deterministic and stochastic terms. Strong-error refinement must couple paths by summing fine increments into the coarse increment. Weak error concerns expectations of test functions, not the discrepancy of one pair of paths. Conditions and pitfalls Under suitable global Lipschitz, moment and smoothness assumptions, Euler–Maruyama typically has strong order 1/2 and weak order 1. Superlinear growth or positivity constraints can invalidate the method and require specialized treatments. Sampling uncertainty may dominate weak discretization error. What to check Use geometric Brownian exact paths and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck moments to test strong and weak convergence separately. Record step size, random streams, sample count and uncertainty, including negative states or boundary violations. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method.
