documents.title: Traced PPM, AUSM variants and curved bow shocks · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Traced PPM, AUSM variants and curved bow shocks Open the new computed comparison. This stage adds a direct-Eulerian characteristic-traced PPM update, specified AUSM+ and AUSM+-up fluxes, and a circular-cylinder forebody diagnostic. The earlier method-of-lines reconstruction and planar odd–even experiment retain their original data and scope. Direct-Eulerian PPM and independent switches# numart.ppm_traced reconstructs primitive density, velocity and pressure from conserved cell means. It uses MC-limited parabolic interpolation, optional density contact steepening, optional shock flattening and componentwise parabolic monotonicity constraints. Mean conserved states are updated by a shared face flux. A primitive profile reconstructed from a conserved mean is a second-order representation; it is not an exact average of primitive variables. For each primitive profile, with local cell coordinate xi in [0,1], q(ξ)=qL+ξ[Δq+q6(1−ξ)],Δq=qR−qL,q6=6qi−3(qL+qR).q(ξ)=qL​+ξ[Δq+q6​(1−ξ)],Δq=qR​−qL​,q6​=6qi​−3(qL​+qR​). Average over a fraction sigma of the domain next to either edge: IR(σ)=qR−σ2[Δq−(1−2σ3)q6],IL(σ)=qL+σ2[Δq+(1−2σ3)q6].IR​(σ)=qR​−2σ​[Δq−(1−32σ​)q6​],IL​(σ)=qL​+2σ​[Δq+(1−32σ​)q6​]. The three wave speeds are u−c, u and u+c. For each incoming family, sigma=|lambda| dt/dx. Starting from the fastest incoming wave's domain average, correct the other incoming characteristic components using a primitive eigenbasis frozen at the cell state. These are time-averaged Riemann inputs for one conservative step. Applying an additional SSPRK3 wrapper to this predictor would define a different method. The default flux is HLLC and CFL is 0.4. The construction follows the direct-Eulerian characteristic-domain approach in the inspected Colella–Woodward author preprint, with the 1984 paper as the original publication. The Cholla author manuscript, Appendix A is an additional algorithmic cross-check. The implementation is independent: it does not reproduce every production-code option, multidimensional CTU, artificial viscosity, Lagrangian evolution or remap. Some displayed Cholla appendix signs/indices are inconsistent with the described neighboring-cell construction; the explicit formulas below and executable checks define this variant. Contact steepening and shock flattening# Steepening changes density edges only. Let D2_i=(rho_(i+1)−2rho_i+rho_(i−1))/6. Require D2_(i−1) D2_(i+1)<0, a relative density jump above 0.01, and a relative pressure jump smaller than 0.1 gamma times the relative density jump. Then η~i=−Di+12−Di−12ρi+1−ρi−1,ηi=clip⁡ ⁣(20(η~i−0.05),0,1).η​i​=−ρi+1​−ρi−1​Di+12​−Di−12​​,ηi​=clip(20(η​i​−0.05),0,1). Blend the density left edge toward rho_(i−1)+delta_rho_(i−1)/2 and the right edge toward rho_(i+1)−delta_rho_(i+1)/2, using MC slopes in those neighboring cells. This suppresses contact spreading but can sharpen an under-resolved smooth density transition. It should not be treated as a universal accuracy improvement. Flattening uses S_i=(p_(i+1)−p_(i−1))/(p_(i+2)−p_(i−2)). The preliminary coefficient is clip(10(S_i−0.75),0,1), enabled only for a relative pressure jump at least 1/3 and a compressive velocity difference. Take the larger coefficient of the cell and its lower-pressure neighbor. Every primitive edge is blended toward its cell value before monotonicity enforcement. A coefficient of 1 removes the spatial variation; 0 leaves it unchanged. Reconstructed inputs that violate density/pressure thresholds of 1e−12 use a common conservative affine scaling about the unchanged cell mean. Invalid completed updates retry with half the time step, up to 14 attempts. These are safeguards, not a fully discrete positivity proof. Failure preserves the last accepted state and actual time. No state clipping, hidden flux substitution or false final-time label is used. The four switch combinations use identical flux, nominal CFL and update algorithm. At N=200 for one moving-contact crossing, steepening reduces density error while pressure and velocity stay constant to roundoff. Smooth entropy-wave grids N=32,64,128 show approximately second-order convergence of the complete traced method; no third- or fourth-order time-accuracy claim is made. AUSM+ and AUSM+-up with stated controls# The older arithmetic-sound-speed AUSM baseline stays separate. The new fluxes use fourth-degree Mach and fifth-degree pressure splitting. For |M|<1, M4±(M)=±[(M±1)24+(M2−1)28],P5±(M)=(M±1)2(2∓M)4±αM(M2−1)2.M4±​(M)=±[4(M±1)2​+8(M2−1)2​],P5±​(M)=4(M±1)2(2∓M)​±αM(M2−1)2. Outside this interval, use signed upwind Mach and pressure fractions. Both variants use the directional critical-enthalpy sound speed employed in the 2006 formulation: a∗,k2=2(γ−1)γ+1Hk,af=min⁡(a∗,L2max⁡(a∗,L,uL),a∗,R2max⁡(a∗,R,−uR)).a∗,k2​=γ+12(γ−1)​Hk​,af​=min(max(a∗,L​,uL​)a∗,L2​​,max(a∗,R​,−uR​)a∗,R2​​). The displayed AUSM+ has alpha=3/16 and no pressure/velocity diffusion terms. It is the specified basic member of this formulation, not a claim to reproduce every 1996 interface-sound-speed option. AUSM+-up uses Kp=0.25, Ku=0.75, sigma=1 and a reference Mach cutoff of 0.1: M‾2=ML2+MR22,M0=min⁡(1,max⁡(M‾2,Mref2)),fa=M0(2−M0),α=316(5fa2−4).M2=2ML2​+MR2​​,M0​=min(1,max(M2,Mref2​))​,fa​=M0​(2−M0​),α=163​(5fa2​−4). Add the pressure diffusion term to the interface Mach number and velocity diffusion to its pressure: Mp=−Kpfamax⁡(1−M‾2,0)pR−pLρ‾af2,pu=−KufaP5+(ML)P5−(MR)(ρL+ρR)af(uR−uL).Mp​=−fa​Kp​​max(1−M2,0)ρ​af2​pR​−pL​​,pu​=−Ku​fa​P5+​(ML​)P5−​(MR​)(ρL​+ρR​)af​(uR​−uL​). Upwind density, velocity and total enthalpy using the resulting mass-flux sign. Add interface pressure to normal momentum. Tests check uniform flow, both supersonic directions, contacts, stationary normal shocks, sonic branch limits, reversal conservation and rotational covariance. Liou (1996) and Liou (2006) are the original references. The sound-speed and diffusion definitions were cross-checked against the official SU2 implementation. Our Python code is independent and supplies no implicit Jacobian or time preconditioning. The low-Mach graph varies the cutoff across 0.01,0.1,1 for a tiny fixed pressure jump. It is a flux sensitivity, not verification of a low-Mach vortex, boundary layer or asymptotic-preserving PDE scheme. A cutoff and the time-step restriction remain part of the numerical method. Matched one-dimensional problems and a recorded failure# All new 1D runs use traced PPM with CFL 0.4. The flux comparison fixes contact steepening off and shock flattening on. It switches HLLC, old AUSM, AUSM+ and AUSM+-up. These are independent adaptive-CFL runs, not matched-step or matched-cost timings. The cases are Sod N=200, moving contact N=200, Shu–Osher N=240, and a strong pressure jump N=200. The first three retain the setups in the earlier comparison. The last uses primitive left (1,0,1000), right (1,0,0.01), gamma=1.4, a jump at x=0.5, extrapolated ends and t=0.01 on [0,1]. Its waves remain away from the boundaries at that time. Sod and strong-jump density errors use front-split 24/48-point quadrature of conserved Riemann states. The moving-contact reference returns to its initial cell means after one crossing. Shu–Osher retains the earlier internal characteristic FD WENO-Z N=960 reference; it is numerical, not exact, and no exact error is reported. Point-reference curves and primitive variables of conserved means have distinct conventions. The stated strong-jump AUSM+ configuration exhausts its admissibility retries before t=0.01. Its table reports failure and the actual stopping time; it is excluded from the final-time curves. The download retains the last accepted conserved state and reason. This demonstrates that the implemented flux, reconstruction safeguards and nominal CFL together do not establish update positivity. Other completed runs can also require retries; inspect their counts. A conservative mesh around the cylinder nose# The 2D experiment covers only the upstream half of a unit circular cylinder: r in [1,4], theta in [pi/2,3pi/2], with flow in the positive x direction. Straight-sided annular quadrilaterals conform to the polygonal approximation of the body. Two grids have 24×48 and 48×96 cells. Radius and angle are uniformly spaced, but physical cells are not squares. Cartesian conserved variables use face-normal numerical fluxes with shared face lengths. Polygon areas, radial chord normals and angular-face normals obey geometric closure to roundoff. This avoids curvilinear momentum source terms. Tests check free-stream preservation when the wall is disabled, reflection of wall-normal momentum, zero wall mass/energy flux and the integrated flux budget. Use rho_inf=1.4, p_inf=1, u_inf=6, v_inf=0, gamma=1.4, giving sound speed 1 and Mach 6. The inner wall is inviscid slip; the outer boundary is fixed free stream and both angular exits extrapolate. Initial conditions are free stream, optionally modified by ρ(r,θ)=ρ∞[1+ϵe−((r−1.5)/0.3)2sin⁡(12(θ−π))],ϵ∈{0,10−4}.ρ(r,θ)=ρ∞​[1+ϵe−((r−1.5)/0.3)2sin(12(θ−π))],ϵ∈{0,10−4}. Velocity and pressure are unchanged initially. The perturbation is a density mode, not a displaced mesh or shock front. The angular wavelength is held fixed under refinement. Both controls and seeded runs use first-order geometric FV, SSPRK2, CFL 0.4 and terminal time 2. CFL uses the sum of all face spectral radii; it is not numerically identical to the 1D CFL rule. There are 20 forebody runs: five fluxes, two grids and two seed amplitudes. Directional HLLE and Roe composition# For a face normal n, choose n1 along the velocity jump and n2 perpendicular to it; orient their signs to make alpha_k=n dot n_k nonnegative. If the velocity jump is below 1e−10 in these nondimensional units, n1 is face-tangential and n2 face-normal. Define F^(n)=α1F^HLLE(n1)+α2F^Roe(n2),n=α1n1+α2n2.F(n)=α1​FHLLE​(n1​)+α2​FRoe​(n2​),n=α1​n1​+α2​n2​. The same left/right physical states are rotated into each local frame. Rotate momentum fluxes back to Cartesian coordinates before combining. A normal velocity jump selects HLLE; a purely tangential shear selects Roe in the face-normal direction. Constant states remain consistent because physical Euler flux is linear in the normal vector. The construction also passes flux-reversal conservation and rotation tests. This is a specified rotated-hybrid experiment, inspired by Nishikawa and Kitamura (2008). It is not the earlier pressure-sensor Roe/HLLE blend, and does not claim an optimized reproduction of the publication's Rotated-RHLL dissipation formula. The tiny-jump fallback and dimensional tolerance are explicit implementation choices. What the forebody results establish# The five fluxes are acoustically smoothed Roe, Einfeldt-type HLLE, AUSM+, AUSM+-up and directional HLLE/Roe. Each image shares one color range across its five field panels. The slip-wall pressure coefficient uses the actual wall-normal momentum flux; the two cells nearest the nose define the reported nose pressure. The normal-shock jump followed by isentropic deceleration gives the inviscid centerline stagnation-pressure reference p0,2=46.8152057161. It is a scalar streamline reference, not an exact bow-shock field. The boundary layer and wake are absent. The nose pressure, reflection defect, remaining normalized update rate, positivity and integrated conservation residual are all saved. On the fine seeded grid, Roe develops a large density reflection defect and its nose pressure falls to about 25.0. The fine HLLE nose pressure is about 47.38; the corresponding coarse value is about 48.81. The directional method and AUSM variants have different perturbation and grid responses. In particular, the directional method can amplify roundoff in its unperturbed control: a symmetric-looking initial state is not an exact discrete symmetry guarantee for that nonlinear direction selection. Inspect both controls and histories rather than selecting a single attractive image. These are terminal snapshots of an evolving calculation. Nonzero update rates and two grid levels do not certify a converged steady solution, an asymptotic convergence order, or universal carbuncle freedom. Longer-time and time-step studies, other Mach numbers, rotated grids, external-code comparisons and further rotated-hybrid variants remain verification work. Full-cylinder viscous drag, lift, shedding and Strouhal validation are a separate task. Reproduction and saved data# Run MPLCONFIGDIR=.mplconfig python scripts/build_shock_expansion.py. The builder caches forebody runs only when the numerical source hashes and full configuration match. Download controls, diagnostics and source hashes and conserved states and mesh vertices/areas. Failed 1D entries include actual times and last accepted states; they must not be compared as if they reached the requested final time. All PNGs and the compressed arrays have hashes in the manifest. The independent checks cover characteristic-domain integrals, switch selectivity, periodic conserved sums, pressure/velocity contact equilibrium, smooth refinement, AUSM branch identities and normal shocks, rotated-flux consistency/covariance, mesh closure and wall/global flux budgets. Passing these checks does not remove the flow-specific limits above. Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Site coverage and counting rules Published web edition, counted 2026-11-22. These are counts of catalog entries and documented examples, not a claim that every entry is a verified end-to-end solver. 46 equation/model entries · 108 methods and building blocks · 213 journal/conference papers · 254 total sources. There are 9 saved-profile equation-gallery cases across 7 equation families, and 76 reading chapters including this inventory. Equations and models# Named equation/model entries, not scalar component equations or mathematically disjoint families. Includes frameworks and auxiliary formulations; variants share one entry except the three separately explained SR/GR fluid systems. Biological entries are imported once from their own catalog. 18 entries have scoped local examples; 28 are reading-only, including all 22 biological survey entries. A coupled system is one entry; its individual component equations do not increase the count. Poisson/Laplace and dimensional variants share entries. Named frameworks and specialized kinetic laws can both appear, so this is not a count of mathematically disjoint families. Equation/model inventory# Physics & mathematical models# Linear advection — Local example. Heat / diffusion — Local example. Poisson / Laplace — Local example. Inviscid Burgers — Local example. LWR traffic flow — Local example. Compressible Euler — Local example. Shallow water, including the rotating linear model — Local example. Wet 1D flow and linear rotating Fourier symbols; no full geophysical dynamical core. Isothermal Euler — Local example. Ideal MHD — Local example. Incompressible Navier–Stokes — Local example. Isothermal lattice BGK — Local example. Hamiltonian oscillators — Local example. Gravitational particle model — Local example. Static force evaluations and boundary kernels; no coupled self-gravitating fluid evolution. Bratu nonlinear boundary-value problem — Local example. Auxiliary hyperbolic diffusion system — Local example. Periodic first-order steady-solution baseline, not physical-time heat diffusion. Relativistic models# Special-relativistic hydrodynamics — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver. General-relativistic hydrodynamics — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver. General-relativistic MHD — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver. Relativistic radiation moments / M1 — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver. Causal relativistic viscous fluid — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver. Biological model survey# Logistic population growth — Reading only. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map. Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics — Reading only. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct. Lotka–Volterra predator–prey — Reading only. McKendrick age-structured population — Reading only. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance. SIR and SEIR compartment models — Reading only. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions. Fisher–KPP invasion front — Reading only. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed. Monod growth and chemostat — Reading only. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model. Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics — Reading only. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey. Turing reaction–diffusion framework — Reading only. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes. FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery — Reading only. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations. Keller–Segel chemotaxis — Reading only. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics. Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor — Reading only. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant. Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries — Reading only. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling. Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA — Reading only. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation. Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback — Reading only. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model. Replicator evolutionary game dynamics — Reading only. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed. Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion — Reading only. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue. Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion — Reading only. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations. Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis — Reading only. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability. Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation — Reading only. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model. Repressilator mRNA–protein network — Reading only. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent. Genetic toggle switch — Reading only. Bistability is not guaranteed for arbitrary Hill exponents or production rates. Induction, mRNA dynamics and noise are additional model choices. Numerical method inventory# Named numerical methods and building blocks with a reading chapter. Aliases count once; RK stages, dimensions, parameter combinations, mesh layouts and theoretical conditions do not add methods. A family and a separately explained algorithm may both appear. Not a count of mutually exclusive end-to-end solvers. 91 entries have scoped local examples; 17 are reading-only. Reconstruction limiters, preconditioners and coupling operators are building blocks, not complete PDE solvers. Mesh layouts, CFL conditions and theorems are not counted as numerical methods. Spatial discretization# Forward spatial difference — Local example. Backward spatial difference — Local example. Centered spatial difference — Local example. Upwind finite differences — Local example. Lax–Friedrichs — Local example. Lax–Wendroff — Local example. Godunov-type finite volumes — Local example. MUSCL reconstruction — Local example. WENO5-JS — Local example. Discontinuous Galerkin / Legendre — Local example. Fourier differentiation and evolution — Local example. Cubic-Hermite CIP — Local example. Continuous P1 Galerkin FEM — Local example. Limited PPM reconstruction — Local example. Method-of-lines parabolic FV and a separate direct-Eulerian traced primitive PPM with contact steepening and shock flattening switches. No Lagrange/remap or multidimensional CTU. Euler characteristic reconstruction — Local example. Local conservative FV basis or face-frozen Roe FD basis; controlled component/characteristic comparisons. FD WENO5-Z — Local example. Global LF splitting, exponent 2, fixed epsilon 1e-6; point values, not FV state interpolation. Riemann fluxes & corrections# Rusanov / local Lax–Friedrichs flux — Local example. HLL — Local example. HLLC — Local example. Roe — Local example. HLLE / Einfeldt wave speeds — Local example. Acoustic Roe entropy correction — Local example. Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver — Local example. Explicit directional HLLE/Roe composition with unit-normal flux checks and conforming cylinder-forebody controls. Distinct from the optimized 2008 Rotated-RHLL formula; no universal carbuncle-free claim. HLLD MHD Riemann solver — Local example. Full-vector adiabatic HLLD/HLLE with Brio-Wu, circular Alfven refinement and weak field-loop tests. CT-Contact and GLM, not UCT-HLLD. AUSM-family flux splitting — Local example. Arithmetic-sound-speed AUSM plus specified critical-sound-speed AUSM+ and AUSM+-up. Matched traced-PPM cases, a recorded strong-jump failure and forebody tests; no low-Mach PDE certification. Limiters & admissibility# Minmod — Local example. Superbee — Local example. Monotonized central / MC — Local example. Van Leer limiter — Local example. Clipped Van Albada limiter — Local example. TVB modified minmod — Local example. Mean-preserving positive-state scaling — Local example. Reconstruction building block; no full Euler-update positivity guarantee. Time integration# Forward Euler — Local example. Backward Euler — Local example. Heun / SSPRK(2,2) — Local example. Explicit midpoint RK2 — Local example. Ralston RK2 — Local example. Kutta RK3 — Local example. SSPRK(3,3) — Local example. SSPRK(4,3) — Local example. Classical RK4 — Local example. SSPRK(5,4) — Local example. Implicit midpoint — Local example. Two-step leapfrog — Local example. Crank–Nicolson — Local example. BDF2 — Local example. L-stable SDIRK2 — Local example. IMEX Euler — Local example. Adaptive SDIRK2 / step doubling — Local example. Symplectic Euler — Local example. Velocity Verlet / particle leapfrog — Local example. Yoshida fourth-order composition — Local example. Linear & nonlinear solvers# Thomas tridiagonal elimination — Local example. Jacobi iteration — Local example. Gauss–Seidel iteration — Local example. Successive over-relaxation / SOR — Local example. Conjugate gradients — Local example. Red-black Gauss–Seidel — Local example. Geometric multigrid V-cycle — Local example. Restarted GMRES — Local example. BiCGSTAB — Local example. Jacobi / diagonal preconditioning — Local example. Unpivoted ILU(0) — Local example. Armijo-damped Newton — Local example. Newton–Krylov with assembled Jacobian — Local example. Coupling, constraints & particles# Dual time stepping — Local example. Scalar residual distribution — Local example. 1D P1 upwind equivalent, not multidimensional Euler RD. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning — Reading only. Constrained transport / CT — Local example. Original arithmetic flux-CT OT baseline plus contact-upwinded CT loop tests. Native face divergence; not UCT-HLLD. GLM divergence cleaning — Local example. Original Rusanov OT baseline plus HLLD/HLLE loop tests with an exact longitudinal cleaning solve and split damping. Native cell-centered divergence. MAC pressure projection — Local example. D2Q9–BGK collision and streaming — Local example. Guo forcing — Local example. Half-way bounce-back — Local example. First-order hyperbolic diffusion baseline — Local example. SPH kernel reconstruction — Local example. ALE uniform-state / geometric-conservation model — Local example. Moving-volume scalar check; no complete ALE Euler solver. Godunov SPH / GSPH — Reading only. Particle fields & gravity# Cloud-in-cell assignment and interpolation — Local example. FFT particle–mesh forces — Local example. Barnes–Hut octree — Local example. Monopole and second-moment expansion — Local example. Isolated doubled-grid FFT convolution — Local example. Horizontal-periodic slab Green-function FFT — Local example. P³M short-range correction — Reading only. TreePM force splitting — Reading only. Fast multipole translations — Reading only. Additional formulations# Original Cartesian KEEP split flux — Local example. Element bases & approximation# Legendre modal basis / orthonormal scaling — Local example. Reference-element tabulation, derivatives, projection and affine mass/stiffness matrices. Lagrange nodal basis / GLL collocation — Local example. Interval cardinal functions, modal transforms, exact versus quadrature mass, and P1/P2 triangle shapes. Papers versus all sources# Unique bibliographic publications classified as journal articles or conference papers, deduplicated by DOI or author/title/year. Includes reviews, translations and explicitly labeled accepted papers; not a claim that every full text was inspected. Books, chapters, reports, preprints and documentation are separate. Unique cataloged works across all publication types. An original publication and a later translation are separate works; duplicate DOI records are not. NASA case links in prose are not catalog records. 207 journal-article records, including reviews, translations and explicitly labeled accepted papers. 3 conference papers. 22 books. 2 book chapters. 3 technical/teaching reports. 10 other records, including documentation and a separately identified preprint. A duplicate Cockburn–Shu 1989 record was merged. Burgers 1948 is classified as a book chapter. The former 146-record total included that duplicate; subsequent source additions are reflected in the current unique-work totals above. An original paper and a separately published translation remain separate works. The bibliography does not claim that every full text has been inspected; source notes preserve the inspection status. Reproduction# The named registry is catalog/coverage.json; biological entries and publication types come from their respective catalogs. python scripts/build_coverage.py checks unique publication identities and local reading links, then generates the counts and this inventory. The website build runs that audit before rendering. Parameter choices, time frames, repeated equations in prose and test function counts do not increase these totals. documents.text: Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald Interfaces often require periodicity in two directions and isolation in the normal direction. Elongating a triply periodic cell is not identical to evaluating the genuinely two-periodic Green function. Problem and representative equations For a neutral cell of volume V, normal z and unit Coulomb prefactor, the Yeh–Berkowitz correction adds a dipole contribution to a specified three-periodic Ewald baseline. Its coordinate derivative gives the normal force correction. The formula assumes neutrality and a conducting-boundary 3D reference. Mz=∑iqizi,ΔE=2πVMz2,ΔFi,z=−4πVqiMz.Mz​=i∑​qi​zi​,ΔE=V2π​Mz2​,ΔFi,z​=−V4π​qi​Mz​. Algorithm Place slabs in an elongated cell with vacuum, converge the 3D sums, and add the dipole correction. Increase the vacuum height to assess residual image interactions. At finite vacuum height, this is not a claim of exact equivalence to a fully two-periodic summation. Conditions and pitfalls Charged slabs, other external dielectric conditions, electrodes and imposed fields require additional formulations. Keep self and k=0 conventions distinct from this correction. Neutral-cell M_z is invariant under an origin shift; net charge destroys that property. What to check Use neutral charge pairs or a dipole layer and vary vacuum height independently of reciprocal/mesh cutoffs. Compare with an independent two-periodic reference when available, and finite-difference the energy for normal forces. Agreement with an uncorrected 3D calculation cannot establish zero slab error. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. In-Chul Yeh and Max L. Berkowitz (1999). Ewald summation for systems with slab geometry. The Journal of Chemical Physics Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Selected source passages consulted · Consulted record Abstract and the slab correction construction; not an audit of all numerical tables. Ewald, P. P. (1921). Die Berechnung optischer und elektrostatischer Gitterpotentiale. documents.title: Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual Implemented: COO-to-CSR assembly, restarted GMRES, BiCGSTAB, Jacobi and unpivoted ILU(0), and Armijo-damped Newton with dense or Krylov inner solves. These are small, inspectable real-arithmetic examples. 1986–1992: nonsymmetric Krylov methods# Saad–Schultz (1986) introduces GMRES; van der Vorst (1992) introduces BiCGSTAB. The implemented GMRES uses Arnoldi reorthogonalization and small Hessenberg least squares, restarting after a specified number of inner iterations. BiCGSTAB has explicit breakdown reporting; it need not have monotone residuals. Both implementations apply a fixed right preconditioner: AM−1z=b,x=M−1z,∥b−Ax∥2≤max⁡(atol,rtol∥b∥2).AM−1z=b,x=M−1z,∥b−Ax∥2​≤max(atol,rtol∥b∥2​). The stopping history recomputes the true residual. Jacobi uses diagonal scaling. ILU(0) retains the supplied nonzero structure, with no fill, pivoting or reordering; tiny pivots raise an explicit failure. This is not a robust replacement for a production sparse factorization. Newton and conditioning# Newton solves J(x)δ=−F(x), then chooses a backtracked step length with an Armijo residual decrease. The Newton–Krylov demonstration assembles J and uses GMRES; it is not matrix free. Bratu's equation is checked against an analytic solution at two spatial resolutions, including inner-solve failures. A small residual is not automatically a small solution error: ∥x−x^∥∥x∥≤κ(A)∥b−Ax^∥∥b∥.∥x∥∥x−x^∥​≤κ(A)∥b∥∥b−Ax^∥​. Condition number, eigenvalue distribution and nonnormality describe different features. A smaller condition number alone does not rank restarted GMRES. CG still requires an SPD operator and suitable SPD preconditioning; generic ILU(0) is not asserted to satisfy that requirement. The nonsymmetric example is first-order upwind advection plus centered diffusion with zero Dirichlet data. Iteration counts have different per-iteration costs; the figure makes no wall-clock ranking. documents.title: Spline interpolation | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Spline interpolation Splines join piecewise low-degree polynomials with specified continuity. Distinguish them from a single global high-degree polynomial and distinguish exact interpolation from smoothing noisy data. Problem and representative equations Use a nondecreasing knot sequence tᵢ and degree p. Nᵢ,₀ is the indicator of [tᵢ,tᵢ₊₁); zero-denominator terms in the recursion are defined as zero. Degree p means order p+1. Ni,p(x)=x−titi+p−tiNi,p−1(x)+ti+p+1−xti+p+1−ti+1Ni+1,p−1(x),s(x)=∑iciNi,p(x).Ni,p​(x)=ti+p​−ti​x−ti​​Ni,p−1​(x)+ti+p+1​−ti+1​ti+p+1​−x​Ni+1,p−1​(x),s(x)=i∑​ci​Ni,p​(x). Algorithm Represent s=ΣcᵢNᵢ,ₚ and determine coefficients by interpolation or least squares. A natural cubic spline sets endpoint second derivatives to zero; clamped conditions prescribe endpoint first derivatives. Determining coefficients and evaluating the spline by de Boor’s algorithm are separate stages. Conditions and pitfalls An interior knot of multiplicity r generally gives Cᵖ⁻ʳ continuity. Cubic splines do not automatically preserve monotonicity or positivity and can overshoot. Extrapolation depends on the chosen endpoint convention and is not covered by an in-interval interpolation argument. What to check Check polynomial reproduction, one-sided derivatives at knots and endpoint conditions. For noiseless functions study refinement; for noisy data separately report held-out prediction errors and smoothing-parameter dependence. documents.title: Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME SPME approximates Ewald structure factors using smooth cardinal B-splines. Treat it as a specific interpolation-and-force construction rather than a synonym for every PME implementation. Problem and representative equations Let uᵢ be particle coordinates in mesh units and Mₚ a cardinal B-spline of order p, not degree p. The product below is the local tensor assignment in three dimensions. Fourier structure factors require a correction for the spline response. Qmxmymz=∑iqi∏d∈{x,y,z}Mp(uid−md),deg⁡Mp=p−1.Qmx​my​mz​​=i∑​qi​d∈{x,y,z}∏​Mp​(uid​−md​),degMp​=p−1. Algorithm Spread charge over p neighboring mesh points in each direction, evaluate a corrected reciprocal mesh energy by FFT, and obtain forces using derivatives of the assignment in analytical differentiation. Record the spline order and mesh together with whether differentiation is analytical or in Fourier space. Conditions and pitfalls Smooth assignment alone does not guarantee both energy consistency and exact net-force cancellation. Ewald neutrality, boundary and self-term conventions still apply. Comparisons with original PME should control error tolerance and differentiation rules, not merely the number of mesh points. What to check Measure force errors against the same converged Ewald reference and check energy finite differences. Report common-translation mesh effects and total force separately. Ensure real-space truncation is not hiding the reciprocal-space convergence trend. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. documents.title: Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax Try the interactive stability laboratory and read the experiment guide to connect the formulas below with live browser calculations. Choose space and time discretizations separately# Forward, backward, and centered spatial differences are D+uj=uj+1−ujh,D−uj=uj−uj−1h,D0uj=uj+1−uj−12h.D+​uj​=huj+1​−uj​​,D−​uj​=huj​−uj−1​​,D0​uj​=2huj+1​−uj−1​​. For smooth functions, the first two are first-order accurate and the centered stencil is second order. Compare them with numart.advection.finite_difference. For linear advection u_t+a u_x=0, upwinding follows information propagation: use a backward difference for a>0 and a forward difference for a<0. A forward difference is therefore not synonymous with an upwind difference. Forward Euler in time gives u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^n; backward Euler gives u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^{n+1} and requires a system solve. A backward spatial stencil alone does not make a method implicit. CFL: can the stencil reach the information it needs?# For constant-coefficient periodic advection with an explicit nearest-neighbor stencil, domain-of-dependence reasoning requires |a|Δt/h ≤ 1. The constant changes with the stencil, Runge–Kutta method, DG degree, and dimension. Explicit diffusion introduces a Δt=O(h²) restriction. A CFL condition is generally necessary rather than sufficient for stability. Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (1928). Forward-time, centered-space (FTCS) advection is a counterexample. Substituting a Fourier mode u_j^n=G^n e^{ijθ} gives G=1−iCsin⁡θ,∣G∣2=1+C2sin⁡2θ,C=aΔt/h.G=1−iCsinθ,∣G∣2=1+C2sin2θ,C=aΔt/h. Some modes grow even when |C|<1. The scheme is unstable under ordinary fixed-CFL grid refinement. Lax–Friedrichs and Lax–Wendroff# The classical Lax–Friedrichs scheme is ujn+1=12(uj+1n+uj−1n)−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n),G=cos⁡θ−iCsin⁡θ.ujn+1​=21​(uj+1n​+uj−1n​)−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​),G=cosθ−iCsinθ. Since |G|²=1-(1-C²)sin²θ, periodic linear advection is stable for |C|≤1. Classical LF uses the numerical-viscosity coefficient h/Δt. Rusanov uses a local maximum wave speed; WENO here uses global LF flux splitting. These are different discrete constructions. Lax (1954). Lax–Wendroff is ujn+1=ujn−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n)+C22(uj+1n−2ujn+uj−1n),ujn+1​=ujn​−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​)+2C2​(uj+1n​−2ujn​+uj−1n​), G=1−iCsin⁡θ+C2(cos⁡θ−1),∣G∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin⁡4(θ/2).G=1−iCsinθ+C2(cosθ−1),∣G∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin4(θ/2). Its stability condition for this problem is also |C|≤1. Second-order accuracy does not itself suppress oscillations near discontinuities. Lax–Wendroff (1960). Tests compare the analytical amplification factors from amplification with actual mode evolution from difference_step. The gallery seeds a small Nyquist perturbation and compares C=0.8 with C=1.1. Dissipation and dispersion: read amplitude and phase separately# The same amplification factor used to test growth also explains two distinct errors: numerical dissipation damps a wave's amplitude; numerical dispersion changes its propagation speed in a wavelength-dependent way. Consider constant-speed scalar advection on a periodic uniform grid. Let h be the grid spacing, Δt the positive time step, k the wavenumber, θ the dimensionless grid wavenumber, and C the signed Courant number. The Fourier convention and exact one-step factor are ut+aux=0,xj=jh,θ=kh,C=aΔth,ujn=u^ neijθ,Gexact=e−iakΔt=e−iCθ.ut​+aux​=0,xj​=jh,θ=kh,C=haΔt​,ujn​=uneijθ,Gexact​=e−iakΔt=e−iCθ.​ The exact solution translates without changing amplitude. This makes the model useful for separating artificial damping from transport error. What the amplification factor measures# For a linear, translation-invariant one-step scheme, write its factor in polar form: G(θ)=∣G(θ)∣e−iϕ(θ),u^ n=G(θ)nu^ 0,∣u^ n∣∣u^ 0∣=∣G(θ)∣n.G(θ)un​=∣G(θ)∣e−iϕ(θ),=G(θ)nu0,∣u0∣∣un∣​=∣G(θ)∣n.​ Thus |G|<1 damps this mode; repeated steps accumulate the loss. |G|=1 preserves its amplitude, while |G|>1 amplifies it. For this scalar periodic problem, the familiar requirement |G|≤1 controls growth, but says nothing about whether the amplitude stays close to its exact value of one. For 0<|G|, the loss can also be expressed as a damping rate σnum per unit time: σnum=−log⁡∣G∣Δt,∣u^ n∣=e−σnumtn∣u^ 0∣,tn=nΔt.σnum​∣un∣​=−Δtlog∣G∣​,=e−σnum​tn​∣u0∣,tn​=nΔt.​ This is a decay rate with units of inverse time, not a diffusion coefficient. At G=0 the mode vanishes in one step; a finite damping rate and phase are undefined. Phase needs a sign convention as well. Use arg₀ for an argument continued from G(0)=1 along a branch on which G never vanishes. The minus sign matches the exact factor above: ϕ(θ)=−arg⁡0G(θ),ωnum=ϕ(θ)Δt,cnuma=ωnum/ka=ϕ(θ)Cθ(ak≠0).ϕ(θ)acnum​​​=−arg0​G(θ),ωnum​=Δtϕ(θ)​,=aωnum​/k​=Cθϕ(θ)​(ak=0).​ Correct transport requires φ=Cθ, as well as |G|=1. A stable wave can travel at the wrong speed and accumulate a large position error. At θ=0, use the low-wavenumber limit for the speed ratio. At G=0 the scheme has removed the mode and its phase is undefined. Principal arguments wrap by 2π; treating that jump as a physical change gives a false dispersion curve. At the Nyquist endpoints θ=±π, the sampled modes coincide, so their propagation direction cannot be uniquely recovered from grid samples. Three examples reveal different errors# For a>0, forward Euler with backward spatial differencing is the first-order upwind scheme. Direct substitution gives Gup=1−C(1−e−iθ),∣Gup∣2=1−4C(1−C)sin⁡2 ⁣(θ2),0≤C≤1(a>0).Gup​∣Gup​∣2​=1−C(1−e−iθ),=1−4C(1−C)sin2(2θ​),0≤C≤1(a>0).​ For 0<C<1, every nonconstant resolved Fourier mode is damped. This is numerical dissipation: the underlying advection equation has no physical decay. Its phase generally also differs from Cθ. For a<0, reverse the upwind stencil. Centered differencing with time still continuous instead gives dujdt=−auj+1−uj−12h,λh=−iahsin⁡θ,ωh=ahsin⁡θ,cha=sin⁡θθ.dtduj​​ωh​​=−a2huj+1​−uj−1​​,λh​=−iha​sinθ,=ha​sinθ,ach​​=θsinθ​.​ The eigenvalue is purely imaginary, so this semidiscrete mode has no amplitude decay. Yet sinθ/θ differs from one: it is dispersive. For θ=π/2, the phase speed is only 2/π≈0.637 times a. At θ=π the centered derivative vanishes, a stationary Nyquist checkerboard annihilated by the centered derivative, rather than correct transport. Time discretization changes the result. With forward Euler, GFE+centered=1−iCsin⁡θ,∣GFE+centered∣2=1+C2sin⁡2θ.GFE+centered​∣GFE+centered​∣2​=1−iCsinθ,=1+C2sin2θ.​ Modes with sinθ≠0 grow for any nonzero C, explaining the FTCS instability discussed above. Other time integrators have different amplitude and phase responses on the same spatial eigenvalues. The linearized centered-wave discussion in KEEP and its RK4 amplitude and phase analysis make this separation explicit. For Lax–Wendroff (1960), the factor already derived above also yields GLW=1−iCsin⁡θ+C2(cos⁡θ−1),∣GLW∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin⁡4 ⁣(θ2).GLW​∣GLW​∣2​=1−iCsinθ+C2(cosθ−1),=1−4C2(1−C2)sin4(2θ​).​ At generic 0<|C|<1 it therefore has amplitude error as well as phase error; calling it “purely dispersive” is incorrect. Its leading smooth-wave error can be dispersive without eliminating higher-order damping. At C=1, both upwind and Lax–Wendroff reduce to G=e−iθ, an exact one-cell shift on this grid. This special Courant number is not representative of other step sizes. For C=0.8 and θ=π/2 (four grid spacings per wavelength), the one-step amplitude gain is about 0.8246 for upwind and 0.8773 for Lax–Wendroff. Their phase-speed ratios are about 1.0551 and 0.9135, respectively: the first travels too fast and the second too slowly. Both are stable, yet both have amplitude and phase errors. Keep the physical and numerical questions distinct# If the physical PDE includes viscosity or another decay mechanism, the exact |G| can itself be below one for the mode considered; compare numerical damping with that exact decay. Likewise, a physically dispersive PDE has a wavenumber-dependent exact phase speed. Error means disagreement with the physical reference. A-stability and L-stability classify a time integrator's response to linear test modes; neither guarantees accurate wave propagation at a chosen resolution. The formulas here concern scalar periodic linear advection. They do not certify nonlinear Euler dynamics, shocks, or wall boundary treatments. A useful diagnostic first fixes h and reduces Δt to expose the time integrator's contribution. Then reduce h with temporal error controlled. Refining with C held fixed changes both scales and does not by itself separate the two errors. For a smooth single mode, compare amplitude and unwrapped phase at the same physical time; agreement in only one of these quantities is incomplete evidence of accuracy. The formulas and worked values here follow by directly substituting Fourier modes into the displayed differences. For the assumptions of the analysis and comparison against the exact amplification factor, see R. R. Rosales’s author lecture notes (2022), §1 and §1.1.2. The Lax–Richtmyer equivalence theorem# Consider a well-posed linear initial-value problem in an appropriate Banach space and a consistent linear difference approximation. When stability means uniform boundedness of the discrete evolution operators over a fixed finite time interval, stability is equivalent to convergence. Lax–Richtmyer (1956), original paper. Writing the error as e^{n+1}=S_h e^n+Δt τ^n, the bound ||S_h^m||≤M_T gives ||e^n||≤M_T||e^0||+M_T T max||τ^k||. Consistency makes the truncation-error term tend to zero, providing the basic stability-to-convergence argument. The converse requires a uniform-boundedness argument. The theorem does not directly certify nonlinear Euler, WENO, shocks, or arbitrary boundary treatments. The Fourier criterion |G|≤1 used here applies to periodic, constant-coefficient scalar problems. Boundaries, variable coefficients, nonnormal matrices, and multistep schemes need additional analysis. Time steps in the first edition# Euler and barotropic systems: Δt=C h/max(|u|+c), with default C=0.3. DG: Δt=C h/((2p+1)|a|), with default C=0.2. 2D MHD: Δt=C/[max(s_x)/h+max(s_y)/h], with default C=0.3. These conservative choices are checked on selected examples. They are not rigorous nonlinear stability limits for every initial condition. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.text: Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions Interpret multistage pseudo-time iterations as smoothers for a steady residual. A Jameson–Schmidt–Turkel-family example connects stage coefficients, stability polynomials, nonlinear order, high-frequency damping and preconditioning. The target is R(U)=0, not a physical-time trajectory For a discrete steady Euler/Navier–Stokes residual R, iterate an artificial ODE in pseudo time τ toward its root. Here R is the conservative residual divided by cell volume. The step is a pseudo-time step; the aim is an adequately converged residual and steady observables, not an accurate physical transient. The following base-state recurrence forms every stage from the same U^(0), unlike chaining forward-Euler increments from the preceding stage. Compare coefficients only after matching residual sign, cell-volume scaling and any preconditioning action. dUdτ=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αkΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s).dτdU​=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αk​ΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s). A representative Jameson-family four-stage iteration Consider these coefficients with the same autonomous residual reevaluated at every stage. For R(U)=AU, the stability polynomial equals classical RK4. The simplified recurrence is not a complete specification of the original fluxes, artificial dissipation and dissipation-update schedule. Equality of linear stability polynomials does not establish nonlinear fourth-order physical-time accuracy. This base-state recurrence is generally second order for nonlinear autonomous ODEs: it fails the third-order condition bᵀ(c⊙c)=1/3. Distinguish its steady-solver purpose and nonlinear order conditions from classical RK4. (α1,α2,α3,α4)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),z=−Δτλ,R4(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24.(α1​,α2​,α3​,α4​)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),z=−Δτλ,R4​(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24. bTc=12,bT(c⊙c)=14≠13for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence.bTc=21​,bT(c⊙c)=41​=31​for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence. Stability and high-frequency damping are different For linearized residual modes, the iteration multiplier is a stability polynomial. |ℛ|≤1 prevents growth, but |ℛ| near one barely damps error. A multigrid smoother seeks small maximum amplification μ on frequencies H not representable on the coarse grid. For a purely decaying z=−2 mode, this four-stage polynomial gives ℛ=1/3, while near-zero low-frequency modes decay slowly. Pushing the step to a stability boundary does not maximize damping or minimize time to convergence. Advection and diffusion occupy different spectral regions. en+1=Rs(−ΔτA)en,μ=max⁡θ∈H∣Rs(−Δτλh(θ))∣.en+1=Rs​(−ΔτA)en,μ=θ∈Hmax​∣Rs​(−Δτλh​(θ))∣. Residual smoothing, preconditioning and multigrid Residual smoothing is a separate spatial filtering operation, not the choice of RK stage coefficients. With dimensionless centered D₂ on a uniform periodic grid and ε≥0, the example below attenuates high-frequency residuals. An invertible filter retains the residual root but changes the iteration spectrum. Low-Mach preconditioning changes acoustic/convective scales, local stepping changes per-cell iteration increments, and coarse correction treats errors poorly reduced by the smoother. Combined iterations still require boundary/variable-coefficient/nonnormality analysis and must be distinguished from physical-time integration. (I−εD2)r‾=r,D^2(θ)=−4sin⁡2(θ/2),r‾^(θ)=r^(θ)1+4εsin⁡2(θ/2).(I−εD2​)r=r,D2​(θ)=−4sin2(θ/2),r(θ)=1+4εsin2(θ/2)r(θ)​. Measure residuals, steady observables and work Measure Fourier-mode damping on a manufactured Poisson-type problem and compare with μ. For compressible flow track true residuals scaled by conservative component and steady quantities such as forces, mass flow and conservation balances. When smoothing residuals, also display the original unsmoothed residual. Report residual evaluations and linear-solve work, final errors and termination reasons, not only stage/cycle counts. Compare methods at the same steady solution and tolerance. This chapter supplies algorithmic reading, not a dedicated Jameson solver or new flow-validation results. Publication scope and related entries This is reading on steady multistage RK iteration. Existing classical RK4, dual-time and multigrid examples do not implement or validate a complete Jameson-type compressible solver. No dedicated solver or new measured results are added. documents.title: Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error Implemented: backward Euler, constant-step BDF2 with backward-Euler startup, two-stage SDIRK2, first-order IMEX Euler, and adaptive SDIRK2 by step doubling. All nonlinear stages use damped Newton and report failure explicitly. Implicit stages and stability# Backward Euler solves y_new−y_old−h f(t_new,y_new)=0. BDF2 solves 3yn+1−4yn+yn−12h=f(tn+1,yn+1).2h3yn+1​−4yn​+yn−1​​=f(tn+1​,yn+1​). Alexander (1977) is the source for the L-stable, two-stage, second-order singly diagonally implicit family used here: γ=1−1/2,A=(γ01−γγ),b=(1−γ,γ),c=(γ,1).γ=1−1/2​,A=(γ1−γ​0γ​),b=(1−γ,γ),c=(γ,1). Each diagonal stage is a separate nonlinear solve. An implicit method can permit steps beyond an explicit stability limit, while accuracy still limits useful step size. A converged Newton residual measures the stage equation, not the temporal discretization error. Adaptive and split steps# The adaptive implementation compares one full SDIRK2 step with two half steps. The local error estimate is (y_half−y_full)/3, scaled by atol+rtol max(|y_old|,|y_half|). It accepts the two-half-step value, without Richardson extrapolation, and adjusts h with exponent −1/3. Rejected trials and accepted steps are counted; reaching a trial limit raises an error. IMEX Euler evaluates one part explicitly and the other implicitly. This minimal first-order split is not the higher-order IMEX RK constructions of Ascher–Ruuth–Spiteri (1997). The explicit part retains its own stability restriction. Variable-step BDF, embedded DIRK pairs and operator splitting remain extensions. The stiff test y′=−1000(y−cos t)−sin t has exact solution cos t when y(0)=1. The manifest records maximum errors at actual integration nodes and adaptive step counts. Separate tests verify order on a nonlinear, nonautonomous ODE and strong damping of a stiff decay mode. The coarse stiff-forced refinement is not in a uniform second-order regime. BDF2 startup and stiff order reduction affect the maximum-over-nodes error; the nonlinear nonstiff order test checks the formal temporal order separately. For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.title: Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise A symplectic integrator advances a Hamiltonian system while preserving its canonical two-form. This is the map property behind the good long-time behavior of many orbital and particle integrators. It does not generally preserve the original Hamiltonian exactly. The Hamiltonian map notebook separates those two questions with computed examples. What the map preserves# For state z = (q,p), Hamilton’s equations and the symplectic condition are z˙=J∇H(z),J=(0I−I0),DΦh(z)TJDΦh(z)=J.z˙=J∇H(z),J=(0−I​I0​),DΦh​(z)TJDΦh​(z)=J. The last identity says that each numerical step is a canonical transformation. For one degree of freedom it is equivalent to det(D Phi) = 1, preserving oriented phase-plane area. In higher dimensions, preservation of total volume alone is weaker than symplecticity. Three separate properties should be tested: preservation of the two-form, preservation of H, and time symmetry Phi_(−h) = Phi_h^(−1). Symplectic Euler already illustrates the distinction: it is symplectic but is neither exactly energy preserving nor time symmetric in general. Split the Hamiltonian, compose exact subflows# For a unit-mass separable system H(q,p) = p²/2 + V(q), the two subflows are a drift and a kick: Dh(q,p)=(q+hp,p),Kh(q,p)=(q,p−h∇V(q)).Dh​(q,p)=(q+hp,p),Kh​(q,p)=(q,p−h∇V(q)). Each is symplectic; compositions remain symplectic. The notebook includes kick–drift symplectic Euler, and the symmetric second-order Störmer–Verlet update pn+1/2=pn−h2∇V(qn),qn+1=qn+hpn+1/2,pn+1=pn+1/2−h2∇V(qn+1).pn+1/2​=pn​−2h​∇V(qn​),qn+1​=qn​+hpn+1/2​,pn+1​=pn+1/2​−2h​∇V(qn+1​). This is the mechanical Leapfrog/velocity-Verlet formulation. It differs from the two-step scalar recurrence in the earlier time-integration notebook. Fourth order by composition# Writing S2(h) for a Verlet step, one fourth-order composition is S4(h)=S2(ah) S2(bh) S2(ah),a=12−21/3,b=−21/32−21/3.S4​(h)=S2​(ah)S2​(bh)S2​(ah),a=2−21/31​,b=−2−21/321/3​. Yoshida (1990) develops higher-order symplectic compositions. Here b is negative: an internal substep goes backward in time. The construction is suitable for the smooth conservative examples used here; simply applying it to irreversible diffusion, shocks, or collision handling is not justified. Higher order also does not establish unconditional stability or an equal-cost advantage. Energy and a modified Hamiltonian# Backward error analysis describes a nearby, generally formal modified Hamiltonian. Under smoothness, bounded-trajectory, small-step, and related hypotheses, this explains small long-time energy errors. It does not assert an exact invariant of the original H for every orbit or step size. Hairer, Lubich, and Wanner (2003) develop this geometric viewpoint and its assumptions. For the special oscillator H = (p²+q²)/2, kick–drift–kick Verlet preserves the quadratic invariant Ih=12p2+12(1−h24)q2Ih​=21​p2+21​(1−4h2​)q2 up to roundoff. H itself oscillates. This invariant is not a claim that its unscaled Hamiltonian flow is exactly the numerical time-h map. The oscillator map is bounded for |h| < 2; above that limit it can be symplectic and unstable. Implicit midpoint and RK4 as comparisons# Implicit midpoint is symplectic and time symmetric when its endpoint equation is solved accurately. It preserves the quadratic oscillator H to roundoff here. It need not exactly conserve a nonquadratic H. Classical RK4 is fourth order but is generally neither symplectic nor time symmetric. Good short-time accuracy alone does not certify the map’s geometry. The second test problem is H = p²/2 + q²/2 + q⁴/4, a smooth nonlinear oscillator. It makes midpoint’s special quadratic-energy conservation visibly distinguishable from a general claim. Reproducible notebook and checks# from numart.hamiltonian import trajectory, energy, canonical_step, J t, z = trajectory(h=0.2, steps=1000, method='yoshida4', system='quartic') print(max(abs((energy(z, 'quartic')-energy(z[0], 'quartic'))/energy(z[0], 'quartic')))) _, M = canonical_step([0.7, 0.4], 0.2, 'yoshida4', 'quartic', True) print(M.T @ J @ M - J) The computed dataset and source manifest supplies 30 Python trajectories: five methods, two Hamiltonians, and h = 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4, all to T = 200 from (q,p) = (1,0.2). Plotted trajectories contain at most 1001 samples; maximum energy errors use every integration step. The phase-patch view applies one step to a square centered at (0.7,0.4). Its sampled polygon boundary is an illustration; the displayed local defect uses an analytic map Jacobian at the patch center. Tests check refinement orders against the exact oscillator, analytic Jacobians against independent finite differences, the canonical identity on both potentials, time reversal for symmetric methods, the Verlet quadratic invariant, and the difference between quadratic and nonquadratic midpoint energy. The gallery and notebook are educational fixed-step examples, not orbit-accuracy or timing rankings. Connecting to particle gravity# A fixed step and a force that is the gradient of a consistent position-dependent potential support the splitting argument. A generic approximate Tree force, changing opening decisions, ad hoc mesh interpolation, or state-dependent step selection does not automatically retain that proof. Force approximation and time integration need joint tests. Continue with particle gravity and Poisson solvers and gravity boundary kernels. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

Choose a book by the question you need to answer; this is a reading guide, not a ranking. Bibliographic years below identify the cited editions, not the invention dates of algorithms. The links lead to publisher records or author-maintained pages. We checked edition metadata and available descriptions or contents, not every derivation in every book. Chapter suggestions describe the atlas connection; they do not claim that all of a textbook has been implemented. A short starting path: Hirsch for the CFD framework; LeVeque for conservation laws and finite-volume reasoning; Toro for Riemann solvers; Patankar for pressure–velocity coupling; Saad for sparse iterative solves. Return to original papers when tracing a particular algorithm. Search the full reference library · All cataloged books · Download BibTeX Covers are supplied by Open Library for the listed ISBN. Each card links to Amazon Japan and the publisher or bibliographic record. The title stays visible when a cover is unavailable. documents.title: Thermostats: temperature control and distributions | Numerical Methods Atlas
documents.text: MOLECULAR DYNAMICS / THERMOSTATS Thermostats: temperature control and distributions Compare fluctuations, ergodicity and time correlations as well as mean temperature, from Nosé–Hoover and velocity rescaling to stochastic and momentum-conserving methods. Comparative introductions and reference entry points for 12 methods. Dedicated code and measured verification results are under construction. Define the controlled temperature With kinetic energy K and f active degrees of freedom, the kinetic temperature is T = 2K / (f k_B). Count constraints and removed center-of-mass motion consistently, and separate thermal motion from streaming. State whether rotational degrees of freedom are included. Equal mean temperature does not imply equal distributions For f independent momentum degrees of freedom with classical quadratic kinetic energy, canonical equilibrium gives 2K/(k_B T₀) a chi-square distribution with f degrees of freedom. Its mean K is f k_B T₀/2 and variance is f(k_B T₀)²/2. Direct rescaling v ← √(T₀/T) v fixes K immediately after application, removing these fluctuations. CSVR instead uses a stochastic factor to generate fluctuations. Separate sampling from dynamics An invariant distribution does not ensure adequate finite-time exploration. Even correct equilibrium sampling can coexist with friction- or collision-induced changes in velocity autocorrelations and diffusion. Assess integration error, heat-bath coupling time and random-seed dependence. Eight foundational entries Direct velocity rescaling Multiply velocities by a common factor to set the kinetic energy at each application. Simple deterministic rescaling does not reproduce canonical kinetic-energy fluctuations. A comparison case for distinguishing temperature control from canonical sampling. Ratio-based rescaling is undefined at T=0; the application interval also matters. Other names: ベロシティースケーリング / ベロシティスケーリング / velocity scaling / simple velocity rescaling Method status, JSON and Markdown GROMACS: temperature coupling Berendsen weak-coupling thermostat Relax the temperature difference over a chosen coupling time using velocity scaling. Fluctuations are suppressed, so this is not a correct canonical sampler. Treat as a historical relaxation method; do not assume correct NVT fluctuations or response properties. Other names: ベルンゼン / Berendsen thermostat / weak coupling Method status, JSON and Markdown Berendsen et al. (1984), Molecular dynamics with coupling to an external bath GROMACS: temperature coupling Andersen thermostat Represent stochastic heat-bath collisions by redrawing selected particle velocities from a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. Canonical sampling and physical time correlations are separate criteria. Independent velocity redraws alter total momentum and transport. Other names: アンダーセン / stochastic collisions Method status, JSON and Markdown Andersen (1980), Molecular dynamics simulations at constant pressure and/or temperature GROMACS: temperature coupling Langevin thermostat Add friction and random forces to the equations of motion. The fluctuation–dissipation relation connects friction and noise at the target equilibrium temperature. Friction changes dynamical correlations and diffusion. Finite-step sampling errors must be assessed together with the integration scheme. Other names: ランジュバン / ランジュヴァン / friction and noise Method status, JSON and Markdown Bussi & Parrinello (2007), Accurate sampling using Langevin dynamics LAMMPS: fix langevin Nosé extended-system thermostat Introduce additional heat-bath degrees of freedom and time scaling: a starting point for deterministic constant-temperature molecular dynamics. Distinguish the original extended Hamiltonian from the real-time Nosé–Hoover equations. An invariant distribution alone does not establish ergodicity. Other names: ノセ / 能勢 / Nose thermostat / extended system Method status, JSON and Markdown Nosé (1984), A unified formulation of the constant temperature molecular dynamics methods Nosé–Hoover thermostat A deterministic method with a dynamically adjusted heat-bath friction variable. The canonical distribution is invariant, but small systems can fail to explore it ergodically. Check nonergodicity in systems such as harmonic oscillators and dependence on bath mass or coupling time. Mean temperature is insufficient validation. Other names: のせフーバー / ノセフーバー / ノセ・フーバー / 能勢・フーバー / Nose-Hoover Method status, JSON and Markdown Hoover (1985), Canonical dynamics: Equilibrium phase-space distributions GROMACS: temperature coupling Nosé–Hoover chains Couple heat-bath variables to further heat baths in a chain. This extension addresses sampling problems of a single thermostat. Chain length, masses and substeps matter. Adding a chain does not universally guarantee ergodicity. Other names: ノセ・フーバー鎖 / NHC / Nose-Hoover chain Method status, JSON and Markdown Martyna, Klein & Tuckerman (1992), Nosé–Hoover chains: The canonical ensemble via continuous dynamics LAMMPS: fix nvt / tchain Stochastic velocity rescaling (CSVR) Use a stochastic global scale factor designed to generate canonical kinetic-energy fluctuations. This is distinct from directly fixing the kinetic energy. Assess equilibrium distributions separately from real-time dynamics. State the coupling time, integration step and degree-of-freedom count. Other names: Bussi–Donadio–Parrinello / Bussi thermostat / v-rescale / canonical velocity rescaling / 確率的速度スケーリング Method status, JSON and Markdown Bussi, Donadio & Parrinello (2007), Canonical sampling through velocity rescaling Author preprint: arXiv:0803.4060 Four further entries Gaussian isokinetic thermostat Constrain kinetic energy continuously using a constraint force, connecting nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with constrained mechanics. Distinguish fixed kinetic energy from the fluctuating canonical kinetic energy at finite system size. Configurational and full phase-space distributions differ. Other names: ガウス等運動エネルギー / isokinetic constraint Method status, JSON and Markdown Evans & Morriss, Statistical Mechanics of Nonequilibrium Liquids, §5.2 Generalized Langevin equation (GLE) Use memory kernels and colored noise, or auxiliary variables representing them, to tailor the frequency response of a heat bath. Separate classical equilibrium fluctuation–dissipation settings from nonequilibrium approximations to nuclear quantum effects; neither is an electronic-structure solver. Other names: 一般化ランジュバン / colored-noise thermostat / 有色雑音 Method status, JSON and Markdown Ceriotti, Bussi & Parrinello (2009), Langevin Equation with Colored Noise for Constant-Temperature Molecular Dynamics Simulations LAMMPS: fix gle DPD pair thermostat Control temperature using dissipative and random pair forces. Standard symmetric pair forces conserve the pair’s total momentum. Relevant when momentum transport matters. Verify matched friction/noise, radial weights and finite-step effects. Other names: 散逸粒子動力学 / dissipative particle dynamics / pairwise thermostat Method status, JSON and Markdown Español & Warren (1995), Statistical Mechanics of Dissipative Particle Dynamics LAMMPS: pair_style dpd / dpd/tstat Lowe–Andersen thermostat Stochastically redraw a component of a nearby pair’s relative velocity while preserving the pair’s center-of-mass momentum. Distinguish from independent-particle Andersen collisions. Collision frequency and neighbor radius affect transport such as viscosity and diffusion. Other names: ロウ・アンダーセン / Lowe Andersen Method status, JSON and Markdown Lowe (1999), An alternative approach to dissipative particle dynamics Planned runnable checks This is a verification plan, not measured results. Start with harmonic oscillators and ideal gases, then a small Lennard–Jones system. Compare mean temperature, kinetic-energy and position distributions, autocorrelations, and coupling-time and step-size dependence. Record multiple independent random streams and correlation-aware uncertainty. Include a small-system example where Nosé–Hoover does not explore adequately. Sources and review scope An introduction linking original-paper DOIs, author preprints and official GROMACS/LAMMPS documentation. Full equation audits and numerical reproductions have not been performed. The Gaussian isokinetic entry currently links an originator-authored monograph; individual original-paper curation remains open. Citation and reuse · Method registry / JSON

documents.title: Time integration and leapfrog · An Atlas of Numerical Methods
documents.text: ← Reading chapters IN THIS EDITION THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data Time integration and leapfrog Spatial reconstruction and time integration are independent choices. After spatial discretization, a PDE becomes an ODE system dU/dt = L(U). Accuracy, stability, monotonicity, dissipation, and cost then depend on both parts. The time integration notebook isolates the temporal choice using y′ = i y, y(0) = 1. Twelve methods on one oscillator# The exact solution exp(i t) follows the unit circle. Forward Euler and backward Euler are first order: the former grows on this undamped oscillator, while the latter damps it. The explicit RK2 family includes Heun / SSPRK(2,2), explicit midpoint, and Ralston. Kutta RK3, SSPRK(3,3), and SSPRK(4,3) are third order; classical RK4 and SSPRK(5,4) are fourth order. Implicit midpoint is second order and preserves the amplitude of this linear oscillator. Its phase still has error. Read the RK family chapter and use the family notebook for stage/order/SSP comparisons and nonlinear tests. For y′ = lambda y, define z = lambda delta t. One-step amplification factors include RFE=1+z,RBE=11−z,Rmidpoint=1+z/21−z/2.RFE​=1+z,RBE​=1−z1​,Rmidpoint​=1−z/21+z/2​. The RK factors are the exponential Taylor polynomial through degree two, three, or four for the three RK2 variants, Kutta RK3 / SSPRK(3,3), or classical RK4 on this scalar linear equation. SSPRK(4,3) instead has a degree-four term z⁴/48; SSPRK(5,4) has an additional degree-five term. Shared scalar amplification does not make nonlinear RK stages identical. SSP properties depend on a forward-Euler bound for the spatial operator; they are not unconditional stability. Leapfrog needs two roots# The centered, two-step first-order-system recurrence is yn+1=yn−1+2zyn,ξ±=z±1+z2.yn+1=yn−1+2zyn,ξ±​=z±1+z2​. The root tending to +1 as z tends to zero carries the physical mode; the root tending to −1 carries a computational mode alternating between steps. Both roots and their multiplicities matter. For z = i sigma, distinct roots have unit modulus when |sigma| < 1. At |sigma| = 1 the repeated root can give linearly growing solutions; do not include that endpoint in a general boundedness claim. Above it, one root grows geometrically. A starting value is required in addition to y(0). This implementation takes one RK4 step, optionally adding a real perturbation epsilon to y(1). At lambda = 0 that perturbation gives even samples equal to 1 and odd samples equal to 1+epsilon: a direct computational-mode demonstration. For the notebook’s oscillator it also perturbs the physical mode. Time filters such as the Robert–Asselin family modify this behavior, with their own damping and accuracy tradeoffs; see Williams (2009). No filter is applied in this edition. Particle leapfrog is a different formulation# A staggered kick–drift scheme for position and velocity, or velocity Verlet for a second-order mechanical system, is often also called leapfrog. Its variables live at different temporal locations and its symplectic interpretation uses that structure. The scalar recurrence above is not a demonstration of a complete SPH particle integrator or a proof of long-time energy conservation for general mechanics. Reproduce and read the notebook# from numart.time_integration import linear_trajectory, leapfrog_roots t, y = linear_trajectory(rate=1j, dt=0.1, steps=200, method='leapfrog') print(leapfrog_roots(0.1j)) The browser selects from Python-computed trajectories with fixed final time 20, twelve methods, seven step sizes, and three leapfrog starting perturbations. Axes expand for unstable samples. A matching time interval is not an equal-cost comparison: implicit solves and RK stages differ. Tests measure temporal refinement orders and check the leapfrog roots, alternating mode, and midpoint amplitude. These oscillator trajectories evaluate the scalar stability factor, which is algebraically equivalent to RK stages on this linear test equation; the separate family notebook evaluates full nonlinear stages. Continue with the spatial stability laboratory, SPH, and ALE. Canonical mechanical maps# The symplectic integration chapter now implements mechanical kick–drift–kick Verlet, a fourth-order Yoshida composition, symplectic Euler, and implicit midpoint on harmonic and quartic Hamiltonians. The map notebook compares them with RK4, separating canonical structure from exact energy conservation. Historical atlas →Computed gallery → ON THIS PAGE

documents.text: Wavelets Wavelets resolve structure in both location and scale. Compared with global Fourier modes, they describe localized changes through a hierarchy of resolutions. Problem and representative equations An orthonormal discrete wavelet system expands a function in coarse scaling coefficients c and detail coefficients d. The factor 2ʲ/² preserves the L2 norm of ψⱼ,ₖ. The stated energy identity assumes a complete orthonormal system and compatible boundary treatment. f=∑kcJ,kϕJ,k+∑j≥J∑kdj,kψj,k,∥f∥22=∑k∣cJ,k∣2+∑j≥J,k∣dj,k∣2.f=k∑​cJ,k​ϕJ,k​+j≥J∑​k∑​dj,k​ψj,k​,∥f∥22​=k∑​∣cJ,k​∣2+j≥J,k∑​∣dj,k​∣2. Algorithm Mallat’s multiresolution algorithm filters and downsamples into coarse and detail coefficients, then recurses on the coarse part. Matched synthesis filters reconstruct the signal. More vanishing moments can sparsify smooth components but affect support width and boundary handling. Conditions and pitfalls On finite intervals specify periodic/symmetric extensions or boundary wavelets. Coefficient thresholding loses information and does not automatically preserve conservation laws or shock positivity. Distinguish continuous transforms, orthonormal discrete transforms and biorthogonal energy relations. What to check Check reconstruction, Parseval energy and vanishing moments on low-degree polynomials. Vary thresholds and report retained coefficients, L2/maximum errors and boundary artifacts. Publication scope and related entries Reading, representative equations and sources are published. Dedicated code and numerical verification remain planned. The suggested checks above are not measured results, and code/results of other methods are not presented as validation of this method. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source. S.G. Mallat (1989). A theory for multiresolution signal decomposition: the wavelet representation. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation. Literature-only. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model. Literature-only. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed. Literature-only. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue. Literature-only. Read this model → Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion Literature only / no dedicated solver ut=Δ[(d1+α11u+α12v)u]+u(a1−b1u−c1v)ut​=Δ[(d1​+α11​u+α12​v)u]+u(a1​−b1​u−c1​v)vt=Δ[(d2+α21u+α22v)v]+v(a2−b2u−c2v)vt​=Δ[(d2​+α21​u+α22​v)v]+v(a2​−b2​u−c2​v) Competition with density-dependent self- and cross-dispersal can produce spatial segregation. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations. Literature-only. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability. Literature-only.
