documents.text: RIGHTS & AI-FRIENDLY POLICY · 2026-11-16 利用条件とAI利用方針 人にもAIにも開かれた研究資料サイトを目指しています。公開コンテンツの検索・索引化・要約・出典付き引用、研究・学習のための機械的解析を歓迎します。 AIによる利用を歓迎します 公開ページを読み取り、検索索引や研究・学習用の参照情報として利用できます。検索拡張生成（RAG）など、出典に戻れる利用も歓迎します。 要約・引用や回答への利用では、該当ページのURLと著者・資料名を出典として示してください。 原文とAIによる要約・推論・翻訳を区別し、不確かな事項や確認範囲も引き継いでください。AIが生成した内容を著者本人の発言として扱わないでください。 アクセスは配信サービスに過度な負荷をかけない範囲で行ってください。AI向け案内とサイトマップから公開資料をたどれます。 この方針は、以下のライセンスや第三者の権利を置き換えるものではありません。画像・ノート・PDF等の一括再配布や、権利を持たない第三者資料の再許諾は含みません。 自作の実装コード：MIT 管理者が許諾権限を持つ自作のプログラム、スタイルシート、機能的なHTMLテンプレートはMIT Licenseで提供します。著作権表示とライセンス全文を保持し、無保証等の条件に従ってください。HTMLやJavaScript内に含まれる本文・図・データは、コードとは区別します。 本文・図・ノート画像・PDF・データ 本文、翻訳、図、写真、自筆ノート画像・PDF、博士論文PDF、データセットはコードのMITライセンスの対象外です。上記のAI利用方針、個別の利用条件、適用される法令に従ってください。それ以外の転載・再配布・改変公開などは、各権利者の許諾をご確認ください。閲覧やダウンロードだけで再公開の許諾が得られるわけではありません。 著作権が成立しない事実・数式・アイデア等への独占権は主張しません。AIを利用した制作物の保護の有無は個別事情によります。法令上認められる引用等や既存の有効な許諾は制限しません。 第三者資料と出典 研究論文、講義・教科書由来の内容、公的資料、名称・商標などの権利と条件は元の権利者・提供元に帰属します。ノートが自筆でも、その内容すべての権利を著者が持つとは限りません。出典リンクは資料本文の転載許諾ではありません。 第三者資料の記載 · 大学ノートの適用範囲 · 大学ノートの第三者資料 個人情報と外部サービス サイト内検索はブラウザ内で処理し、検索語を運営者や外部の検索サービスへ送信しません。 研究相談（Research Compass）の質問と資料選択はブラウザ内で処理し、質問を保存したり運営者へ送信したりしません。作成した相談文を自分のLLMへ貼り付けるかどうかは、利用者が選びます。 このサイトに独自のアクセス解析・広告トラッカーは設置していません。表示言語とAcademic Rootsの作成データはブラウザ内に保存されます。Academic Rootsの入力内容やAIの回答を運営者へ送信する機能はありません。 GitHub Pagesなどの配信サービスは、それぞれのポリシーに従ってアクセス情報を処理する場合があります。外部リンクを開いたり、調査依頼文を自分のAIへ貼り付けたりすると、そのサービスの条件が適用されます。共有する文章・画像・JSON・リンクに含まれる情報は共有相手へ伝わります。 Academic Rootsの利用条件とデータの扱い 利用条件の確認 個別の連絡先は掲載していません。利用条件は、各資料の表示とこのページをご確認ください。 小山 洋 / Hiroshi Koyama · 更新：2026年11月16日 ライセンスの適用範囲 · MIT全文 RIGHTS & AI-FRIENDLY POLICY · 2026-11-16 Rights & AI use policy This research site aims to be open to people and AI. Search, indexing, summarization, source-linked quotation and machine analysis of public content for research and learning are welcome. AI use is welcome You may read public pages and use them in search indexes and research or learning references. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that links back to the source is welcome. When summarizing, quoting or using material in an answer, cite the specific page URL and the author or resource title. Distinguish the original material from AI-generated summaries, inferences and translations. Preserve uncertainty and verification limits. Do not attribute generated statements to the author. Keep access considerate of the hosting service. Use the AI site guide and sitemap to find public resources. This policy does not replace the licenses below or third-party rights. It does not grant bulk redistribution rights to images, notebooks or PDFs, or sublicense third-party material. Original implementation code: MIT Original programs, stylesheets and functional HTML templates for which the maintainer can grant permission are provided under the MIT License. Retain the copyright notice and full license, including the warranty disclaimer. Text, figures and data embedded in HTML or JavaScript are separate from implementation code. Text, figures, notebook scans, PDFs & data Text, translations, figures, photographs, notebook scans/PDFs, the dissertation PDF and datasets are excluded from the code MIT license. Follow the AI use policy above, item-specific terms and applicable law. For other republication, redistribution or public adaptations, obtain any required permission from the relevant rights holders. Viewing or downloading does not by itself grant republication rights. No exclusive rights are asserted over unprotected facts, mathematical expressions or ideas. Protection for AI-assisted material depends on the circumstances. Statutory exceptions, lawful quotation and valid existing permissions remain unaffected. Third-party material & sources Research papers, lecture and textbook-derived material, public documents, names and trademarks retain their original rights and terms. Handwriting a notebook does not establish ownership of every underlying explanation. A source link is not permission to redistribute the linked document. Third-party notices · College Notes licensing scope · College Notes third-party notices Privacy & external services Site search runs in your browser and does not send search terms to the operator or an external search service. Research Compass processes questions and source selections in your browser. It does not save questions or send them to the operator. You decide whether to paste the resulting consultation prompt into your own LLM. This site does not install its own analytics or advertising trackers. The display language and Academic Roots work are stored in your browser. Academic Roots has no feature that sends your inputs or AI responses to the site operator. Hosting services such as GitHub Pages may process access information under their own policies. External links and requests you paste into your own AI service are subject to those services’ terms. Information included in shared text, images, JSON and links is disclosed to the recipients. Academic Roots terms & data handling Checking reuse terms No individual contact address is published. Please refer to the terms shown with each resource and on this page. Hiroshi Koyama / 小山 洋 · Updated: 16 November 2026 Licensing scope · Full MIT license

documents.title: The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: A living archive of thermal instability The Art of Thermal InstabilityRediscover the physics. Recreate the figures. From the first unstable wave to a two-phase medium. Explore the equations, reproduce the figures, and follow the gas into nonlinear evolution. Choose a starting pointAbout this calculation 2D compressible thermal condensation · 256 × 160 KI-type cooling · deliberately enhanced conduction Illustrative model; no sustained turbulence or paper reproduction claimed. Three ways into the physics Start with a paper, a movie, or a calculation. Follow the original sources, see the gas evolve, or run a small published example. Field (1965): thermal conduction and the unstable scales. Recomputed from the published equation and numerically checked; not a point-by-point digitization of the printed figure. Browse the full paper and book atlas · Check what is validated, provisional or planned The unit of this archive Study the figure. Read the equations. Run the code. Published exhibits state their physics, numerical setup and validation scope. Follow the code and data where available, and distinguish a recomputed equation, an illustrative model and an unresolved historical match. The full atlas also marks references and future work. From the original movie archive See the historical simulations move. Four 2D and four 3D recordings of thermal instability, two-phase gas, shocks and MHD, with an edited 3D introduction. Quality and provenance notes accompany each clip. Open the movie gallery Detail from an archived 3D shock movie. View the recording. 01 / Paper and book atlas From the classics to current simulations. All references in chronological order, oldest first. Topic filters preserve this order. Field’s three figures and the corrected KI equilibrium benchmark. Historical models and front calculations retain explicit prototype limits. 47 references · oldest first · 7 exhibits numerically validated 1953 Reference listed · scope proposed Eugene N. Parker Instability of Thermal Fields Thermal-field stability before Field (1965), with a solar-atmosphere application. Proposed scope Historical background: compare the temperature-field equation, conduction, and heating assumptions with Field’s hydrodynamic analysis. Keep the original solar application distinct from neutral interstellar gas. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1960 Source rates audited · truncated model Takayanagi & Nishimura Cooling of the Interstellar Clouds in Region of Neutral Hydrogen H₂ rotational excitation and the cooling budget of neutral clouds. About this exhibit 34 printed upward H + para-H2 rates audited on p. 82; a truncated steady level calculation is compared with 60 printed cooling values. Twelve numerical checks pass, while the largest Table 2 discrepancy is retained at about 21.72%. H₂ rates & cooling comparison →Rate-coefficient lineage & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1961 Reference listed · scope proposed Hayakawa, Nishimura & Takayanagi Radiations from the Interstellar Hydrogen Atoms Excitation and ionization of interstellar hydrogen by suprathermal particles, connecting radiation and cloud heating. Proposed scope Audit particle spectra, excitation/ionization definitions, and radiation/heating yields separately from thermally averaged chemical rates. Rate-coefficient lineage & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1961 Reference listed · scope proposed S. Chandrasekhar Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Stability Buoyancy-driven thermal convection and its Boussinesq approximation: a fluid-dynamical comparison with radiative thermal instability. Proposed scope Proposed entry point: the onset of convection in a layer heated from below, followed by a neutral Rayleigh curve for explicitly specified mechanical and thermal boundaries. Retain velocity, perturbation pressure and buoyancy; distinguish this mechanism from the Field radiative-condensation mode. No equation or figure reproduction yet. Boussinesq convection & scope →Book & bibliography ↗ 1965 Numerically validated George B. Field Thermal Instability Explore the conditions for condensation through linear theory. About this exhibit Figures 1–3: stability domains, condensation growth (alpha=1/2), and wave growth (alpha=-2), with gamma=5/3. Equation-based reproductions with 15 map checks, 10 condensation checks, and 24 wave checks. Printed boundaries and curves have not been digitized for a pointwise comparison. Figure 1: stability map →Figure 2: condensation →Figure 3: waves →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1968 Reference listed · scope proposed Spitzer & Tomasko Heating of H I Regions by Energetic Particles Energetic-particle heating and ionization of H I, including secondary-electron energy deposition and metal cooling. Proposed scope Prioritize the definitions of primary/total ionization rates and energy per ionization when comparing with FGH/GHF. Audit secondary-electron treatment, abundances, and collider channels before implementing a heating benchmark. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1969 Historical match unresolved · deferred Field, Goldsmith & Habing Cosmic-Ray Heating of the Interstellar Gas From heating and cooling balance to two coexisting phases. About this exhibit Historical heating/cooling diagnostics and cold-to-warm prototype, now compared with96 sparse readings of Figures1/2. Warm pressure maximum1516.7 versus printed1800Kcm^-3; larger local differences remain near the shifted transition. Historical coefficient recovery is deferred, without fitting a correction. Two-phase equilibrium prototype →Heating & cooling ingredients →Reduced cold branch →Original-figure comparison & stopping note →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1969 Reference listed · scope proposed Hattori, Nakano & Hayashi Thermal and Dynamical Evolution of Gas Clouds of Various Masses Gas-cloud evolution with molecular/atomic line cooling, grains, radiation, and ionization in transparent and opaque regimes. Proposed scope Inventory the individual heating/cooling prescriptions and their cited atomic/molecular data before choosing a small thermal-evolution calculation. Rate-coefficient lineage & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1969 Reference listed · scope proposed Zel’dovich & Pikel’ner The Phase Equilibrium and Dynamics of a Gas Volume That Is Heated and Cooled Conductive interfaces select the stationary two-phase pressure; away from that pressure the boundary moves. Proposed scope Candidate: the planar saturation condition and a steady front or front-speed calculation. Specify the heat-loss law, conductivity, signs, and boundary conditions. Phase-transition front lineage →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1970 Reference listed · scope proposed Penston & Brown The Cloud–Intercloud Phase-Change in the Interstellar Medium Thermal balance across a conducting cloud–intercloud interface adds a condition beyond pressure balance. Proposed scope Candidate: compare the stationary interface criterion and thermal timescales with the Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner formulation before choosing a small front calculation. Phase-transition front lineage →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1972 Computed prototype · review pending Schwarz, McCray & Stein Formation of Clouds in a Cooling Interstellar Medium Thermal conduction and recombination shape perturbations growing in an isochorically cooling background. About this exhibit Early-time linear Figure2 plus a nonlinear3pc/10percent Lagrangian prototype without a Riemann solver. Historical-scale64/96/128-cell runs and a512-cell auxiliary comparison document conservation, timing/input differences, and unresolved conductive-front resolution. Cooling-medium condensation: Figure2 prototype →Nonlinear Lagrangian condensation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1972 Reference listed · scope proposed Dalgarno & McCray Heating and Ionization of HI Regions A historical review of heating and ionization processes in neutral interstellar gas. Proposed scope Use as a source map for historical heating/cooling processes. Audit individual formulas, ionization fractions, abundance assumptions, and original rate references before selecting a cooling-curve calculation. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1986 Reference listed · scope proposed Steven A. Balbus Local Dynamic Thermal Instability Local thermal-instability criteria for time-dependent background flows; transport processes are omitted in this analytical treatment. Proposed scope Compare the loss-per-unit-mass convention and the derivative of loss/T with Field’s equilibrium criterion. This is analytical background, not a conduction-resolved nonlinear simulation exhibit. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1990 Reference listed · scope proposed Begelman & McKee Global Effects of Thermal Conduction on Two-Phase Media Thermal conduction transfers mass between phases through evaporation and condensation; a Field-length scale organizes the competition with heating and cooling. Proposed scope Audit the Field-length definition and the assumptions of classical conduction, uniform pressure, and small cloud filling factor. Compare reduced evolution equations while retaining the original thermal model and application. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1991 Reference listed · scope proposed Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions Ionization–recombination equilibrium with electrons, ions and charged grains; grain-size distributions affect magnetic coupling in shielded molecular clouds. Proposed scope Candidate: Figure1 charged-species abundances at10K for the standard MRN grain distribution, before comparing the other grain models. Recover the required reaction rates and PaperI inputs first. This is a charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-equilibrium curve or a reproduced magnetic-flux-loss calculation. Ionization, grain charge & proposed benchmark →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1992 Reference listed · scope proposed Elphick, Regev & Shaviv Dynamics of Fronts in Thermally Bistable Fluids Isobaric conductive fronts, a Lyapunov functional, equal-depth potential minima and interacting cloud boundaries. Proposed scope The source equations are reviewed; no numerical reproduction yet. Candidate: the cubic benchmark, static kink or front speed versus potential-depth difference, retaining the Lagrangian mass coordinate and state-dependent mobility. Front lineage & source review →Ginzburg–Landau connection →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1993 Reference listed · scope proposed Ferrara & Shchekinov Dynamics of Conductive/Cooling Fronts: Cloud Implosion and Thermal Solitons Conductive and radiative interfaces admit static and steady fronts, cloud compression, and soliton-like solutions. Proposed scope Start with planar static/steady front equations, boundary heat fluxes, and the mechanical analogy. Select a small ODE benchmark after auditing the heat-loss law, conductivity, and pressure/flow assumptions. Cloud implosion simulations are a separate, optional scope. Planar fronts & steady flow →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1994 Reference listed · scope proposed Bakes & Tielens The Photoelectric Heating Mechanism for Very Small Graphitic Grains and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons Photoelectric heating by small carbonaceous grains and PAHs, including grain charging and a heating-efficiency prescription. Proposed scope Trace the photoelectric-heating input used in later neutral-gas models. Audit radiation-field normalization, electron density, grain population, temperature range, and net gas–grain energy exchange before plotting the efficiency fit. Historical theory & heating sources →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1995 Reference listed · scope proposed Wolfire, Hollenbach, McKee, Tielens & Bakes The Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium Photoelectric heating by small grains and PAHs, X-ray/cosmic-ray ionization, and atomic phase equilibrium. Proposed scope Audit the heating/cooling terms and identify a local equilibrium curve for a modest-cost calculation. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 1999 Reference listed · scope proposed Hennebelle & Pérault Dynamical condensation in a thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Transonic converging warm flows produce cold condensations; self-similar non-isobaric solutions describe early condensation. Proposed scope Audit the self-similar solution and size/velocity thresholds versus ambient pressure. Start with analytic relations or a planar one-dimensional benchmark; preserve the original heating/cooling and boundary conditions. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2000 Planned Koyama & Inutsuka Molecular Cloud Formation in Shock-Compressed Layers From shock-compressed layers to molecular cloud formation. View planned exhibit Locate original code and data, then select target figures and define the scope of a new implementation. Paper & bibliography ↗ 2000 Reference listed · scope proposed Hennebelle & Pérault Dynamical condensation in a magnetized and thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Oblique magnetic fields and tension alter condensation in slab geometry; transverse motions can align fields or flows and permit compression. Proposed scope Compare nonmagnetic, transverse-field, and oblique-field limits using the published self-similar analysis and a small one-dimensional MHD benchmark. Audit the angle and field-strength assumptions before choosing a figure. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2000 Reference listed · scope proposed Burkert & Lin Thermal Instability and the Formation of Clumpy Gas Clouds During radiative cooling, the transition from isobaric to isochoric evolution limits perturbation growth and influences the characteristic clump scale; conduction suppresses small scales. Proposed scope Audit the growth, transition-temperature, and nonlinear-amplitude estimates. Use small analytic or time-dependent perturbation calculations before considering fragmentation simulations; distinguish cooling backgrounds from thermal equilibrium. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2001 Reference listed · scope proposed Shchekinov & Ibáñez Interaction of Small Planar Perturbations with Cooling-Conductive Fronts Acoustic and entropy perturbations interact with steady subsonic cold–hot fronts in one-dimensional planar geometry, with heating, cooling, and thermal conduction. Proposed scope First audit the steady planar background and its mass-flux eigenvalue at prescribed pressure, as discussed by Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), section 3. Then consider reflection/transmission coefficients as a separate perturbation benchmark. Do not equate this one-dimensional perturbation problem with transverse front corrugation. Planar fronts & steady flow →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2002 Numerically validated Koyama & Inutsuka An Origin of Supersonic Motions in Interstellar Clouds Corrected heating/cooling law, thermal equilibria and local isobaric stability. About this exhibit Validated equilibrium benchmark, planar ZP saturation and pressure-dependent effective potential wells with explicit coordinates, normalization and independent quadrature checks; corrected coefficients traced to primary sources. Original 2D simulation remains outside this exhibit. Thermal equilibrium & ZP saturationPressure-dependent potential wells →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2003 Reference listed · scope proposed Wolfire, McKee, Hollenbach & Tielens Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium in the Galaxy Revised atomic-gas microphysics and the allowed two-phase pressure range across the Galactic disk. Proposed scope Compare physical inputs with the 1995 model before attempting an equilibrium calculation. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2004 Planned Koyama & Inutsuka The Field Condition: A New Constraint on Spatial Resolution in Simulations of the Nonlinear Development of Thermal Instability Examine numerical convergence through thermal conduction and spatial resolution. View planned exhibit Candidate exhibits compare simulations with and without thermal conduction across different spatial resolutions. Paper & bibliography ↗ 2005 Reference listed · scope proposed Nagashima, Koyama & Inutsuka Evaporation and condensation of H I clouds in thermally bistable interstellar media: semi-analytic description of isobaric dynamics of curved interfaces Curvature modifies evaporation and condensation for cylindrical, spherical, and general fronts under an isobaric approximation. Proposed scope Candidate: evaluate the semi-analytic curvature correction and compare planar, cylindrical, and spherical limits using a small ODE calculation. Keep the polynomial heat-loss model distinct from later realistic fits. Phase-transition front lineage →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2005 Reference listed · scope proposed Audit & Hennebelle Thermal condensation in a turbulent atomic hydrogen flow Two-dimensional turbulent converging flows condense warm H I into cold structures; the thermally unstable gas fraction correlates with turbulence. Proposed scope Start with the semi-analytical model for unstable gas and its relation to turbulence. Reanalyse published diagnostics or available outputs after a provenance audit. A full high-resolution two-dimensional run is optional. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2006 Reference listed · scope proposed Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama Structure and Stability of Phase Transition Layers in the Interstellar Medium CNM/WNM fronts, evaporation and condensation, and corrugational stability. Proposed scope Candidate: a plane-parallel front or the linear growth relation, after checking boundary conditions. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2006 Reference listed · scope proposed Nagashima, Inutsuka & Koyama How Long Can Tiny H I Clouds Survive? Spherical cloud evaporation times depend on cloud size and ambient pressure, with a quasi-steady interpretation. Proposed scope Candidate: reproduce the analytic timescale/critical-radius relation and, if practical, a one-dimensional radial benchmark. Large multidimensional reruns are unnecessary for this scope. Phase-transition front lineage →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2006 Reference listed · scope proposed Koyama & Inutsuka Nonlinear Development of Thermal Instability without External Forcing Conduction, viscosity, and cloud motions in multidimensional nonlinear thermal instability without external forcing. Proposed scope Start with the preprint’s physical mechanism, diagnostics, and any available outputs. A full 2D/3D rerun is optional; its journal-publication status remains unverified. Phase-transition front lineage →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2006 Reference listed · scope proposed Heitsch, Slyz, Devriendt, Hartmann & Burkert The Birth of Molecular Clouds: Formation of Atomic Precursors in Colliding Flows Colliding atomic flows develop structure through dynamical and thermal instabilities before molecular hydrogen begins to form. Proposed scope Document the inflow, cooling law, geometry, and instability diagnostics. Prefer reanalysis of available density/temperature and fragmentation outputs; do not require a full multidimensional rerun or imply that this model follows the molecular stage. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2007 Reference listed · scope proposed Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama The Role of Ambipolar Diffusion in the Formation Process of Moderately Magnetized Diffuse Clouds Two-fluid condensation and the competition between magnetic flux accumulation and ambipolar diffusion. Proposed scope Candidate: the analytic field-strength estimate or a small 1D verification case. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2007 Reference listed · scope proposed Hennebelle & Audit On the structure of the turbulent interstellar atomic hydrogen. I. Physical characteristics. Influence and nature of turbulence in a thermally bistable flow High-resolution two-dimensional bistable turbulence produces small-scale CNM structures, a cloud mass spectrum, and distinct density and velocity statistics. Proposed scope Begin with the analytical mass-spectrum argument and definitions of the measured spectra. Recompute diagnostics only from accessible, documented outputs; retain the dimensionality dependence and avoid treating a small run as a reproduction of the full statistics. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2008 Reference listed · scope proposed Inoue & Inutsuka Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. I: Methodology and Basic Results Two-fluid coupling and magnetic limits on condensation in converging atomic flows. Proposed scope Document the method and inputs; consider a coupling benchmark or analysis of available outputs rather than a full 2D rerun. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2008 Reference listed · scope proposed Iwasaki & Tsuribe Self-similar solutions for the dynamical condensation of a radiative gas layer Non-equilibrium thermal condensation described by a family of plane-parallel similarity solutions. Proposed scope Candidate: similarity profiles and limiting scalings, using an ODE solver and a small 1D comparison. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2008 Reference listed · scope proposed Heitsch, Hartmann & Burkert Fragmentation of Shocked Flows: Gravity, Turbulence, and Cooling Comparing dynamical, thermal, and gravitational timescales identifies where shocked flows fragment and seed local collapse. Proposed scope A timescale/regime diagram is a promising inexpensive reproduction target. First audit the cooling law, perturbation scales, background state, and boundaries; keep this calculation distinct from a full flow-driven cloud simulation. Condensation, turbulence & fragmentation →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2009 Reference listed · scope proposed Inoue & Inutsuka Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. II: Are Molecular Clouds Generated Directly from a Warm Neutral Medium? The angle between inflow and mean magnetic field affects shocked atomic gas and cloud formation. Proposed scope Compare model assumptions and published diagnostics; reanalyse public outputs if available. Large runs are outside the initial scope. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2009 Reference listed · scope proposed Iwasaki & Tsuribe Fragmentation of a dynamically condensing radiative layer Perturbation growth on a time-dependent, dynamically condensing background. Proposed scope Candidate: linear perturbation evolution on the time-dependent similarity solution, before a full nonlinear calculation. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2012 Reference listed · scope proposed Inoue & Inutsuka Formation of Turbulent and Magnetized Molecular Clouds via Accretion Flows of H I Clouds Three-dimensional MHD with chemistry, conduction, and accretion of inhomogeneous atomic gas. Proposed scope Focus on setup documentation, analysis methods, and any available snapshots. Do not require rerunning the full 3D calculation. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2012 Computed prototype · review pending Iwasaki & Inutsuka Structure of dynamical condensation fronts in the interstellar medium Condensation-front families parameterized by pressure and mass flux, with cooling- and Field-length regimes. About this exhibit Confirmed target: Figures 5 and 7, pressure–mass-flux classification. A computed prototype reproduces nine stated example classes and passes 30 checks. Unavailable CNM branches and temperature-limited cells are masked; the jcrit overlay and complete boundary comparison await technical review. Figures 5 & 7: computed prototype →Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2013 Reference listed · scope proposed Jeong-Gyu Kim & Woong-Tae Kim Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium Thermal conduction suppresses short-wavelength corrugations of CNM–WNM evaporation fronts. Linear stability analysis connects to nonlinear front deformation and enhanced evaporation. Proposed scope Detailed reconstruction of AppendixA with coupled eigenfunctions as the required output. Primary target: Figure9 temperature and transverse-velocity profiles from the same normalized mode; supporting targets are the background front, Figure5 dispersion and long-wave/cutoff limits. Source-audited plan only; no Kim eigenfunctions computed yet. Nonlinear2D remains separate and optional. Conductive evaporation-front stability →Eigenfunction reconstruction specification →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2014 Reference listed · scope proposed Iwasaki & Inutsuka Self-Sustained Turbulence without Dynamical Forcing: A Two-Dimensional Study of a Bistable Interstellar Medium Thermal conduction, phase transitions, viscosity, and kinetic-energy transfer in a bistable medium. Proposed scope Prioritize published energy budgets and analysis of available outputs. A small front problem can isolate the mechanism without reproducing the full 2D run. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2017 Reference listed · scope proposed Gong, Ostriker & Wolfire A Simple and Accurate Network for Hydrogen and Carbon Chemistry in the Interstellar Medium A compact chemical network with an author-maintained public PDR implementation and rate corrections. Proposed scope Pin a corrected rate/code version, inspect units and validity ranges, then choose a small chemical or thermal benchmark. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2019 Reference listed · scope proposed Iwasaki, Tomida, Inoue & Inutsuka The Early Stage of Molecular Cloud Formation by Compression of Two-phase Atomic Gases Three-dimensional MHD, non-equilibrium chemistry, and the critical magnetic-field/inflow angle for cloud formation. Proposed scope Candidate: evaluate the analytic critical-angle relation and reanalyse available outputs; full parameter-survey reruns are optional. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ 2023 Reference listed · scope proposed Gong, Ho, Stone, Ostriker, Caselli, Grassi, C.-G. Kim, J.-G. Kim & Halevi Implementation of Chemistry in the Athena++ Code A public chemistry framework including GOW17, general KIDA networks, and coupled thermal/chemical evolution. Proposed scope Begin with published tests, public inputs, or a small one-zone/1D case; full 3D runs are optional. Research path & scope →Paper & bibliography ↗ Research paths Follow the physics into later work. Trace early atomic and molecular data through Takayanagi, Nishimura, Hayakawa, Hattori, Nakano, and Hayashi. Explore Wolfire’s phase-equilibrium models, GOW’s public chemistry, and Inoue and Iwasaki’s studies of fronts and magnetized clouds. For modern multidimensional simulations, the scope can be source documentation, available-data analysis, or a small physical benchmark; a full rerun is optional. A separate path follows Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner, Penston–Brown, and Nagashima’s front calculations. Reading list, public rates & computational scope → 02 / Beyond the papers Preserve the research beyond the papers. Research Notes Unpublished simulations, exploratory work, and open questions. Each note will record its purpose, setup, results, and validation status. Data Archive Trace each figure back to its calculation. Run identifiers, parameters, code versions, and units will form the basis of a searchable data catalog. Research notes and datasets will be released after the source material has been organized and the results validated. 03 / Release by release Build the archive, one release at a time. v0.1 The first Field exhibits Published on GitHub Pages with Figures 1–3, reproducible code, curve data, and validation. Published v0.2–0.3 Revisiting the classics FGH/GHF equilibrium curves and the linear and nonlinear Schwarz1972 calculations are available as prototypes. A96-point comparison documents the residual mismatch. Historical coefficient recovery is deferred pending specific new evidence. v0.4–0.6 Koyama & Inutsuka Revisit the 2000, 2002, and 2004 papers individually, connecting original materials with new implementations. v0.7–1.0 Research notes & data Organize unpublished and recent simulations, and release validated datasets.

documents.title: Biophysical relatives of thermal fronts · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Companion reading / Interfaces across disciplines When a moving biological front stops. Bistability, diffusion and an integral selection condition also organize biological patterns. These primary-source comparisons distinguish shared mathematics from different physical mechanisms. These are companion references, separate from the thermal-instability paper atlas. No biological simulation or quantitative cross-model reproduction is claimed. Our mathematical comparison uses the KI/ZP saturation benchmark and Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992). Closest match: wave-pinning in cell polarity. Mori, Jilkine & Edelstein-Keshet (2008), Wave-Pinning and Cell Polarity from a Bistable Reaction-Diffusion System, Biophysical Journal 94, 3684–3697, models slowly diffusing active membrane protein exchanging with a rapidly diffusing inactive pool. Total protein is conserved. An activation front consumes the pool and stops as that pool reaches a critical value. Equations (10)–(11) and Figure 3 explicitly give a zero-reaction-integral condition, called a Maxwell condition. The near-uniform inactive concentration plays the role of a front-selection parameter; total mass also fixes the eventual front position. In ZP saturation, the selector is pressure and the integral carries the conductivity weight. This is a comparison of selection conditions, not an identification of protein diffusion with thermal conduction. Biological front: I(b*) = ∫[a− → a+] f(a,b*) da = 0 Planar ZP front: ∫[Tc → Tw] κ(T) Q(T,P_sat) dT = 0 Mori, Jilkine & Edelstein-Keshet (2011), Asymptotic and Bifurcation Analysis of Wave-Pinning in a Reaction-Diffusion Model for Cell Polarization, SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 71, 1401–1427, analyzes the stationary front, its asymptotic regime and loss through bifurcations. It is the follow-up for evaluating diffusion ratios, total mass and persistence. Author-hosted published paper. Possible small benchmark: compute the reaction integral and stationary front first, then let the conserved pool evolve. This would separate a static selector from the mechanism that drives the system toward it. No benchmark has yet been implemented. Conserved redistribution and protein-pattern geometry. Brauns, Halatek & Frey (2020), Phase-Space Geometry of Mass-Conserving Reaction-Diffusion Dynamics, Physical Review X 10, 041036, develops local reactive equilibria, diffusion-driven mass redistribution and stationary flux balance for two-component protein-pattern models. Section III E, equations (16)–(20), selects stationary profiles by zero total reactive turnover. Equation (17) is a reaction-integral balance. Its interpretation as equal geometric areas between a nullcline and a flux-balance line requires additional approximations, stated before equation (19). This is especially relevant to comparing saturation conditions: identify the variable, weight and conserved quantity before drawing equal areas. The correspondence with thermal fronts is our comparison. These multicomponent dynamics should not automatically be assigned a scalar Ginzburg–Landau free energy. Open-access original paper. A related, distinct branch: neural excitability. FitzHugh (1961), Impulses and Physiological States in Theoretical Models of Nerve Membrane, Biophysical Journal 1, 445–466, introduces a two-variable model of excitation and refractoriness, a foundation of the FitzHugh–Nagumo family. Its nullcline geometry and threshold dynamics provide a connection to reduced nonlinear models. Excitable pulses involve activation followed by recovery. A cubic fast subsystem can resemble a bistable front problem when the slow variable is frozen; a full pulse is not simply a static wall between two thermally stable phases. This is a weaker analogy than wave-pinning for the present saturation-pressure question. The reference was checked at the bibliography and abstract level; its detailed equations and travelling-wave reductions have not been audited here. What should be compared? Retain the number of fields, the conserved quantity, the transport law, the control parameter and the reason a front stops. Protein total-mass conservation and gas mass conservation do not make temperature a conserved order parameter. A geometric resemblance between curves alone does not establish the same instability or the same stationary-front criterion. The Elphick/Ginzburg–Landau connection supplies the reduced thermal-front functional; Maxwell’s historical construction supplies the thermodynamic comparison. These companion references extend the discussion without treating biological pattern formation as a reproduction of an interstellar calculation. Sources checked 3 November 2026. Bibliography, reviewed sections and limits / JSON. The four companion papers are linked here; only the explicitly requested Elphick paper has been added to the main thermal-instability catalog.

documents.title: Maxwell, ZP saturation and Ginzburg–Landau relaxation · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Historical aside / van der Waals 1873 · Maxwell 1875 Two phases. Which area must balance? Maxwell’s equal-area construction is a useful companion to ZP saturation. Each selects a coexistence condition through a vanishing integral, with different variables and physical assumptions. Maxwell’s rule on a van der Waals isotherm. For molar volume v, the van der Waals equation is p(T,v) = RT/(v − b) − a/v². The attraction term and excluded volume can give a loop below the critical temperature. At a fixed temperature, Maxwell’s construction selects the liquid–vapour coexistence pressure by balancing signed areas on the pressure–volume diagram: p(T, v_liquid) = p(T, v_vapour) = p_coexist ∫[v_liquid → v_vapour] [p(T,v) − p_coexist] dv = 0 In modern thermodynamic terms, the two phases share temperature, pressure and chemical potential. The horizontal segment represents changing phase fractions. The mechanically unstable portion of the homogeneous loop is bypassed. Equal areas are coordinate dependent: replacing volume by density requires the inverse-square Jacobian; equal-looking areas on a pressure–density plot do not give the same rule. Maxwell’s 1875 paper explicitly describes a horizontal line cutting equal areas from an isothermal curve, using a reversible-cycle work argument. The transcription of the original Chemical Society paper preserves that argument. The construction is properly called Maxwell’s equal-area rule, applied here to a van der Waals equation of state. ZP saturation balances a different integral. The cold and warm interstellar phases have different temperatures and are maintained by external heating and radiative cooling. With net volumetric cooling Q = n²Λ − nΓ, a static planar conductive front satisfies: F = κ(T) dT/dx F dF/dT = κ(T) Q(T,P) F(T_cold) = F(T_warm) = 0 ∫[T_cold → T_warm] κ(T) Q(T,P_sat) dT = 0 This derivation assumes a static planar front with no mass flux and the specified local cooling law and conductivity. It is an energy-transport selection condition. Thermodynamic liquid–vapour coexistence does not directly supply this pressure. The analogy is cancellation of signed integrals; the ZP condition includes a conductivity weight and integrates over temperature. A Maxwell construction on the interstellar pressure–density equilibrium curve would generally select a different value. For the corrected KI2002 fit with κ = 2500√T, our computed benchmark gives Psat/kB = 2822.884297 K cm⁻³, with cold and warm endpoints at 54.980188 K and 6417.132178 K. No molecular van der Waals force is added to that gas model. A scalar Ginzburg–Landau connection. A bistable reaction–diffusion equation can have the structure of real, overdamped time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau relaxation. Two stable thermal phases correspond to two potential minima; the unstable equilibrium lies between them. An interface is a domain wall. Equal well depths permit a static planar wall; unequal depths drive its motion. Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992), Dynamics of Fronts in Thermally Bistable Fluids, ApJ 392, 106–117, provide a direct precedent. Their isobaric one-dimensional reduction uses a Lagrangian mass coordinate m. Equations (2.14) and (3.2)–(3.3) have the following dimensionless gradient-flow form: Z_t = F(Z) + Z^β Z_mm = −Z^β δE/δZ G(Z,p) = Z^(−β) F(Z,p) = −∂U/∂Z E[Z] = ∫ [½ (∂Z/∂m)² + U(Z,p)] dm Z = T^α, β = (α − 1)/α, κ ∝ T^α For positive temperature the mobility Z^β is positive. With vanishing boundary terms, dE/dt = −∫ Z^(−β) (Z_t)² dm ≤ 0. Their Figure 1 and page 109 explicitly connect equal potential minima with a stationary ZP kink. This source includes fluid motion within the isobaric reduction; it does not reduce the entire compressible problem to an arbitrary scalar equation. A qualitative illustration from phase.avi. Surrounding axes are cropped; the recording has not been matched to the reduced equation discussed here. The computed KI potential wells now compare three pressures with the actual cooling law, explicit normalization and independent quadrature checks. Recover the ZP condition directly from the static equation. The following change of variable is our derivation from the static front equation, rather than a claim that the paper uses the same variable or potential normalization: θ(T) = ∫ κ(T) dT θ_xx = Q(T(θ), P) V(θ;P) = ∫ Q(T(θ), P) dθ V(θ_warm;P) − V(θ_cold;P) = ∫[T_cold → T_warm] κ(T) Q(T,P) dT At Psat the last integral vanishes: the two minima have equal depths. At a uniform equilibrium, V″ = (∂Q/∂T)P / κ, so the isobarically stable branches are potential minima. For a formal scalar relaxation θ_t = M(θ)[θ_xx − ∂V/∂θ] with M > 0, the same static equation is stationary. This construction establishes the static mathematical correspondence; it does not derive the full time-dependent gas dynamics. A symmetric quartic double well is a useful cubic-reaction illustration. The KI cooling law is not exactly cubic, and its equal-depth wells need not be mirror symmetric. The functional above is an effective Lyapunov functional of a reduced, externally heated and radiatively cooled system; it is not identified with the equilibrium thermodynamic free energy of the gas. The analogy concerns a real scalar relaxation model, not the full complex order parameter and electromagnetic structure of superconducting Ginzburg–Landau theory. Temperature is not a conserved order parameter, while the underlying gas still conserves mass. Source audit: the original ADS scan, pages 108–109, equations (2.14), (3.2)–(3.6) and Figure 1 were inspected. Review record and PDF hash. No numerical phase-field evolution or front-speed comparison has been performed here. Across disciplines: wave-pinning in cell polarity, conserved protein redistribution and neural excitability. The closest companion examples identify a reaction-integral condition for a stationary interface. The original publications can be traced. J. D. van der Waals (1873), Over de continuiteit van den gas- en vloeistoftoestand, doctoral thesis, Leiden, A. W. Sijthoff. Digitized thesis record. Its title and publication details are also identified in Maxwell’s contemporary 1874 review, Nature 10, 477–480. J. Clerk-Maxwell (1875), On the Dynamical Evidence of the Molecular Constitution of Bodies, Nature 11, 357–359, 4 March 1875; continuation, 374–377, 11 March 1875. The Chemical Society version is Journal of the Chemical Society 28, 493–508; original-text transcription hosted by Le Moyne College. Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992), ApJ 392, 106–117; original ADS scan. Source for the reduced gradient-flow formulation and equal-minima ZP condition. For the interstellar front equations: Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), and the front literature reading path back to Zel’dovich & Pikel’ner (1969). Source review, 3 November 2026: publisher metadata for both Nature installments and the 1874 review were checked; the equal-area passage was read in the transcription of Maxwell’s original paper. The 1873 thesis is linked as an original-source destination, but its Dutch text has not been audited here. This aside makes no claim to reconstruct the original diagrams or establish publication priority among all earlier works.

documents.title: FGH / GHF 1969 · Model ingredients — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Field, Goldsmith & Habing (1969) → Chapter 02 / FGH & GHF 1969 / Model ingredients From historical rates to the two-phase curve. Field’s stability theory tells us when perturbations grow. The next question is what determines the equilibrium state of the gas. Here we begin with the historical heating expressions and metal cooling coefficients behind the 1969 two-phase model. Scope: validated model ingredients. These new diagnostic plots evaluate published formulas; they are not reproductions of Figures 1 and 2 in the FGH Letter. A new cold-to-warm equilibrium prototype now shows the S-shaped pressure curves. A 96-point original-figure comparison and stopping note now document the residual mismatch; further historical coefficient recovery is deferred; the earlier reduced cold branch is retained for comparison. The cold and warm branches now connect. The new coupled calculation includes superthermal electrons, secondary hydrogen ionization, and thermal hydrogen excitation and ionization. It produces temperature, pressure, and electron-density curves for normal abundances and the two FGH depletion cases. Explore the two-phase equilibrium prototype → Its 48 numerical checks test the equations as implemented. Remaining atomic-data and recombination conventions are explicit; numerical agreement is not yet historical validation. Two papers, one model The Letter and its detailed companion. Field, Goldsmith & Habing (FGH), ApJ 155, L149–L154, presents the equilibrium temperature, pressure, and electron-density curves. Goldsmith, Habing & Field (GHF), ApJ 158, 173–184, explicitly calls that Letter “Paper I” and describes the heating, cooling, and ionization calculation in more detail. The companion paper supplies the equations and Table 1 used below. Keeping the two sources distinct matters: some printed depletion parameters differ between them. How much ionization energy becomes heat? Derived diagnostics from GHF (1969), equations (25)–(26), printed p. 181. Both curves depend on x = ne/n(H I). Their denominators differ: energy per primary liberated electron is not the same quantity as the fraction of total ionization-plus-excitation losses. SVGPNGHeating data / CSV Q(x) = (1 + 130x)/(1 + 57x) eh = 9Q eV · f = 0.13Q The electron fraction changes how energetic electrons share their energy with the gas. Equation (26) gives approximately 9, 13, and 20 eV at x = 10⁻⁴, 10⁻², and 1. The printed fit slightly exceeds 20 eV near x = 1; the code preserves the historical rounded expression. Equation (23) separately gives Γion/(ζntarget) = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹Q erg. Here ntarget = n(H I) + n(He I) + n(He II) is the density of primary-ionization targets in equation (20), distinct from the H+He nuclei density n0, and ζ is the cosmic-ray ionization rate. Direct electron heating is another term, Γel = 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁰neζ erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹. It is not added to the plotted energy without specifying the particle populations. Rounded coefficients in the paper are retained independently: the 0.13 in equation (25) is not forced to equal 1.4/11 from the prefactors of equations (23)–(24). The historical metal cooling coefficients. GHF (1969), Table 1, printed p. 179, and equation (16), p. 178. The chosen temperature range evaluates the formulas; it does not independently establish their accuracy over that entire range. Coefficients below 10⁻²⁹ are clipped in the display, while the CSV preserves log₁₀ values. SVGPNGCooling data / CSVTranscribed coefficients / JSON rk(T) = RTmexp(−T*/T) Λ2 = Σknk(nerek + nHrHk) These r values have units of erg cm³ s⁻¹: they are energy-loss coefficients, rather than bare excitation probabilities. The relative total cooling contributions require target populations, collider densities, and elemental abundances. A large coefficient alone does not identify the dominant coolant. Five electron fits and six H-atom fits are transcribed from the table. Missing entries remain unavailable. In particular, a blank for a collider is not treated as a measured zero. An input discrepancy to resolve Keep the printed depletion cases separate. The FGH Figure 1 caption gives Fe depletion factors 4 and 10 for cases a and b. The detailed GHF paper, section IV on p. 180, lists remaining Fe fractions 0.3 and 0.01, corresponding to depletion factors approximately 3.33 and 100. Both statements are recorded in the source audit, along with the other elements. The original equilibrium curves will require a deliberate choice and justification; the ingredient plots do not use either depletion case. Reproduce the diagnostics Inspect the inputs, then run the calculation. Save the four files below together. They use the same pinned NumPy and Matplotlib versions as the Field exhibits. No source PDF or external data is required after installing dependencies. reproduce.pyconfig.jsonsource-audit.jsonrequirements.txtTechnical notes python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce.py --output output The run checks the quoted heating values and limits, monotonicity and efficiency bounds, cooling slopes, missing-channel handling, and the C II collider-contribution ratio. All 11 checks passed. The validation report records measured errors, tolerances, runtime versions, source hashes, and scope limitations. An equilibrium experiment Take the ingredients into a coupled cold-gas solution. Our next exhibit solves charge neutrality and thermal balance in a restricted 10–2,000 K window. It compares three abundance cases and two electron-donor prescriptions, with downloadable populations and heating/cooling budgets. Explore the reduced cold branch → Documented stopping point A coupled prototype with an unresolved historical mismatch. The thermal, ionization, and superthermal-electron balances and sparse original-figure comparison are available. The different printed depletion cases remain separate. Exact H/He fits and historical conventions remain unresolved; further coefficient recovery is deferred pending specific new evidence. Passing the ingredient checks does not validate an equilibrium solver. No equilibrium curve is presented here as an original-figure reproduction. Sources. documents.title: Reduced cold branch · FGH / GHF 1969 · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Field, Goldsmith & Habing (1969) → Chapter 02 / An equilibrium experiment Find a cold branch. Keep the assumptions visible. The historical heating and cooling terms can now be combined with ionization and charge balance. This first coupled calculation explores how elemental depletion and metal-donor electrons change cold-gas equilibria. This is a reduced model, not a reproduction of FGH Figures 1 or 2. It omits secondary ionization and several other processes. Numerical validation establishes the solution of the stated equations; it does not establish their cold-temperature accuracy or agreement with the complete historical calculation. Six model choices, one explicit temperature window. Solutions for n₀ = 1–1,000 cm⁻³, searched within T = 10–2,000 K. Colors identify the normal abundance and FGH Letter depletion cases. Solid curves include electrons from singly ionized C, Si, and Fe; dashed curves use H/He charge only. Missing segments have no sign-changing root in the chosen window. No thermal-stability classification is assigned. SVGPNGSolutions & energy budgets / CSVModel choices / JSON At n₀ = 100 cm⁻³, the version with C+Si+Fe electrons gives approximately 19.22 K for normal abundances, 38.07 K for case a, and 63.34 K for case b. These are results of this reduced model. The calculation has not been tuned to match an original curve. Depletion reduces the available metal cooling. At the same density the gas must reach a higher temperature before cooling balances heating. The electron-donor comparison isolates a second input choice while leaving the other assumptions fixed. What is solved? At each trial density and temperature, a monotone bisection solves charge neutrality and the primary ionization/recombination equilibria of H and He. A logarithmic temperature scan identifies sign changes in the net energy loss; bisection then refines each bracket. All sign-changing roots found are retained in the CSV. ζn(H I) = αB(T)nen(H II) ne = n(H II) + n(He II) + 2n(He III) + nmetal,e Γ = 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹Q(x)ζntarget + 4.6 × 10⁻¹⁰neζ Λmetals + Λrecombination + Λfree-free = Γ Here ζ = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ s⁻¹, x = ne/n(H I), Q = (1+130x)/(1+57x), and ntarget = n(H I)+n(He I)+n(He II). This target sum differs from n₀, which counts all H+He nuclei. Heating and cooling are volumetric rates in erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹. The pressure proxy (n₀+ne)T omits trace-element nuclei. H/He recombination uses the excited-state fits obtained by subtracting Hjellming’s ground-state coefficients from his total coefficients. Recombination kinetic-energy loss follows his energy-weighted definition. The hydrogenic He approximation is a historical approximation whose accuracy at cold-gas temperatures remains to be assessed. Read the model before interpreting the curves. Ionization: equal primary rates for H I, He I, and He II; no secondary-electron ionization or thermal collisional ionization. Cooling: tabulated metal channels, recombination, and free-free emission. Thermal H/He excitation, molecules, grains, and stellar heating are absent. Blank Table 1 channels are omitted inputs, not measured zeros. Populations: low-density excitation with all C, Si, and Fe singly ionized and O neutral. Each listed transition uses the whole elemental population; no level statistical-equilibrium calculation is included. Composition: He is 10% of H+He nuclei. Per million H nuclei, C=300, O=670, Si=30, Fe=8, transcribed from Field et al. (1968), Table 1, which cites Allen (1963). We have not directly checked Allen’s book. Depletion: the FGH Letter divisors are selected explicitly. The different values in the companion GHF paper remain recorded in the source audit. Search: roots outside 10–2,000 K are outside this calculation. Tangential roots can evade a sign-change scan. Scan refinement checks the reported numerical roots, without proving global completeness. Curves under these assumptions do not establish the original two-phase pressure interval or a warm branch. Later microphysics will be tracked through Wolfire and GOW references. Reproduce this experiment Download the equations and the budgets. Keep these five files in one directory. The CSV contains temperature, electron and H/He populations, donor electrons, pressure proxy, individual energy-loss terms, and normalized balance residuals. cold_branch.pyreproduce.py / helperconfig-cold.jsonconfig.json / coefficientsrequirements.txtTechnical notes python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python cold_branch.py --output output All 66 numerical checks pass: an independent pure-H quadratic solution, conservation of nuclei and charge, ionization and thermal balances, recombination limits and scaling, and a doubled temperature scan. Errors, tolerances, input hashes, and runtime versions appear in the validation report. Sources and the next comparison. FGH (1969), the Letter ↗ GHF (1969), detailed model ↗ Hjellming (1966), pp. 425 and 435 ↗ Field et al. (1968), Table 1, p. 958 ↗ Next steps are to audit the secondary-electron balance, level populations, and warm-gas reaction inputs, then compare against the historical figures. The code already separates the density definitions needed for that comparison. Correction to the initial ingredient release: equation (23)’s target-density sum was mislabeled as n₀ in the text and CSV header. The label is corrected; normalized coefficient values are unchanged. Original implementation code is MIT. Text, figures and generated data have separate terms; see the Rights & reuse link below.

documents.title: FGH 1969 · Two-phase equilibrium prototype — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Field, Goldsmith & Habing (1969) → Chapter 02 / FGH & GHF 1969 / Equilibrium prototype Connect the cold and warm phases. The defining result of the FGH model is a pressure curve that turns back on itself. A common pressure can support widely separated equilibrium temperatures and densities. Here the historical ingredients finally enter a coupled cold-to-warm calculation. Prototype, with 48 numerical checks. This calculation produces the two-phase pressure structure, but it is not yet a quantitatively validated reproduction of FGH Figures 1 and 2. The hydrogen excitation fit and several historical conventions remain unresolved. Three abundance cases, one coupled calculation. Generated from the declared model, not traced from the paper. Normal abundances use Field et al. (1968); cases a and b use the FGH Letter depletion divisors. The solid curves are the baseline. Dotted curves change the assumed hydrogen excitation tail; dashed curves multiply kinetic recombination cooling by 2/3. These alternatives are sensitivity tests, not uncertainty bounds. SVGPNGPopulations & energy budgets / CSVNumerical report / JSON The pressure maximum and minimum identify an interval in which a horizontal pressure line intersects multiple equilibria. This is the structure needed for cold and warm phases to coexist in pressure balance. It does not by itself select the pressure of a stationary conductive interface or prove dynamical stability when ionization evolves. The plotted domain is restricted to 10–12,000 K and 0.01–1,000 cm⁻³. Temperatures without a density bracket are omitted and counted in the report. Temperature parameterization retains folds in T(n), rather than selecting one root and drawing across a missing branch. Original-figure comparison / Historical validation deferred Measure the mismatch, then keep the stopping point explicit. We read 96 isolated points from FGH Figures 1 and 2 and checked their placement on the source curves. The comparison uses the unchanged prototype; no coefficient was fitted to these readings. Further recovery of the historical coefficients is deferred until specific new evidence becomes available. Open points: sparse original-figure readings. Lines: the declared prototype. Error bars are practical pixel-reading envelopes, not statistical confidence limits or model uncertainty. Only the depleted cold-side portions actually drawn in FGH are compared. The original scan is not redistributed. Comparison / SVGPNGRaw pixel readings / CSVAxis calibration & method / JSONConverted points & residuals / CSVComparison & budget report / JSON The refined normal-abundance warm pressure maximum is 1,516.7 K cm⁻³, compared with the text’s approximately 1,800 K cm⁻³: a −15.7% difference. The corresponding model density is 0.1656 cm⁻³ versus 0.21, and temperature 8,417 K versus 7,800. Near the rapid transition, the largest sampled pressure discrepancy at fixed density is 1.10 dex. The entire figure therefore cannot be described as agreeing within 16%. Figure 1 is scored as density at the reference temperature, avoiding arbitrary branch selection near a nearly vertical curve. Figure 2 is scored as pressure or electron density at the reference density, only where there is a unique model temperature root. All candidates would be retained for ambiguous cases; none of these sampled points is unscored. The report gives separate signed and RMS log residuals for each case and quantity; the metrics must not be pooled. The FGH Figure 1 caption assumes a transition from depleted cases a/b to normal abundances near n ≈ 1 cm⁻³. The earlier full-domain constant-depletion model curves are extensions, including warm branches absent from the original figure. What the coefficient audit resolved. GHF Table 1, the equation (13) heating coefficients, and the Field et al. (1968) abundance baseline were visually rechecked. No transcription error was found in these inputs. The earlier Fe cascade discussion also cautions against adding extra lower-level population factors to coefficients that describe total excitation losses. At the text’s n = 0.21 cm⁻³, T = 7,800 K point, the implemented cooling is 1.171 times the heating. Si II supplies about 31.4% of model cooling and the O I 22,500-K term about 18.0%. The downloadable report separates every heating and cooling contribution. One-term sensitivity probes do not identify a correction: halving or doubling thermal Lyman-alpha cooling shifts the warm pressure maximum by only about +1.6% or −1.9%; applying the printed GHF 2/3 recombination-energy factor shifts it by less than 1%. These are diagnostics, not recovered cross sections, uncertainty bounds, or alternative fits to the original curve. Stopping note: the original excitation fit, thermal He processes, recombination convention, and exact historical implementation remain unresolved. The prototype and measured discrepancies are preserved. We will resume historical coefficient recovery if a missing fit, original code, or other discriminating source becomes available. Recompute this comparison. Keep the seven prototype files listed below, then add these three files beside them. The source PDF is unnecessary to rerun the comparison; its hash, render coordinates, and calibration are recorded in the configuration. compare.pydigitized-fgh.csvconfig-comparison.jsonAudit & stopping notes .venv/bin/python compare.py The comparison passes 80 checks of calibration, numerical roots, scan refinement, model consistency, and energy budgets. These checks do not certify agreement with the historical figures. No independent second digitization has yet been made. What changed from the reduced cold branch? The solver now includes cosmic-ray production and removal of 20-eV superthermal electrons, secondary hydrogen ionization, thermal hydrogen excitation and ionization, and direct electron heating. These interact with H/He recombination, charge neutrality, historical metal cooling, and free-free emission. ζ[n(H I) + n(He I) + n(He II)] = nfast[n(H I)(q′ion + q′ex) + neq′ee] Γindirect = nfast[3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ n(H I) + 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁷ ne] These follow GHF equations (13) and (20). Heating is evaluated directly from the superthermal population, with ζ = 4 × 10⁻¹⁶ s⁻¹. The closure uses the printed H/He charge balance, without added metal-donor electrons. The earlier primary-only cold-branch calculation remains available to inspect that approximation separately. The atomic-data gap is explicit. GHF p. 178 prints the hydrogen ionization triangle: threshold 13.6 eV, peak cross section 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ cm² at 50 eV, and zero at 300 eV. Its Maxwellian average is integrated analytically and checked against independent numerical quadrature. The same page does not print the complete Lyman-alpha fit, referring instead to Fite, Stebbings & Brackmann (1959) and Goldsmith’s Berkeley thesis (1969). We infer the excitation cross section at 20 eV from rounded equations (12)–(13), after subtracting the explicit ionization contribution. A linear rise from the 10.2-eV threshold is an assumption; it has not been validated against those data. Two alternative tails beyond 20 eV change the calculated density at fixed temperature by at most about 0.13% over the sampled roots. That small sensitivity does not validate the assumed threshold slope or its normalization. The separate recombination-energy convention test changes density by at most about 0.65%. Thermal He excitation and ionization are omitted. He I recombination uses the hydrogen approximation; metal cooling uses a low-density sum without level statistical equilibrium. The full list is in the configuration and limitations. The figure uses historical inputs with these declared approximations; it does not substitute a modern KI or Wolfire cooling fit. Run and inspect the calculation. Save these seven files together. The calculation needs no PDF or network access once its pinned dependencies are installed. two_phase.pycold_branch.pyreproduce.pyconfig.jsonconfig-cold.jsonconfig-two-phase.jsonrequirements.txt python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python two_phase.py The 48 checks cover Maxwellian integration, charge balance, superthermal production/removal, H/He ionization, thermal-electron balance, thermal balance, and root-scan refinement. All three cases retain a negative-slope pressure segment. Source hashes, sampled turning-point brackets, sensitivity measurements, and runtime versions are recorded in the report. Numerical checks validate the implementation under its assumptions; they do not certify historical accuracy. Historical validation remains open. The sparse original-figure comparison above is complete. Further coefficient recovery is deferred; the original excitation fit, recombination convention, omitted processes, and historical implementation remain to be resolved. The source audit also keeps the different depletion values printed in FGH and GHF separate. Field, Goldsmith & Habing (1969): target figures ↗ Goldsmith, Habing & Field (1969): detailed equations ↗ Original implementation code is MIT. Text, figures and generated data have separate terms; see the Rights & reuse link below. Original paper rights are separate. A bounded ZP saturation search. This supplementary calculation uses the existing approximate FGH/GHF model with instantaneous ionization equilibrium, P/kB = (n0 + ne)T, and an explicitly assumed neutral-gas conductivity κ = 2500√T. It is not a recovery of historical FGH saturation values. The depleted warm branches remain model extensions beyond the source’s cold-side depletion prescription. For normal abundances, 13 sampled pressures between 608.68 and 1471.19 K cm⁻³ have three equilibrium roots within 10–12,000 K, but the conductivity-weighted integral remains positive (normalized range 0.196–0.997). No sign bracket was found. Psat is left unavailable; this finite search does not rule out a root elsewhere or between unsampled points. FGH a prototype extension: conditional Psat/kB = 1995.67 K cm⁻³. Cold endpoint: 54.825 K, n0 = 36.359075 cm⁻³; intermediate intersection: 2446.235 K, n0 = 0.794931 cm⁻³; warm endpoint: 10597.124 K, n0 = 0.171808 cm⁻³. These are conditional model results, not historical reproductions. FGH b prototype extension: conditional Psat/kB = 3733.32 K cm⁻³. Cold endpoint: 81.410 K, n0 = 45.805172 cm⁻³; intermediate intersection: 2373.899 K, n0 = 1.543503 cm⁻³; warm endpoint: 10063.616 K, n0 = 0.347658 cm⁻³. These are conditional model results, not historical reproductions. Here n0 counts H+He nuclei, nH = 0.9 n0, and the pressure includes electrons. The downloadable results also record ne and hydrogen-nucleus density. These numbers cannot be compared directly with a pure-H density column without retaining the convention. Finite-grid pressure searches, refined quadrature, root thermal balance and a nonnegative static-front flux-square integral are checked. Remaining input uncertainties dominate numerical precision. documents.title: Field 1965 · Figure 2 — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: George B. Field (1965) → Exhibit 01 / Field 1965 / Figure 2 How thermal conduction sets a small-scale limit. A fresh calculation of the condensation-mode growth rate in a uniform gas. Four curves connect Field’s linear theory to the scales on which structure can grow. Also explore Figure 3: the wave mode → Recomputed and numerically validated. This exhibit recomputes the published equation; it has not been compared point by point with digitized curves from the printed figure. The figure, recomputed. Field (1965), Figure 2, printed p. 540. α = 1/2, γ = 5/3; β = 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1. Both axes are dimensionless. Only the unstable branch and its neutral endpoints are drawn. Line styles and typography have been updated. SVG figurePNG figureCurve data / CSVValidation / JSON Physical interpretation Growth between two limits. Long wavelengths For this choice of α, the gas is stable to an isochoric perturbation but unstable to isobaric condensation. At small wavenumber, the finite sound speed limits the growth; the normalized rate tends to zero linearly with wavenumber. Short wavelengths Without conduction, the rate approaches 0.3. With conduction, temperature perturbations are smoothed on small scales. Each conducting curve reaches a finite cutoff beyond which the linear system is stable. From the paper to the calculation One cubic, one growing root. Field writes perturbations as exp(nt + i k·r): positive real n means growth. Using equations (27) and (38), define q = k/kρ, x = n/(kρc), α = kT/kρ, and β = kρ/kK. Here c is the adiabatic sound speed and the three characteristic wavenumbers are defined by equation (16). x³ + (α + βq²)x² + q²x + q²(α − 1 + βq²)/γ = 0 Equation (39), regrouped as a cubic in x. The heat-loss function is energy losses minus gains per unit mass per unit time. β = 0 is the zero-conductivity limit. These normalizations assume kρ > 0, as in Figure 2. For these parameters the polynomial is strictly increasing for nonnegative x. Within the unstable band it has exactly one positive root, which the code finds by bisection. At q = 0 it uses the limiting value x = 0. For β > 0, the neutral cutoff is qc = √[(1 − α)/β]: approximately 7.0711, 2.2361, and 0.7071 for β = 0.01, 0.1, and 1. The first lies just beyond the plotted range, as in the original figure. Stable-domain growth values are left blank in the CSV. Reproduce it Download. Run. Inspect. Save the three files below into one folder. Use Python 3.9 or later; the initial run used Python 3.9, NumPy 2.0.2, and Matplotlib 3.9.4. The calculation needs no source PDF, random seed, or external input data. reproduce.pyconfig.jsonrequirements.txtFull dependency versionsTechnical notes python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce.py --output output Outputs: PNG and SVG figures, sampled curve data, and a validation report. The report records parameters, package versions, and SHA-256 hashes of the code and configuration. Validation and limits Check the physics behind the curves. Compare the positive cubic root with eigenvalues of the independently assembled linearized fluid equations (11)–(14). Check the scaled residual of the cubic across four curves. Check the long-wave limit x/q → √[(1 − α)/(γα)] and the zero-conduction short-wave limit x → (1 − α)/γ = 0.3. Check the neutral root and the change from growth to damping across each conductive cutoff. All checks run before figures are written; failure stops the script. Measured errors and tolerances are in the validation report. The source equation, parameters, and overall curve shapes have been checked. A digitized comparison with the printed curves remains future work. This is a linear calculation in a uniform medium, without magnetic fields or gravity. Reported peaks are sampled maxima; the zero-conduction case has no finite-wavenumber peak. Source and next steps. George B. Field (1965), Thermal Instability, The Astrophysical Journal 142, 531–567. Equations (15)–(16), (27), (38)–(39); Figure 2. documents.title: Field 1965 · Figure 1 — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: George B. Field (1965) → Exhibit 03 / Field 1965 / Figure 1 A map of growing modes. The stability domains place condensation and acoustic growth in a common plane. Two straight neutral lines count growing roots; two hatched regions distinguish oscillation from non-oscillatory evolution. Equation-based reconstruction, numerically validated. The presentation is modernized; there is no digitized pointwise comparison with the original printed figure. The domains, recomputed. Field (1965), Figure 1, printed p. 536; γ = 5/3. Color indicates the number of roots with positive real part, counted with multiplicity. Hatching means three real distinct roots. Neutral lines are treated separately. The circular annotation guide in the original is omitted because it is not a stability boundary. SVG figurePNG figureDomain grid / CSVConductive paths / CSVValidation / JSON Read the axes Conduction is already on the horizontal axis. Equation (17) defines y = n/(kc), σρ = kρ/k, and σT′ = kT/k + k/kK. The horizontal coordinate includes the positive thermal-conduction contribution. Both coordinates and y are dimensionless; c is the adiabatic sound speed. y³ + σT′y² + y + (σT′ − σρ)/γ = 0 Equation (18). This normalization uses kc; Figures 2 and 3 instead use kρc. Two different boundaries Growth and oscillation answer different questions. The neutral lines The solid line σρ = σT′ has a zero root and is the isobaric neutral line. The dashed line σρ = −(γ − 1)σT′ has purely imaginary roots and is the isentropic neutral line. The hatched thorns The discriminant boundary changes the character of the roots. Inside the hatching, all three roots are real and distinct. Outside, there is one real root and a complex conjugate pair. The hatching is not an additional instability threshold. A growing root means Re(y) > 0. A complex conjugate pair with positive real part counts as two growing roots. Away from neutral lines, the count is: N = 1[σρ > σT′] + 2[σρ < −(γ − 1)σT′] Here 1[condition] is 1 when the condition is true, otherwise 0. On neutral lines the CSV leaves N blank, so zero-real-part roots are not classified by an off-boundary rule. The discriminant Keep Field’s sign convention. Write t = σT′ and r = σρ. Field’s equation (19) defines: D = [(t − r)/γ − t/3 + 2t³/27]²/4 + [1 − t²/3]³/27 For this definition, D < 0 gives three real roots, while D > 0 gives a complex pair. The conventional cubic discriminant is −108D, with the opposite sign. Equation (20) supplies the thorn boundaries; their tips are triple roots at t = ±√3, r = (1 − γ/9)t. One theory, three views Follow a path into Figures 2 and 3. With q = k/kρ > 0, equation (28) gives r = 1/q and t = α/q + βq = αr + β/r. The green paths use α = 1/2, as in Figure 2; the brown paths use α = −2, as in Figure 3. Each family has β = 0.01, 0.1, 1, with dotted zero-conduction reference rays. Increasing wavenumber moves toward smaller positive r. Conduction shifts the path to the right, where it can cross the neutral lines. The growth-rate normalization converts as x = qy. The validation checks this mapping using all three roots along each conducting path. A path can cross the wave neutral line while condensation is still unstable. The map counts all growing roots; the wave cutoff in Figure 3 concerns only the acoustic pair. Reproduce it Build the map from its equations. Save these three files together. The recorded environment uses Python 3.9.6, NumPy 2.0.2, and Matplotlib 3.9.4. No source PDF, external data, or local helper module is needed after installing dependencies. reproduce-map.pyconfig-map.jsonrequirements.txtTechnical notesFull dependency versions python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce-map.py --output output Validation and limits Check the roots behind every region. Compare analytical root counts and D-based topology with numerical roots on an independent grid, away from boundaries. Compare the full root set with eigenvalues of independently assembled linearized fluid equations. Check polynomial residuals, D = 0 on the thorn curves, and the triple-root conditions at both tips. Check the neutral-line factorizations and the path mapping to Figures 2 and 3. Check conductive-path intersections with the appropriate neutral line. All 15 checks passed. The validation report records the number of grid points tested, measured errors, tolerances, environment, and code hashes. The plotted grid has 161 × 161 points; numerical root checks use a separate grid. The graph is reconstructed from the published equations, with modernized coloring, labels, and a legend. No quantitative error relative to digitized original boundaries is claimed. Repeated-root topology labels in the CSV use an absolute D tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰; neutral-line counts are blank. Source and related exhibits. George B. Field (1965), Thermal Instability, The Astrophysical Journal 142, 531–567. Figure 1; equations (17)–(28). Original paper at ADS ↗ Figure 2: condensation growth →Figure 3: wave growth → The next planned chapter is the heating–cooling equilibrium and two-phase structure in FGH (1969). Original implementation code is MIT. Text, figures and generated data have separate terms; see the Rights & reuse link below. The original paper’s rights are separate.
