documents.title: Field 1965 · Figure 3 — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: George B. Field (1965) → Exhibit 02 / Field 1965 / Figure 3 When sound waves grow. An oscillation can grow while it travels. Figure 3 follows the real part of the acoustic wave pair in Field’s dispersion relation, with α = −2. Recomputed and numerically validated. The calculation selects the complex wave pair explicitly: the fastest-growing root belongs to a different mode. No digitized pointwise comparison with the printed curves has been performed. The wave mode, recomputed. Field (1965), Figure 3, printed p. 540. α = −2, γ = 5/3; β = 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1. Both axes are dimensionless. Growing branches and neutral endpoints are shown; the CSV also includes signed damping rates and frequencies. SVG figurePNG figureGrowth & frequency / CSVValidation / JSON Growth and oscillation Two parts of a complex root. The real part: growth Write x = ξ + iη, with time normalized by kρc. The real part ξ sets the exponential growth or decay of the disturbance. Positive ξ is an oscillatory instability, also called overstability. The imaginary part: frequency The two conjugate roots have opposite frequencies and equal growth rates. The code keeps the positive-frequency member, η > 0. The figure plots ξ; the CSV retains both ξ and η. At long wavelengths, Re(x) tends to zero quadratically with q = k/kρ. Without conduction it approaches 0.1 at short wavelengths. Increasing conduction reduces growth and introduces a finite wave cutoff. Mode selection The growing wave is not the fastest root. As in Figure 2, define x = n/(kρc), q = k/kρ, α = kT/kρ, β = kρ/kK, and s = α + βq². The same dispersion relation applies: x³ + sx² + q²x + q²(s − 1)/γ = 0 At q = 0, the wave pair tends to x = 0, whereas the condensation root tends to −α = 2. Selecting the root with the largest real part would draw the condensation mode instead of Figure 3. The script identifies the unique root with positive imaginary part and fails if no unique wave pair exists. Equation (40) provides a separate check on ξ = Re(x): ξ³ + sξ² + (s² + q²)ξ/4 + q²[(1 − 1/γ)s + 1/γ]/8 = 0 What a cutoff means A damped wave can coexist with condensation. The wave cutoff follows equation (26): qc = √[(−α − 1/(γ − 1))/β] = √(0.5/β). For β = 0.01, 0.1, and 1 this is approximately 7.0711, 2.2361, and 0.7071. The first is just outside the plotted interval. At the cutoff, s = −1.5 and the cubic factors as (x + s)(x² + q²). The wave roots are purely imaginary, x = ±iq, but the condensation root remains x = 1.5. The wave mode is damped above its cutoff. This does not imply stability of the whole gas: for these parameters the condensation mode remains unstable until a higher wavenumber. Reproduce it Run the second calculation. Download these four files into the same folder. reproduce.py supplies the shared dispersion relation and fluid matrix; reproduce-wave.py selects and validates the wave pair. The recorded environment used Python 3.9.6, NumPy 2.0.2, and Matplotlib 3.9.4. reproduce-wave.pyreproduce.pyconfig-wave.jsonrequirements.txt python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce-wave.py --output output Technical notesFull dependency versions No source PDF, network access, or external input data is needed after installing dependencies. Output includes figures, signed growth rates and frequencies, validation results, and source-code hashes. Validation and limits Follow the wave all the way to damping. Compare both members of the complex pair against the eigenvalues of the linearized fluid equations. Check the complex residual of equation (39) and the real-part residual of equation (40). Check Re(x)/q² → 0.025 and Im(x)/q → √0.9 at long wavelengths. For zero conduction, check Re(x) → 0.1 and Im(x)/q → 1 at short wavelengths. Check zero growth, frequency η = q, and the change to damping at each conductive wave cutoff. Confirm that the selector excludes the faster condensation root and that condensation can still grow when the waves are damped. All 24 checks passed in the recorded run. The script stops on a validation failure. Measured errors and tolerances are available in the validation report. The plotted geometry has been inspected against the scan, but no error relative to digitized original curves is claimed. Peaks are sampled maxima. The β = 0 endpoint at q = 7 is not a physical finite-wavenumber maximum. Magnetic fields, gravity, and nonlinear evolution are outside this calculation. Source and related exhibit. George B. Field (1965), Thermal Instability, The Astrophysical Journal 142, 531–567. Figure 3, equations (15), (26)–(27), (30), (38)–(40). Original paper at ADS ↗ Compare Figure 2: the condensation mode with α = 1/2 → Figure 1 now places both modes in a common map of stability domains → Original implementation code is MIT. documents.text: From the original movie archive / recovered November 2026 An archive in motion. Clouds emerge, shocks gather gas, and magnetized structures evolve. Four 2D and four 3D recordings bring the historical calculations back to the browser. Browse 2D movies → Archival footage, selected for visual demonstration. These movies have not been matched to recovered run inputs or independently validated against a paper. Original frame captions are retained in the full-frame versions. An edited introduction A short introduction in 3D. Download the edited selection 18 seconds, four distinct 3D excerpts. New English headings replace the old top title frames; the 3D scenes and their source cadence are preserved. Cuts separate different calculations. Repeated frames encode the low-cadence sources at 15 fps; no intermediate simulation states have been invented. Download MP4. The full-frame collection Keep the original picture in view. Play one recording at a time. Each retains its original aspect ratio, annotations and temporal sequence. Small lettering is best inspected at native size using the MP4 link. Downloading or enlarging a recording does not recover detail absent from the source. 2D recordings 2D / shock layer A developing layer and its close-up Download MP4 The wide view and close-up show an increasingly structured interface. Both original panels and color bars are retained. 800 × 600 px · 10 fps · 14.5 s Viewing quality: One of the stronger 2D presentation sources: 800 x 600 at 10 fps. Small labels still require native-size viewing. Source and editing record Descriptive title based on visible panels; original file demo1.avi. Original: sim/demo1.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 2D / phase diagram Two-phase gas and its pressure-density track Download MP4 Spatial structure is displayed alongside the pressure-density plane and equilibrium curve. Original time annotations, arrows and axes are retained. 680 × 340 px · 10 fps · 28.6 s Viewing quality: Useful for explaining the spatial/phase-plane connection. At 680 x 340, fine annotations are too small for a large-screen hero. Source and editing record Descriptive title based on visible panels; original file 1024CC.avi. The filename is not treated as a verified mesh size. Original: sim/1024CC.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 2D / MHD layer An MHD-labelled layer Download MP4 The recording follows the evolution of a thin layer, with overlaid lines and arrows. 640 × 640 px · 10 fps · 10.1 s Viewing quality: Useful for a layer-focused exhibit. The bottom axis caption is partly clipped in the original frame; this has not been reconstructed. Source and editing record Original file mhd_layer.avi and visible log-density scale; numerical run inputs are not recovered. Original: sim/asj2002b/mhd_layer.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 2D / phase separation Growing and merging structures Download MP4 Small initial variations develop into separated, evolving structures. Use this clip for qualitative morphology. 500 × 500 px · 10 fps · 20.7 s Viewing quality: Qualitative use only: the lower axis caption is clipped and the recording does not provide a complete visible color scale. Source and editing record Descriptive title based on visible evolution; original file phase.avi. Original: sim/movie/phase.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 3D recordings 3D / condensation Thermal instability in 3D Download MP4 A nearly uniform rendering develops into separated structures. The original title identifies thermal instability with conduction and viscosity. 700 × 668 px · 5 fps · 10.6 s Viewing quality: Good for compact gallery display. Grain-like texture and limited rendering detail are already visible in the source. Source and editing record Embedded caption: Thermal Instability + conduction + viscosity; Koyama & Inutsuka 2002. Original: sim/tw_mov/i256v.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 3D / shock A shock sweeps up warm gas Download MP4 A corrugated layer develops behind the advancing shock. The original caption gives a shock speed of 14.4 km/s. 700 × 600 px · 5 fps · 16.4 s Viewing quality: Good for compact display; small structures soften when enlarged. Source presentation is only 5 fps. Source and editing record Embedded caption: WNM Swept-Up by 14.4km/s Shock (3D); Koyama & Inutsuka 2002. Original: sim/tw_mov/shock.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 3D / MHD shock A magnetized shock in 3D Download MP4 A shock-compressed structure evolves in the MHD-labelled recording. Compare the visible evolution with the hydrodynamic-labelled clip; these are not yet established as a controlled matched pair. 700 × 600 px · 5 fps · 8.2 s Viewing quality: Good at native or smaller size. Fine structures are soft in the recording; native cadence is 5 fps. Source and editing record Embedded caption: WNM Swept-Up by MHD Shock (3D); Koyama & Inutsuka 2002. Original: sim/tw_mov/shockb.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG 3D / MHD Thermal instability with MHD Download MP4 The initially filled box develops connected structures as the viewpoint rotates. 608 × 588 px · 3 fps · 32.7 s Viewing quality: Useful as a historical rotating view. Only 3 fps; expect visibly stepped motion, not smooth modern animation. Source and editing record Embedded caption: Thermal Instability + MHD; Koyama & Inutsuka 2002. Original: sim/tw_mov/zpmhd128.avi. Complete original frame and timing retained in this version; H.264/yuv420p conversion only. No audio was present. Exact paper figure and run parameters remain unverified. MP4 · Poster / PNG What these recordings can tell us. They are effective visual demonstrations at compact gallery sizes. Their native resolutions are 500–800 pixels wide and their cadences are 3–10 fps. Fine textures can look grainy, and low-frame-rate motion is visibly stepped. They are suitable as historical exhibits; they are not high-resolution, full-screen source material. The 3D recordings carry the embedded credit “Koyama & Inutsuka 2002”. This identifies the caption on the recording; it does not establish a match to a specific paper figure, simulation dimensionality in that paper, or verified numerical parameters. The 2D titles here describe the visible panels and evolution. A number in a filename is not treated as a confirmed computational mesh size. The gallery was curated from 87 video files, representing 55 byte-distinct recordings after SHA-256 deduplication. Astronomy candidates were visually inspected at several times. The eight selected originals and their MP4 derivatives were decoded completely; dimensions and frame counts were checked. These are technical media checks, not numerical or physical validation of the simulations. Materials molecular-dynamics movies and related materials CG are excluded, along with unrelated footage and journal-supplement movies from other collections. Source originals remain untouched. Full-frame versions use H.264/yuv420p, retain the original dimensions and cadence, and add no spatial or temporal interpolation. The showreel has its own explicit crop and excerpt log. documents.title: Front classification prototype · Iwasaki & Inutsuka 2012 · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) → Iwasaki & Inutsuka 2012 / Figures 5 and 7 / Computed prototype Classify the interface by following its trajectory. A pressure and a mass flux can select very different connections between cold and warm gas. We solve the steady front equations behind the paper’s classification diagrams, starting from the cold neutral medium. This is a computed subset prepared for technical review, not a completed reproduction of every published region or auxiliary curve. Nine published example classifications agree. The map marks unavailable CNM branches and unresolved or temperature-limited cases instead of filling them from the source figure. The KI2002 equilibrium benchmark documents the corrected coefficients used here, stable and unstable branches, and all three equilibrium intersections at the ZP saturation pressure. Toward Figure 5: pressure and condensation flux. 29 pressure samples × 45 flux samples. Each cell is computed from the printed model. The white dashed curve is the condensation ZP separatrix, found by matching phase integrations from the cold and warm equilibria. Gray inputs lack the outgoing CNM saddle on the implemented density branch. White is unresolved. The source jcrit overlay remains to be audited. PNGSVGAll decisions / CSVComputed boundaries / CSV C–U–o approaches unstable gas with a temperature overshoot; C–U approaches it monotonically. C–c reaches the critical point, while C–C connects cold equilibria. A local node at the unstable equilibrium is insufficient to establish C–U: the paper explicitly notes that the global trajectory can still overshoot. The condensation flux is plotted as −j divided by mH × (1 cm⁻³) × (1 km s⁻¹). Positive plotted values therefore mean negative physical j. The physical mass flux has units g cm⁻² s⁻¹; the density unit implicit in the source’s compact axis label is explicit here. Toward Figure 7: extend the pressure range. 33 × 49 samples. The dark dashed curve marks Tcrit = 10,000 K. Here the white region consists of 669 samples with no terminal point inside the declared 20,000 K search window; it is not assigned a physical class by extrapolating the rate fit. It must not be read as an absence of steady solutions in the paper. PNGSVGAll decisions / CSVComputed boundaries / CSV The published Figure 7 extends beyond the bistable-pressure interval. This prototype keeps a temperature window and an explicit CNM boundary branch; those restrictions explain much of the difference in displayed coverage. The exported decisions distinguish restricted coverage from the paper’s classifications. Check the equilibrium landmarks first. Equations (5)–(7) set the thermal equilibrium curve. Equation (16), the conductivity-weighted net-loss integral, selects the saturation pressure. Equilibrium data / CSVSVG The printed cooling fit gives Pmin/kB = 1,597.45, Pmax/kB = 5,007.00, and Psat/kB = 2,822.88 K cm⁻³. The source quotes 1596 in the text / 1598 in Figure 1, 5012, and 2823. These small differences are retained. At Pc/kB = 3,000 K cm⁻³, the matched condensation ZP flux is −j = 0.00315993 in the plotted normalization, close to the quoted 0.0032. The calculation preserves constant mass and momentum flux and uses the full plus-density branch of equation (11), rather than imposing constant pressure throughout the front. What is being solved? ρv = j · ρv² + P = M ρ(T) = [M + √(M²−4ℛj²T)]/(2ℛT) d(F²)/dT = ℛj[(γ+1)/(γ−1)+M/√(M²−4ℛj²T)]F + 2κρℒ Here dθ = κdT and F = dθ/dx = κdT/dx. The physical conductive heat flux is −F. The CNM boundary is a thermal equilibrium with F = 0, approached along its outgoing saddle eigenvector. The source heating/cooling fit, pure atomic hydrogen, γ = 5/3, and κ = 2500√T are used. For node-like targets, the solver follows log(F) and refines the remaining temperature distance. A captured trajectory has F proportional to that distance; a crossing retains finite F. Two consecutive refinements must agree. Ambiguous cases remain white. Grid boundaries have not been digitized against the published figure. Prepared for technical review Two implementation questions to discuss with the authors. Continuation of the CNM boundary: at large imposed flux, the implemented plus-density branch can lose its outgoing CNM saddle. How should the boundary or branch be continued to recover the rest of the published C–C coverage? The reference state for jcrit: what temperature interval and loss normalization were used to choose Tm in section 4.1.2? The prototype does not infer an unprinted selection, so it omits that overlay. These are questions about the present implementation and interpretation. They are not assertions of errors in the paper. A useful first review package is this page, the nine example checks, the source audit, and the two grid CSVs. The first technical milestone is agreement on these model choices. Quantitative boundary comparisons, finer sampling, and broader continuation can then follow. The front lineage provides the context connecting Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner, Penston–Brown, Nagashima, and later front studies. Run the steady calculation. Download the five files below into one directory. This is a small steady ODE calculation rather than a multidimensional simulation. The report records actual runtime; changing the grid or solver settings changes the cost. front_model.pyreproduce.pyconfig.jsonsource-audit.jsonrequirements.txtTechnical notes python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce.py --output output All 30 checks pass, including nine published classification examples and their refinement, matched ZP integrations, equilibrium landmarks, mass and momentum conservation, critical-point pressure, and an independent finite-difference derivative. The validation report records every measurement and tolerance, the map’s coverage counts, runtime, and hashes. Passing these checks does not validate the masked regions, the omitted jcrit overlay, shock continuation, or a complete reproduction of Figures 5 and 7. Source. Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), source preprint ↗ Published article, MNRAS 423, 3638–3645 ↗ The inspected PDF is arXiv:1204.5532v2, 14 May 2012. The template’s 2002/2018 header is not its publication date. Original implementation code is MIT. documents.title: Thermal equilibrium · Koyama & Inutsuka 2002 · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Koyama & Inutsuka (2002) → Koyama & Inutsuka 2002 / Corrected analytic fit / Equilibrium benchmark One cooling law. Two stable phases. Balance heating and cooling, follow the stable and unstable branches, and locate the pressure that supports a static planar conductive front. A new diagnostic of the corrected model, with numerical validation. This does not reproduce the original two-dimensional simulation or claim to digitize an equilibrium figure from the 2002 paper. The same cooling law underlies our Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) front prototype. Temperature, density and pressure. Pure atomic H: n = ρ/mH and P/kB = nT. The corrected fit gives isobaric instability between 184.000 and 5039.419 K, corresponding to densities between 0.993567 and 8.681810 cm⁻³. The endpoints are marginal. Dots mark the cold, intermediate and warm intersections at the ZP saturation pressure. PNGSVGEquilibria / CSV With net volumetric cooling Q = n²Λ − nΓ, thermal equilibrium gives n = Γ/Λ(T) and P/kB = TΓ/Λ(T). Here Γ = 2 × 10⁻²⁶ erg per H atom per second; Λ is in erg cm³ s⁻¹. Let β = d ln Λ / d ln T. At equilibrium, (∂Q/∂T)P = nΓ(β − 1)/T. The local isobaric thermal mode is stable for β > 1 and unstable for β < 1. These branch labels omit the wavelength dependence of conduction, which stabilizes sufficiently small scales. The isochoric derivative is positive throughout the displayed interval. The plotted 10–10,000 K range is a diagnostic choice, not a claim that a temperature-only fit describes all chemistry or ionization there. The turning pressures are Pmin/kB = 1597.453 and Pmax/kB = 5007.000 K cm⁻³. Two stable equilibria share a pressure between these limits; a static conductive front imposes an additional condition. ZP saturation and its equilibrium points. Psat/kB = 2822.884297 K cm⁻³. For a planar, static front with zero conductive flux at each end, integrate d(κ dT/dx)/dx = Q to obtain ∫TcTw κ(T) Q(T,P) dT = 0. We use κ = 2500√T erg cm⁻¹ K⁻¹ s⁻¹. An unweighted equal-area construction on the pressure–density plot would give a different condition. Cold endpoint T = 54.980188 K n = 51.343664 cm⁻³ Isobarically stable Intermediate intersection T = 1364.881273 K n = 2.068227 cm⁻³ Isobarically unstable Warm endpoint T = 6417.132178 K n = 0.439898 cm⁻³ Isobarically stable The intermediate point is the third intersection of the common-pressure line with the equilibrium curve. It is not a third asymptotic endpoint of this cold-to-warm static front. Uniform equilibria have no temperature gradient; conduction selects the connecting front without moving the equilibrium curve. Pressure and all three points / CSVPrecision and checks / JSONCross-model landmark registry / JSON Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), equations (4)–(7), use the same pure-H pressure convention, corrected rates and conductivity. Our two implementations agree on Psat to better than 10⁻¹⁰ relative precision. The paper prints Psat/kB = 2823, Pmax/kB = 5012, and Pmin/kB = 1596 in the text or 1598 in Figure 1. We retain these small numerical differences instead of fitting coefficients to the labels. A nonzero mass flux changes the front problem; uniform thermal equilibrium alone does not determine the pressure–mass-flux classification. For the FGH/GHF prototype, the bounded saturation search is recorded separately. Its density includes H and He nuclei plus electrons in the pressure. Its unresolved historical coefficients prevent assigning a historical FGH saturation value. Pressure tilts the two thermal wells. Compare P/Psat = 0.9, 1 and 1.1 using the same corrected cooling law, pure-H density convention and Parker conductivity as the equilibrium benchmark. This is a new static-front diagnostic of the model, not an original-paper figure reproduction. The cold minimum sets V = 0 separately at each pressure; all curves share one vertical scale, the intermediate barrier at saturation. Blue marks cold equilibria, orange intermediate equilibria, and green warm equilibria. The wide figure compares logarithmic temperature (top) with the natural conduction coordinate (bottom). On narrow screens the temperature panels are stacked vertically. The minima are strongly asymmetric in the conduction coordinate. Full comparison / SVGFull comparison / PNGStacked temperature panels / SVGAll curves / CSVEquilibria, depths & checks / JSON The coordinate and potential have explicit definitions. Q(T,P) = n²Λ(T) − nΓ, n = (P/kB)/T κ(T) = 2500 √T θ(T) = ∫κ(T) dT = (5000/3) T^(3/2) V(θ(T),P) = ∫[Tcold(P) → T] κ(s) Q(s,P) ds ∂V/∂θ = Q θ has units erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ and V has units erg² cm⁻⁴ s⁻², the square of an energy flux. V is an effective static-front potential, not the thermodynamic free energy of the gas. Its additive constant is arbitrary; choosing Vcold = 0 makes the difference between the two minima directly visible. The shared scale is Vbarrier,sat = 3.425672655 × 10⁻¹⁸ erg² cm⁻⁴ s⁻². At a thermal equilibrium, ∂²V/∂θ² = (∂Q/∂T)P / κ. Thus the two isobarically stable equilibria are minima and the unstable intersection is a maximum. A monotonic relabeling from θ to log T preserves these extrema and their depths; it changes the apparent shape and width of the wells. Below saturation P/kB = 2540.596 K cm⁻³. documents.title: Eigenfunction reconstruction specification · Kim & Kim2013 · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Kim & Kim2013 / Source-audited specification / Not yet computed Reconstruct the mode. Keep its components coupled. Matching a growth-rate curve is only part of the task. The required result is the spatial eigenfunction, with its temperature, velocity, flux and pressure information preserved under one amplitude and phase convention. This page defines the reconstruction and its acceptance criteria. No Kim2013 background front, eigenvalue, eigenfunction or source digitization has been computed in this project yet. Public specification and status. The original study is Kim & Kim, Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium. Figure9 is the primary comparison. The MU69 example compares temperature and transverse velocity on two different transverse cuts. The reconstruction must produce both curves from the same mode: Temperature panel: δT/Tbackground at y = 0.5Ly. Velocity panel: δvy/vx1 at y = 0.25Ly. Source comparison time: t/tgr = 2; pressure P/kB = 1800 K cm⁻³. Table3 uses Ly = 1.06 pc; Table1 quotes the fastest wavelength as 1.05 pc. Keep that rounding distinction when selecting k. Compare signs, extrema, zero crossings, relative amplitudes and far-field decay. Digitization must distinguish the source’s analytical solid curves from its simulation dots, and retain axis calibration and reading uncertainty. A common amplitude alignment can test shape and relative amplitude; matching the absolute amplitude after the source’s initially shifted front requires a separate initial-mode projection or linear initial-value calculation. The origin is fixed by T = √(T1T2). Temperature divided by Tbackground is a pointwise conversion from the solver’s δT/T1, rather than the same plotted variable. Match the paper’s background model first. The source uses the corrected KI cooling fit but a constant conductivity κ = 10⁵ erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ K⁻¹, with m = 1.37mH, n = ρ/m and γ = 5/3. Its reported saturation pressure is Psat/kB = 2282 K cm⁻³. The existing KI/Iwasaki benchmark instead uses κ = 2500√T and has a different computed saturation pressure. Copying its front unchanged would change the problem. Reconstruct the steady boundary-value problem and its mass-flux eigenvalue from equations (9)–(13), before assembling the linear operator. Figures2–3 and Table1 provide background comparisons. Report residuals against the rounded source values; do not fit coefficients or redefine the origin to force agreement. Five state components, one eigenfunction. xi = x / ell_D1 nu = k ell_D1 sigma = Omega / (k vx1) state = (J, V, M, Theta, dTheta/dxi) Theta = temperature Fourier amplitude / T1 AppendixA equations (A7)–(A10) form a five-dimensional first-order problem. The source’s state-vector order differs from the presentation order in (A6); it must be explicit in code. The upstream regular basis contains incompressible and thermal modes. Downstream it contains incompressible, vortex and thermal modes. Match the full state, using the regularity and outgoing-mode conditions of (A11)–(A21). delta vy / vx1 = Re[ -i V(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ] delta T / Tbackground = (T1/Tbackground) Re[ Theta(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ] The growing branch may use real state amplitudes; the transverse-velocity Fourier amplitude still carries the explicit −i factor. This gives the transverse phase relation used by the two Figure9 cuts. Independent component normalizations or phase rotations would destroy that information. Use the paper’s C1 = 1 convention, or a documented equivalent single gauge. Export all five state components, the basis coefficients and reconstructed physical perturbations, with units and the retained approximation order. The source’s low-Mach/isobaric reduction retains hydrodynamic coupling; it must not be replaced by setting pressure and velocity perturbations to zero or advertised as an exact full-compressible spectrum. Required verification gates. Background: converge the thermal front, mass flux and energy balance before solving for perturbations. Operator: independently check the linearization and heat-loss derivative, and substitute every far-field basis vector into the constant-state equations. Eigenfunction: retain equation, matching and boundary residuals for all components. Use scale-aware norms without ratios through zero components. Convergence: enlarge both far fields, refine the spatial representation and tighten tolerances. Both the eigenvalue and the normalized mode shape must converge. Mode identity: follow the same branch by eigenfunction overlap as k changes. Recover the k = 0 translation mode and long-wave displacement limit without imposing them on finite-k modes. Source comparison: reconstruct both Figure9 cuts with a common normalization. Validate a representative mode with an independent discretization or small-amplitude linear evolution. Dispersion: then reproduce Figure5 at P/kB = 1700, 1800 and 1900 K cm⁻³. Its ordinate is ΩellD1/vx1 = νσ, not σ alone. Check (A24), the peak and the cutoff; the downstream vortex tail becomes long as σ approaches zero. A full nonlinear two-dimensional run is a separate, optional task. The coupled Fourier-mode eigenproblem is the required core. Source questions remain visible. The inspected v2 text on page5 gives Lf = 0.13 pc for the 1800 K cm⁻³ evaporation example, whereas Table1 gives 0.29 pc. This must be checked against the journal version and definitions. It is not a reason to tune a coordinate scale. The Figure9 initial-value amplitude convention also needs clarification before claiming an absolute-amplitude reproduction. Source review: arXiv1310.2940v2, 6 December2013. Sections2–3 and AppendixA read; pages3,5,6,9,14–16 visually inspected. Source hash, conventions, targets and open questions / JSON. Cross-model pressure registry distinguishes source-reported values from computed results.

documents.text: Public progress · reviewed 2026-11-21 Published results. Bounded next questions. Make the published research resources discoverable and usable, with working code/data links and explicit verification limits. New scientific implementations remain queued. This page is the public work record. Read the status and limits here without a GitHub account. Planned work has not been implemented; one scientific implementation is normally active at a time. Work record / JSONGet code and data Published outcomes KI2002: pressure-dependent potential wells Published. Shared normalization at 0.9, 1 and 1.1 saturation pressure; code, configuration, CSV and independent checks. No compressible front speed is inferred. Illustrative 2D thermal-condensation movie Published. Movie, initial/final states and numerical benchmarks. Enhanced conduction broadens interfaces; this is not a historical reproduction or sustained turbulence. Next scientific questions Kim & Kim2013: coupled Figure9 eigenfunctions Planned. Source-audited specification only; no solver yet. Completion requires coupled components, one common amplitude/phase convention, boundary/domain convergence and an independent comparison. Compressible flow versus reduced reaction–diffusion models Planned. Explain pressure, momentum, advection and compressional work using existing equations. Nearly uniform pressure does not imply zero flow. A new simulation is a separate task. Iwasaki2012: one missing branch or critical-flux example Planned. Choose one bounded trajectory diagnostic and preserve the nine existing classifications. A full map recomputation is not required. Schwarz1972: timing and mesh sensitivity Planned. Reuse existing resolution studies and separate source-reading, model and discretization uncertainties. Continuum convergence of the narrow conductive layer is not established. Deferred until new evidence FGH1969: historical coefficient recovery Deferred. Restart only with a recoverable historical rate/cross-section, a checkable convention explaining a residual, or equivalent new evidence. Do not tune rates to force the original curve. Keep the scientific limits visible. Field1965 calculations are derived from the source equations; pointwise digitization is a separate task. Historical movie provenance is documented, but exact original run inputs and paper-figure matches remain unverified. The archive does not reproduce every result in every cataloged paper. Specifications, implementations, numerical checks and historical agreement are separate milestones. See each exhibit for units, boundary conditions, source editions and unresolved questions. Further directions Small comparisons of reduced and compressible models, bounded front diagnostics, KI2000/2004, and analysis of available multidimensional outputs remain candidates. Full high-cost reruns are optional; no release date is assigned to these scientific extensions.

documents.title: Research paths · The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Research paths / Reading list From two phases to chemistry and cloud formation. FGH established a two-phase picture. Later work changed the heating and chemical inputs, then followed fronts, turbulence, and magnetized clouds. This reading list connects those questions to the calculations we can document and explore. Listed references are not completed reproductions. Bibliography and abstracts have been checked; equations, target figures, and data availability need individual review. This page groups papers by research path; each path runs from oldest to newest. For one chronological list across all paths, open all papers by year. Publication years are used where confirmed, with preprint dates noted separately. Scope for modern simulations Choose the scientific question before the computing budget. Reproducing a large multidimensional simulation can require substantial computing time, storage, and access to original inputs. Our modern-paper exhibits can instead provide a source guide, documented setup, analysis of available outputs, or a small benchmark that isolates a physical mechanism. Source and method: link the paper and any public code, inputs, and datasets; record what is actually available. Reuse and analysis: regenerate a diagnostic from released outputs where possible, preserving units, provenance, and processing steps. Small calculations: evaluate an analytic relation, a one-zone chemical model, a front, or a convergence test within an explicit reduced scope. Optional full runs: record the resolution, solver, hardware, wall time, and storage needed. A full 2D/3D rerun is not a condition for completing a source or analysis exhibit. For new nonlinear thermal-instability simulation exhibits, the thermal-conduction treatment and resolution of its relevant scales are selection criteria to audit explicitly. Analytical theory and microphysical rate references are documented separately. Digitized published curves will be identified as digitizations. Reduced models will state their omissions; their results will not be labeled as full-simulation reproductions. Reading path Foundations: thermal stability, buoyancy and conductive phase exchange Parker (1953) provides a pre-Field historical starting point. Chandrasekhar (1961) supplies the buoyancy-driven convection and Boussinesq comparison. Balbus (1986) extends the local stability analysis to evolving backgrounds, while Begelman & McKee (1990) treats conductive mass exchange between phases. Analytical background references and conduction-resolved simulation exhibits have different roles. 1953 / Reference listed Instability of Thermal Fields Eugene N. Parker ApJ 117, 431 Thermal-field stability before Field (1965), with a solar-atmosphere application. Proposed scope: Historical background: compare the temperature-field equation, conduction, and heating assumptions with Field’s hydrodynamic analysis. Keep the original solar application distinct from neutral interstellar gas. Source & bibliography ↗ 1961 / Reference listed Hydrodynamic and Hydromagnetic Stability S. Chandrasekhar Monograph: Clarendon Press, Oxford (1961); later Dover edition, ISBN 9780486640716 Buoyancy-driven thermal convection and its Boussinesq approximation: a fluid-dynamical comparison with radiative thermal instability. Proposed scope: Proposed entry point: the onset of convection in a layer heated from below, followed by a neutral Rayleigh curve for explicitly specified mechanical and thermal boundaries. Retain velocity, perturbation pressure and buoyancy; distinguish this mechanism from the Field radiative-condensation mode. No equation or figure reproduction yet. Source & bibliography ↗ 1972 / Computed prototype / technical review pending Formation of Clouds in a Cooling Interstellar Medium Schwarz, McCray & Stein ApJ175,673–686 Thermal conduction and recombination shape perturbations growing in an isochorically cooling background. Proposed scope: Early-time linear Figure2 plus a nonlinear3pc/10percent Lagrangian prototype without a Riemann solver. Historical-scale64/96/128-cell runs and a512-cell auxiliary comparison document conservation, timing/input differences, and unresolved conductive-front resolution. Source & bibliography ↗Cooling-medium condensation: Figure2 prototype →Nonlinear Lagrangian condensation → 1986 / Reference listed Local Dynamic Thermal Instability Steven A. Balbus ApJ Letters 303, L79–L82 Local thermal-instability criteria for time-dependent background flows; transport processes are omitted in this analytical treatment. Proposed scope: Compare the loss-per-unit-mass convention and the derivative of loss/T with Field’s equilibrium criterion. This is analytical background, not a conduction-resolved nonlinear simulation exhibit. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1990 / Reference listed Global Effects of Thermal Conduction on Two-Phase Media Begelman & McKee ApJ 358, 375–391 Thermal conduction transfers mass between phases through evaporation and condensation; a Field-length scale organizes the competition with heating and cooling. Proposed scope: Audit the Field-length definition and the assumptions of classical conduction, uniform pressure, and small cloud filling factor. Compare reduced evolution equations while retaining the original thermal model and application. Source & bibliography ↗ Convection and radiative condensation are distinct: Chandrasekhar’s textbook is included as a foundational monograph, not a journal paper. Its proposed benchmark is buoyancy-driven convection of a layer heated from below. Rayleigh-number onset must not be identified with the cooling-derivative criterion for the Field condensation mode, which does not require gravity. The Boussinesq comparison retains velocity, a pressure constraint and buoyancy while filtering acoustic compressibility. It does not mean zero flow or zero pressure gradient. The resulting hierarchy for the proposed explanation is: selected reaction–diffusion models → Boussinesq fluid dynamics → compressible thermal gas. These are different approximations and drivers, not a single universal equation. Spiegel & Veronis (1960), On the Boussinesq Approximation for a Compressible Fluid, gives a primary-source account of its assumptions: a thin layer relative to scale heights and suitably small fluctuations. Density variations remain in the buoyancy force. The compressible-fluid reduction also requires care with the adiabatic temperature gradient. The textbook’s bibliography is checked; its exact equations, sections and figures are not yet audited because full-text access attempts failed. No textbook figure is claimed reproduced. Source review and proposed scope / JSON. Reading path Rate and ionization lineage: atomic data, grains and charge balance A separate branch follows the atomic and molecular data, radiative yields, and heating/cooling prescriptions behind gas models. Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) extends the path to grain-size-dependent charge equilibrium in shielded molecular gas. These papers are not all chemical-network rate catalogs. 1960 / Source rates audited / truncated model Cooling of the Interstellar Clouds in Region of Neutral Hydrogen Takayanagi & Nishimura PASJ 12, 77–105 H₂ rotational excitation and the cooling budget of neutral clouds. Proposed scope: 34 printed upward H + para-H2 rates audited on p. 82; a truncated steady level calculation is compared with 60 printed cooling values. Twelve numerical checks pass, while the largest Table 2 discrepancy is retained at about 21.72%. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗H₂ rates & cooling comparison → 1961 / Reference listed Radiations from the Interstellar Hydrogen Atoms Hayakawa, Nishimura & Takayanagi PASJ 13, 184–206 Excitation and ionization of interstellar hydrogen by suprathermal particles, connecting radiation and cloud heating. Proposed scope: Audit particle spectra, excitation/ionization definitions, and radiation/heating yields separately from thermally averaged chemical rates. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1968 / Reference listed Heating of H I Regions by Energetic Particles Spitzer & Tomasko ApJ 152, 971 Energetic-particle heating and ionization of H I, including secondary-electron energy deposition and metal cooling. Proposed scope: Prioritize the definitions of primary/total ionization rates and energy per ionization when comparing with FGH/GHF. Audit secondary-electron treatment, abundances, and collider channels before implementing a heating benchmark. Source & bibliography ↗ 1969 / Reference listed Thermal and Dynamical Evolution of Gas Clouds of Various Masses Hattori, Nakano & Hayashi Progress of Theoretical Physics 42, 781–798 Gas-cloud evolution with molecular/atomic line cooling, grains, radiation, and ionization in transparent and opaque regimes. Proposed scope: Inventory the individual heating/cooling prescriptions and their cited atomic/molecular data before choosing a small thermal-evolution calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1972 / Reference listed Heating and Ionization of HI Regions Dalgarno & McCray ARA&A 10, 375–426 A historical review of heating and ionization processes in neutral interstellar gas. Proposed scope: Use as a source map for historical heating/cooling processes. Audit individual formulas, ionization fractions, abundance assumptions, and original rate references before selecting a cooling-curve calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1991 / Reference listed Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi ApJ 368, 181–194 Ionization–recombination equilibrium with electrons, ions and charged grains; grain-size distributions affect magnetic coupling in shielded molecular clouds. Proposed scope: Candidate: Figure1 charged-species abundances at10K for the standard MRN grain distribution, before comparing the other grain models. Recover the required reaction rates and PaperI inputs first. This is a charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-equilibrium curve or a reproduced magnetic-flux-loss calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Field et al. (1968) discusses Takayanagi and Nishimura’s H₂ excitation data. FGH (1969) cites Hayakawa, Nishimura and Takayanagi’s cosmic-ray heating work. Hattori, Nakano and Hayashi’s reference list includes both papers. These links identify a route for source tracing; they do not establish that later models use identical coefficients. For each future rate record, we will distinguish cross sections, rate coefficients, energy-loss coefficients, volumetric rates, and yields. Species, colliders, units, normalization, validity range, population assumptions, source equation/table, and correction/code version will accompany the numerical formula. The Takayanagi–Nishimura rate audit now transcribes 34 coefficients and tests a finite level model. Its Table 2 mismatches remain visible. Other coefficient sets still require equation/table review; the citation links alone do not validate them. Lineage evidence and proposed coefficient-record fields / JSON Ionization fraction is a separate branch: Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) calculates electron, ion and charged-grain abundances before magnetic coupling. Figures1–4 compare grain distributions. Figure1 is a possible small charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-balance calculation. Its axes use abundances relative to total hydrogen nuclei and nH/ζ, with ζ the ionization rate per hydrogen molecule; these conventions must not be silently interchanged with FGH’s atomic-gas definitions. The paper calls Umebayashi & Nakano (1990), Magnetic flux loss from interstellar clouds, MNRAS243,103–113, PaperI and builds on its reaction scheme. The publisher’s abstract confirms an ionization–recombination equilibrium calculation; its full rate-table audit remains pending. Distinguish the ionization rate ζ from the resulting electron fraction, and distinguish both from a cooling coefficient. Source review and parameter conventions / JSON. Reading path Heating, cooling, and public chemistry Cosmic-ray heating in FGH, grain photoelectric heating in Bakes & Tielens (1994), Wolfire (1995, 2003), and GOW (2017) provide a path to public chemistry implementations. These models use different physical assumptions; they are not interchangeable cooling prescriptions. 1994 / Reference listed The Photoelectric Heating Mechanism for Very Small Graphitic Grains and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons Bakes & Tielens ApJ 427 (1994) Photoelectric heating by small carbonaceous grains and PAHs, including grain charging and a heating-efficiency prescription. Proposed scope: Trace the photoelectric-heating input used in later neutral-gas models. Audit radiation-field normalization, electron density, grain population, temperature range, and net gas–grain energy exchange before plotting the efficiency fit. Source & bibliography ↗ 1995 / Reference listed The Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium Wolfire, Hollenbach, McKee, Tielens & Bakes ApJ 443, 152–168 Photoelectric heating by small grains and PAHs, X-ray/cosmic-ray ionization, and atomic phase equilibrium. Proposed scope: Audit the heating/cooling terms and identify a local equilibrium curve for a modest-cost calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2003 / Reference listed Neutral Atomic Phases of the Interstellar Medium in the Galaxy Wolfire, McKee, Hollenbach & Tielens ApJ 587, 278–311 Revised atomic-gas microphysics and the allowed two-phase pressure range across the Galactic disk. Proposed scope: Compare physical inputs with the 1995 model before attempting an equilibrium calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2017 / Reference listed A Simple and Accurate Network for Hydrogen and Carbon Chemistry in the Interstellar Medium Gong, Ostriker & Wolfire ApJ 843, 38 A compact chemical network with an author-maintained public PDR implementation and rate corrections. Proposed scope: Pin a corrected rate/code version, inspect units and validity ranges, then choose a small chemical or thermal benchmark. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2023 / Reference listed Implementation of Chemistry in the Athena++ Code Gong, Ho, Stone, Ostriker, Caselli, Grassi, C.-G. Kim, J.-G. Kim & Halevi ApJS 268, 42 A public chemistry framework including GOW17, general KIDA networks, and coupled thermal/chemical evolution. Proposed scope: Begin with published tests, public inputs, or a small one-zone/1D case; full 3D runs are optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Reading path Phase-transition fronts: from planar balance to curved clouds Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner (1969) and Penston–Brown (1970) connect to Elphick–Regev–Shaviv (1992), Ferrara–Shchekinov (1993), Shchekinov–Ibáñez (2001), Nagashima and collaborators’ curved-front work, and Kim & Kim’s (2013) conductive evaporation-front instability. Static balance, steady mass flux, perturbations, and spherical survival times are distinct computational questions. 1969 / Reference listed The Phase Equilibrium and Dynamics of a Gas Volume That Is Heated and Cooled Zel’dovich & Pikel’ner Soviet Physics JETP 29, 170–173; Russian original: ZhETF 56, 310–315 Conductive interfaces select the stationary two-phase pressure; away from that pressure the boundary moves. Proposed scope: Candidate: the planar saturation condition and a steady front or front-speed calculation. Specify the heat-loss law, conductivity, signs, and boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗ 1970 / Reference listed The Cloud–Intercloud Phase-Change in the Interstellar Medium Penston & Brown MNRAS 150, 373–388 Thermal balance across a conducting cloud–intercloud interface adds a condition beyond pressure balance. Proposed scope: Candidate: compare the stationary interface criterion and thermal timescales with the Zel’dovich–Pikel’ner formulation before choosing a small front calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1992 / Reference listed Dynamics of Fronts in Thermally Bistable Fluids Elphick, Regev & Shaviv ApJ 392, 106–117 Isobaric conductive fronts, a Lyapunov functional, equal-depth potential minima and interacting cloud boundaries. Proposed scope: The source equations are reviewed; no numerical reproduction yet. Candidate: the cubic benchmark, static kink or front speed versus potential-depth difference, retaining the Lagrangian mass coordinate and state-dependent mobility. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 1993 / Reference listed Dynamics of Conductive/Cooling Fronts: Cloud Implosion and Thermal Solitons Ferrara & Shchekinov ApJ 417, 595 Conductive and radiative interfaces admit static and steady fronts, cloud compression, and soliton-like solutions. Proposed scope: Start with planar static/steady front equations, boundary heat fluxes, and the mechanical analogy. Select a small ODE benchmark after auditing the heat-loss law, conductivity, and pressure/flow assumptions. Cloud implosion simulations are a separate, optional scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2001 / Reference listed Interaction of Small Planar Perturbations with Cooling-Conductive Fronts Shchekinov & Ibáñez ApJ 563, 209–220 Acoustic and entropy perturbations interact with steady subsonic cold–hot fronts in one-dimensional planar geometry, with heating, cooling, and thermal conduction. Proposed scope: First audit the steady planar background and its mass-flux eigenvalue at prescribed pressure, as discussed by Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012), section 3. Then consider reflection/transmission coefficients as a separate perturbation benchmark. Do not equate this one-dimensional perturbation problem with transverse front corrugation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2005 / Reference listed Evaporation and condensation of H I clouds in thermally bistable interstellar media: semi-analytic description of isobaric dynamics of curved interfaces Nagashima, Koyama & Inutsuka MNRAS Letters 361, L25–L29 Curvature modifies evaporation and condensation for cylindrical, spherical, and general fronts under an isobaric approximation. Proposed scope: Candidate: evaluate the semi-analytic curvature correction and compare planar, cylindrical, and spherical limits using a small ODE calculation. Keep the polynomial heat-loss model distinct from later realistic fits. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed How Long Can Tiny H I Clouds Survive? Nagashima, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ Letters 652, L41–L44 Spherical cloud evaporation times depend on cloud size and ambient pressure, with a quasi-steady interpretation. Proposed scope: Candidate: reproduce the analytic timescale/critical-radius relation and, if practical, a one-dimensional radial benchmark. Large multidimensional reruns are unnecessary for this scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed Nonlinear Development of Thermal Instability without External Forcing Koyama & Inutsuka arXiv:astro-ph/0605528 (2006 preprint; journal publication not verified) Conduction, viscosity, and cloud motions in multidimensional nonlinear thermal instability without external forcing. Proposed scope: Start with the preprint’s physical mechanism, diagnostics, and any available outputs. A full 2D/3D rerun is optional; its journal-publication status remains unverified. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2013 / Reference listed Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium Jeong-Gyu Kim & Woong-Tae Kim ApJ 779, 48 Thermal conduction suppresses short-wavelength corrugations of CNM–WNM evaporation fronts. Linear stability analysis connects to nonlinear front deformation and enhanced evaporation. Proposed scope: Detailed reconstruction of AppendixA with coupled eigenfunctions as the required output. Primary target: Figure9 temperature and transverse-velocity profiles from the same normalized mode; supporting targets are the background front, Figure5 dispersion and long-wave/cutoff limits. Source-audited plan only; no Kim eigenfunctions computed yet. Nonlinear2D remains separate and optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Gradient-flow connection: Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) gives an isobaric reduction in Lagrangian mass coordinates, a Lyapunov functional, equal-minima ZP fronts and front interactions. The biophysical comparisons follow wave-pinning, conserved protein redistribution and neural excitability, with their distinct conservation laws and scope. Conductive front instability: Kim & Kim (2013) explicitly includes thermal conduction in the linear stability analysis and nonlinear evolution of evaporation fronts. This provides a comparison with Inoue et al. (2006), while Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) supplies a related steady-front classification. A stability spectrum, a steady-solution classification, and nonlinear saturation are different reproduction targets. The user requires detailed coupled eigenfunctions, especially Figure9, as the Kim2013 reconstruction target; a dispersion curve alone will not complete that task. Steady flow and perturbations: Ferrara & Shchekinov (1993) studies static/steady front properties and their dynamical evolution. Shchekinov & Ibáñez (2001) studies planar acoustic/entropy perturbations interacting with steady subsonic fronts. In section 3, Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) explicitly describes the latter work as determining the ZP mass flux j(P) through an eigenvalue problem. We will audit the steady background before attempting perturbation coefficients. This citation does not establish identical cooling laws or numerical parameters. Related entries: Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama (2006) addresses front stability; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) studies dynamical condensation fronts; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2014) studies interfacial energy transfer in a bistable medium. The Field-condition paper provides a connection to conduction and resolution. Different heat-loss laws, geometries, and dynamical approximations must be preserved when comparing these studies. A reading path is not proof of identical assumptions or coefficients. Reading path Hennebelle, Burkert, and collaborators: condensation and fragmentation Converging flows connect thermal bistability to cloud formation. Hennebelle and collaborators examine dynamical condensation, magnetic fields, and turbulent two-phase gas; Burkert and collaborators examine cooling perturbations, colliding flows, and fragmentation. These are related research paths, not a claim that the listed papers share the same authors or physical model. 1999 / Reference listed Dynamical condensation in a thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Hennebelle & Pérault A&A 351, 309–322 Transonic converging warm flows produce cold condensations; self-similar non-isobaric solutions describe early condensation. Proposed scope: Audit the self-similar solution and size/velocity thresholds versus ambient pressure. Start with analytic relations or a planar one-dimensional benchmark; preserve the original heating/cooling and boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗ 2000 / Reference listed Dynamical condensation in a magnetized and thermally bistable flow. Application to interstellar cirrus Hennebelle & Pérault A&A 359, 1124–1138 Oblique magnetic fields and tension alter condensation in slab geometry; transverse motions can align fields or flows and permit compression. Proposed scope: Compare nonmagnetic, transverse-field, and oblique-field limits using the published self-similar analysis and a small one-dimensional MHD benchmark. Audit the angle and field-strength assumptions before choosing a figure. Source & bibliography ↗ 2000 / Reference listed Thermal Instability and the Formation of Clumpy Gas Clouds Burkert & Lin ApJ 537, 270–282 During radiative cooling, the transition from isobaric to isochoric evolution limits perturbation growth and influences the characteristic clump scale; conduction suppresses small scales. Proposed scope: Audit the growth, transition-temperature, and nonlinear-amplitude estimates. Use small analytic or time-dependent perturbation calculations before considering fragmentation simulations; distinguish cooling backgrounds from thermal equilibrium. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2005 / Reference listed Thermal condensation in a turbulent atomic hydrogen flow Audit & Hennebelle A&A 433, 1–13 Two-dimensional turbulent converging flows condense warm H I into cold structures; the thermally unstable gas fraction correlates with turbulence. Proposed scope: Start with the semi-analytical model for unstable gas and its relation to turbulence. Reanalyse published diagnostics or available outputs after a provenance audit. A full high-resolution two-dimensional run is optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2006 / Reference listed The Birth of Molecular Clouds: Formation of Atomic Precursors in Colliding Flows Heitsch, Slyz, Devriendt, Hartmann & Burkert ApJ 648, 1052–1065 Colliding atomic flows develop structure through dynamical and thermal instabilities before molecular hydrogen begins to form. Proposed scope: Document the inflow, cooling law, geometry, and instability diagnostics. Prefer reanalysis of available density/temperature and fragmentation outputs; do not require a full multidimensional rerun or imply that this model follows the molecular stage. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2007 / Reference listed On the structure of the turbulent interstellar atomic hydrogen. I. Physical characteristics. Influence and nature of turbulence in a thermally bistable flow Hennebelle & Audit A&A 465, 431–443 High-resolution two-dimensional bistable turbulence produces small-scale CNM structures, a cloud mass spectrum, and distinct density and velocity statistics. Proposed scope: Begin with the analytical mass-spectrum argument and definitions of the measured spectra. Recompute diagnostics only from accessible, documented outputs; retain the dimensionality dependence and avoid treating a small run as a reproduction of the full statistics. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2008 / Reference listed Fragmentation of Shocked Flows: Gravity, Turbulence, and Cooling Heitsch, Hartmann & Burkert ApJ 683, 786–795 Comparing dynamical, thermal, and gravitational timescales identifies where shocked flows fragment and seed local collapse. Proposed scope: A timescale/regime diagram is a promising inexpensive reproduction target. First audit the cooling law, perturbation scales, background state, and boundaries; keep this calculation distinct from a full flow-driven cloud simulation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Publication years determine the order: Audit & Hennebelle (2005) has a 2004 preprint, and Hennebelle & Audit (2007) has a 2006 preprint. For modest computing budgets, the self-similar, perturbation-growth, semi-analytical, and timescale arguments offer entry points. High-resolution multidimensional statistics require suitable released outputs or a separately documented computing plan. Reading path Inoue: fronts, two-fluid gas, and magnetic fields A path from the stability of phase-transition fronts to converging flows and turbulent molecular clouds. 2006 / Reference listed Structure and Stability of Phase Transition Layers in the Interstellar Medium Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ 652, 1331–1338 CNM/WNM fronts, evaporation and condensation, and corrugational stability. Proposed scope: Candidate: a plane-parallel front or the linear growth relation, after checking boundary conditions. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2007 / Reference listed The Role of Ambipolar Diffusion in the Formation Process of Moderately Magnetized Diffuse Clouds Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama ApJ 658, L99–L102 Two-fluid condensation and the competition between magnetic flux accumulation and ambipolar diffusion. Proposed scope: Candidate: the analytic field-strength estimate or a small 1D verification case. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2008 / Reference listed Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. I: Methodology and Basic Results Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 687, 303–310 Two-fluid coupling and magnetic limits on condensation in converging atomic flows. Proposed scope: Document the method and inputs; consider a coupling benchmark or analysis of available outputs rather than a full 2D rerun. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2009 / Reference listed Two-Fluid MHD Simulations of Converging H I Flows in the Interstellar Medium. II: Are Molecular Clouds Generated Directly from a Warm Neutral Medium? Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 704, 161–169 The angle between inflow and mean magnetic field affects shocked atomic gas and cloud formation. Proposed scope: Compare model assumptions and published diagnostics; reanalyse public outputs if available. Large runs are outside the initial scope. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2012 / Reference listed Formation of Turbulent and Magnetized Molecular Clouds via Accretion Flows of H I Clouds Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 759, 35 Three-dimensional MHD with chemistry, conduction, and accretion of inhomogeneous atomic gas. Proposed scope: Focus on setup documentation, analysis methods, and any available snapshots. Do not require rerunning the full 3D calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ Reading path Iwasaki: condensation, interfaces, and cloud formation Similarity solutions and front structure offer modest-cost entry points. Later multidimensional calculations can be explored through their diagnostics and available data. 2008 / Reference listed Self-similar solutions for the dynamical condensation of a radiative gas layer Iwasaki & Tsuribe MNRAS 387, 1554–1562 Non-equilibrium thermal condensation described by a family of plane-parallel similarity solutions. Proposed scope: Candidate: similarity profiles and limiting scalings, using an ODE solver and a small 1D comparison. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2009 / Reference listed Fragmentation of a dynamically condensing radiative layer Iwasaki & Tsuribe A&A 508, 725–735 Perturbation growth on a time-dependent, dynamically condensing background. Proposed scope: Candidate: linear perturbation evolution on the time-dependent similarity solution, before a full nonlinear calculation. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2012 / Computed prototype / technical review pending Structure of dynamical condensation fronts in the interstellar medium Iwasaki & Inutsuka MNRAS 423, 3638–3645 Condensation-front families parameterized by pressure and mass flux, with cooling- and Field-length regimes. Proposed scope: Confirmed target: Figures 5 and 7, pressure–mass-flux classification. A computed prototype reproduces nine stated example classes and passes 30 checks. Unavailable CNM branches and temperature-limited cells are masked; the jcrit overlay and complete boundary comparison await technical review. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗Figures 5 & 7: computed prototype → 2014 / Reference listed Self-Sustained Turbulence without Dynamical Forcing: A Two-Dimensional Study of a Bistable Interstellar Medium Iwasaki & Inutsuka ApJ 784, 115 Thermal conduction, phase transitions, viscosity, and kinetic-energy transfer in a bistable medium. Proposed scope: Prioritize published energy budgets and analysis of available outputs. A small front problem can isolate the mechanism without reproducing the full 2D run. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ 2019 / Reference listed The Early Stage of Molecular Cloud Formation by Compression of Two-phase Atomic Gases Iwasaki, Tomida, Inoue & Inutsuka ApJ 873, 6; preprint first posted in 2018 Three-dimensional MHD, non-equilibrium chemistry, and the critical magnetic-field/inflow angle for cloud formation. Proposed scope: Candidate: evaluate the analytic critical-angle relation and reanalyse available outputs; full parameter-survey reruns are optional. Source & bibliography ↗Publication / DOI ↗ GOW / Code and rate provenance Follow the corrected rates to their implementation. The original paper, its erratum, a revised preprint, and an evolving code repository are separate references. This is a live page, not a frozen rate version. gow-pdr-code ↗ — Commit recorded for provenance only. Not built or benchmarked here. Model-specific landmarks retain density conventions and unresolved cases. The Maxwell equal-area historical aside traces the primary publications and distinguishes its integral from ZP selection. The same aside develops a scalar Ginzburg–Landau connection, with Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) as a direct precedent. Field’s stability map connects to front and perturbation problems. FGH/GHF two-phase equilibrium prototype, historical ingredients, and reduced cold branch give a starting point for comparing historical and later microphysics.

documents.title: Schwarz, McCray & Stein 1972 · Cooling-medium condensation — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Schwarz, McCray & Stein (1972) → Chapter 03 / Schwarz, McCray & Stein (1972) / Linear prototype Let the background cool. Watch the perturbations grow. Cloud formation can begin while the surrounding gas cools, rather than departing from steady thermal equilibrium. Here the background temperature and ionization evolve together with density perturbations at four wavelengths. First target: the early-time part of Figure 2. The linear equations include conduction and recombination. Cooling is reconstructed from Figure 1, rather than independently recovered from every atomic rate. The run stops at the input-data boundary, about 1.68 Myr. Late-time Figure 2 remains unfinished. A separate nonlinear Lagrangian prototype now follows the 3 pc, 10% perturbation into condensation. A time-dependent background changes the instability problem. Solid lines: the declared linear prototype. Dashed black: background temperature, read on the right axis. Open circles: Figure 2 density readings; black crosses: its temperature readings. Gray: beyond the input domain. The right panel shows the reconstructed cooling input. There is no fitted time rescaling. SVGPNGBackground & perturbations / CSVFigure 2 comparison / CSVNumerical report / JSON Initial conditions: n(H) =0.3 cm⁻³, T =8,200 K, x =n(e)/n(H) =0.05; neutral He/H =0.1. Wavelengths are 0.3,1,3,10 pc. The historical conduction prescription is K(T) =2,500√T in cgs units. No continuing heating is applied. The 0.3 pc mode initially decreases, showing short-wavelength conduction damping. Within the computed window it later reaches about 14.8 times its initial amplitude, while the 1 pc mode reaches about 107. The latter maximum occurs at the domain stop and is not an established peak. These are normalized linear amplitudes, not nonlinear cloud density contrasts. The original curves are not matched exactly. The report gives separate log-RMS discrepancies and scored-point counts for temperature and each wavelength. Points past the domain stop have no model prediction. These descriptive differences are not numerical pass tolerances. Integrate the background and perturbations together. Equations (16)–(18) evolve uniform cooling and recombination. Equations (19)–(24) evolve relative density, pressure, velocity divergence, and ionization perturbations; the equation of state supplies the temperature perturbation. The coefficients change with time, so a single constant exponential growth rate is insufficient. d ln T₀/dt = −1/τC + (2−γ)[x₀/(1.1+x₀)]/τR d ln x₀/dt = −1/τR τC = (1.1+x₀)kT₀ / [n₀(γ−1)Λ] τR = 1/[n₀x₀α⁽²⁾(T₀)] The pressure perturbation contains the conduction term in equation (19). Density amplitudes are normalized to n₁(0) =1; the actual perturbation may be arbitrarily small. Pressure, velocity and relative ionization perturbations initially vanish. This declared initial-mode choice has not been confirmed as the unique Figure 2 initialization. DOP 853 and Radau agree on the computed evolution. Equation (19) is also compared with a centered-difference Jacobian of the original primitive pressure equation, including the changing background normalization. Keep the historical input limits visible. The 39 Figure 1 readings cover x =0.001,0.01,0.1 and T ≈13.93–8,429.74 K. PCHIP interpolates logΛ(logT), with Λ piecewise linear in ionization fraction. A logarithmic-ionization alternative changes the stopping time to about 1.51 Myr, illustrating reconstruction sensitivity. The accepted solution stops at the lowest supported temperature,13.93 K, after 1.679 Myr. It is not continued through an invented cold cooling law. Raw pixels, crop origins, calibration ticks and source hashes accompany the input. Figure 2 readings use the 0–2 Myr ticks bracketing the sampled interval; a single exact affine scale is not assumed for the slightly distorted full scan. Reading envelopes are practical limits, not statistical confidence intervals, and there is no independent second digitization. H recombination uses Hjellming’s (1966) excited-state approximation; the exact fit used by Schwarz and collaborators remains unidentified. Nonpositive linear amplitudes remain in the CSV but are omitted from the log plot; they do not mean negative physical gas density. This paper adopts Fe/H =5 ×10⁻⁵, compared with 8 ×10⁻⁶ in the earlier FGH baseline. Neither FGH nor KI cooling is silently substituted. Jura & Dalgarno’s Table 1 supplies several electron-impact rates but does not alone specify all required neutral channels. Equation (7) contains 1.4m(H) in the power-per-mass normalization; the Figure 1 caption omits 1.4. The implementation follows equations (7)–(9) without adjusting the time axis to improve agreement. The note added in proof on p.686 revises the discussion of trace-element ionization and cooling but supplies no replacement numerical rate table. See the source audit. Run the prototype. Save the five required files together. No PDF or network access is needed after dependency installation. reproduce.pyconfig.jsoncooling-readings.csvreference-readings.csvrequirements.txtSource auditTechnical notesConverted cooling data / CSV python 3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce.py All 31 checks pass: calibration, interpolation, coefficient derivatives, the independent pressure-equation Jacobian, integrator agreement, valid domains, background evolution and conduction controls. These validate the stated implementation, not full historical reproduction. Next: the nonlinear 3 pc example. First establish the cold cooling input, recombination fit and initial mode for the complete Figure 2. The nonlinear prototype and mesh study now computes profiles corresponding to Figures 3–6 in a periodic one-dimensional calculation with a 3 pc wavelength and 10% initially isobaric density modulation. This requires conduction, recombination, shock handling and grid/time convergence; a large linear amplification alone does not reproduce cloud thickness or density contrast. documents.title: Schwarz1972 · Nonlinear Lagrangian condensation — The Art of Thermal Instability
documents.text: Paper overview: Schwarz, McCray & Stein (1972) → Chapter03 / Schwarz, McCray & Stein (1972) / Nonlinear prototype Follow the gas into a cold, dense layer. A 10% density wave grows beyond the linear regime in a cooling 3 pc box. Moving mass cells follow the compression, while thermal conduction, recombination and shock heating act together. A nonlinear numerical prototype, using 96 mass cells for the displayed profiles. There is no Riemann solver. The method uses pressure forces, compatible pressure work and compression-only artificial viscosity. Figures 3–6 motivate the outputs; original cooling inputs, timing and front resolution remain imperfect, so this is not certified historical reproduction. Density, velocity, temperature and ionization. Times are the same as the published snapshots; no temporal or phase shift was fitted. The displayed run uses 96 equal-H-mass cells. Both the mass coordinate and physical positions/cell widths are exported. The original figure labels zone number; its exact grid-to-mass mapping has not been recovered. Profiles / SVGPNGFull profiles / CSVMesh histories / CSVValidation & source comparison / JSON At 0.985 Myr the displayed model has peak n(H) ≈ 31.1 cm⁻³, a density contrast ≈ 187, minimum temperature ≈ 12.7 K and minimum ionization fraction ≈ 0.0010. The surrounding warm minimum-density gas is about 1430 K. These are computed quantities, not prescribed cloud conditions. The paper’s text gives approximate cloud values of 15 K, x ≈ 0.002, a 0.007 pc extent and 20% of the mass, with an intercloud temperature about 1,800 K. Our density-excess FWHM is 0.0078 pc, while the broader selection T < 100 K and n > 10 times the mean gives 0.0155 pc and 28.1% of the mass. These definitions need not coincide with the original cloud edge. The condensation timing differs: by 0.955 Myr this prototype already has a strongly condensed layer, whereas the corresponding original profile is still growing. The resemblance of the late cloud does not establish pointwise agreement throughout the evolution. A classical Lagrangian calculation. The periodic domain contains a sinusoidal physical-space density perturbation of amplitude 0.1 and wavelength 3 pc, with mean n(H) = 0.3 cm⁻³. The unperturbed temperature is 8,200 K, x = 0.05, and neutral He/H = 0.1. Initial pressure is uniform, so the local temperature varies inversely with density; velocities start at zero. Equal-H-mass cells move with the gas. A compatible midpoint pressure-work update balances changes in internal and kinetic energy. Compression-only quadratic and linear artificial viscosity handle shocks. Conduction uses a conservative periodic implicit solve, and a coupled local energy/recombination solve accounts for radiative losses and changing particle number. This is not the recovered original program. The paper describes von Neumann–Richtmyer viscosity and 100–200 spatial mesh points. The 64/96-cell cases explore historical-scale calculations below that reported range; the 128-cell case lies within it. We keep these experiments separate from any claim about the authors’ exact mesh. The semi-implicit conduction update is backward Euler. We therefore do not claim global second-order time accuracy; timestep refinement is measured directly. No temperature floor, clipped density, imposed cold layer or fitted time shift is used. Compare mesh counts without declaring every front resolved. 64, 96 and 128 cells are the historical-scale study; 512 cells provide an auxiliary comparison. The dashed temperature line is the input boundary. The four-cell Field-length line is a stated diagnostic, not a universal theorem, and is not met throughout these runs. Mesh comparison / SVGPNG At 0.985 Myr the 96-to-128 density-profile L1 difference on mass coordinate is about 3.2%; 128 versus 512 differs by about 4.7%. Halving the timestep in the 96-cell calculation changes the density profile by about 0.02%. Profiles are compared without shifting the cloud. Spatial front resolution is still limited. The auxiliary 512-cell run reaches a minimum Field-length proxy of only 1.37 cells. The proxy is √[K(T)T/(n²Λ)]. A small difference between these cloud profiles is not proof that the thin conductive interface or a continuum solution is fully resolved. All 33 numerical self-checks pass, including compatible hydro energy accounting, a periodic conduction Fourier mode, independent cooling/recombination ODEs, the small-amplitude linear limit, box length, momentum, positivity and timestep agreement. The unmet spatial-resolution diagnostic is recorded separately and is not counted as a passed check. Track where the cooling input is extended. The nonlinear cooling table adds 12 warm-end readings to the earlier 39 points from Figure 1. These cover the locally warmer cells in the initially isobaric wave. The earlier linear input and results are preserved. Below the lowest graph temperature, about 13.93 K, the model uses a continuous C II-like asymptote with exp(−92/T), neutral-collider T⁰ and electron-collider T⁻¹ᐟ² factors. Below x = 0.001 the two low-ionization curves continue to a nonnegative neutral-collider contribution. These are explicit extrapolations, not recovered historical coefficients. The 96-cell density contrast first reaches 100 near 0.948 Myr. It enters the cold temperature extension near 0.974 Myr and the low-ionization extension near 0.986 Myr. Thus the initial formation of the high-contrast layer precedes those extensions, while the later cloud state depends on them. Exposure of each accepted state is recorded in the report. Changing the cold electron temperature power from −1/2 to 0 is included as a sensitivity probe. It does not bound every uncertainty in the historical cooling rates. The recombination fit, normalization caveat and proof note described in the linear exhibit remain relevant. Run the nonlinear study. Save the four nonlinear files plus reproduce.py, config.json, cooling-readings.csv and requirements.txt from the linear exhibit. No source PDF is required after installing the pinned dependencies. nonlinear.pyreproduce-nonlinear.pyconfig-nonlinear.jsoncooling-nonlinear-readings.csvreproduce.pyconfig.jsoncooling-readings.csvrequirements.txtTechnical notesSource audit python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python reproduce-nonlinear.py The single-run solver also accepts a chosen mesh and end time, for example: .venv/bin/python nonlinear.py --cells 96 --end 1.05 Schwarz, McCray & Stein (1972): source paper ↗ Original implementation code is MIT.
